subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Introduction to Medical-Surgical Nursing
question: (a) Define pre-operative care and list the phases of peri-operative care. (2 marks) (b) Explain the physical and psychological preparation of a patient for major surgery. (8 marks) (c) Describe the immediate pre-operative care on the day of surgery. (5 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Definition and phases of peri-operative care (2 marks) Peri-operative nursing is the care given to a surgical patient before, during and after surgery. Pre-operative care is the physical and psychological preparation of the patient from the time the decision for surgery is made until the patient is transferred to the operating table. Its aim is to bring the patient to surgery in the best possible physical and mental condition so that anaesthesia and surgery are safe and recovery is smooth.

Phases of peri-operative care

  1. Pre-operative phase – from the decision for surgery to the transfer of the patient onto the operating table.
  2. Intra-operative phase – from transfer onto the operating table until admission to the recovery room (post-anaesthesia care unit, PACU).
  3. Post-operative phase – from admission to the PACU until complete recovery and the last follow-up visit.

(b) Physical and psychological preparation for major surgery (8 marks) 1. Pre-operative assessment

  • History – present illness, previous operations and any problem with anaesthesia, allergies (drugs, latex, iodine, plaster), chronic diseases (diabetes, hypertension, asthma, heart disease, kidney disease, tuberculosis, epilepsy), bleeding tendency, current medicines, smoking, alcohol and tobacco chewing (gutkha, kharra), and family history of anaesthetic problems.
  • Physical examination – vital signs, height, weight, BMI, nutritional and hydration status, condition of skin at the operative site, veins for IV access, loose teeth or dentures.
  • Pre-anaesthetic check-up (PAC) by the anaesthetist – airway assessment, fitness, ASA physical status grading and the anaesthesia plan.
  • Risk screening – risk of DVT, pressure injury, falls and malnutrition.

2. Investigations (as ordered)

  • Blood – haemoglobin/CBC, blood grouping and cross-matching (units reserved according to the surgery), bleeding and clotting time, PT/INR, blood sugar (and HbA1c in diabetics), urea, creatinine, electrolytes, LFT if needed.
  • Serology – HIV, HBsAg, anti-HCV as per hospital policy (with counselling and consent); standard precautions are used for every patient anyway.
  • Urine routine; ECG (usually above 40 years or with heart disease); chest X-ray when indicated; echocardiography, pulmonary function tests and imaging of the operative area for selected patients; pregnancy test in women of reproductive age if indicated.

3. Improving the general condition

  • Correct anaemia, dehydration and electrolyte imbalance; transfuse if ordered.
  • Control blood sugar and blood pressure; treat infections such as dental caries, UTI and skin infections before elective surgery.
  • Nutrition – high-protein, high-calorie diet with vitamin C and zinc for wound healing; oral supplements or tube feeding for malnourished patients before major elective surgery.
  • Respiratory preparation – advise the patient to stop smoking (ideally 4–8 weeks before surgery; even 24 hours helps), practise breathing exercises and incentive spirometry, and treat chest infection.

4. Review of medicines (as per surgeon and anaesthetist)

  • Anticoagulants and antiplatelets – warfarin is usually stopped about 5 days before surgery with an INR check; clopidogrel 5–7 days before; heparin bridging for high-risk patients as ordered.
  • Diabetic drugs – metformin is usually withheld on the day of surgery; insulin doses are adjusted and blood glucose is monitored.
  • Antihypertensives are usually continued with a sip of water, except some (ACE inhibitors, ARBs) that the anaesthetist may withhold on the morning of surgery.
  • Patients on long-term steroids may need extra steroid cover.
  • Herbal remedies (garlic, ginkgo, ginseng) increase bleeding – ask about them and stop as advised.

5. Pre-operative teaching (patient and family)

  • Explain in simple words what to expect – the OT, anaesthesia, waking up in the recovery room, drains, urinary catheter, IV lines, nasogastric tube and oxygen mask.
  • Teach and get a return demonstration of deep breathing, coughing with splinting of the incision with a pillow, incentive spirometry, leg exercises (ankle pumps, quadriceps setting), turning in bed and early ambulation.
  • Explain the pain scale (0–10) and assure the patient that pain relief will be given – he should report pain rather than bear it silently.
  • Use the teach-back method and leaflets in the patient's language (Marathi, Hindi).

6. Gastrointestinal preparation

  • Fasting (NPO) as per current anaesthesia guidelines: light meal – stop 6 hours before; heavy or fatty meal – 8 hours; clear fluids (water, clear juice without pulp, black tea) up to 2 hours before anaesthesia; breast milk 4 hours before (infants).
  • Purpose – to prevent vomiting and aspiration of gastric contents (aspiration pneumonitis) during anaesthesia.
  • Bowel preparation only when ordered (for example, colorectal surgery); nasogastric tube insertion if ordered (intestinal obstruction).

7. Skin preparation

  • Bath with soap or chlorhexidine the night before or the morning of surgery.
  • Hair removal only if it interferes with surgery, using electric clippers just before surgery; shaving with a razor causes small cuts and increases surgical site infection.
  • Clean the umbilicus for abdominal surgery; trim nails and remove nail polish (to observe colour and use the pulse oximeter).

8. Elimination, rest and sleep

  • The patient voids before going to the OT; a catheter is passed only if ordered (long or pelvic surgery).
  • Ensure a good night's sleep; a sedative may be given as ordered.

9. Psychological preparation

  • Assess fears – fear of death, pain, anaesthesia, disfigurement, cancer diagnosis, loss of income and cost of treatment.
  • Build rapport, encourage questions, give honest and accurate information, and involve the family.
  • Respect religious and cultural practices – allow prayer; a sacred thread or amulet may be taped as per hospital policy.
  • Teach relaxation, slow breathing or music; for children use play preparation and allow a parent to stay where permitted.
  • Informed consent – the surgeon explains the nature, benefits, risks and alternatives of the operation in a language the patient understands; the patient must be an adult, mentally competent and not sedated; parents or guardians sign for minors; the nurse checks that the consent is signed, dated and witnessed. Separate consent is taken for anaesthesia and blood transfusion.

(c) Immediate pre-operative care on the day of surgery (5 marks)

  1. Identify the patient – identity band with name, age and hospital number; allergy band if allergic.
  2. Confirm fasting status and note the time of the last food and drink.
  3. Personal hygiene – bath, clean OT gown, hair tied and covered with a cap; remove make-up, nail polish, contact lenses, hairpins, jewellery (if the patient refuses to remove a ring or mangalsutra, tape it and document as per policy), dentures (labelled and kept safely), wigs and prostheses.
  4. Record baseline vital signs, weight, SpO₂ and blood sugar (diabetics); report fever, cough, high BP or a new complaint to the surgeon and anaesthetist.
  5. Empty the bladder and record the time.
  6. Give pre-medication as ordered and on time – anxiolytic (midazolam), antacid or proton-pump inhibitor, antiemetic; the prophylactic antibiotic is usually given within 60 minutes before the skin incision. After sedation keep the side rails up and do not allow the patient to walk.
  7. Site marking for limbs, eyes, kidneys and other paired organs is checked.
  8. Documents ready – case file, signed consents, investigation reports, X-ray/CT films, PAC notes, details of cross-matched blood and implants.
  9. Complete the pre-operative checklist, sign it, and hand over the patient to the OT nurse using a structured handover (ISBAR). Transfer by trolley with side rails up, keeping the patient covered and warm.
  10. Prepare the post-operative bed and unit – warm operation bed, oxygen, suction, IV stand, BP apparatus, kidney tray and monitor.

Pre-operative checklist (common items) | Item | Check | |---|---| | Identity band, allergy status | Present and correct | | Consent (surgery, anaesthesia, blood) | Signed and witnessed | | NPO status | Time of last intake recorded | | Investigations, blood arranged | Reports in file; units cross-matched | | Jewellery, dentures, prostheses | Removed and documented | | Bladder | Voided/catheterised – time noted | | Pre-medication, antibiotic | Given – time and dose recorded | | Site marking | Done by the surgeon | | Vital signs | Recorded within the last hour |

Special considerations

  • Elderly – risk of dehydration, confusion and fragile skin; keep glasses and hearing aids till induction where allowed.
  • Diabetic patients – schedule first on the list, monitor blood glucose, and manage insulin and dextrose infusions as ordered.
  • Emergency surgery – essential steps are done quickly: consent, blood sample for grouping and cross-matching, IV access, nasogastric aspiration if needed and informing the anaesthetist about the last meal.

Common nursing diagnoses

  • Anxiety related to the unknown outcome of surgery.
  • Deficient knowledge regarding post-operative exercises and care.
  • Risk for infection and risk for peri-operative positioning injury.

Nursing importance Good pre-operative preparation prevents cancellation of surgery, wrong-site surgery, aspiration, surgical site infection, DVT and post-operative chest complications, and it reduces the patient's fear.

Conclusion Pre-operative care prepares the patient's body and mind for surgery; careful assessment, teaching, fasting, skin preparation, consent and a completed checklist make surgery safe.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Introduction to Medical-Surgical Nursing
question: (a) Explain the immediate post-operative care of a patient in the post-anaesthesia care unit (PACU). (7 marks) (b) Describe the care of the post-operative patient in the surgical ward. (3 marks) (c) Explain the common post-operative complications and their prevention and management. (5 marks)
answer_html:
Introduction The post-operative phase begins when the patient is admitted to the post-anaesthesia care unit (PACU) or recovery room and continues until complete recovery. The first few hours after anaesthesia are the most dangerous because the patient may have airway obstruction, bleeding, shock or hypothermia. Close observation and timely action by the nurse are life-saving.

(a) Immediate post-operative care in the PACU (7 marks) 1. Receiving the patient

  • The PACU is located next to the operation theatre and has oxygen, suction, monitors, airway equipment, defibrillator and emergency drugs at every bed.
  • Receive a handover from the anaesthetist and the scrub nurse – name, surgery done, type of anaesthesia, drugs and fluids given, blood loss, urine output, intra-operative problems, drains and catheters, and post-operative orders.

2. Airway (first priority)

  • Until protective reflexes return, keep the unconscious patient in the lateral or semi-prone (recovery) position with the head slightly extended, unless contraindicated.
  • Support the jaw (jaw thrust); leave the oropharyngeal airway in place until the patient begins to reject it (gagging); then remove it.
  • Suction secretions or vomitus from the mouth.
  • Watch for airway obstruction – snoring, stridor, use of accessory muscles, falling SpO₂ – and for laryngospasm; call the anaesthetist at once.

3. Breathing

  • Give oxygen by face mask as ordered and monitor respiratory rate, depth and SpO₂ (keep 94% or above).
  • Watch for respiratory depression due to opioids or residual muscle relaxants (respiratory rate below 10/min); keep naloxone and reversal drugs ready as ordered.
  • Encourage deep breathing as soon as the patient is awake.

4. Circulation

  • Check pulse and BP every 15 minutes for the first hour (or until stable), then every 30 minutes and then hourly, as per policy; note skin colour, temperature and capillary refill.
  • Hypotension with tachycardia suggests bleeding or hypovolaemia; also watch for arrhythmias on the ECG monitor.

5. Level of consciousness and temperature

  • Note the response to name and commands, orientation, and pupils (after neurosurgery).
  • Hypothermia is common after long surgery – cover with warm blankets or use a forced-air warmer; shivering increases oxygen demand and is treated as ordered.

6. Wound, drains, IV lines and urine output

  • Check the dressing for soakage (mark the edge of any stain and recheck); note the amount and colour of drain output; keep drains patent and below wound level; report fresh bleeding.
  • Maintain IV fluids at the prescribed rate; check urine output – at least 0.5 ml/kg/hour (about 30 ml/hour in an adult).

7. Pain and nausea

  • Assess pain on the 0–10 scale and give analgesics as ordered (paracetamol, NSAIDs, opioids, epidural or patient-controlled analgesia).
  • Manage post-operative nausea and vomiting (PONV) with antiemetics (ondansetron) and lateral positioning to prevent aspiration.

8. Safety and documentation

  • Side rails up; never leave the patient alone; record all observations, drugs and events.

9. Criteria for discharge from the PACU – modified Aldrete score | Parameter | 2 | 1 | 0 | |---|---|---|---| | Activity | Moves 4 limbs | Moves 2 limbs | Cannot move | | Respiration | Breathes deeply, coughs | Shallow breathing | Apnoeic | | Circulation | BP within 20% of pre-op | 20–50% change | More than 50% change | | Consciousness | Fully awake | Arousable | Not responding | | SpO₂ | Above 92% on room air | Needs oxygen | Below 90% with oxygen | A score of 9 or more (with pain and nausea controlled, and regression of a spinal block) allows transfer to the ward.

(b) Care in the surgical ward (3 marks)

  • Receive and position the patient – Fowler's position after abdominal or chest surgery once conscious and stable; as ordered after spinal anaesthesia.
  • Vital signs as scheduled; maintain the intake–output chart.
  • Respiratory care – deep breathing and coughing every hour while awake, and incentive spirometry about 10 times an hour.
  • Early ambulation – dangle the legs, sit out of bed and walk with support, usually the same evening or the next day.
  • DVT prevention – leg exercises, compression stockings, intermittent pneumatic compression and low-molecular-weight heparin as ordered.
  • Nutrition – sips of water and then oral fluids once nausea settles and bowel activity returns; progress from clear liquids to a normal diet (early feeding is encouraged after most surgeries).
  • Wound care with aseptic technique; the first dressing is usually opened after 48 hours unless soaked.
  • Elimination – watch for urinary retention and constipation; give fibre, fluids and stool softeners as ordered.
  • Comfort, hygiene, sleep and emotional support, followed by discharge teaching – wound care, date of suture removal, diet, activity limits (no heavy lifting for about 6 weeks after abdominal surgery), medicines, warning signs and follow-up.

(c) Common post-operative complications – prevention and management (5 marks) | Complication | Usual time | Features | Prevention and nursing management | |---|---|---|---| | Airway obstruction, hypoxaemia | PACU | Snoring, stridor, cyanosis, falling SpO₂ | Recovery position, jaw thrust, airway, suction, oxygen; call anaesthetist | | Haemorrhage – primary (during surgery), reactionary (within 24 hours), secondary (7–10 days, due to infection) | Variable | Soaked dressing, drain blood, rising pulse, falling BP, pallor | Monitor vitals and wound; pressure dressing; IV fluids, blood as ordered; prepare for re-exploration | | Hypovolaemic shock | First 24–48 hours | Tachycardia, hypotension, cold clammy skin, low urine output | Elevate legs, oxygen, IV fluids and blood as ordered; monitor urine output | | Atelectasis, pneumonia | 24–72 hours | Fever, breathlessness, reduced breath sounds, crepitations | Deep breathing, coughing, incentive spirometry, early ambulation, adequate pain relief | | Urinary retention | 6–12 hours | No voiding, bladder distension, discomfort | Privacy, sit or stand to void, running water, warm compress; catheterise if no voiding in 6–8 hours as ordered | | Paralytic ileus | 2–3 days | Distension, absent bowel sounds, vomiting, no flatus | Nil by mouth, nasogastric aspiration, IV fluids, correct potassium, early ambulation | | Surgical site infection | 3–7 days | Redness, swelling, pus, pain, fever | Hand hygiene, aseptic dressing, glucose control, antibiotics as ordered, culture of discharge | | Wound dehiscence/evisceration | 5–10 days | Gush of serosanguinous fluid, wound opens | Low Fowler's position with knees flexed, cover with sterile saline-soaked dressing, NPO, inform surgeon | | Deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism | 7–14 days | Calf pain and swelling; sudden breathlessness, chest pain | Leg exercises, stockings, early ambulation, anticoagulants; for PE – oxygen, emergency help | | Post-operative delirium | First few days, elderly | Confusion, agitation | Orientation, glasses and hearing aids, sleep, treat cause, family presence |

Post-operative fever – the "5 Ws" (memory aid)

  • Wind (day 1–2) – atelectasis, pneumonia.
  • Water (day 3–5) – urinary tract infection (catheter).
  • Wound (day 5–7) – surgical site infection.
  • Walking (day 5–10) – DVT and thrombophlebitis.
  • Wonder drugs (any time) – drug fever, transfusion reaction.

Nursing importance Most post-operative deaths and complications can be prevented by vigilant airway care, frequent monitoring, early detection of bleeding, good pain relief, breathing exercises and early ambulation.

Conclusion Post-operative care moves from intensive monitoring in the PACU to promotion of recovery in the ward; the nurse's observation, prevention of complications and discharge teaching ensure a safe and quick recovery.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Introduction to Medical-Surgical Nursing
question: Explain the role of the nurse in medical-surgical settings (OPD, ward and ICU).
answer_html:
Introduction Medical-surgical nursing is the care of adults with medical illnesses or surgical conditions, before and after treatment. The nurse works in the outpatient department (OPD), wards and intensive care unit (ICU) and performs many roles as a member of the health team.

1. General roles of the medical-surgical nurse

  • Care provider – assesses the patient, plans and gives holistic care using the nursing process.
  • Educator – teaches patients and families about the disease, medicines, diet, exercises and self-care (insulin injection, stoma care, crutch walking).
  • Advocate – protects the patient's rights, dignity, privacy and informed consent.
  • Coordinator/collaborator – works with doctors, physiotherapists, dietitians, social workers and pharmacists.
  • Counsellor – supports patients facing chronic illness, surgery, cancer or disability.
  • Manager – manages the ward, staff, supplies, equipment and records.
  • Researcher – uses evidence-based practice and takes part in audits and research.

2. Role in the outpatient department

  • Arrange the clinic, maintain flow and triage patients so that the seriously ill are seen first.
  • Check vital signs, weight, blood sugar and BP; screen for TB, diabetes, hypertension and cancers.
  • Assist doctors in examination and minor procedures (dressings, injections, suture removal).
  • Give health education in the waiting area and individual counselling.
  • Guide patients for investigations, admission and referral; maintain OPD records.

3. Role in the medical and surgical wards

  • Admission – orient the patient to the ward, collect history, do a baseline assessment, and obtain consent.
  • Implement care plans – medicines, IV therapy, wound care, drains, catheters and nutrition.
  • Monitor and report changes early; use early warning scores.
  • Pre- and post-operative care; prevention of complications such as pressure ulcers, falls, DVT and infection.
  • Maintain infection control and biomedical waste management.
  • Discharge planning and teaching from the day of admission; follow-up and referral.

4. Role in the intensive care unit

  • Continuous monitoring of ECG, SpO₂, invasive BP, CVP, urine output and level of consciousness.
  • Care of patients on mechanical ventilators, inotropes and multiple infusions.
  • Quick recognition of emergencies and participation in CPR and code blue.
  • Strict prevention of ventilator-associated pneumonia, catheter-related bloodstream infection and CAUTI using bundles.
  • Comfort, communication, eye and mouth care for unconscious patients; family support and help with difficult decisions.
  • Accurate documentation and safe handover.

5. Professional qualities required Sound knowledge, skill, alertness, compassion, good communication, ethical and legal awareness, teamwork and commitment to lifelong learning (for example, the Nurse Practitioner in Critical Care programme in India).

Nursing importance The quality of care, patient safety and patient satisfaction in medical-surgical units depend mainly on the nurse, who is with the patient round the clock.

Conclusion The medical-surgical nurse is a caregiver, teacher, advocate and coordinator whose roles change according to the setting – OPD, ward or ICU.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Introduction to Medical-Surgical Nursing
question: Explain the current trends in medical-surgical nursing.
answer_html:
Introduction Medical-surgical nursing has changed from simple bedside care under the doctor's orders to a specialised, evidence-based and technology-supported profession. Changes in disease patterns (more lifestyle diseases and cancers), technology and patient expectations have created new trends.

1. Specialisation and advanced practice

  • Specialties such as cardiac, oncology, nephrology, orthopaedic, neuroscience, critical care and wound care nursing.
  • Nurse Practitioner in Critical Care (NPCC) and other advanced practice roles; post-basic diplomas in specialty areas.

2. Evidence-based practice and quality

  • Care based on research rather than routine (for example, clipping rather than shaving, early feeding after surgery).
  • Clinical protocols, care bundles, audits and quality indicators.
  • Hospital accreditation by NABH and quality certification (NQAS) for public hospitals; focus on patient safety – identification, safe medication, falls and infection prevention.

3. Changes in surgical care

  • Minimally invasive surgery – laparoscopic, endoscopic and robotic surgery with smaller wounds and faster recovery.
  • Day-care (ambulatory) surgery – patient goes home the same day.
  • Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) programmes.
  • Organ transplantation and joint replacement are now common.

4. Technology and informatics

  • Electronic health records, bar-code medication administration, smart infusion pumps, central monitoring.
  • Telemedicine and tele-nursing – for example, eSanjeevani consultations and telephone follow-up after discharge.
  • Digital health IDs under the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM).

5. Shift towards the community and home

  • Shorter hospital stays; more care at home – home health care, home dialysis, palliative care.
  • Early discharge planning and self-care education.
  • Health and Wellness Centres (Ayushman Arogya Mandirs) for screening of non-communicable diseases.

6. Patient-centred and holistic care

  • Respect for patient rights and shared decision-making; informed consent.
  • Attention to pain, nutrition, mental health, spirituality and family.
  • Use of complementary therapies such as yoga and music therapy.

7. Changing health problems

  • Increase in diabetes, hypertension, cancers, trauma and elderly patients with many diseases; continued burden of infections such as TB and dengue; antimicrobial resistance.

8. Education and legal awareness

  • Competency-based nursing education (INC 2021 curriculum), simulation laboratories and continuing nursing education.
  • Greater awareness of legal responsibilities, documentation and consumer protection.

Nursing importance Knowing these trends helps nurses update their knowledge and skills, give safe modern care and take up new career opportunities.

Conclusion Medical-surgical nursing is moving towards specialised, evidence-based, technology-supported and patient-centred care across hospital and home.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Introduction to Medical-Surgical Nursing
question: Explain the principles of wound care and the types of wound dressings.
answer_html:
Introduction A wound dressing is a covering applied to a wound to protect it, absorb discharge, prevent infection and promote healing. Modern wound care is based on the principle of moist wound healing – a clean, moist (not wet) wound heals faster than a dry, scabbed wound.

1. Principles of wound care

  • Asepsis – hand hygiene and aseptic non-touch technique; sterile instruments and dressings.
  • Clean from clean to less clean – for a surgical incision, clean from the top to the bottom or from the centre outwards, using a fresh swab for each stroke.
  • Assess the wound at every dressing – site, size, depth, wound bed (granulation, slough, necrosis), exudate (amount, colour, smell), edges and surrounding skin, and signs of infection.
  • Maintain a moist environment, remove dead tissue (debridement), control infection and protect the surrounding skin.
  • Minimise pain and trauma – give analgesia before painful dressings; soak adherent dressings with saline.
  • Treat the cause – nutrition, blood sugar control, pressure relief, circulation.
  • TIME framework for chronic wounds: Tissue (remove non-viable tissue), Infection/inflammation (control), Moisture balance, Edge of wound (promote advancement).

2. Types of wound dressings | Dressing | Features | Best used for | |---|---|---| | Dry gauze | Cheap, absorbent; may stick to the wound | Clean surgical incisions, as a secondary dressing | | Paraffin gauze (tulle) | Non-adherent | Burns, skin graft donor sites, superficial wounds | | Transparent film | Waterproof, allows viewing of the wound | IV cannula sites, superficial wounds, stage I pressure injury | | Hydrocolloid | Gel forms over the wound; keeps it moist | Light-to-moderate exudate, pressure injuries | | Hydrogel | Adds moisture; softens slough and dry necrotic tissue | Dry wounds, slough | | Alginate (seaweed) | Highly absorbent; forms gel; helps haemostasis | Heavy exudate, cavity wounds | | Foam | Absorbent and cushioning | Moderate-to-heavy exudate, pressure areas | | Antimicrobial (silver, iodine, honey) | Reduces bacterial load | Infected or colonised wounds | | Negative pressure wound therapy (vacuum dressing) | Sealed foam with suction | Large, deep, chronic or open abdominal wounds |

3. Steps in changing a surgical dressing (brief)

  1. Check the order, explain the procedure, provide privacy and give analgesia if needed.
  2. Hand hygiene; open the sterile dressing set; wear gloves.
  3. Remove the old dressing gently and discard into the correct BMW bin; observe the dressing.
  4. Clean the wound with normal saline (or antiseptic as per policy), dry the surrounding skin.
  5. Apply the new dressing and secure it; make the patient comfortable.
  6. Document the wound condition, exudate and the dressing used; report signs of infection.

Nursing importance Choosing the right dressing and good technique speed healing, reduce infection, pain and hospital stay, and lower the cost of care.

Conclusion Wound care follows the principles of asepsis and moist healing; the dressing is chosen according to the type of wound and the amount of exudate.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Introduction to Medical-Surgical Nursing
question: Explain Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) and the nurse's role.
answer_html:
Definition Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) is an evidence-based, multidisciplinary care pathway that aims to reduce surgical stress, maintain normal body function and speed up recovery after surgery. It was first used in colorectal surgery and is now used in gynaecological, orthopaedic, urological and other surgeries in many Indian hospitals.

1. Aims

  • Reduce complications and length of hospital stay.
  • Early return to normal eating, walking and activity.
  • Better pain control with fewer opioids; lower cost.

2. Pre-operative elements

  • Counselling and education of the patient and family about the plan and their active role.
  • Optimisation of anaemia, diabetes, nutrition; stopping smoking and alcohol.
  • Avoid prolonged fasting – clear fluids up to 2 hours before anaesthesia; carbohydrate drink (carbohydrate loading) the night before and 2–3 hours before surgery (except in some diabetics).
  • No routine bowel preparation for most surgeries.
  • No long-acting sedative pre-medication.
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis and DVT prophylaxis.

3. Intra-operative elements

  • Minimally invasive surgery (laparoscopic) where possible.
  • Short-acting anaesthetic drugs; regional anaesthesia (spinal/epidural, nerve blocks).
  • Goal-directed fluid therapy – avoid both too much and too little IV fluid.
  • Maintain normal body temperature (warm air blankets, warm fluids).
  • PONV prophylaxis; avoid routine nasogastric tubes and drains.

4. Post-operative elements

  • Early oral feeding – fluids within a few hours and solid food from the first day when tolerated.
  • Early mobilisation – sitting out of bed on the day of surgery and walking on day 1.
  • Multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia – paracetamol, NSAIDs, regional blocks.
  • Early removal of urinary catheter, IV lines and drains.
  • Chewing gum to reduce ileus; prevention of nausea.
  • Clear discharge criteria and telephone follow-up.

5. Nurse's role in ERAS

  • Educate the patient before surgery; give carbohydrate drinks and ensure safe fasting times.
  • Encourage and record early feeding and mobilisation targets (for example, walking a set distance on day 1).
  • Assess pain regularly and give multimodal analgesia on time.
  • Monitor for complications – nausea, ileus, bleeding, infection.
  • Remove catheters and lines early as per protocol; maintain the ERAS checklist and audit.
  • Prepare the patient for early discharge and follow up by phone.

Nursing importance Nurses spend the most time with the patient; ERAS succeeds only when nurses actively drive early feeding, mobilisation and pain control.

Conclusion ERAS is a modern pathway of care in which small evidence-based steps before, during and after surgery together give faster and safer recovery.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Introduction to Medical-Surgical Nursing
question: Explain complementary and alternative therapies and their use in medical-surgical nursing.
answer_html:
Definition Complementary therapies are healing practices used along with conventional (allopathic) treatment, while alternative therapies are used in place of conventional treatment. Together they are called complementary and alternative medicine (CAM); when combined thoughtfully with conventional care it is called integrative care. In India, traditional systems are promoted by the Ministry of AYUSH (Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa and Homoeopathy).

1. Classification | Group | Examples | |---|---| | Whole medical systems | Ayurveda, homoeopathy, Unani, Siddha, naturopathy | | Mind–body therapies | Yoga, meditation, pranayama, relaxation, guided imagery, music therapy, prayer | | Biologically based therapies | Herbal medicines (tulsi, ashwagandha, turmeric), special diets, vitamins | | Manipulative and body-based therapies | Massage, chiropractic, reflexology, acupressure | | Energy therapies | Reiki, therapeutic touch, magnet therapy | | Others | Aromatherapy, hydrotherapy, laughter therapy, pet therapy |

2. Uses in medical-surgical settings

  • Pain and anxiety before and after surgery – music, guided imagery, relaxation and massage.
  • Nausea after surgery or chemotherapy – acupressure at the P6 (wrist) point, ginger.
  • Chronic diseases – yoga and pranayama for hypertension, diabetes, asthma and COPD; stress reduction in heart disease.
  • Cancer and palliative care – comfort, sleep and well-being (aromatherapy, massage, meditation).
  • Rehabilitation – yoga and hydrotherapy for musculoskeletal problems.

3. Precautions

  • Many herbal products interact with drugs – garlic, ginkgo and ginseng increase bleeding; St John's wort reduces the effect of many drugs; some products may contain heavy metals or steroids.
  • Herbs are usually stopped one to two weeks before surgery as advised.
  • Alternative therapy should not delay effective treatment (for example, cancer surgery or insulin in type 1 diabetes).
  • Massage is avoided over DVT, fractures, open wounds and tumours.

4. Role of the nurse

  • Ask every patient about the use of herbal, AYUSH or home remedies and record it.
  • Respect the patient's beliefs and culture; provide unbiased, evidence-based information.
  • Inform the doctor and pharmacist about possible interactions.
  • Use simple safe therapies within nursing practice – relaxation, music, positioning, touch, breathing exercises – after training and as per hospital policy.
  • Observe and document the effects.

Nursing importance CAM therapies, used wisely, improve comfort, reduce anxiety and pain and increase patient satisfaction, but the nurse must guard against unsafe interactions.

Conclusion Complementary therapies support conventional treatment; the nurse should assess their use, respect the patient's choice and ensure safety.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Introduction to Medical-Surgical Nursing
question: Write the stages (phases) of wound healing.
answer_html:
Phases of wound healing

  1. Haemostasis phase (immediately – minutes to hours) – vasoconstriction, platelet plug and fibrin clot stop bleeding.
  2. Inflammatory phase (days 1–4) – redness, warmth, swelling; neutrophils and macrophages clean the wound of bacteria and debris.
  3. Proliferative phase (days 4–21) – granulation tissue, new blood vessels, collagen formation, wound contraction and epithelialisation.
  4. Maturation (remodelling) phase (day 21 to 1–2 years) – collagen reorganises; the scar becomes stronger and paler (reaches about 70–80% of original strength).

Nursing relevance: protect the wound from infection and trauma, give protein, vitamin C and zinc, control blood sugar and avoid smoking.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Introduction to Medical-Surgical Nursing
question: What is the International Classification of Diseases (ICD)? State its uses.
answer_html:
The International Classification of Diseases (ICD) is the global standard system published by the WHO for classifying and coding diseases, injuries, symptoms and causes of death. ICD-11 came into effect on 1 January 2022; ICD-10 is still widely used in India. Each condition has an alphanumeric code (for example, ICD-10 E11 – type 2 diabetes mellitus; A15 – respiratory tuberculosis).

Uses

  1. Recording and comparing morbidity and mortality statistics nationally and internationally.
  2. Medical records coding, indexing and retrieval.
  3. Health insurance claims and hospital billing (for example, under PM-JAY).
  4. Planning health services and allocating resources; research and epidemiology.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Introduction to Medical-Surgical Nursing
question: Classify surgery according to urgency, with examples.
answer_html:
Classification of surgery according to urgency

  1. Emergency – must be done immediately to save life or limb; for example, ruptured spleen, perforated peptic ulcer, ruptured ectopic pregnancy, obstructed airway.
  2. Urgent – needs attention within about 24–48 hours; for example, acute cholecystitis, fracture fixation, kidney stone with obstruction.
  3. Required (planned) – should be done within weeks to months; for example, cataract, thyroid nodule, prostate enlargement.
  4. Elective – the patient can choose the time; delay is not harmful; for example, inguinal hernia repair, varicose veins.
  5. Optional – done at the patient's request; for example, cosmetic surgery.

Surgery may also be classified by purpose (diagnostic, curative, reconstructive, palliative, transplant, cosmetic) and degree of risk (major, minor).

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Introduction to Medical-Surgical Nursing
question: Differentiate between wound dehiscence and evisceration. State the immediate nursing action.
answer_html:
• Wound dehiscence – partial or complete separation of the layers of a surgical wound.
  • Evisceration – protrusion of abdominal organs (bowel) through the opened wound – a surgical emergency.
  • Usually occur 5–10 days after surgery; risk factors – obesity, malnutrition, diabetes, steroids, wound infection, coughing, vomiting and distension. A gush of pinkish (serosanguinous) fluid from the wound is an early sign.

Immediate nursing action

  1. Stay with the patient; call for help and inform the surgeon.
  2. Place in low Fowler's position with knees flexed to reduce tension.
  3. Cover with sterile dressing soaked in warm normal saline; never push organs back.
  4. Keep NPO, monitor vital signs for shock and prepare for surgery.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Introduction to Medical-Surgical Nursing
question: List the benefits of early ambulation after surgery.
answer_html:
Early ambulation means getting the patient out of bed and walking as early as possible after surgery (usually within 24 hours), as allowed by the surgeon.

Benefits

  1. Prevents deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism by improving venous return.
  2. Improves lung expansion – prevents atelectasis and pneumonia.
  3. Stimulates peristalsis – reduces paralytic ileus, gas pain and constipation.
  4. Helps voiding and reduces urinary retention.
  5. Prevents pressure ulcers, muscle wasting and joint stiffness.
  6. Improves circulation and wound healing, appetite and sleep.
  7. Improves the patient's morale and independence and shortens hospital stay.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Intraoperative Care
question: (a) Describe the location and design of an operation theatre complex, including its zones. (6 marks) (b) List the members of the OT team. (3 marks) (c) Explain the duties of the scrub nurse and the circulating nurse. (6 marks)

diagram.caption: Layout of an operation theatre complex showing zones
labels: separate exit); one-way flow of clean and dirty traffic

answer_html:
Introduction The operation theatre (OT) is a specially designed unit where surgical procedures are performed under strict asepsis. A well-planned OT complex with proper zoning, trained staff and clear duties ensures patient safety, infection prevention and efficient work.

(a) Location and design of the OT complex (6 marks) 1. Location

  • A separate wing or block, away from main hospital traffic, noise and dust; preferably not on the ground floor.
  • Close to surgical wards, ICU, emergency department, CSSD, blood bank, radiology and laboratory, connected by wide corridors and lifts.

2. Planning principle

  • The complex is planned so that asepsis increases progressively from the outside to the inside, and clean and dirty traffic do not cross (separate clean and dirty corridors, or a double-corridor design).

3. Operating room design

  • Size – about 6 m × 6 m (36 m²) for general surgery; larger rooms for orthopaedic, cardiac and neurosurgery; ceiling height about 3 m.
  • Walls and floor – smooth, seamless, non-porous, washable, with rounded (coved) corners; antistatic flooring; light pastel colours to reduce glare.
  • Doors – wide enough for trolleys, sliding or self-closing, kept closed; no windows or only sealed windows.
  • Ventilation – positive pressure (air flows out of the OT, not in), at least 20 air changes per hour, HEPA filters, and laminar airflow for joint replacement and implant surgery.
  • Temperature about 20–24 °C and relative humidity about 40–60%, as per hospital norms.
  • Lighting – shadowless operating lamp (LED) plus good general lighting; emergency power back-up (UPS and generator).
  • Services – piped medical gases (oxygen, nitrous oxide, air, vacuum), anaesthetic gas scavenging, many earthed electrical sockets, and communication systems.
  • Supporting areas – scrub area outside each OT, sterile store, anaesthesia room, pre-operative holding area, recovery room (PACU), staff changing rooms, rest room, doctors' and nurses' duty rooms, dirty utility and pass-boxes for specimens and instruments.

4. Zones of the OT complex | Zone | Areas included | Rules | |---|---|---| | Protective (outer, unrestricted) zone | Reception, waiting area, patient transfer area, changing rooms, offices, general stores | Street clothes only up to the changing room; staff change into OT dress | | Clean (semi-restricted) zone | Pre-operative holding area, recovery room, corridors, sterile stores, staff rest room | OT dress, cap and OT footwear | | Aseptic (sterile, restricted) zone | Operating rooms, scrub area, instrument set-up room | Full OT attire with mask; only the scrubbed team in sterile gowns near the sterile field | | Disposal (dirty) zone | Dirty utility, sluice room, instrument washing area, waste collection | Separate exit route; used items never pass through clean areas |

5. Traffic control

  • Keep doors closed and limit the number of people in the OT; avoid unnecessary movement and talking.
  • Staff with infections (boils, respiratory infection) should not work in the OT.

(b) Members of the OT team (3 marks)

  • Sterile (scrubbed) team – operating surgeon, assistant surgeon(s) and scrub nurse (instrument nurse).
  • Non-sterile (unscrubbed) team – anaesthesiologist, anaesthesia technician or nurse, circulating nurse, OT technician, radiographer or perfusionist when needed, OT attendants and housekeeping staff.
  • Supporting staff – OT in-charge sister/nursing supervisor, CSSD staff, biomedical engineer and store-keeper.

(c) Duties of the scrub nurse and the circulating nurse (6 marks) | Phase | Scrub nurse (sterile) | Circulating nurse (non-sterile) | |---|---|---| | Before surgery | Checks the OT list and the required instrument sets; performs surgical scrub, gowning and gloving; arranges the instrument trolley and Mayo tray; prepares sutures and blades; does the initial count with the circulating nurse; helps the surgeon to gown and glove; helps with draping | Checks that the OT is clean and ready – lights, suction, diathermy, warming device, OT table, temperature; receives the patient and verifies identity, consent, site marking and the checklist (Sign In); helps in transferring and positioning the patient; opens sterile packs; ties gowns; applies the diathermy return pad | | During surgery | Anticipates the surgeon's needs and passes instruments correctly (handle first, firmly into the palm); maintains the sterile field; keeps track of sponges, needles and instruments; loads needle holders; receives specimens; keeps the trolley tidy; does the count before closure | Supplies extra items to the sterile field without contaminating it; records counts, specimens, implants and times; takes part in the Time Out; watches for breaks in asepsis; adjusts the light; collects and labels specimens; keeps doors closed; communicates with the outside; acts as the patient's advocate | | After surgery | Does the final count; applies the dressing; removes drapes carefully; separates sharps; sends instruments for decontamination; reports any problem with instruments | Completes the Sign Out with the team; helps transfer the patient to the PACU with a proper handover; completes OT records and registers; arranges cleaning of the OT for the next case |

Qualities of an OT nurse Sound knowledge of anatomy, surgical steps and instruments; strict surgical conscience (admitting and correcting any break in asepsis even when no one sees it); alertness, speed, physical fitness, calmness in emergencies and good teamwork.

OT attire and infection-control rules

  • Scrub suits are freshly laundered, worn only inside the OT complex and changed when soiled or wet; staff do not go outside the complex in OT dress (or cover it with a gown if they must).
  • Caps cover all hair, including sideburns and beards; masks cover the nose and mouth fully, are changed between cases and are never left hanging around the neck.
  • Dedicated OT footwear or shoe covers; protective eyewear or face shields when splashes are expected.
  • No jewellery, watches, artificial nails or nail polish; mobile phones are kept to a minimum and cleaned.
  • Staff with boils, open wounds, diarrhoea or respiratory infection report to the in-charge and stay away from the sterile zone.

Equipment of an operating room

  • Operating table with attachments (arm boards, stirrups, head rest, kidney rest), shadowless operating lamp, anaesthesia work station and multi-parameter monitors.
  • Suction machines (wall and portable), electrosurgical (diathermy) unit, defibrillator and emergency (crash) trolley.
  • Instrument trolleys, Mayo stand, kick buckets, IV stands, patient warming devices, X-ray viewing screen or digital display, a clock with an elapsed-time timer, and closed storage cabinets.

Role of the OT nurse in-charge

  • Prepares the OT list with the surgeons and anaesthetists, plans duties of nurses and technicians, and ensures enough staff for emergencies.
  • Maintains stocks of sterile supplies, sutures, drugs and implants; plans preventive maintenance of equipment.
  • Supervises asepsis, cleaning and biomedical waste management; conducts audits of hand hygiene and checklist use.
  • Maintains records – OT register, count sheets, specimen register, implant register, narcotic register and incident reports.
  • Orients and trains new staff and students in OT routines.

Nursing importance Correct design and zoning reduce surgical site infections, while clear duties of scrub and circulating nurses prevent errors such as retained sponges, wrong-site surgery and breaks in sterility.

Conclusion A safe OT depends on correct location and design, strict zoning and traffic control, and a well-coordinated team in which the scrub and circulating nurses play complementary roles.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Intraoperative Care
question: (a) Define anaesthesia and classify it. (3 marks) (b) Explain the stages of general anaesthesia. (4 marks) (c) Describe the nursing responsibilities before, during and after general and spinal anaesthesia. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Stages of general anaesthesia (Guedel's classification)
labels: stage III surgical anaesthesia with four planes
stage IV medullary paralysis; changes in respiration

answer_html:
(a) Definition and classification (3 marks) Anaesthesia (Greek: an = without, aesthesis = sensation) is the reversible loss of sensation, with or without loss of consciousness, produced by drugs so that surgery and procedures can be done painlessly.

Classification

  1. General anaesthesia (GA) – reversible loss of consciousness with analgesia, amnesia, muscle relaxation and loss of reflexes.
    • Inhalational – sevoflurane, isoflurane, desflurane, nitrous oxide (halothane in older practice).
    • Intravenous – propofol, thiopentone, ketamine, etomidate.
    • Balanced anaesthesia – combination of IV induction agent, inhalational agent, opioid (fentanyl, morphine) and muscle relaxant (succinylcholine, atracurium, vecuronium).
  2. Regional anaesthesia – loss of sensation in one part of the body while the patient is awake.
    • Spinal (subarachnoid) anaesthesia, epidural (including caudal), peripheral nerve blocks (brachial plexus block), IV regional anaesthesia (Bier's block).
  3. Local anaesthesia – topical (lignocaine jelly or spray), local infiltration and field block.
  4. Sedation (monitored anaesthesia care) – conscious sedation for endoscopy, cardioversion and minor procedures (midazolam, propofol, fentanyl).

ASA physical status classification (brief) – I healthy; II mild systemic disease; III severe systemic disease; IV severe disease that is a constant threat to life; V moribund; VI brain-dead organ donor; "E" is added for emergency surgery.

(b) Stages of general anaesthesia – Guedel's classification (4 marks) | Stage | Extent | Main features | |---|---|---| | I – Stage of analgesia | From start of induction to loss of consciousness | Drowsiness, reduced pain perception, amnesia; patient can still talk | | II – Stage of excitement (delirium) | From loss of consciousness to the start of regular breathing | Irregular breathing, breath-holding, struggling, coughing, vomiting, dilated pupils, rise in pulse and BP – dangerous stage; avoid noise and stimulation | | III – Stage of surgical anaesthesia | From regular breathing to paralysis of respiratory muscles; four planes | Regular, deep breathing; loss of eyelash and corneal reflexes; muscles relax; eyeballs become fixed; surgery is done in planes 2–3 | | IV – Stage of medullary paralysis (overdose) | From respiratory arrest to circulatory failure | Apnoea, widely dilated fixed pupils, severe hypotension – death unless anaesthesia is reduced and life support given | With modern rapid IV induction, stages I and II are passed within seconds. The three phases of GA in practice are induction, maintenance and emergence (recovery).

(c) Nursing responsibilities (8 marks) 1. Before anaesthesia

  • Ensure that the pre-anaesthetic check-up (PAC) is done, investigations are available and the ASA grade and plan are recorded.
  • Check consent for anaesthesia, fasting status, removal of dentures, jewellery and nail polish, and note loose teeth.
  • Give pre-medication as ordered (anxiolytic, antacid, antiemetic) and record it.
  • Check the anaesthesia work station – oxygen supply and back-up cylinder, anaesthesia machine, suction, breathing circuits, masks, oropharyngeal airways, laryngoscope with working bulb, endotracheal tubes of different sizes, stylet, bougie, laryngeal mask airway, Ambu bag and the difficult-airway cart.
  • Keep drugs ready and labelled – induction agents, muscle relaxants, reversal agents (neostigmine with glycopyrrolate), opioids, and emergency drugs (adrenaline, atropine, ephedrine, phenylephrine); keep a defibrillator nearby.
  • Attach monitors – ECG, non-invasive BP, SpO₂, end-tidal CO₂ (capnography), temperature; secure a working IV line.

2. During induction

  • Keep the OT quiet; stay at the patient's side and reassure; pre-oxygenate as directed.
  • Assist intubation – hand the laryngoscope and tube, apply cricoid pressure (Sellick's manoeuvre) when asked during rapid sequence induction, inflate the cuff, confirm tube position (EtCO₂ trace, bilateral chest movement and breath sounds) and secure the tube.
  • After induction, position the patient safely, protect the eyes (tape closed or eye pads), pad pressure points and apply the safety strap.

3. During maintenance

  • Monitor and record vital signs, SpO₂, EtCO₂, urine output, blood loss (suction volume, weighing of swabs) and fluids given; keep blood ready.
  • Maintain body temperature with warmers and warm fluids.
  • Watch for complications – hypotension, arrhythmias, bronchospasm, anaphylaxis, malignant hyperthermia, air embolism.

4. During emergence and after anaesthesia

  • Keep suction ready during extubation; turn the patient to the side once extubated; give oxygen.
  • Transfer to the PACU with the anaesthetist; give a full handover.
  • Observe for complications of GA – airway obstruction, laryngospasm, aspiration, hypoxia, respiratory depression, hypotension, nausea and vomiting, shivering, sore throat, delirium and urinary retention – and report promptly.

5. Spinal anaesthesia – specific nursing care

  • Procedure – the patient sits or lies on the side with the back flexed (knees to chest, chin down); under strict asepsis the anaesthetist injects local anaesthetic (for example, 0.5% heavy bupivacaine) into the subarachnoid space at L3–L4 or L4–L5. Help the patient hold the position still and reassure him.
  • Monitor BP every 2–3 minutes initially – hypotension and bradycardia are common due to sympathetic block; treat as ordered with IV fluids, leg elevation, ephedrine or phenylephrine, and atropine for bradycardia.
  • Watch for high spinal block (breathing difficulty, numb hands, difficulty speaking), nausea and shivering.
  • After surgery – check the return of sensation and movement of the legs (Bromage score), protect numb limbs from injury and pressure, turn the patient carefully, and watch for urinary retention and post-dural puncture headache (encourage fluids and analgesics as ordered).

6. Epidural and local anaesthesia

  • Epidural – secure the catheter, label the line, monitor sensory level, BP and respiration; give top-ups or infusions only as prescribed; remove the catheter at the correct time in relation to anticoagulant doses.
  • Local anaesthesia – check allergy; know the maximum safe dose (for example, plain lignocaine about 3 mg/kg, with adrenaline about 7 mg/kg); watch for toxicity – numbness around the mouth, metallic taste, tinnitus, confusion, seizures, arrhythmias; keep resuscitation equipment and lipid emulsion (20%) available. Adrenaline-containing solutions are traditionally avoided in fingers, toes, penis, nose and ear lobes.

7. Common complications of general anaesthesia and nursing action

  • Airway obstruction (tongue falling back) – jaw thrust, oropharyngeal airway, lateral position, suction.
  • Laryngospasm – 100% oxygen with gentle positive pressure, call the anaesthetist; drugs as ordered.
  • Aspiration of vomitus – head low and turned to the side, suction immediately, oxygen; inform the anaesthetist.
  • Respiratory depression due to opioids or residual muscle relaxant – stimulate the patient, give oxygen, keep reversal drugs (naloxone, neostigmine) ready as ordered.
  • Hypotension and arrhythmias – check bleeding and fluids, raise the legs, IV fluids and vasopressors as ordered, ECG monitoring.
  • Nausea and vomiting – antiemetics, lateral position, mouth care.
  • Hypothermia and shivering – warm blankets, forced-air warming, warm fluids.
  • Sore throat and hoarseness after intubation – reassure; warm saline gargles and lozenges when allowed.
  • Emergence delirium – protect from falls (side rails), reassure, rule out hypoxia and a full bladder.

8. Teaching after day-care anaesthesia For 24 hours after anaesthesia the patient should not drive, operate machines, drink alcohol or sign legal documents; he must go home with a responsible adult, take light food first, and contact the hospital if he has bleeding, severe pain, persistent vomiting or fever.

Nursing importance Most anaesthetic emergencies – difficult airway, aspiration, hypotension, toxicity – can be prevented or controlled when the nurse prepares equipment properly, monitors closely and acts quickly.

Conclusion Anaesthesia may be general, regional, local or sedation; knowledge of its stages, drugs, complications and the nurse's role before, during and after anaesthesia is essential for safe surgery.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Intraoperative Care
question: Explain the steps of surgical scrub, gowning and gloving.

diagram.caption: Steps of surgical hand scrub
labels: scrubbing four sides of each finger
rinsing from fingertips to elbows with hands held up

answer_html:
Definition Surgical scrub (surgical hand antisepsis) is the process of removing transient organisms and reducing resident organisms on the hands and forearms using an antiseptic agent before putting on a sterile gown and gloves. It is done by every member of the sterile team before every operation.

1. Preparation

  • Nails short and clean; no nail polish, artificial nails, rings, bangles or watch.
  • Wear OT dress, cap covering all hair and mask covering nose and mouth; adjust eye protection before scrubbing.
  • Check hands for cuts or skin infection.
  • Antiseptic – 4% chlorhexidine gluconate or 7.5% povidone-iodine scrub; or an alcohol-based surgical hand rub; elbow, foot or sensor-operated tap.

2. Steps of surgical scrub (antiseptic soap and water)

  1. Wash hands and forearms with plain soap to remove dirt; clean under the nails with a nail cleaner under running water (at least for the first scrub of the day).
  2. Wet hands and forearms, always keeping the hands higher than the elbows so that water flows from the cleanest area (hands) to the less clean area (elbows).
  3. Apply antiseptic and scrub systematically from fingertips to elbow: each finger as having four sides, the web spaces, palm, back of the hand, wrist and forearm up to about 5 cm above the elbow.
  4. Repeat for the other hand and arm.
  5. Rinse from fingertips to elbows in one direction; let water drip off the elbows.
  6. Total scrub time is usually 3–5 minutes, as per hospital policy or the antiseptic manufacturer.
  7. Hold the hands up and away from the body, above the waist and below the shoulders; enter the OT by pushing the door with the back.
  8. Dry with a sterile towel – one end for one hand and arm (blotting from the fingers towards the elbow), the other end for the other arm; discard the towel. - Alcohol-based surgical hand rub – after a plain hand wash, apply the rub to hands and forearms up to the elbows and rub until dry (about 3 minutes); no towel is needed.

3. Gowning

  1. Pick up the folded sterile gown from the inside at the neck and step back from the table.
  2. Let the gown unfold with the inside facing you; insert both arms into the sleeves without touching the outside.
  3. The circulating nurse ties the back and neck ties, touching only the inside.
  4. Keep hands inside the cuffs for closed gloving; the wrap-around tie is completed after gloving with a sterile team member or a tie card.
  5. The sterile area of the gown is the front from the chest to the level of the sterile field and the sleeves from 5 cm above the elbow to the cuff.

4. Gloving

  • Closed gloving (preferred in the OT) – hands stay inside the gown sleeves while the gloves are picked up and pulled over the cuffs, so bare skin never touches the outside of the glove.
  • Open gloving – used for procedures without a gown (catheterisation, dressings).
  • Assisted gloving – the scrub nurse holds the glove open for the surgeon.
  • Double gloving is advised in orthopaedic and high-risk surgeries; change gloves immediately if punctured.

Nursing importance Correct scrubbing, gowning and gloving are the first line of defence against surgical site infection; any break must be corrected at once (surgical conscience).

Conclusion Surgical scrub, gowning and gloving follow a fixed sequence that keeps the hands and the sterile field free from contamination.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Intraoperative Care
question: Classify sutures and suture materials. Add a note on the nurse's responsibilities.
answer_html:
Definition A suture is a strand of material used to tie (ligate) blood vessels or bring tissues together (approximate) until healing occurs. A ligature is a suture tied around a vessel to stop bleeding.

1. Qualities of an ideal suture Adequate tensile strength, secure knots, minimal tissue reaction, easy handling, sterility, predictable absorption, non-allergenic, does not wick bacteria, and low cost.

2. Classification (a) According to absorption | Type | Natural | Synthetic | |---|---|---| | Absorbable (broken down by enzymes or hydrolysis) | Plain catgut (absorbed in about 7–10 days); chromic catgut (about 2–3 weeks) | Polyglactin 910 (Vicryl), polyglycolic acid (Dexon), polydioxanone (PDS – long-lasting), poliglecaprone (Monocryl) | | Non-absorbable (remain permanently or are removed) | Silk, linen, cotton | Nylon (Ethilon), polypropylene (Prolene), polyester (Ethibond); metal – stainless steel wire, staples | (b) According to structure

  • Monofilament – single strand (nylon, Prolene, PDS) – slides easily through tissues, less infection, but knots need care.
  • Multifilament (braided) – several strands (silk, Vicryl) – easy to handle and knot but can harbour bacteria.

3. Sizes The USP size runs from thick (5, 2, 1, 0) to very fine (2-0, 3-0 … 10-0); the more zeros, the finer the suture. For example, 1 or 1-0 for abdominal fascia, 3-0 or 4-0 for skin of the trunk, 5-0 or 6-0 for the face, and 8-0 to 10-0 for eye and microvascular surgery.

4. Common uses

  • Vicryl – subcutaneous tissue, bowel anastomosis, ligatures, episiotomy.
  • PDS/looped nylon – closure of the abdominal wall.
  • Silk – securing drains and tubes, ligatures.
  • Nylon/Prolene – skin closure, hernia repair (with mesh), vascular surgery.
  • Steel wire – closure of the sternum, orthopaedic use; staples – skin and bowel.
  • Other wound-closure methods: skin adhesive (cyanoacrylate glue) and adhesive strips.

5. Suture needles

  • Round-bodied (taper) – soft tissues such as bowel, vessels and muscle.
  • Cutting and reverse cutting – tough tissues such as skin and tendons.
  • Blunt – friable organs such as liver and kidney.
  • Atraumatic (swaged) needles, with the suture attached to the needle, cause less tissue damage than eyed needles.

6. Nurse's responsibilities

  • Keep the commonly used sutures ready; check the type, size, expiry date and packet integrity; open packets aseptically onto the sterile field.
  • Load the needle holder correctly (needle held about one-third of the way from the swaged end) and pass it with the needle pointing in the direction of use.
  • Count needles along with swabs and instruments; dispose of used needles in a puncture-proof sharps container.
  • Record the sutures and implants used.
  • Removal of skin sutures (as ordered) – face and neck 3–5 days; scalp, abdomen and trunk 7–10 days; limbs 10–14 days; over joints about 14 days (later in elderly, diabetic or malnourished patients). Use aseptic technique; cut the suture close to the skin and pull it out so that the exposed part does not pass through the tissue; observe the wound and document.

Nursing importance Knowledge of sutures helps the scrub nurse anticipate the surgeon's needs and helps the ward nurse remove sutures at the correct time.

Conclusion Sutures are classified by absorption, source and structure; the right suture and needle for each tissue, with careful handling by the nurse, promote safe wound healing.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Intraoperative Care
question: Explain the safety measures in the operation theatre, including the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist.
answer_html:
Introduction Surgery carries risks of wrong patient or wrong site surgery, retained instruments, burns, falls, infection and anaesthetic accidents. Most of these are preventable. The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist and standard safety practices make every operation safer.

1. WHO Surgical Safety Checklist | Phase | When | Key checks | |---|---|---| | Sign In | Before induction of anaesthesia | Patient confirms identity, site, procedure and consent; site marked; anaesthesia machine and medication check complete; pulse oximeter working; known allergy; difficult airway or aspiration risk; risk of blood loss above 500 ml (7 ml/kg in children) – IV access and blood planned | | Time Out | Before skin incision | All team members introduce themselves by name and role; confirm patient, site and procedure; antibiotic prophylaxis given within the last 60 minutes; critical events reviewed by surgeon, anaesthetist and nurse; sterility confirmed; essential imaging displayed | | Sign Out | Before the patient leaves the OT | Nurse confirms the name of the procedure, instrument, sponge and needle counts are correct, specimens labelled, equipment problems addressed; team reviews key concerns for recovery |

2. Other safety measures

  • Correct patient, site and procedure – identity band, site marking, verification at every handover.
  • Positioning safety – adequate staff to lift, padding of pressure points, safety strap, protection of nerves and eyes.
  • Prevention of retained items – systematic counts; X-ray-detectable sponges.
  • Electrosurgical (diathermy) safety – return electrode pad on a clean, dry, hairless, well-muscled area close to the site and away from metal implants; remove jewellery; patient should not touch metal parts of the table; check cables; keep the active electrode in a holster.
  • Fire safety – the "fire triangle" (oxygen, fuel, ignition source); let alcohol skin preparation dry fully, avoid high oxygen near the face during head and neck surgery, keep saline and extinguishers ready.
  • Infection prevention – surgical attire, scrubbing, sterile field, traffic control, timely antibiotic.
  • Medication safety – label all syringes and solutions on the sterile field; read back verbal orders.
  • Sharps safety – use a neutral zone or tray for passing sharps; no recapping.
  • Prevention of hypothermia – warm room, blankets, warm fluids.
  • Radiation and laser safety – lead aprons, thyroid shields, protective eyewear.
  • Latex allergy – latex-free trolley for allergic patients.
  • Specimen safety – correct labelling and register entry.
  • Equipment safety – daily checks and maintenance of lights, tables and machines.

3. Role of the nurse The circulating nurse often leads the checklist, speaks up when anything is unclear, ensures that counts and specimens are correct and documents everything.

Nursing importance Using the WHO checklist has been shown to reduce surgical deaths and complications; it changes safety from individual memory to a team routine.

Conclusion OT safety depends on the three-phase WHO checklist and on daily practices that prevent wrong-site surgery, retained items, burns, fire and infection.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Intraoperative Care
question: Describe the common surgical positions and the nurse's responsibilities in positioning the patient.
answer_html:
Introduction Surgical positioning is placing the patient on the operating table so that the operative site is well exposed while breathing, circulation, nerves and skin are protected. Under anaesthesia the patient cannot feel pain or move, so the nurse must protect him.

1. Common surgical positions | Position | Description | Used for | |---|---|---| | Supine (dorsal recumbent) | Lying flat on the back, arms on arm boards (less than 90°) | Most abdominal, chest, face, neck and limb surgeries | | Trendelenburg | Supine with head lowered and legs raised | Lower abdominal and pelvic surgery (bowel falls away from pelvis) | | Reverse Trendelenburg | Head raised, feet lowered | Upper abdominal (gallbladder, stomach), head and neck surgery | | Lithotomy | Supine with hips and knees flexed and legs in stirrups | Perineal, vaginal, rectal surgery, cystoscopy, deliveries | | Lateral (kidney position) | Lying on the side with kidney rest raised | Kidney, chest (thoracotomy) and hip surgery | | Prone | Lying face down with chest supports | Spine, back of legs, posterior neck surgery | | Jack-knife (Kraske) | Prone with hips flexed over the table break | Rectal and pilonidal sinus surgery | | Sitting (beach chair/Fowler's) | Sitting upright | Shoulder surgery, some neurosurgery |

2. Hazards of positioning

  • Nerve injury – brachial plexus (arm abducted more than 90°), ulnar nerve (elbow pressure), common peroneal nerve (lithotomy stirrups pressing on the lateral knee).
  • Pressure injuries over the sacrum, heels, elbows, occiput, face and chest.
  • Breathing difficulty – Trendelenburg and prone positions reduce chest expansion.
  • Circulatory problems – hypotension when the position is changed quickly, DVT, compartment syndrome in long lithotomy.
  • Eye injury in the prone position; falls from the table.

3. Nurse's responsibilities

  1. Check the planned position and keep supports, pads, arm boards, stirrups and straps ready.
  2. Use enough staff to move the patient; move slowly and gently, especially an anaesthetised patient; coordinate with the anaesthetist who protects the head and airway.
  3. Keep the body in good alignment; no limb should hang off the table.
  4. Pad bony prominences and pressure points; keep arms on arm boards at less than 90°.
  5. In lithotomy, raise and lower both legs together to prevent hip dislocation and back strain.
  6. In the prone position, support the chest and pelvis so that the abdomen moves freely; protect eyes, face, breasts and genitals.
  7. Apply the safety strap above the knees; ensure no contact with metal parts (diathermy burns).
  8. Keep IV lines, catheters and tubes free of kinks.
  9. Recheck the position after any table movement; document the position, supports used and skin condition before and after surgery.

Nursing importance Correct positioning prevents painful and sometimes permanent nerve injuries, pressure ulcers and breathing problems after surgery.

Conclusion Each surgical position gives good exposure for a particular operation, but the nurse must protect nerves, skin, breathing and circulation while the patient is anaesthetised.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Intraoperative Care
question: Explain the cleaning and disinfection of the operation theatre.
answer_html:
Introduction The OT environment can be a source of surgical site infection if dust, blood and body fluids are not removed properly. Systematic cleaning and disinfection of the OT, done at fixed times with the correct methods and agents, keeps the environment safe.

1. Principles

  • Clean from clean areas to dirty areas and from top to bottom (high surfaces first, floor last).
  • Use damp/wet methods – never dry dusting or sweeping, which spreads dust and microbes.
  • Use separate colour-coded mops, cloths and buckets (two-bucket method – one with detergent/disinfectant, one for rinsing).
  • Staff wear PPE – gloves, apron, mask; follow BMW rules for waste.

2. Schedule of cleaning (a) Before the first case of the day

  • Damp dust all horizontal surfaces – OT table, lights, trolleys, anaesthesia machine, monitors, shelves – with a detergent or low-level disinfectant. (b) Between cases

  • Remove used linen, waste and sharps in the correct BMW bags and containers.

  • Clean and disinfect surfaces that touched the patient or were splashed – OT table, mattress, arm boards, straps, suction outlets, equipment – and the floor around the table (about 1–1.5 m).
  • Blood or body-fluid spills – absorb, then disinfect with sodium hypochlorite (0.5–1% available chlorine), leave for the contact time and wipe.

  • Use 70% alcohol for small surfaces and equipment where suitable. (c) End of the day – terminal cleaning

  • Clean and disinfect all surfaces, equipment, doors and handles, walls up to reachable height, scrub sinks and the whole floor (wet mopping with detergent followed by disinfectant).

  • Clean suction jars, waste bins and trolleys; restock supplies. (d) Weekly

  • Walls, ceilings, air-conditioning grills, light fixtures, cupboards and shelves; remove all movable items and clean the room thoroughly.

3. "Infected" cases

  • Standard precautions and routine between-case cleaning are sufficient after cases such as HIV, HBV or TB; the OT does not need to be closed for special fumigation. Schedule such cases at the end of the list where policy requires.

4. Fumigation and fogging

  • Traditional formalin fumigation has been abandoned in most hospitals because it is toxic and carcinogenic. Current national infection-control guidelines do not recommend routine fumigation or fogging; thorough surface cleaning is the key. Where hospital policy still requires fogging (for example, after construction), hydrogen peroxide–silver nitrate based agents are used.

5. Monitoring

  • Cleaning checklists signed by housekeeping and checked by the OT in-charge.
  • Microbiological surveillance (surface swabs, settle plates) is not routine but is done after construction, outbreaks or as per hospital policy.
  • Regular maintenance of AHU filters and air-change monitoring.

Nursing importance The OT nurse supervises housekeeping staff, ensures correct dilution and contact time of disinfectants, and maintains records, which directly reduces surgical site infections.

Conclusion Planned daily, between-case, terminal and weekly cleaning with wet methods and correct disinfectants keeps the OT safe; routine fumigation is no longer necessary.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Intraoperative Care
question: Classify surgical instruments with examples and explain their care.
answer_html:
Introduction Surgical instruments are tools used to cut, hold, clamp, retract, suture and suction tissues during surgery. Most are made of stainless steel. Knowing their names and uses helps the scrub nurse pass the right instrument quickly, and proper care increases their life.

1. Classification with examples | Group | Examples | Use | |---|---|---| | Cutting and dissecting | Scalpel – Bard-Parker handle No. 3 (blades 10, 11, 12, 15) and No. 4 (blades 20–24); scissors – Mayo (heavy), Metzenbaum (fine), suture scissors | Incising and dissecting tissues, cutting sutures | | Grasping and holding | Toothed and non-toothed dissecting forceps, Allis, Babcock (bowel), sponge-holding forceps (Rampley) | Holding tissues, swabbing | | Clamping (haemostatic) | Mosquito, Kelly, Kocher's, Crile artery forceps, bowel clamps | Stopping bleeding, clamping vessels and bowel | | Retracting | Hand-held – Langenbeck, Deaver, Morris; self-retaining – Balfour, Weitlaner | Holding wound edges and organs away | | Suturing | Needle holders (Mayo-Hegar), needles, skin stapler | Closing tissues | | Suction | Yankauer, Poole suction tips | Removing blood and fluid | | Probing and dilating | Probes, Hegar dilators, uterine sounds | Exploring tracts, dilating openings | | Accessory | Towel clips, catheters, diathermy pencil | Holding drapes, others | | Specialised | Laparoscopic, orthopaedic, ophthalmic and microsurgical sets | Specialty surgeries |

2. Care of instruments

  1. During surgery – keep instruments wiped of blood with a moist sponge; use each instrument only for its purpose (do not use fine scissors to cut sutures); pass instruments handle first, in the closed position.
  2. Point-of-use pre-cleaning – after surgery, remove gross debris, open the ratchets and joints, and keep the instruments moist (enzymatic spray or damp towel); transport in a closed container.
  3. Cleaning and decontamination in the CSSD/washing area – soak in enzymatic detergent, clean manually with a soft brush under water or use an ultrasonic washer or washer-disinfector; rinse and dry.
  4. Inspection – check for rust, cracks, blunt edges, misaligned jaws and loose screws; send damaged instruments for repair.
  5. Lubrication of hinged instruments with water-soluble instrument milk.
  6. Packing in sets with an instrument list and chemical indicator; sharp tips protected.
  7. Sterilisation – steam (autoclave) for most; low-temperature methods (ethylene oxide, hydrogen peroxide plasma) for heat-sensitive items.
  8. Storage in a clean, dry, closed sterile store; first-in, first-out use; record the sterility date.
  9. Never drop, throw or pile heavy instruments on delicate ones.

Nursing importance Well-maintained instruments shorten operating time, prevent injury and infection, and save hospital money.

Conclusion Surgical instruments are grouped by function – cutting, holding, clamping, retracting, suturing and suction – and need careful cleaning, inspection, sterilisation and storage.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Intraoperative Care
question: When and how are surgical counts done?
answer_html:
Surgical count is the systematic counting of sponges (gauze, mops), sharps (needles, blades) and instruments by the scrub nurse and the circulating nurse together and aloud, and recording on the count board/sheet.

When

  1. Before the incision (baseline count).
  2. Before closing a cavity within a cavity (for example, uterus, bladder).
  3. Before closure of the wound (peritoneum/fascia).
  4. At skin closure.
  5. Whenever scrub or circulating staff change.

If a count is incorrect – inform the surgeon, recount, search the field, floor and bins, take an X-ray as ordered and document; a retained surgical item is a "never event".

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Intraoperative Care
question: What is malignant hyperthermia? Write its emergency management.
answer_html:
Malignant hyperthermia is a rare, inherited, life-threatening hypermetabolic reaction of skeletal muscle triggered by volatile inhalational anaesthetics (halothane, sevoflurane, isoflurane) and succinylcholine. Uncontrolled calcium release in muscle causes rigidity and heat production.

Features: unexplained rise in end-tidal CO₂ (earliest sign), tachycardia, masseter and muscle rigidity, rapidly rising temperature, acidosis, hyperkalaemia, arrhythmias and dark urine (myoglobin).

Emergency management

  1. Stop the triggering agent; call for help; hyperventilate with 100% oxygen.
  2. Give dantrolene sodium 2.5 mg/kg IV, repeated until symptoms subside.
  3. Cool the patient (cold IV saline, ice packs); treat hyperkalaemia, acidosis and arrhythmias; monitor urine output.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Intraoperative Care
question: How are surgical specimens handled in the OT?
answer_html:
Handling of surgical specimens

  1. Receive the specimen from the surgeon in a suitable container; never discard any tissue removed from the patient.
  2. Label the container (not just the lid) with the patient's name, age, hospital number, specimen name and site, date and time, and surgeon.
  3. Histopathology – put in 10% neutral buffered formalin (about 10 times the specimen volume).
