  4. Frozen section, culture or cytology – send fresh, without formalin, immediately.
  5. Complete the requisition form, enter in the specimen register, and send promptly; use gloves; maintain chain of custody for medico-legal specimens.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Intraoperative Care
question: State the rules for maintaining a sterile field.
answer_html:
Rules for maintaining a sterile field

  1. Only sterile items are placed on a sterile field; check sterility indicators and expiry dates.
  2. Sterile persons touch only sterile items; non-sterile persons do not reach over the field.
  3. Tables are sterile only at table level; items falling below are contaminated.
  4. The outer edge (about 2.5 cm) of a sterile wrapper is considered non-sterile.
  5. A sterile gown is sterile only in front from chest to table level and on the sleeves.
  6. Never turn your back on the sterile field; keep it always in view.
  7. Moisture through a sterile drape contaminates it.
  8. When in doubt, consider it contaminated and replace it.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Intraoperative Care
question: What is post-dural puncture headache? How is it managed?
answer_html:
Post-dural puncture headache (PDPH) is a headache that occurs after spinal anaesthesia or lumbar puncture due to leakage of CSF through the dural hole, causing low CSF pressure and traction on pain-sensitive structures.

Features: starts 24–72 hours after the puncture; frontal or occipital headache that is worse on sitting or standing and relieved on lying flat; may have neck stiffness, nausea and tinnitus.

Prevention: use of fine, pencil-point spinal needles (25–27 G).

Management: lying flat for comfort, plenty of oral fluids, analgesics (paracetamol), caffeine as ordered, and an epidural blood patch for severe or persistent headache.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Fluid and Electrolyte Imbalance, Shock and Pain
question: (a) Define hypovolaemic shock and list its causes. (3 marks) (b) Explain its pathophysiology and clinical features, with the classes of haemorrhage. (4 marks) (c) Describe the medical and nursing management of a patient with hypovolaemic shock. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Vicious cycle of hypovolaemic shock
labels: fall in stroke volume and cardiac output
organ failure; compensatory sympathetic and RAAS activation

answer_html:
(a) Definition and causes (3 marks) Shock is a life-threatening state of inadequate tissue perfusion, in which the cells do not receive enough oxygen and nutrients for their needs. Hypovolaemic shock is shock caused by a decrease in the circulating (intravascular) blood volume, usually a loss of 15% or more, leading to low cardiac output. It is the commonest type of shock, especially after trauma and in obstetric and surgical bleeding.

Causes

  1. Haemorrhagic (loss of whole blood)
    • Trauma – road traffic accidents, falls, stab wounds, fractures of the pelvis and femur.
    • Upper and lower GI bleeding – peptic ulcer, oesophageal varices.
    • Obstetric haemorrhage – postpartum haemorrhage, ruptured ectopic pregnancy, antepartum haemorrhage.
    • Surgical bleeding, ruptured aortic aneurysm, bleeding disorders, anticoagulant overdose.
  2. Non-haemorrhagic (loss of plasma or fluid)
    • Severe vomiting and diarrhoea – cholera, acute gastroenteritis.
    • Burns – loss of plasma from burnt surfaces.
    • Excessive urination – diabetic ketoacidosis, diabetes insipidus, overuse of diuretics.
    • Third-space losses – acute pancreatitis, intestinal obstruction, peritonitis, ascites.
    • Excessive sweating (heat exhaustion), dengue with plasma leakage.

(b) Pathophysiology and clinical features (4 marks) Pathophysiology

  • Loss of volume → decreased venous return (preload) → fall in stroke volume and cardiac output → fall in BP → poor tissue perfusion.
  • Compensation – the sympathetic system releases adrenaline and noradrenaline (tachycardia, vasoconstriction); the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system and ADH retain sodium and water (low urine output, thirst); fluid moves from tissues into vessels.
  • If the loss continues, compensation fails – cells change to anaerobic metabolism, lactic acid accumulates (metabolic acidosis), cell membranes fail and organs are damaged (kidneys, lungs, gut, brain) – multiple organ dysfunction and death.

Clinical features

  • Tachycardia (often the first sign), weak thready pulse, narrow pulse pressure, later hypotension.
  • Tachypnoea; anxiety and restlessness progressing to confusion and coma.
  • Cold, pale, clammy skin, delayed capillary refill (more than 2 seconds), collapsed neck veins, low CVP.
  • Thirst, dry mouth, oliguria (urine output below 0.5 ml/kg/hour).
  • Laboratory – falling haemoglobin (after some hours), raised lactate, metabolic acidosis on ABG, raised urea and creatinine.

Classes of haemorrhage (ATLS, adult of 70 kg) | Feature | Class I | Class II | Class III | Class IV | |---|---|---|---|---| | Blood loss | Up to 15% (750 ml) | 15–30% (750–1500 ml) | 30–40% (1500–2000 ml) | More than 40% (above 2000 ml) | | Pulse/min | Below 100 | 100–120 | 120–140 | Above 140 | | BP | Normal | Normal | Decreased | Markedly decreased | | Respiration/min | 14–20 | 20–30 | 30–40 | Above 35 | | Urine (ml/hour) | Above 30 | 20–30 | 5–15 | Negligible | | Mental state | Slightly anxious | Mildly anxious | Anxious, confused | Confused, lethargic | Remember: BP falls late – a young adult may lose up to 30% of blood volume before the BP drops.

(c) Medical and nursing management (8 marks) 1. Immediate assessment and resuscitation – ABC

  • Call for help; assess airway, breathing and circulation; give high-flow oxygen (by face mask with reservoir) to keep SpO₂ at 94% or above.
  • Control external bleeding – direct pressure, pressure dressing, elevation; tourniquet for life-threatening limb bleeding; pelvic binder for pelvic fracture as ordered.
  • Position – lie flat with the legs raised (passive leg raising) unless there is head, chest or spinal injury; avoid the steep Trendelenburg position (it compromises breathing).

2. Vascular access and investigations

  • Insert two large-bore IV cannulas (14–16 G) in the forearms or antecubital veins; intraosseous or central access if veins are collapsed.
  • Draw blood for grouping and cross-matching, CBC, coagulation profile, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, blood sugar, lactate and ABG.

3. Fluid and blood replacement

  • Give warmed crystalloids (Ringer's lactate or normal saline) – about 1 litre bolus in adults (20 ml/kg in children) – and reassess the response.
  • Blood transfusion early in haemorrhagic shock – O-negative packed red cells in extreme emergency, then group-specific cross-matched blood.
  • Massive transfusion protocol for major bleeding – packed red cells, fresh frozen plasma and platelets in about a 1:1:1 ratio; check calcium and temperature.
  • Tranexamic acid in trauma and postpartum haemorrhage – 1 g IV over 10 minutes within 3 hours of injury, followed by 1 g over 8 hours, as ordered.
  • In bleeding trauma patients the doctor may allow "permissive hypotension" (systolic BP about 80–90 mmHg) until bleeding is controlled – except in head injury.
  • In non-haemorrhagic shock (diarrhoea, burns) – crystalloids according to calculated losses (for example, the Parkland formula in burns).
  • Vasopressors are not the first treatment; they are used only after adequate volume replacement if hypotension persists.

4. Definitive treatment of the cause

  • Surgery to stop bleeding (laparotomy, repair of vessels), endoscopic therapy for GI bleeding, uterotonics and surgery for PPH, correction of coagulopathy.
  • Antiemetics, antidiarrhoeals and ORS as appropriate in fluid-loss shock.

5. Monitoring (nursing)

  • Pulse, BP, respiration and SpO₂ every 5–15 minutes until stable; ECG monitoring.
  • Urine output hourly through an indwelling catheter – target at least 0.5 ml/kg/hour (30 ml/hour in adults).
  • Level of consciousness, skin colour, temperature and capillary refill.
  • CVP (if a central line is present), shock index (pulse ÷ systolic BP – above 0.9 is a warning), lactate and ABG as ordered.
  • Strict intake–output chart and accurate recording of all fluids, blood and losses (drains, vomitus, stools).

6. Prevention of the "lethal triad"

  • Hypothermia – warm blankets, warmed IV fluids and blood, warm room.
  • Acidosis and coagulopathy – adequate oxygenation, perfusion and early blood products.

7. Safe transfusion and fluid administration

  • Two-person bedside check, use of a blood warmer for rapid transfusion, monitoring for transfusion reactions and fluid overload (crepitations, breathlessness, rising JVP).

8. Comfort and psychological care

  • Keep the patient calm, explain procedures briefly, relieve pain carefully (small IV doses of opioids as ordered), maintain privacy, and keep the family informed.

9. Prevention and early detection of complications

  • Acute kidney injury (falling urine output, rising creatinine), ARDS (breathlessness, falling SpO₂), DIC (oozing from puncture sites), stress ulcers, multiple organ dysfunction – report early.

Common nursing diagnoses

  • Deficient fluid volume related to active blood loss.
  • Decreased cardiac output and ineffective tissue perfusion related to reduced circulating volume.
  • Anxiety related to the sudden serious illness; risk for injury related to altered consciousness.

10. Health education and prevention

  • Teach first aid for bleeding (direct pressure, elevation) and early transport to hospital after injury – the "golden hour" of trauma.
  • Teach families to give ORS early in diarrhoea and to recognise danger signs of dehydration (sunken eyes, very little urine, drowsiness).
  • Encourage institutional deliveries and active management of the third stage of labour to prevent postpartum haemorrhage.
  • Advise patients on anticoagulants about regular INR checks and bleeding warning signs.

Nursing importance In hypovolaemic shock "time is life": the nurse is usually the first to notice tachycardia, restlessness and falling urine output; early action before the BP falls saves lives.

Conclusion Hypovolaemic shock results from loss of blood or fluid; rapid control of bleeding, oxygen, large-bore IV access, fluids and blood, treatment of the cause and close nursing monitoring are the keys to survival.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Fluid and Electrolyte Imbalance, Shock and Pain
question: Explain the causes, clinical features and management of: (a) Hyponatraemia (4 marks) (b) Hypernatraemia (3 marks) (c) Hypokalaemia (4 marks) (d) Hyperkalaemia (4 marks)

diagram.caption: ECG changes in potassium imbalance
labels: normal ECG; hypokalaemia – flat or inverted T wave
prominent U wave; hyperkalaemia – tall peaked T waves

answer_html:
Introduction Sodium is the main cation of the extracellular fluid and controls water balance and nerve–muscle function; potassium is the main intracellular cation and is vital for the heart, muscles and nerves. Imbalances are very common in hospitalised patients – after vomiting, diarrhoea, surgery, diuretics, kidney disease and IV therapy – and can cause seizures, paralysis and cardiac arrest. Normal values: serum sodium 135–145 mEq/L; serum potassium 3.5–5.0 mEq/L.

(a) Hyponatraemia – serum sodium below 135 mEq/L (4 marks) Causes

  • Loss of sodium – vomiting, diarrhoea, NG aspiration, diuretics (especially thiazides), Addison's disease, burns, heavy sweating replaced with plain water.
  • Gain of water (dilution) – SIADH (lung cancer, head injury, meningitis, drugs such as carbamazepine and antidepressants), excessive hypotonic IV fluids (plain 5% dextrose) after surgery, psychogenic polydipsia, heart failure, cirrhosis and kidney failure, absorption of irrigation fluid during TURP.

Clinical features (depend on the level and speed of fall)

  • Anorexia, nausea, vomiting, headache, lethargy, muscle cramps and weakness.
  • Confusion, irritability, seizures and coma due to cerebral oedema (water moves into brain cells), especially when sodium falls below 120 mEq/L or falls rapidly.

Management

  • Treat the cause – stop the offending drug, correct vomiting and diarrhoea.
  • Sodium loss with dehydration – isotonic (0.9%) normal saline IV, oral salt.
  • Water excess (SIADH, dilutional) – fluid restriction (for example, 800–1000 ml/day), drugs such as tolvaptan as ordered.
  • Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizures, coma) – 3% hypertonic saline in small boluses in the ICU, as ordered.
  • Correct slowly – a rise of not more than 8–10 mEq/L in 24 hours, because rapid correction causes osmotic demyelination syndrome (paralysis, difficulty speaking and swallowing).
  • Nursing – monitor sodium every 4–6 hours as ordered, neurological status and seizure precautions; daily weight; strict intake and output; avoid giving plain water or hypotonic fluids to high-risk patients; explain the reason for fluid restriction and spread allowed fluids over the day.

(b) Hypernatraemia – serum sodium above 145 mEq/L (3 marks) Causes

  • Water loss – fever, sweating, rapid breathing, diabetes insipidus, osmotic diuresis (hyperglycaemia), severe watery diarrhoea.
  • Inadequate water intake – elderly, unconscious and bedridden patients, infants, patients on tube feeds without extra water.
  • Sodium excess – hypertonic saline or sodium bicarbonate infusion, salt poisoning.

Clinical features

  • Intense thirst, dry sticky mucous membranes, dry swollen tongue, flushed skin, fever, low urine output (except in diabetes insipidus).
  • Restlessness, irritability, confusion, muscle twitching, seizures and coma due to shrinkage of brain cells.

Management

  • Replace water slowly – oral water, or IV 5% dextrose or 0.45% saline as ordered; reduce sodium by not more than about 10 mEq/L in 24 hours to avoid cerebral oedema.
  • Treat the cause – desmopressin for central diabetes insipidus, fever control.
  • Nursing – offer water regularly to elderly and unconscious patients, give free water with tube feeds, record intake–output and daily weight, monitor neurological status, provide mouth care and seizure precautions.

(c) Hypokalaemia – serum potassium below 3.5 mEq/L (4 marks) Causes

  • GI losses – vomiting, NG suction, diarrhoea, laxative abuse, fistulas.
  • Renal losses – loop and thiazide diuretics, hyperaldosteronism, corticosteroids, osmotic diuresis.
  • Shift into cells – insulin therapy (especially in DKA), alkalosis, salbutamol.
  • Poor intake – starvation, alcoholism, elderly on poor diet.

Clinical features

  • Muscle weakness, leg cramps, fatigue, reduced reflexes; severe cases – paralysis and respiratory muscle weakness.
  • Reduced bowel movement – constipation, abdominal distension, paralytic ileus.
  • Cardiac – palpitations, arrhythmias; increased risk of digoxin toxicity.
  • ECG – flat or inverted T waves, ST depression and prominent U waves.
  • Polyuria (inability to concentrate urine).

Management

  • Treat the cause; review diuretics (a potassium-sparing diuretic may be added).
  • Oral potassium chloride (syrup or tablets, given with or after food and diluted to reduce gastric irritation) and potassium-rich foods – bananas, oranges, coconut water, tomatoes, potatoes, green leafy vegetables, dry fruits.
  • IV potassium chloride for severe hypokalaemia or when oral intake is not possible:
    • Never give KCl as an IV push or bolus – it can cause cardiac arrest.
    • Always dilute in IV fluid and give by an infusion pump at a controlled rate (usually not more than 10 mEq/hour through a peripheral line; higher rates only through a central line with ECG monitoring, as ordered).
    • Check that urine output is adequate before and during potassium replacement.
    • Watch the IV site for pain and phlebitis; mix the bag well.
  • Correct low magnesium, otherwise potassium will not rise.
  • Nursing – monitor serum potassium, ECG and muscle strength; watch for digoxin toxicity; record intake–output; teach diet.

(d) Hyperkalaemia – serum potassium above 5.0 mEq/L (4 marks) Causes

  • Kidney failure (acute or chronic) – the most common cause.
  • Drugs – potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone), ACE inhibitors and ARBs, NSAIDs, excess potassium supplements.
  • Release from cells – crush injury, burns, rhabdomyolysis, tumour lysis, haemolysis, acidosis (DKA), massive transfusion of old stored blood.
  • Addison's disease (low aldosterone).
  • False (pseudo) hyperkalaemia – haemolysed sample due to a tight tourniquet, fist clenching or a fine needle; always confirm before treating.

Clinical features

  • Muscle weakness, tingling, numbness; flaccid paralysis in severe cases.
  • Nausea, intestinal colic, diarrhoea.
  • Bradycardia, arrhythmias, ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest – the most dangerous effect.
  • ECG – tall peaked (tented) T waves → prolonged PR interval → loss of P waves → wide QRS → sine-wave pattern → VF/asystole.

Emergency management (potassium above 6.5 mEq/L or ECG changes), as ordered

  1. Continuous ECG monitoring; stop all potassium intake and offending drugs.
  2. Stabilise the heart – 10% calcium gluconate 10 ml IV slowly over 5–10 minutes (repeat if ECG changes persist); it does not lower potassium but protects the heart.
  3. Shift potassium into cells – IV regular insulin 10 units with 25–50 g dextrose (for example, 50 ml of 50% dextrose); salbutamol nebulisation; sodium bicarbonate if acidotic. Monitor blood sugar for hypoglycaemia for several hours after insulin.
  4. Remove potassium from the body – loop diuretics (furosemide) if the kidneys work, potassium-binding resins (calcium or sodium polystyrene sulfonate orally or rectally), and haemodialysis in kidney failure or refractory cases.

Nursing management

  • Draw blood samples correctly to avoid haemolysis; recheck potassium as ordered.
  • Monitor ECG, pulse, BP and muscle strength; keep resuscitation equipment ready.
  • Low-potassium diet for kidney patients – limit bananas, oranges, coconut water, potatoes, tomatoes and dry fruits; leaching of vegetables (peeling, cutting, soaking and boiling in excess water, then discarding the water) reduces potassium.
  • Teach patients on ACE inhibitors and spironolactone about regular potassium checks and avoiding salt substitutes (which contain potassium chloride).

Summary table | Imbalance | Key danger | Key nursing caution | |---|---|---| | Hyponatraemia | Seizures, cerebral oedema | Correct slowly (risk of osmotic demyelination) | | Hypernatraemia | Confusion, seizures | Correct slowly (risk of cerebral oedema) | | Hypokalaemia | Arrhythmia, ileus, digoxin toxicity | Never give KCl IV push; use a pump | | Hyperkalaemia | Cardiac arrest | Calcium gluconate, insulin–dextrose, ECG monitoring |

Nursing importance Nurses give IV fluids, potassium infusions and diuretics and are the first to notice confusion, weakness or ECG changes; accurate monitoring and safe administration prevent fatal complications.

Conclusion Sodium imbalances mainly affect the brain and must be corrected slowly, while potassium imbalances mainly affect the heart and muscles; identifying the cause, careful replacement or removal and close monitoring are essential.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Fluid and Electrolyte Imbalance, Shock and Pain
question: Explain the stages of shock with the assessment findings in each stage.
answer_html:
Introduction Shock is a state of inadequate tissue perfusion that progresses through stages if it is not treated. Whatever the cause – hypovolaemic, cardiogenic, distributive or obstructive – the body passes through the initial, compensatory, progressive and refractory (irreversible) stages. Early recognition in the compensatory stage saves lives.

1. Initial stage

  • Cardiac output begins to fall; cells start anaerobic metabolism and lactic acid begins to rise.
  • No obvious clinical signs; there may be a slight increase in heart rate.

2. Compensatory (non-progressive) stage

  • The body tries to maintain BP and blood flow to vital organs:
    • Sympathetic stimulation (adrenaline, noradrenaline) → tachycardia, peripheral vasoconstriction.
    • Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system and ADH → sodium and water retention.
    • Increased respiration to correct acidosis.
  • Assessment findings
    • BP normal or slightly low, narrow pulse pressure.
    • Heart rate above 100/min; rapid breathing.
    • Cool, pale skin (except warm, flushed skin in early septic shock).
    • Decreased urine output, thirst.
    • Anxiety, restlessness – an early sign of reduced brain perfusion.
    • Hyperglycaemia; slight metabolic acidosis or respiratory alkalosis.
  • This stage is reversible if the cause is treated quickly.

3. Progressive (decompensated) stage

  • Compensatory mechanisms fail; poor perfusion damages organs.
  • Assessment findings
    • Hypotension (systolic BP below 90 mmHg or MAP below 65 mmHg).
    • Weak, thready pulse, marked tachycardia, arrhythmias, chest pain.
    • Cold, clammy, mottled skin, cyanosis, slow capillary refill.
    • Rapid, shallow breathing, crepitations (ARDS may begin).
    • Oliguria (below 0.5 ml/kg/hour) – acute kidney injury.
    • Confusion and lethargy.
    • Metabolic acidosis, raised lactate, raised liver enzymes, stress ulcers, early DIC.

4. Refractory (irreversible) stage

  • Severe cell death and organ failure; the patient does not respond to fluids or vasopressors.
  • Assessment findings – profound hypotension, bradycardia or serious arrhythmias, anuria, unresponsiveness or coma, severe acidosis, bleeding due to DIC, multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS) – usually ending in death.

Summary | Stage | BP | Pulse | Urine | Mental state | |---|---|---|---|---| | Initial | Normal | Normal/slightly high | Normal | Normal | | Compensatory | Normal/slightly low | Raised | Reduced | Anxious, restless | | Progressive | Low | Rapid, weak | Oliguria | Confused, lethargic | | Refractory | Very low | Slow/irregular | Anuria | Unconscious |

Nursing responsibilities

  • Recognise early signs – tachycardia, restlessness, falling urine output and narrow pulse pressure – rather than waiting for a fall in BP.
  • Monitor vital signs, SpO₂, urine output hourly, capillary refill, mental status and lactate; use early warning scores.
  • Start oxygen and IV access, and inform the doctor at once; assist in fluid resuscitation and drug therapy; record everything.

Nursing importance The compensatory stage is the "golden window" in which nurses can detect shock and start treatment before irreversible organ damage.

Conclusion Shock progresses from silent cellular changes to compensation, decompensation and finally irreversible organ failure; early recognition and treatment stop this progression.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Fluid and Electrolyte Imbalance, Shock and Pain
question: Explain the clinical features and emergency management of anaphylactic shock.
answer_html:
Definition Anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening, generalised hypersensitivity reaction that develops rapidly, with airway, breathing or circulation problems, usually with skin and mucosal changes. When it causes hypotension and poor perfusion it is called anaphylactic shock – a type of distributive shock. It is a type I (IgE-mediated) reaction in which mast cells release histamine and other mediators, causing vasodilatation, capillary leakage and bronchospasm.

1. Common causes (triggers)

  • Drugs – penicillins, cephalosporins, NSAIDs, IV contrast media, anaesthetic drugs and muscle relaxants, anti-snake venom, anti-rabies serum, iron injections, some vaccines (rare).
  • Foods – peanuts, shellfish, eggs, milk.
  • Insect stings – bees, wasps, hornets.
  • Latex, blood transfusion.

2. Clinical features (usually within minutes)

  • Skin – itching, flushing, urticaria (hives), angioedema of lips, tongue and eyelids.
  • Airway and breathing – hoarseness, throat tightness, stridor, wheeze, breathlessness, cyanosis.
  • Circulation – tachycardia, hypotension, dizziness, fainting, collapse, cardiac arrest.
  • GI – nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, diarrhoea.
  • Feeling of impending doom, anxiety.

3. Emergency management

  1. Stop the trigger immediately – stop the injection or infusion (keep the line open with saline).
  2. Call for help; assess airway, breathing and circulation.
  3. Position – lie flat with legs raised; if breathless, allow to sit up; pregnant women on the left side.
  4. Adrenaline intramuscular – the first and most important drug: 0.5 mg (0.5 ml of 1:1000 adrenaline) in adults, into the anterolateral thigh; children – 0.3 mg (6–12 years), 0.15 mg (under 6 years) or 0.01 mg/kg; repeat every 5 minutes if there is no improvement.
  5. High-flow oxygen (10–15 L/min).
  6. IV fluids – rapid bolus of crystalloid (500–1000 ml in adults, 10–20 ml/kg in children) for hypotension.
  7. Additional drugs as ordered – salbutamol nebulisation for wheeze; antihistamine (chlorpheniramine) for skin symptoms; corticosteroid (hydrocortisone) in some cases; IV adrenaline infusion by the doctor for refractory shock.
  8. CPR if cardiac arrest occurs.
  9. Observe for at least 6–12 hours (longer for severe reactions) because of the risk of a biphasic (second) reaction.

4. Nursing responsibilities and prevention

  • Take a careful allergy history before giving any drug; mark allergies clearly on the file and use an allergy band.
  • Keep an anaphylaxis (emergency) kit with adrenaline in every injection room, OT, ward and vaccination site.
  • Observe patients for at least 15–30 minutes after injections, vaccines, ASV and contrast media.
  • Document the reaction, the drug and the treatment; report as an adverse drug reaction (PvPI) or AEFI.
  • Teach the patient to avoid the trigger, carry an allergy card and, where prescribed, an adrenaline auto-injector.

Nursing importance Anaphylaxis can kill within minutes; a nurse who recognises it quickly and gives IM adrenaline without delay saves lives.

Conclusion Anaphylactic shock is a rapid, IgE-mediated reaction with skin, airway and circulatory involvement; stopping the trigger and giving IM adrenaline, oxygen and fluids immediately are the keys to survival.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Fluid and Electrolyte Imbalance, Shock and Pain
question: Explain the management of septic shock with reference to the sepsis hour-1 bundle and the nurse's role.
answer_html:
Definitions

  • Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection.
  • Septic shock is sepsis in which, despite adequate fluid resuscitation, vasopressors are needed to keep the mean arterial pressure (MAP) at 65 mmHg or above and the serum lactate remains above 2 mmol/L. It carries a high death rate.
  • Common sources in Indian hospitals – pneumonia, urinary tract infection, intra-abdominal infection, skin and soft-tissue infection, infected IV lines, and infections such as malaria and typhoid complications.

1. Early recognition

  • Warning signs – fever or hypothermia, respiratory rate 22/min or more, altered mental state, systolic BP 100 mmHg or less, tachycardia, warm flushed skin early (cold later), low urine output, mottled skin.
  • Use early warning scores (NEWS) and sepsis screening tools in wards.

2. Sepsis hour-1 bundle (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) – started within one hour of recognition

  1. Measure lactate; re-measure if the initial value is above 2 mmol/L.
  2. Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics (two sets from different sites).
  3. Give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics without delay.
  4. Give 30 ml/kg crystalloid rapidly for hypotension or lactate of 4 mmol/L or more, with reassessment of the response.
  5. Start vasopressors – noradrenaline is the first choice – if hypotension persists during or after fluids, to keep MAP at 65 mmHg or above.

3. Other management

  • Source control – drain abscesses, remove infected catheters and lines, surgery for perforation.
  • Oxygen, and ventilatory support if needed.
  • Hydrocortisone for shock not responding to vasopressors, as ordered.
  • Blood glucose control (about 140–180 mg/dl), DVT prophylaxis, stress ulcer prophylaxis, early nutrition.
  • Review and narrow antibiotics once culture reports arrive (antimicrobial stewardship).

4. Nurse's role

  • Recognise and escalate early; start the bundle as per protocol; document the time of each element (cultures, antibiotic, fluids).
  • Collect blood cultures aseptically before the first antibiotic dose; give antibiotics on time.
  • Give fluid boluses and watch for fluid overload (crepitations, falling SpO₂).
  • Administer vasopressors through a central line (or a large, well-secured peripheral vein for a short time), using an infusion pump, and watch for extravasation.
  • Monitor MAP, pulse, respiration, SpO₂, temperature, mental status, hourly urine output, capillary refill, lactate and blood sugar.
  • Strict infection prevention – hand hygiene, line and catheter bundles.
  • Comfort, skin care, nutrition and family support.

Nursing importance Every hour of delay in antibiotics increases deaths in septic shock; nurses who screen, escalate and start the bundle make the biggest difference.

Conclusion Septic shock needs early recognition and the hour-1 bundle – lactate, cultures, antibiotics, fluids and vasopressors – along with source control and close nursing monitoring.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Fluid and Electrolyte Imbalance, Shock and Pain
question: Explain the causes, clinical features and management of hypocalcaemia and hypercalcaemia.
answer_html:
Introduction Calcium is needed for bones and teeth, nerve conduction, muscle contraction, heart rhythm and blood clotting. Normal total serum calcium is 8.5–10.5 mg/dl (ionised calcium about 4.5–5.3 mg/dl). Calcium is regulated by parathyroid hormone (PTH), vitamin D and calcitonin.

1. Hypocalcaemia (serum calcium below 8.5 mg/dl) Causes

  • Hypoparathyroidism – especially after thyroidectomy or parathyroidectomy.
  • Vitamin D deficiency (very common in India), chronic kidney disease.
  • Acute pancreatitis, massive transfusion of citrated blood, low magnesium, alkalosis (reduces ionised calcium).
  • Low albumin (total calcium appears low).

Clinical features

  • Tingling and numbness around the mouth and in fingers and toes; muscle cramps.
  • Tetany – carpopedal spasm; positive Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs.
  • Laryngospasm (stridor), bronchospasm, seizures.
  • Prolonged QT interval, arrhythmias, hypotension.

Management

  • Acute symptomatic – 10% calcium gluconate 10–20 ml IV slowly over about 10 minutes, followed by an infusion as ordered, with ECG monitoring; prevent extravasation (tissue necrosis); never mix with sodium bicarbonate; caution in patients on digoxin.
  • Chronic – oral calcium carbonate and vitamin D (calcitriol); correct magnesium.
  • Nursing – seizure precautions; keep a tracheostomy set and calcium gluconate at the bedside after thyroidectomy; watch for tingling and stridor; teach a calcium-rich diet (milk, curd, ragi, sesame, green leafy vegetables).

2. Hypercalcaemia (serum calcium above 10.5 mg/dl) Causes

  • Primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy (bone metastases, multiple myeloma) – the two main causes.
  • Prolonged immobilisation, excess vitamin D or calcium intake, thiazide diuretics, sarcoidosis.

Clinical features – "bones, stones, groans, moans"

  • Bones – bone pain, fractures.
  • Stones – kidney stones, polyuria, thirst, dehydration.
  • Groans – abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, constipation, peptic ulcer, pancreatitis.
  • Moans – fatigue, depression, confusion, coma.
  • Short QT interval, arrhythmias; increased sensitivity to digoxin.

Management

  • IV normal saline hydration to promote calcium excretion; loop diuretic (furosemide) after rehydration, as ordered.
  • Bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid, pamidronate), calcitonin, corticosteroids (myeloma, vitamin D toxicity); dialysis in severe cases; treat the cause (parathyroidectomy, cancer therapy).
  • Nursing – encourage 2–3 litres of fluid daily (unless restricted) and mobility; strain urine for stones if ordered; monitor ECG, intake–output and mental status; avoid thiazides and calcium supplements; safety measures for confused patients.

Nursing importance Nurses caring for post-thyroidectomy, cancer and immobilised patients must watch for early signs of calcium imbalance, which can cause laryngospasm, seizures or arrhythmias.

Conclusion Hypocalcaemia causes neuromuscular excitability and tetany, while hypercalcaemia causes "bones, stones, groans and moans"; both need treatment of the cause and careful monitoring.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Fluid and Electrolyte Imbalance, Shock and Pain
question: Explain the causes, clinical features and nursing management of acid–base imbalances.
answer_html:
Introduction The body keeps the blood pH between 7.35 and 7.45 using buffers, lungs (CO₂) and kidneys (HCO₃⁻). Normal PaCO₂ is 35–45 mmHg and HCO₃⁻ 22–26 mEq/L. A pH below 7.35 is acidosis and above 7.45 is alkalosis; the cause may be respiratory (CO₂) or metabolic (HCO₃⁻).

1. Respiratory acidosis (pH low, PaCO₂ high)

  • Causes – hypoventilation: COPD, severe asthma, pneumonia, opioid or sedative overdose, chest injury, Guillain–Barré syndrome, obesity hypoventilation.
  • Features – headache, drowsiness, confusion, flushed warm skin, tachycardia, CO₂ narcosis and coma.
  • Management – improve ventilation: clear the airway, upright position, deep breathing and coughing, bronchodilators; controlled oxygen in COPD (target SpO₂ 88–92%); non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP) or mechanical ventilation; naloxone for opioid overdose as ordered.

2. Respiratory alkalosis (pH high, PaCO₂ low)

  • Causes – hyperventilation: anxiety and panic, pain, fever, hypoxia, early salicylate poisoning, high altitude, excessive mechanical ventilation.
  • Features – light-headedness, tingling of fingers and around the mouth, carpopedal spasm (low ionised calcium), palpitations.
  • Management – treat the cause; calm the patient and coach slow breathing; relieve pain and fever; adjust ventilator settings as ordered.

3. Metabolic acidosis (pH low, HCO₃⁻ low)

  • Causes – diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis (shock, sepsis), kidney failure, severe diarrhoea (loss of bicarbonate), poisoning (methanol, salicylates).
  • Features – Kussmaul breathing (deep, rapid – the lungs try to blow off CO₂), headache, confusion, nausea, vomiting, hypotension, arrhythmias; often hyperkalaemia.
  • Management – treat the cause: insulin and fluids in DKA, fluids and oxygen in shock, dialysis in kidney failure; sodium bicarbonate only in severe acidosis as ordered; monitor potassium (it falls as acidosis is corrected).

4. Metabolic alkalosis (pH high, HCO₃⁻ high)

  • Causes – vomiting and NG suction (loss of HCl), diuretics, hypokalaemia, excessive antacid or bicarbonate intake.
  • Features – slow shallow breathing (compensation), confusion, muscle twitching, tetany, arrhythmias (with hypokalaemia).
  • Management – normal saline with potassium chloride as ordered, antiemetics, proton-pump inhibitors during prolonged NG suction, stop excess alkali; replace NG losses.

5. Nursing management (common to all)

  • Recognise high-risk patients and early signs; monitor ABG, electrolytes (especially potassium), respiratory rate and pattern, SpO₂, mental status, ECG and intake–output.
  • Collect ABG samples correctly (heparinised syringe, no air bubbles, on ice if delayed, note oxygen therapy).
  • Maintain airway and correct positioning; give oxygen and drugs as prescribed.
  • Ensure safety (side rails, seizure precautions) in confused patients.
  • Explain care to the patient and family; document trends.

Nursing importance Acid–base imbalances are usually signs of a serious underlying illness; correcting the cause, rather than only the numbers, is the key nursing principle.

Conclusion Respiratory imbalances are corrected by improving ventilation, and metabolic imbalances by treating the cause (DKA, shock, vomiting, kidney failure), with close ABG and electrolyte monitoring.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Fluid and Electrolyte Imbalance, Shock and Pain
question: Explain the management of acute post-operative pain, including patient-controlled analgesia and epidural analgesia.
answer_html:
Introduction Acute post-operative pain is pain caused by surgical tissue injury; it is usually most severe in the first 24–72 hours. Poorly controlled pain is not only cruel but also dangerous – it slows recovery and can lead to chronic post-surgical pain.

1. Harmful effects of unrelieved pain

  • Shallow breathing and poor coughing → atelectasis and pneumonia.
  • Immobility → DVT, pressure ulcers, ileus.
  • Tachycardia and hypertension → myocardial ischaemia in heart patients.
  • Stress hormones → hyperglycaemia, poor wound healing, low immunity.
  • Anxiety, insomnia, delirium, longer hospital stay and chronic pain.

2. Principles of post-operative pain management

  • Assess regularly – pain is the "fifth vital sign"; use the 0–10 numerical rating scale or the Wong–Baker FACES scale; assess at rest and on movement and coughing.
  • Prevent rather than chase pain – give analgesics around the clock in the first 48–72 hours, not only on demand.
  • Multimodal (balanced) analgesia – combine drugs acting at different sites to get better relief with fewer side effects:
    • Paracetamol (oral/IV) regularly;
    • NSAIDs (diclofenac, ketorolac) if there is no contraindication (bleeding, kidney disease, peptic ulcer);
    • Opioids (morphine, tramadol, fentanyl) for moderate to severe pain;
    • Local and regional techniques – wound infiltration, nerve blocks, epidural analgesia.
  • Reassess after giving analgesia – about 30 minutes after IV and 60 minutes after oral drugs – and document.

3. Patient-controlled analgesia (PCA)

  • A programmed infusion pump allows the patient to press a button and receive a small preset bolus dose of opioid (for example, morphine 1 mg) IV.
  • Safety settings – lockout interval (for example, 5–10 minutes, during which further presses give no drug) and a maximum dose per hour or 4 hours.
  • Advantages – quick relief, patient feels in control, steady drug levels, less total opioid.
  • Nursing care – teach the patient before surgery; only the patient presses the button (no "PCA by proxy" by relatives); monitor respiratory rate, SpO₂ and sedation score hourly at first; keep naloxone ready; check the pump settings, syringe and line; record doses used.

4. Epidural analgesia

  • A catheter in the epidural space delivers a local anaesthetic, often with an opioid, as a continuous infusion or patient-controlled boluses – excellent for abdominal, thoracic and lower-limb surgery.
  • Nursing care – monitor BP (hypotension), respiration and sedation, sensory level and leg movement; check the catheter site for leakage and infection; label the line clearly as "epidural"; watch for urinary retention, itching and nausea; report severe back pain or new leg weakness (possible epidural haematoma or abscess); remove the catheter as per protocol in relation to anticoagulant doses.

5. Opioid side effects and nursing actions

  • Respiratory depression and over-sedation – stop the opioid, stimulate, oxygen, naloxone as ordered.
  • Nausea and vomiting – antiemetics; constipation – fluids, fibre, laxatives; itching; urinary retention.

6. Non-pharmacological measures

  • Splinting the incision with a pillow during coughing and moving, comfortable positioning, cold packs where suitable, early mobilisation, relaxation and slow breathing, music and distraction, reassurance and adequate sleep.

Nursing importance Good pain control allows early breathing exercises, mobilisation and feeding, which prevent complications and shorten hospital stay.

Conclusion Post-operative pain is best managed by regular assessment and multimodal analgesia, using PCA and epidural techniques safely with close monitoring for opioid side effects.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Fluid and Electrolyte Imbalance, Shock and Pain
question: Enlist the types of shock with one example each.
answer_html:
Types of shock

  1. Hypovolaemic shock – loss of blood or fluid: haemorrhage, severe diarrhoea (cholera), burns.
  2. Cardiogenic shock – failure of the heart as a pump: acute myocardial infarction, severe arrhythmia.
  3. Distributive (vasogenic) shock – abnormal vasodilatation:
    • Septic shock – severe infection;
    • Anaphylactic shock – penicillin or insect-sting allergy;
    • Neurogenic shock – spinal cord injury.
  4. Obstructive shock – obstruction to blood flow: tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, massive pulmonary embolism. (Endocrine shock – Addisonian crisis – is sometimes added.)

Memory aid: shock may be due to an empty tank (hypovolaemic), a failing pump (cardiogenic), leaking or dilated pipes (distributive) or a blocked pipe (obstructive).

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Fluid and Electrolyte Imbalance, Shock and Pain
question: What are Chvostek's sign and Trousseau's sign?
answer_html:
Both are signs of latent tetany, seen in hypocalcaemia (for example, after thyroidectomy with parathyroid damage), low magnesium and alkalosis.

  1. Chvostek's sign – tapping the facial nerve in front of the ear (below the zygomatic arch) causes twitching of the upper lip and facial muscles on the same side.
  2. Trousseau's sign – inflating a BP cuff on the arm above the systolic pressure for 3 minutes produces carpal spasm: flexion of the wrist and knuckle joints, extension of the fingers and adduction of the thumb ("main d'accoucheur", obstetrician's hand). Trousseau's sign is more specific than Chvostek's sign.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Fluid and Electrolyte Imbalance, Shock and Pain
question: What is pre-emptive analgesia?
answer_html:
Pre-emptive analgesia is the administration of analgesia before the painful stimulus (before the surgical incision) to prevent the pain pathways from becoming over-sensitive (central sensitisation or "wind-up").

Examples

  1. Local anaesthetic infiltration of the incision site before cutting.
  2. Epidural or nerve block started before surgery.
  3. Pre-operative oral paracetamol, NSAIDs or gabapentinoids as ordered.

Benefits – less post-operative pain, smaller doses of opioids (and so fewer opioid side effects), earlier breathing exercises and mobilisation, and possibly less chronic post-surgical pain. It works best when combined with continued multimodal analgesia after surgery.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Fluid and Electrolyte Imbalance, Shock and Pain
question: What is the shock index? State its significance.
answer_html:
Shock index (SI) = Heart rate ÷ Systolic blood pressure.

  • Normal: 0.5–0.7.
  • Above 0.9 (and especially 1.0 or more) suggests significant blood loss or shock, even when the BP still looks "normal".

Significance

  1. Simple bedside tool for early detection of hidden (compensated) shock in trauma, GI bleeding and sepsis.
  2. Used in obstetrics – an obstetric shock index above 0.9–1.0 in postpartum haemorrhage indicates the need for urgent resuscitation and referral.
  3. Helps in triage and in monitoring the response to fluids. Example: pulse 120/min, BP 100 mmHg systolic → SI = 1.2 (shock).

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Fluid and Electrolyte Imbalance, Shock and Pain
question: What is central venous pressure (CVP)? Give its normal value and significance.
answer_html:
Central venous pressure (CVP) is the pressure of blood in the superior vena cava/right atrium, measured through a central venous catheter. It reflects the right ventricular filling pressure (preload) and the patient's fluid status.

Normal value: about 2–8 mmHg (approximately 3–10 cm H₂O).

Significance

  • Low CVP – hypovolaemia (bleeding, dehydration) – needs fluids.
  • High CVP – fluid overload, right heart failure, cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax, pulmonary hypertension.
  • Measured with the patient supine, the transducer or zero point at the phlebostatic axis (4th intercostal space, mid-axillary line), reading at end-expiration; trends are more useful than a single value.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Respiratory Disorders
question: (a) Define pneumonia and classify it. (3 marks) (b) Explain the causes, clinical features and diagnostic evaluation of pneumonia. (4 marks) (c) Describe the medical and nursing management of a patient with pneumonia. (8 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Definition and classification (3 marks) Pneumonia is an acute inflammation of the lung parenchyma (alveoli and small airways), usually caused by infection, in which the alveoli fill with exudate and the lung becomes consolidated. It is a leading cause of death in children under five and in the elderly in India.

Classification

  1. According to the setting (most useful for treatment)
    • Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) – develops outside hospital or within 48 hours of admission.
    • Hospital-acquired (nosocomial) pneumonia (HAP) – develops 48 hours or more after admission.
    • Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) – develops 48 hours or more after endotracheal intubation.
    • Aspiration pneumonia – after inhaling gastric contents or oral secretions.
    • Pneumonia in the immunocompromised – HIV, cancer chemotherapy, transplant (Pneumocystis, fungi, CMV).
  2. According to anatomy – lobar pneumonia (whole lobe), bronchopneumonia (patchy, around bronchi), interstitial pneumonia.
  3. According to organism – bacterial (typical), atypical (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella), viral (influenza, SARS-CoV-2, RSV), fungal, parasitic.

(b) Causes, clinical features and diagnostic evaluation (4 marks) Causative organisms

  • CAP – Streptococcus pneumoniae (commonest), Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus aureus (after influenza), Mycoplasma, respiratory viruses.
  • HAP/VAP – Gram-negative bacteria (Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, E. coli) and MRSA – often multidrug-resistant.
  • Aspiration – mouth anaerobes.

Risk factors Extremes of age, smoking, alcoholism, malnutrition, COPD, diabetes, heart and kidney disease, HIV, immobility, reduced consciousness or impaired swallowing (stroke, sedation), NG tube feeding, recent surgery, mechanical ventilation and poor oral hygiene.

Clinical features

  • Sudden high fever with chills and rigors, malaise, body ache.
  • Cough – dry at first, then with purulent or rusty sputum (pneumococcal).
  • Pleuritic chest pain – sharp, worse on breathing and coughing.
  • Breathlessness, tachypnoea, tachycardia, use of accessory muscles, central cyanosis.
  • On examination – reduced chest movement, dull percussion, bronchial breath sounds, crackles (crepitations), increased vocal resonance over the affected area.
  • Elderly patients may show only confusion, falls, loss of appetite or low-grade fever.

Diagnostic evaluation

  • Chest X-ray – consolidation (lobar or patchy shadows), effusion.
  • Sputum – Gram stain and culture and sensitivity (before antibiotics); AFB and CBNAAT to exclude TB.
  • Blood – CBC (leucocytosis), blood culture, CRP/procalcitonin, urea and electrolytes, blood sugar; ABG and SpO₂.
  • Urinary antigen tests (pneumococcus, Legionella); RT-PCR for influenza and COVID-19 when indicated.
  • Severity assessment – CURB-65 (1 point each): Confusion, Urea above 7 mmol/L (BUN above 19 mg/dl), Respiratory rate 30/min or more, BP – systolic below 90 or diastolic 60 mmHg or less, age 65 years or more. Score 0–1: home treatment; 2: hospital admission; 3 or more: severe – consider ICU.

(c) Medical and nursing management (8 marks) 1. Medical management

  • Antibiotics – started early, according to the setting and local antibiogram, later adjusted to culture reports:
    • Mild CAP – oral amoxicillin or a macrolide (azithromycin), or doxycycline.
    • Hospitalised CAP – a β-lactam (amoxicillin-clavulanate or ceftriaxone) with a macrolide.
    • HAP/VAP – broad-spectrum anti-pseudomonal antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, carbapenems) ± MRSA cover, as per hospital policy.
    • Usual duration 5–7 days for uncomplicated pneumonia; longer for complications.
  • Oxygen therapy to keep SpO₂ at 94–98% (88–92% in COPD with CO₂ retention).
  • IV fluids for dehydration; antipyretics and analgesics (paracetamol).
  • Bronchodilator nebulisation if wheeze; chest physiotherapy.
  • Non-invasive or mechanical ventilation for respiratory failure.
  • Treatment of complications – pleural effusion, empyema (chest tube), lung abscess, sepsis and septic shock.

2. Nursing management – nursing diagnoses and interventions (i) Ineffective airway clearance related to excessive secretions and pain

  • Encourage deep breathing and coughing; teach splinting of the chest with a pillow.
  • Fluids 2–3 litres a day (unless restricted) to thin secretions; steam inhalation or nebulisation as ordered.
  • Chest physiotherapy, postural drainage and suctioning when the patient cannot cough effectively.
  • Change position every 2 hours; ambulate as tolerated.

(ii) Impaired gas exchange related to consolidation

  • Semi-Fowler's or high Fowler's position; oxygen as prescribed with humidification.
  • Monitor respiratory rate, SpO₂, colour, mental status and ABG; report increasing breathlessness, cyanosis or confusion.
  • Position with the good lung down in unilateral pneumonia (improves oxygenation), unless contraindicated.

(iii) Hyperthermia related to infection

  • Monitor temperature 4-hourly; tepid sponging, light clothing, antipyretics as ordered; change damp linen.

(iv) Acute pain (pleuritic chest pain)

  • Analgesics as ordered; supportive positioning; splinting during coughing.

(v) Risk for deficient fluid volume and imbalanced nutrition

  • Intake–output chart; oral and IV fluids; small, frequent, high-calorie, high-protein meals; oral care before meals.

(vi) Activity intolerance and fatigue

  • Bed rest in the acute phase; plan care to allow rest; gradual increase in activity.

(vii) Risk for infection spread and complications

  • Hand hygiene, cough etiquette, safe sputum disposal; droplet precautions where needed (influenza, COVID-19).
  • Watch for signs of complications – persistent fever, increasing pleuritic pain (effusion/empyema), hypotension (septic shock), confusion, falling SpO₂.
  • Give antibiotics on time and complete the full course.

(viii) Deficient knowledge

  • Teach about medicines, rest, nutrition, fluids, smoking cessation and follow-up X-ray.

3. Prevention of pneumonia

  • Vaccination – pneumococcal vaccine (PCV in the Universal Immunisation Programme for infants; PCV/PPSV for elderly and high-risk adults) and annual influenza vaccine.
  • Stop smoking; reduce indoor air pollution (clean cooking fuel – LPG under Ujjwala Yojana).
  • Prevention of hospital pneumonia – hand hygiene, head-end elevation 30–45°, oral care, early mobilisation, aspiration precautions during feeding, and the VAP bundle for ventilated patients (head elevation, daily sedation interruption and assessment for extubation, oral care, subglottic suction, DVT and stress ulcer prophylaxis).
  • Early treatment of upper respiratory infections; good nutrition (Poshan Abhiyaan for children).

4. Complications to watch for

  • Pleural effusion and empyema – persistent fever and pleuritic pain, dull percussion.
  • Lung abscess – foul-smelling sputum, cavity on X-ray.
  • Sepsis and septic shock – hypotension, confusion, low urine output.
  • Respiratory failure and ARDS – rising respiratory rate, falling SpO₂ despite oxygen.
  • Spread of infection – meningitis, endocarditis, arthritis (pneumococcal); delirium and falls in the elderly.

5. Discharge teaching

  • Complete the full course of antibiotics even if feeling well.
  • Rest for one to two weeks and increase activity gradually; continue deep breathing exercises.
  • Eat a nourishing diet and drink plenty of fluids; stop smoking and avoid alcohol.
  • Attend follow-up; a repeat chest X-ray after about 6 weeks is advised in smokers and older adults to make sure the shadow has cleared (to exclude an underlying cancer).
  • Return immediately if fever returns, breathlessness increases, chest pain worsens or blood appears in sputum.
  • Take pneumococcal and influenza vaccines as advised.

Nursing importance Pneumonia kills mainly through hypoxia and sepsis; regular respiratory assessment, oxygen, airway clearance, timely antibiotics and prevention measures by nurses greatly reduce deaths, especially in the elderly and children.

Conclusion Pneumonia is an acute infection of the lung parenchyma classified mainly by setting; early diagnosis, correct antibiotics, oxygen, airway clearance and good nursing care lead to recovery, while vaccination and infection control prevent it.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Respiratory Disorders
question: (a) Define bronchial asthma and list its triggers. (3 marks) (b) Explain its pathophysiology and clinical features. (4 marks) (c) Describe the management of acute severe asthma and the long-term nursing management with patient education. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Airway changes in bronchial asthma
labels: normal bronchiole compared with asthmatic bronchiole showing bronchospasm of smooth muscle
inflammatory cells and thick mucus plug narrowing the lumen

answer_html:
(a) Definition and triggers (3 marks) Bronchial asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease of the airways characterised by airway hyper-responsiveness and reversible (variable) airflow obstruction, causing recurrent episodes of wheeze, breathlessness, chest tightness and cough, especially at night and early morning. It affects all ages; in India it is common in children and is worsened by air pollution.

Types

  • Extrinsic (allergic, atopic) – starts in childhood, linked to allergens, eczema and allergic rhinitis; raised IgE.
  • Intrinsic (non-allergic) – usually starts in adults; triggered by infections, exercise, drugs or stress.
  • Others – exercise-induced, occupational, aspirin-induced, cough-variant asthma.

Triggers

  1. Allergens – house dust mite, pollen, mould, animal dander, cockroaches.
  2. Air pollution and irritants – smoke (tobacco, biomass chulha, mosquito coils, incense), vehicle exhaust, crop-burning smoke, festival firecrackers, strong perfumes, dust.
  3. Respiratory infections – common cold, influenza.
  4. Exercise, especially in cold dry air; cold weather and sudden temperature changes.
  5. Drugs – aspirin and NSAIDs, β-blockers (propranolol, even eye drops).
  6. Emotional stress, laughing or crying.
  7. Occupational agents – flour, wood dust, chemicals, cotton dust.
  8. Gastro-oesophageal reflux, some foods and preservatives (sulphites).

(b) Pathophysiology and clinical features (4 marks) Pathophysiology

  • A trigger activates mast cells, eosinophils and T-lymphocytes in the sensitive airway.
  • Release of histamine, leukotrienes and prostaglandins causes:
    1. Bronchospasm – contraction of bronchial smooth muscle.
    2. Mucosal oedema and inflammation.
    3. Excessive thick mucus forming plugs.
  • The airway lumen narrows → increased airway resistance, air trapping and hyperinflation, ventilation–perfusion mismatch → hypoxaemia.
  • Repeated inflammation leads to airway remodelling (thickened walls) and less reversible obstruction.

Clinical features

  • Episodic breathlessness, wheezing (mostly expiratory), chest tightness and cough (often at night or early morning); symptoms vary over time.
  • During an attack – tachypnoea, tachycardia, prolonged expiration, use of accessory muscles, patient sits upright leaning forward, anxiety.
  • Auscultation – bilateral expiratory wheeze (rhonchi).
  • Peak expiratory flow (PEF) is reduced and improves after a bronchodilator; spirometry shows reduced FEV₁/FVC with reversibility (12% or more and 200 ml increase in FEV₁).
  • Features of acute severe asthma – cannot complete sentences in one breath, respiratory rate 25/min or more, pulse 110/min or more, PEF 33–50% of best.
  • Life-threatening features – silent chest, cyanosis, SpO₂ below 92%, PEF below 33%, exhaustion, confusion, bradycardia, hypotension; a normal or rising PaCO₂ is a danger sign (fatigue).

(c) Management (8 marks) 1. Management of acute severe asthma (status asthmaticus) – an emergency

  1. Position – sit the patient upright, supported, leaning slightly forward; stay with the patient and reassure.
  2. Oxygen – to maintain SpO₂ about 93–95%.
  3. Inhaled short-acting β₂-agonist – salbutamol nebulisation 2.5–5 mg (oxygen-driven), repeated every 20 minutes in the first hour or given continuously, as ordered; or salbutamol MDI with spacer.
  4. Ipratropium bromide nebulisation (0.5 mg) added in severe attacks.
  5. Systemic corticosteroids early – oral prednisolone 40–50 mg or IV hydrocortisone 100 mg 6-hourly, as ordered.
  6. IV magnesium sulphate 2 g over 20 minutes for severe attacks not responding to initial treatment.
  7. IV fluids (patients are often dehydrated), correction of potassium (salbutamol and steroids lower it).
  8. Avoid sedatives (they depress breathing).
  9. Monitoring – respiratory rate, pulse, BP, SpO₂, PEF before and 15–30 minutes after nebulisation, ability to speak, level of consciousness, ABG; chest X-ray to exclude pneumothorax.
  10. Escalation – transfer to ICU for intubation and mechanical ventilation if there is exhaustion, confusion, rising PaCO₂ or respiratory arrest.
  11. Before discharge – PEF above 75% of best, stable on oral treatment and inhaler, written action plan given and inhaler technique checked.

2. Long-term management (stepwise approach – GINA)

  • Controller (preventer) medicines – inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) such as budesonide, beclomethasone, fluticasone, used every day to reduce airway inflammation; combined with a long-acting β₂-agonist (formoterol) when needed; leukotriene antagonists (montelukast); biologics for severe asthma.
  • Reliever medicines – for quick relief during symptoms; current guidelines prefer ICS–formoterol as reliever (or salbutamol in some settings). Inhalers are preferred to tablets.
  • Treatment is stepped up when asthma is uncontrolled and stepped down when well controlled for three months.

3. Nursing management and patient education

  • Teach the difference between controller and reliever medicines; explain that ICS must be used daily even when well, and that rinsing the mouth after ICS prevents oral thrush and hoarseness.
  • Check inhaler technique at every visit (MDI with spacer, dry powder inhaler) – poor technique is a common cause of poor control.
  • Identify and avoid triggers – no smoking at home, use LPG instead of chulha, damp-dust instead of sweeping, wash bed linen in hot water and sun-dry, control cockroaches, avoid outdoor exercise on high-pollution days (check AQI), wear a mask in dust, avoid firecracker smoke.
  • Peak flow monitoring and a written asthma action plan:
    • Green zone (PEF above 80% of best) – continue usual treatment.
    • Yellow zone (50–80%) – use reliever, increase treatment as per plan, contact the doctor.
    • Red zone (below 50%) – take reliever and go to hospital immediately.
  • Breathing exercises and yoga (pranayama) as supportive therapy; regular exercise with pre-exercise reliever if needed.
  • Annual influenza vaccination; treat allergic rhinitis and reflux.
  • Tell the patient to avoid aspirin, NSAIDs and β-blockers unless approved.
  • Psychological support – reduce anxiety and correct myths (fear of "addiction" to inhalers or steroids is common in India).
  • Special groups – in pregnancy, continue asthma medicines (uncontrolled asthma is more dangerous than the drugs); school teachers should know the child's action plan.
  • Regular follow-up to review symptoms, PEF and medicines.

4. Assessing asthma control (in the last 4 weeks) Ask four questions: (1) daytime symptoms more than twice a week? (2) any night waking due to asthma? (3) reliever needed more than twice a week? (4) any limitation of activity? None – well controlled; 1–2 – partly controlled; 3–4 – uncontrolled (treatment needs review, after checking inhaler technique and adherence).

5. Correcting common myths

  • "Inhalers are addictive" or "inhalers are the last stage" – false; inhalers are the first, safest and most effective treatment because the drug goes directly to the airways.
  • "Steroid inhalers are dangerous" – inhaled doses are in micrograms, far smaller than tablets in milligrams, and side effects are minimal.
  • "Asthma is contagious" – false; it cannot spread from person to person.
  • "Children with asthma should not play sports" – false; with good control and a pre-exercise reliever when needed, they can take part fully in games and yoga.
  • "Stop medicines when you feel well" – false; controllers must be continued and reduced only by the doctor.

Nursing importance Most asthma deaths are preventable; nurses play a key role by managing acute attacks quickly, recognising life-threatening signs and teaching inhaler technique, trigger control and the action plan.

Conclusion Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disease with reversible bronchospasm; acute severe attacks need oxygen, repeated bronchodilators and early steroids, while long-term control depends on daily controllers, trigger avoidance and good self-management education.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Respiratory Disorders
question: (a) Classify chest injuries. (3 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features and emergency management of tension pneumothorax, haemothorax and flail chest. (8 marks) (c) Describe the nursing care of a patient with chest injury. (4 marks)

diagram.caption: Flail chest with paradoxical movement
labels: multiple adjacent ribs fractured in two places; flail segment moving inward on inspiration and outward on expiration; underlying lung contusion

answer_html:
Introduction Chest (thoracic) injuries cause about a quarter of trauma deaths; most result from road traffic accidents, falls, assaults and stab wounds. Many are life-threatening within minutes (airway obstruction, tension pneumothorax, massive haemothorax, cardiac tamponade), but most can be managed with simple measures such as oxygen, decompression and a chest tube.

(a) Classification (3 marks) 1. According to mechanism

  • Blunt (non-penetrating) – road accidents, falls, crush injuries, blows.
  • Penetrating – stab wounds, gunshot wounds, sharp objects.

2. According to the structure injured

  • Chest wall – rib fractures, flail chest, sternal fracture, soft-tissue injury.
  • Pleura – pneumothorax (simple, open/sucking, tension), haemothorax, haemopneumothorax.
  • Lungs – pulmonary contusion, laceration.
  • Heart and great vessels – cardiac contusion, cardiac tamponade, aortic rupture.
  • Others – diaphragmatic rupture, tracheobronchial and oesophageal injuries, traumatic asphyxia, subcutaneous emphysema.

(b) Clinical features and emergency management (8 marks) 1. Tension pneumothorax

  • What happens – air enters the pleural space with each breath through a one-way valve in the lung or chest wall but cannot escape. Pressure rises, the lung collapses, the mediastinum shifts to the opposite side, the vena cava is kinked and venous return falls → obstructive shock. It can kill within minutes.
  • Clinical features
    • Severe respiratory distress, air hunger, anxiety, cyanosis.
    • Tachycardia, hypotension, distended neck veins.
    • Absent breath sounds and hyper-resonance on the affected side.
    • Tracheal deviation away from the affected side (a late sign).
  • Emergency management
    • It is a clinical diagnosis – treat immediately without waiting for an X-ray.
    • High-flow oxygen; call for help.
    • Needle decompression by the doctor – a large-bore cannula (14 G) inserted into the pleural space (2nd intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line, or 4th/5th space just anterior to the mid-axillary line in adults); a hiss of air confirms the diagnosis.
    • Followed by an intercostal chest drain (ICD) in the 5th intercostal space anterior to the mid-axillary line ("safe triangle") connected to an underwater seal.
  • Open pneumothorax (sucking chest wound) – cover the wound with a sterile occlusive dressing taped on three sides (or a vented chest seal) so that air can escape but not enter; then ICD and surgical closure.

2. Haemothorax

  • What happens – blood collects in the pleural space from injured lung, intercostal or internal mammary vessels or the heart and great vessels. Massive haemothorax is more than 1500 ml of blood (about one-third of the blood volume).
  • Clinical features
    • Signs of hypovolaemic shock – tachycardia, hypotension, pallor, cold clammy skin.
    • Breathlessness, dull percussion and reduced or absent breath sounds on the affected side.
    • Chest X-ray – fluid level or white-out; ultrasound (e-FAST) detects blood quickly.
  • Emergency management
    • Oxygen, two large-bore IV lines, blood for grouping and cross-matching; fluid and blood resuscitation.
    • Large-bore ICD to drain blood and re-expand the lung; record the initial drainage.
    • Thoracotomy if the initial drainage is 1500 ml or more, or continuing drainage is about 200 ml/hour for 2–4 hours, or the patient remains unstable.
    • Autotransfusion of drained blood where facilities exist.

3. Flail chest

  • What happens – two or more adjacent ribs are fractured in two or more places, producing a free-floating segment of chest wall that moves paradoxically – inward during inspiration and outward during expiration. The underlying pulmonary contusion is the main cause of hypoxia.
  • Clinical features
    • Severe chest pain, breathlessness, rapid shallow breathing, cyanosis.
    • Paradoxical movement of the flail segment; crepitus of fractured ribs; bruising.
    • Hypoxaemia and hypercapnia on ABG; may develop respiratory failure.
  • Emergency management
    • Oxygen; adequate analgesia (IV opioids, intercostal nerve block or thoracic epidural) so that the patient can breathe deeply and cough.
    • Careful fluid management (to avoid worsening lung contusion).
    • Chest physiotherapy, incentive spirometry, non-invasive ventilation.
    • Intubation and mechanical ventilation (internal pneumatic stabilisation) for respiratory failure; surgical rib fixation in selected patients.
    • Do not strap the chest tightly – it restricts breathing and causes atelectasis.

4. Simple rib fractures (brief)

  • Pain on breathing and coughing, local tenderness; risk of pneumonia, especially in the elderly. Treat with analgesics, breathing exercises and early mobilisation; avoid chest strapping.

(c) Nursing care of a patient with chest injury (4 marks)

  1. Primary survey (ABCDE) – ensure a clear airway, give high-flow oxygen, assess breathing (rate, depth, symmetry, paradoxical movement, breath sounds), circulation (pulse, BP, bleeding) and level of consciousness; protect the cervical spine if indicated.
  2. Positioning – semi-Fowler's or upright position if the spine is not injured and BP allows; in unilateral injury, positioning on the injured side may help splint the chest, as ordered.
  3. Continuous monitoring – respiratory rate, SpO₂, pulse, BP, ECG, urine output, ABG; watch for signs of tension pneumothorax, increasing haemothorax and cardiac tamponade (Beck's triad – hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds).
  4. Pain relief – give analgesics on time; support the chest with a pillow during coughing; assist with epidural or nerve-block care.
  5. Chest drain care – keep the drainage bottle below chest level, maintain the water seal, check for swinging (tidaling) and bubbling, record the amount and colour of drainage hourly in haemothorax; never clamp the tube routinely; keep two artery forceps and a sterile dressing at the bedside; watch for subcutaneous emphysema.
  6. Respiratory care – deep breathing, coughing, incentive spirometry, chest physiotherapy and early ambulation to prevent atelectasis and pneumonia.
  7. Fluid and nutrition – maintain IV fluids and blood as ordered; intake–output chart; nutritious diet once oral intake starts.
  8. Infection prevention – aseptic care of wounds and drain sites; tetanus prophylaxis for open wounds.
  9. Psychological support – reassure the frightened, breathless patient; explain procedures; keep the family informed.
  10. Health education – use of seat belts and helmets, safe driving, workplace safety, and follow-up for lung function after recovery.

Other life-threatening chest injuries (brief)

  • Cardiac tamponade – blood in the pericardial sac after penetrating injury; Beck's triad (hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds); needs urgent pericardiocentesis or surgery.
  • Pulmonary contusion – bruising of lung tissue causing hypoxia over 24–48 hours; oxygen, careful fluids, ventilation if needed.
  • Traumatic aortic rupture – after rapid deceleration (high-speed accidents); widened mediastinum on X-ray; urgent surgery or stent.
  • Diaphragmatic rupture – abdominal organs move into the chest; bowel sounds heard in the chest; surgical repair.
  • Traumatic asphyxia – severe crushing of the chest causing bluish face and neck, swollen face and subconjunctival haemorrhages; oxygen and supportive care.
  • Subcutaneous emphysema – air under the skin of the chest and neck with a crackling feel (crepitus); it points to an underlying pneumothorax or airway injury that must be looked for and treated.

Nursing importance Rapid recognition of tension pneumothorax, massive haemothorax and flail chest, followed by immediate oxygen, decompression, chest drainage and pain relief, prevents many deaths after chest trauma.

Conclusion Chest injuries may be blunt or penetrating and involve the chest wall, pleura, lungs or heart; tension pneumothorax, haemothorax and flail chest are emergencies that need prompt treatment and skilled nursing care.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Respiratory Disorders
question: Explain the medical and nursing management of a patient with emphysema (COPD).
answer_html:
Introduction Emphysema is a form of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) in which the alveolar walls are destroyed and airspaces are permanently enlarged, causing loss of elastic recoil and air trapping. In India the main causes are tobacco smoking (including bidis) and indoor smoke from biomass fuels (chulhas). The disease cannot be cured, but good management relieves breathlessness and prevents exacerbations.

1. Medical management

  • Smoking cessation – the single most effective measure; counselling, nicotine replacement and the national quitline (1800-112-356).
  • Bronchodilators (inhaled) – short-acting salbutamol for relief; long-acting LAMA (tiotropium) and LABA (formoterol, salmeterol) for maintenance; inhaled corticosteroids for patients with frequent exacerbations.
  • Vaccination – annual influenza and pneumococcal vaccines.
  • Pulmonary rehabilitation – exercise training, breathing retraining, education and nutritional support.
  • Long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) – at least 15 hours a day when PaO₂ is 55 mmHg or less (SpO₂ 88% or less) at rest.
  • Surgery in selected patients – bullectomy, lung volume reduction surgery, lung transplantation.
  • Acute exacerbation – controlled oxygen (target SpO₂ 88–92%) by Venturi mask, nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone (about 40 mg for 5 days), antibiotics when sputum is purulent, and non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP) for hypercapnic respiratory failure.

2. Nursing management

  • Positioning – high Fowler's or tripod position (sitting, leaning forward with arms on a table) to ease breathing.
  • Breathing retraining – pursed-lip breathing and diaphragmatic (abdominal) breathing to reduce air trapping and slow the breathing rate.
  • Airway clearance – adequate fluids (if not restricted), huff coughing, chest physiotherapy; teach correct inhaler use with a spacer.
  • Oxygen safety – give only the prescribed flow (excess oxygen can raise CO₂ in some patients); no smoking or open flame near oxygen; humidify as needed.
  • Energy conservation – plan rest periods; sit while bathing and dressing; avoid hurrying; use simple aids.
  • Nutrition – small, frequent, high-calorie, high-protein meals; rest before meals; avoid gas-forming foods; oxygen during meals if prescribed; monitor weight (many patients are underweight).
  • Prevent infection – hand hygiene, avoid crowds during flu season, oral hygiene, early reporting of change in sputum colour.
  • Psychological support – breathlessness causes anxiety and depression; teach relaxation and involve the family.
  • Monitoring – respiratory rate, SpO₂, use of accessory muscles, ABG, signs of cor pulmonale (ankle oedema, raised JVP) and CO₂ narcosis (drowsiness, headache, flapping tremor).

3. Patient education

  • Recognise an exacerbation early – more breathlessness, more sputum or change to yellow-green, fever – and seek help.
  • Continue regular exercise (walking) within limits; continue pursed-lip breathing.
  • Avoid smoke, dust, firecrackers and cold air; use LPG for cooking.

Nursing importance Good nursing care – breathing exercises, correct inhaler and oxygen use, nutrition and education – improves quality of life and reduces hospital admissions in emphysema.

Conclusion Emphysema is managed by stopping smoke exposure, bronchodilators, vaccination, rehabilitation and oxygen when needed, supported by breathing retraining, energy conservation and nutrition.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Respiratory Disorders
question: Define acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Explain its causes, clinical features and management.
answer_html:
Definition Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a form of acute, diffuse, inflammatory lung injury leading to increased permeability of the alveolar–capillary membrane, non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema and severe hypoxaemia that does not respond to oxygen alone.

Berlin definition (2012)

  • Onset within one week of a known insult.
  • Bilateral opacities on chest X-ray or CT, not fully explained by effusions, collapse or nodules.
  • Respiratory failure not fully explained by heart failure or fluid overload.
  • PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio (with PEEP 5 cm H₂O or more): mild 201–300, moderate 101–200, severe 100 or less.

1. Causes

  • Direct lung injury – pneumonia (including COVID-19 and influenza), aspiration of gastric contents, near-drowning, inhalation of smoke or toxic gases, lung contusion.
  • Indirect injury – sepsis (commonest cause), severe trauma and fractures (fat embolism), massive blood transfusion, acute pancreatitis, burns, drug overdose, and tropical infections such as falciparum malaria, leptospirosis and dengue.

2. Pathophysiology (brief) Damage to the alveolar–capillary membrane → protein-rich fluid leaks into alveoli → loss of surfactant → alveolar collapse → stiff lungs, shunting and refractory hypoxaemia; later fibrosis may develop.

3. Clinical features

  • Develops within hours to days of the insult: severe breathlessness, tachypnoea, use of accessory muscles, cyanosis, tachycardia, restlessness and confusion.
  • Crackles on auscultation; low SpO₂ despite high-flow oxygen.
  • Chest X-ray – bilateral diffuse infiltrates ("white-out"); ABG – low PaO₂, initially low PaCO₂, later rising.

4. Management

  • Treat the cause – antibiotics and source control for sepsis, management of pancreatitis or trauma.
  • Oxygen; high-flow nasal oxygen or non-invasive ventilation in mild cases.
  • Mechanical ventilation with a lung-protective strategy – low tidal volume (about 6 ml/kg of predicted body weight), plateau pressure 30 cm H₂O or less, adequate PEEP to keep alveoli open.
  • Prone positioning for 12–16 hours a day in moderate to severe ARDS – improves oxygenation and survival.
  • Conservative (restrictive) fluid strategy once shock is controlled.
  • Sedation, muscle relaxants in severe early ARDS, ECMO for refractory cases.
  • Nutrition, DVT and stress ulcer prophylaxis, glucose control.

5. Nursing responsibilities

  • Continuous monitoring of SpO₂, ABG, respiratory rate, ventilator settings and pressures, haemodynamics and urine output.
  • VAP prevention bundle, closed suctioning, oral care and head-end elevation.
  • Safe prone positioning – enough trained staff, protect the eyes, face and pressure points, secure the endotracheal tube and lines.
  • Accurate fluid balance; sedation and pain assessment; skin care.
  • Communication and support for the family.

Nursing importance ARDS has a high mortality; skilled ICU nursing – ventilator care, prone positioning and prevention of infection – directly affects survival.

Conclusion ARDS is acute non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema with refractory hypoxaemia, most often due to sepsis or pneumonia; treatment of the cause, lung-protective ventilation, prone positioning and expert nursing care are essential.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Respiratory Disorders
question: Explain the causes, clinical features and management of pleural effusion, with the nursing care during thoracentesis.
answer_html:
Definition Pleural effusion is an abnormal collection of fluid in the pleural space (normally only about 10–20 ml of fluid is present). It is not a disease itself but a sign of an underlying condition.

1. Causes

  • Transudate (pressure imbalance) – congestive heart failure (commonest overall), cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminaemia.
  • Exudate (inflammation) – tuberculosis (commonest cause of exudative effusion in India), pneumonia (parapneumonic effusion), malignancy (lung, breast, lymphoma), pulmonary embolism, rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, pancreatitis.
  • Other types – empyema (pus), haemothorax (blood), chylothorax (lymph).

2. Clinical features

  • Breathlessness (depends on size and speed of collection), pleuritic chest pain, dry cough.
  • Features of the cause – fever, night sweats and weight loss (TB), oedema (heart failure).
