  • Signs – reduced chest movement, stony dull percussion, decreased breath sounds and vocal fremitus on the affected side; trachea shifted to the opposite side in large effusions.

3. Investigations

  • Chest X-ray – blunting of the costophrenic angle, meniscus sign; ultrasound detects small effusions and guides tapping; CT scan.
  • Diagnostic thoracentesis – fluid for protein, LDH, glucose, cell count, ADA (raised in TB), Gram stain, culture, CBNAAT and cytology.

4. Management

  • Treat the cause – anti-TB treatment, antibiotics, diuretics for heart failure, cancer therapy.
  • Therapeutic thoracentesis for breathlessness – usually not more than 1–1.5 litres at one time to avoid re-expansion pulmonary oedema.
  • Intercostal chest drain for empyema or large recurrent effusion.
  • Pleurodesis (talc) or an indwelling pleural catheter for recurrent malignant effusion.

5. Nursing care during thoracentesis Before

  • Explain the procedure, obtain consent; check coagulation reports and allergy; record baseline vital signs and SpO₂.
  • Position – sitting upright on the edge of the bed, leaning forward over a bedside table with arms resting on a pillow; if unable to sit, lie on the unaffected side with the head end raised.
  • Prepare a sterile thoracentesis set, local anaesthetic, specimen containers and drainage bottle.

During

  • Maintain asepsis; support the patient; ask him not to cough or move suddenly.
  • Monitor pulse, BP, SpO₂, colour and breathing; watch for faintness, sweating, persistent cough, chest tightness or pain – inform the doctor to stop the procedure.
  • Label specimens correctly and send them promptly.

After

  • Apply a sterile dressing; position comfortably; record the amount, colour and character of fluid.
  • Monitor vital signs and breathing; arrange a chest X-ray if ordered to exclude pneumothorax.
  • Watch for complications – pneumothorax, bleeding, re-expansion pulmonary oedema, vasovagal reaction, infection and leakage at the site.

Nursing importance Correct positioning, monitoring and specimen handling make thoracentesis safe and help in early diagnosis of TB and cancer.

Conclusion Pleural effusion is fluid in the pleural space due to heart failure, TB, infection or cancer; treatment of the cause and safe thoracentesis with good nursing care relieve breathlessness.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Respiratory Disorders
question: Explain the causes, clinical features and nursing management of lung abscess.
answer_html:
Definition A lung abscess is a localised area of suppurative necrosis of lung tissue forming a pus-filled cavity, usually more than 2 cm in diameter.

1. Causes

  • Aspiration (commonest) of oral secretions or vomitus containing anaerobic bacteria – in alcoholics, unconscious patients, epilepsy, stroke, anaesthesia, swallowing disorders and poor dental hygiene.
  • Necrotising pneumonia – Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella.
  • Bronchial obstruction – tumour, foreign body.
  • Septic emboli – infective endocarditis, IV drug use; spread from an amoebic liver abscess (right lower lobe).
  • Aspiration abscesses are commoner in the right lung (wider, more vertical right bronchus), usually in the posterior segment of the upper lobe or the superior segment of the lower lobe.

2. Clinical features

  • High fever with chills, malaise, night sweats, loss of appetite and weight.
  • Cough with large amounts of foul-smelling, purulent sputum, sometimes blood-stained; sudden expectoration of a large amount of pus when the abscess ruptures into a bronchus.
  • Pleuritic chest pain, breathlessness, bad breath (halitosis), clubbing in chronic cases.
  • Chest X-ray – a cavity with an air-fluid level; CT scan; sputum culture and AFB; bronchoscopy to exclude tumour or foreign body.

3. Medical and surgical management

  • Prolonged antibiotics (usually 4–6 weeks or until the X-ray clears) covering anaerobes – amoxicillin-clavulanate, clindamycin, or as per culture.
  • Postural drainage and chest physiotherapy.
  • Bronchoscopy to remove a foreign body or aspirate pus; percutaneous drainage for large peripheral abscesses.
  • Surgical resection (lobectomy) if there is no response, massive haemoptysis or suspected cancer.

4. Nursing management

  • Postural drainage – position the patient so that the affected segment is uppermost, 2–3 times a day before meals, combined with percussion and coughing (as taught in fundamentals of nursing).
  • Collect sputum for culture before antibiotics; record the daily amount, colour and smell of sputum; give sputum cups with lids and disinfectant; dispose of safely.
  • Oral hygiene after each episode of expectoration and before meals – reduces bad taste and improves appetite.
  • Fluids 2–3 litres a day; high-protein, high-calorie diet with vitamins.
  • Give antibiotics on time; watch for side effects (diarrhoea with clindamycin).
  • Monitor temperature, respiration and for haemoptysis or signs of empyema.
  • Rest, comfortable position and emotional support (foul sputum may embarrass the patient).
  • Prevention – aspiration precautions (head-end elevation, careful feeding of stroke and unconscious patients, suction), good dental care, treatment of alcoholism.

Nursing importance Effective postural drainage, oral care and nutrition speed the healing of the abscess and prevent complications such as empyema and bronchiectasis.

Conclusion Lung abscess is a pus-filled cavity usually due to aspiration; long-term antibiotics, drainage and good nursing care lead to recovery, while aspiration precautions prevent it.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Respiratory Disorders
question: Explain the medical and nursing management of a patient with bronchiectasis.
answer_html:
Introduction Bronchiectasis is the permanent abnormal dilatation of bronchi due to destruction of their walls, leading to pooling of secretions and repeated infections. In India, post-tuberculosis bronchiectasis and childhood infections (measles, whooping cough, severe pneumonia) are common causes; others include cystic fibrosis, immune deficiency and bronchial obstruction.

1. Clinical features (brief) Chronic cough with large amounts of purulent sputum, worse in the morning and on changing posture; recurrent chest infections; haemoptysis; breathlessness; clubbing; coarse crackles. Diagnosis is by high-resolution CT (HRCT) of the chest, sputum culture and tests for the cause.

2. Medical management

  • Airway clearance is the foundation – postural drainage, chest physiotherapy, active cycle of breathing technique, oscillating devices (flutter valve), and nebulised hypertonic saline as ordered.
  • Antibiotics for exacerbations, chosen by sputum culture (Pseudomonas is common), usually for 14 days; long-term macrolide (azithromycin) for frequent exacerbations.
  • Bronchodilators when there is airflow obstruction.
  • Vaccination – influenza and pneumococcal.
  • Treat the cause – immunoglobulin replacement, management of TB sequelae or ABPA.
  • Haemoptysis – bronchial artery embolisation for significant bleeding; surgery (lobectomy) for localised disease or massive haemoptysis.

3. Nursing management

  • Teach and supervise postural drainage 2–4 times a day (before meals and at bedtime), with percussion and huff coughing; teach a family member to help at home.
  • Record sputum daily – amount, colour, smell, blood; an increase in volume or purulence suggests an exacerbation.
  • Hydration (2–3 litres a day unless restricted) to keep secretions thin; steam inhalation.
  • Oral hygiene frequently – foul sputum causes bad taste and poor appetite.
  • Nutrition – high-calorie, high-protein diet; small frequent meals.
  • Infection control – sputum cups with lids, hand hygiene, safe disposal; avoid contact with people having colds.
  • Haemoptysis care – keep the patient calm, position on the affected side (to protect the good lung), give oxygen, keep suction ready, measure blood loss and inform the doctor at once.
  • Smoking cessation and avoidance of smoke and dust.
  • Exercise and pulmonary rehabilitation as tolerated.

4. Patient education

  • Daily airway clearance even when feeling well; complete antibiotic courses.
  • Recognise warning signs – fever, increased or discoloured sputum, increased breathlessness, blood in sputum.
  • Regular follow-up and vaccinations.

Nursing importance Regular airway clearance taught and supervised by the nurse is the most effective way to reduce infections and hospital admissions in bronchiectasis.

Conclusion Bronchiectasis is managed by daily airway clearance, prompt antibiotics for exacerbations, treatment of the cause and supportive nursing care including nutrition, oral hygiene and haemoptysis care.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Respiratory Disorders
question: Write a note on carcinoma of the lung with its nursing management.
answer_html:
Introduction Lung cancer (bronchogenic carcinoma) is a malignant tumour arising from the epithelium of the bronchi or lung tissue. It is one of the commonest cancers in Indian men and is increasing in women. It is often diagnosed late because its symptoms are mistaken for tuberculosis.

1. Types

  • Non-small cell lung cancer (about 85%) – adenocarcinoma (commonest; also in non-smokers and women), squamous cell carcinoma (central, linked to smoking), large cell carcinoma.
  • Small cell lung cancer (about 15%) – highly aggressive, strongly linked to smoking, spreads early; may produce hormones (SIADH, Cushing's syndrome).

2. Risk factors Smoking (cigarettes and bidis – most important), passive smoking, indoor biomass smoke, air pollution, occupational exposure (asbestos, silica, arsenic), radon, previous lung scarring (TB), family history.

3. Clinical features

  • Persistent cough or change in a chronic cough, haemoptysis, chest pain, breathlessness, wheeze, recurrent pneumonia.
  • Weight loss, loss of appetite, fatigue, clubbing.
  • Local spread – hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal nerve), superior vena cava obstruction (swelling of face and arms), Horner's syndrome and arm pain (Pancoast tumour), pleural effusion.
  • Metastases – bone pain, headache and seizures (brain), jaundice (liver).

4. Diagnosis Chest X-ray, CT scan, bronchoscopy with biopsy, CT-guided needle biopsy, sputum cytology, pleural fluid cytology, PET-CT for staging, and molecular tests (EGFR, ALK) to guide targeted therapy.

5. Management

  • Surgery for early non-small cell cancer – lobectomy, pneumonectomy or segmentectomy (open or VATS).
  • Chemotherapy and radiotherapy (curative or palliative).
  • Targeted therapy (EGFR inhibitors such as gefitinib, osimertinib) and immunotherapy for advanced disease.
  • Palliative care – pain relief, oxygen, drainage of effusion, stenting for airway or SVC obstruction.

6. Nursing management

  • Post-thoracotomy care – pain control (epidural, PCA), deep breathing and coughing, incentive spirometry, early ambulation, chest drain care, arm and shoulder exercises on the operated side.
  • Positioning – after lobectomy, the patient may lie on either side or back; after pneumonectomy, usually on the back or the operated side, avoiding complete turning to the non-operated side (as ordered), so that the remaining lung can expand fully.
  • Breathlessness – upright position, oxygen, breathing techniques, fan, energy conservation.
  • Chemotherapy and radiation care – manage nausea, mucositis, low blood counts (infection precautions), skin care in the radiation field, fatigue.
  • Nutrition – high-calorie, high-protein small meals.
  • Haemoptysis – calm the patient, lie on the affected side, suction, oxygen, inform the doctor.
  • Psychological and spiritual support; involve the family; link with palliative care services.
  • Prevention – tobacco cessation counselling (COTPA, NTCP), clean fuels, workplace protection.

Nursing importance Nurses help in early detection (suspecting cancer when "TB-like" symptoms do not respond), prepare patients for surgery and support them through treatment and palliative care.

Conclusion Lung cancer, closely linked to smoking, presents with cough, haemoptysis and weight loss; treatment includes surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and targeted therapy, with compassionate nursing care at every stage.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Respiratory Disorders
question: Explain acute tonsillitis and the post-operative nursing care after tonsillectomy.
answer_html:
Introduction Acute tonsillitis is acute inflammation of the palatine tonsils, common in children and young adults. It is caused by viruses or by bacteria, especially group A β-haemolytic streptococci, which can lead to rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis.

1. Clinical features

  • Sore throat, pain on swallowing, fever, malaise, headache; referred ear pain.
  • Enlarged, red tonsils with white exudate in the crypts; tender enlarged neck (jugulodigastric) lymph nodes; bad breath.

2. Treatment

  • Rest, plenty of fluids, soft diet, warm saline gargles, analgesics and antipyretics (paracetamol).
  • Antibiotics for bacterial tonsillitis – penicillin or amoxicillin for 10 days to prevent rheumatic fever.
  • Complications – peritonsillar abscess (quinsy), chronic tonsillitis, rheumatic fever, acute glomerulonephritis.

3. Indications for tonsillectomy

  • Recurrent tonsillitis – 7 or more episodes in one year, 5 per year for 2 years or 3 per year for 3 years.
  • Recurrent peritonsillar abscess; enlarged tonsils causing obstructive sleep apnoea or difficulty in swallowing; suspected malignancy; diphtheria carriers.

4. Post-operative nursing care

  • Position – tonsillar (semi-prone/lateral) position with the head turned to one side and slightly lower until fully conscious, so that blood and saliva drain out of the mouth and are not aspirated.
  • Observe for haemorrhage (the most important complication):
    • Frequent swallowing (especially in children), vomiting of dark or fresh blood, restlessness, rising pulse, falling BP, pallor.
    • Primary (during surgery), reactionary (within 24 hours) and secondary (5–10 days, due to infection).
    • Report immediately; keep suction, ice, adrenaline-soaked packs and a tray for re-exploration ready.
  • Suction gently, avoiding the tonsillar bed; keep a kidney tray and tissues at the bedside.
  • Ice collar to the neck may reduce pain and bleeding.
  • Pain relief – paracetamol and other analgesics as ordered; avoid aspirin (increases bleeding).
  • Diet – once fully awake and not bleeding, start cold fluids and soft foods (cold milk, ice cream, custard, curd rice); then soft solid foods; avoid hot, spicy, hard or rough foods (chips, toast) for about 10 days; encourage fluids.
  • Oral hygiene – gentle mouthwash or saline gargles as advised; no vigorous gargling or clearing the throat in the first days.
  • Discharge teaching – the white slough (membrane) in the tonsillar bed for 5–10 days is normal; ear pain is common; report any bleeding, high fever or inability to swallow; avoid crowds and people with infections for two weeks; rest from school or work for about 10–14 days.

Nursing importance Close observation for bleeding and correct positioning after tonsillectomy prevent aspiration and fatal haemorrhage, especially in children.

Conclusion Acute tonsillitis is treated with symptomatic care and antibiotics; after tonsillectomy, the nurse's main duties are safe positioning, early detection of bleeding, pain relief and suitable diet.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Respiratory Disorders
question: Explain the nursing care of a patient with a tracheostomy.

diagram.caption: Parts of a tracheostomy tube
labels: cuff with pilot balloon and inflation valve
tapes; position in trachea below cricoid cartilage

answer_html:
Definition A tracheostomy is a surgical opening in the anterior wall of the trachea (usually through the 2nd–4th tracheal rings) into which a tube is inserted to provide an airway. The opening is called the tracheostome.

1. Indications

  • Upper airway obstruction – tumours of the larynx, trauma, foreign body, bilateral vocal cord paralysis, severe infections (diphtheria, Ludwig's angina).
  • Prolonged mechanical ventilation (usually more than 7–14 days).
  • Removal of secretions (bronchial toilet) in unconscious or neuromuscular patients.
  • Protection of the airway from aspiration.

2. Types of tubes Cuffed (for ventilation and to prevent aspiration) or uncuffed; with or without inner cannula; fenestrated (allows speech); metal (Jackson's silver tube) or plastic (PVC, silicone).

3. Nursing care (a) Bedside preparation (emergency kit)

  • Keep a spare tube of the same size and one size smaller, obturator, tracheal dilator, suction apparatus with catheters, oxygen, Ambu bag and a syringe for the cuff at the bedside at all times.

(b) Humidification

  • The nose and upper airway are bypassed, so inspired air must be humidified – heat-moisture exchanger (HME), humidified oxygen, saline nebulisation – to prevent thick secretions and tube blockage.

(c) Suctioning

  • Sterile technique; hand hygiene and sterile gloves.
  • Pre-oxygenate; use a catheter not more than half the internal diameter of the tube.
  • Insert without suction; apply suction (about 100–150 mmHg in adults) only while withdrawing, rotating the catheter; each pass not more than 10–15 seconds.
  • Allow rest and oxygen between passes; observe SpO₂, heart rate and the secretions.

(d) Inner cannula and stoma care

  • Remove and clean the inner cannula every 4–8 hours or as needed (with saline/hydrogen peroxide and a brush), rinse and replace; or change a disposable one.
  • Clean the stoma with normal saline; dry and apply a Y-shaped (keyhole) dressing; observe for redness, discharge and bleeding.
  • Change tapes with two people (one holds the tube); tie securely so that one finger can be slipped under the tape.

(e) Cuff care

  • Maintain cuff pressure at 20–30 cm H₂O (check with a manometer every 8 hours) to prevent tracheal damage and aspiration.

(f) Communication, nutrition and comfort

  • Provide a writing board, picture cards or a call bell; speaking valves when allowed.
  • Check swallowing before oral feeds; elevate the head during and after feeds.
  • Oral care, positioning, psychological support.

4. Complications and their care

  • Accidental decannulation (especially within the first 72 hours, before the tract forms) – call for help, keep the stoma open with the tracheal dilator, give oxygen and reinsert as per protocol.
  • Tube blockage with secretions – suction, change the inner cannula.
  • Bleeding, subcutaneous emphysema, pneumothorax, infection, tracheal stenosis, tracheo-oesophageal fistula.

5. Discharge teaching (permanent tracheostomy) Cleaning the tube and stoma, suctioning, humidification, covering the stoma with a gauze bib, avoiding water entry (no swimming, care while bathing), and recognising signs of infection or blockage.

Nursing importance A tracheostomy patient depends on the nurse for a patent airway; proper humidification, suctioning and emergency preparedness are life-saving.

Conclusion Tracheostomy care includes humidification, aseptic suctioning, cleaning of the inner cannula and stoma, cuff care, communication support and readiness for emergencies.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Respiratory Disorders
question: Explain the nursing assessment of a patient with a respiratory disorder.
answer_html:
Introduction Respiratory assessment is the systematic collection of information about the patient's breathing through history, physical examination and investigations. It helps the nurse detect problems early, plan care and monitor progress.

1. Health history

  • Cough – duration (more than 2 weeks → test for TB), dry or productive, timing (night, morning).
  • Sputum – amount, colour (white, yellow, green, rusty), smell, blood (haemoptysis).
  • Breathlessness – onset, on exertion or at rest, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea; graded by the MRC dyspnoea scale.
  • Chest pain (pleuritic or not), wheeze, fever, night sweats, weight loss, hoarseness.
  • Smoking history – cigarettes or bidis, in pack-years (packs per day × years smoked); passive smoke; biomass fuel exposure.
  • Occupational exposure (dust, silica, cotton, chemicals), TB contact, allergies, previous lung disease, medicines, vaccination status.

2. General examination

  • Level of consciousness, distress, posture (tripod position), ability to speak in full sentences.
  • Cyanosis (central – lips, tongue; peripheral – nails), clubbing, pallor, lymph nodes, ankle oedema, raised JVP.
  • Vital signs, SpO₂.

3. Inspection of the chest

  • Respiratory rate (normal 12–20/min), depth and rhythm – Cheyne–Stokes, Kussmaul.
  • Shape – normal, barrel chest (emphysema), pigeon chest, funnel chest, kyphoscoliosis.
  • Symmetry of movement, use of accessory muscles, intercostal retractions, nasal flaring, scars, wounds and chest drains.

4. Palpation

  • Tracheal position (shift in effusion, collapse, pneumothorax).
  • Chest expansion (symmetry), tactile vocal fremitus (increased in consolidation, decreased in effusion and pneumothorax), tenderness, crepitus (subcutaneous emphysema).

5. Percussion

  • Resonant – normal lung.
  • Dull – consolidation, collapse; stony dull – pleural effusion.
  • Hyper-resonant – pneumothorax, emphysema.

6. Auscultation

  • Breath sounds – vesicular (normal), bronchial (consolidation), diminished or absent (effusion, pneumothorax, collapse).
  • Added (adventitious) sounds – crackles (fine – pulmonary oedema, fibrosis; coarse – secretions, pneumonia), wheeze (rhonchi) – asthma, COPD; pleural rub – pleurisy; stridor – upper airway obstruction.
  • Vocal resonance.

7. Investigations (nurse's role in preparation and collection) Pulse oximetry, ABG, chest X-ray, CT scan, sputum for Gram stain, culture, AFB and CBNAAT, spirometry and peak flow, bronchoscopy, thoracentesis and pleural biopsy, CBC and other blood tests.

Nursing importance Careful respiratory assessment allows early recognition of deterioration (rising respiratory rate, falling SpO₂, new crackles) and guides oxygen therapy, positioning and airway care.

Conclusion Respiratory assessment combines a focused history, general examination, inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation and investigations to identify and monitor respiratory problems.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Respiratory Disorders
question: Define pulmonary embolism. Write its clinical features and management.
answer_html:
Pulmonary embolism (PE) is the obstruction of the pulmonary artery or one of its branches by an embolus, most often a thrombus from deep vein thrombosis (DVT) of the legs or pelvis.

Risk factors – immobility, surgery (especially hip and knee), pregnancy and postpartum period, oral contraceptives, cancer, obesity, long journeys.

Clinical features – sudden breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain, tachypnoea, tachycardia, cough, haemoptysis, hypoxia, anxiety, fainting; massive PE causes shock and cardiac arrest.

Management – oxygen, anticoagulation (heparin/LMWH followed by oral anticoagulants), thrombolysis for massive PE, embolectomy; prevention by early ambulation and DVT prophylaxis.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Respiratory Disorders
question: What is empyema thoracis? How is it treated?
answer_html:
Empyema thoracis is the collection of pus in the pleural cavity.

Causes – pneumonia (commonest), tuberculosis, lung abscess, chest injury or surgery, spread from a subphrenic abscess. Features – persistent fever, chest pain, breathlessness, weight loss, dull percussion and reduced breath sounds; thick pus on pleural aspiration.

Treatment

  1. Drainage – intercostal chest tube (underwater seal); intrapleural fibrinolytics in loculated empyema.
  2. Antibiotics according to culture (anti-TB drugs for TB empyema).
  3. Decortication (VATS or open surgery) for thick chronic empyema.
  4. Nutrition, chest physiotherapy and breathing exercises.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Respiratory Disorders
question: Define sinusitis and list its management.
answer_html:
Sinusitis is inflammation of the mucous membrane lining the paranasal sinuses (maxillary is most commonly involved). It is acute if less than 4 weeks and chronic if more than 12 weeks.

Causes – common cold, allergic rhinitis, dental infection, deviated nasal septum, nasal polyps. Features – nasal blockage, thick purulent discharge, facial pain and pressure worse on bending forward, headache, fever, post-nasal drip, reduced smell.

Management

  1. Steam inhalation and saline nasal irrigation.
  2. Nasal decongestant drops for not more than 3–5 days; analgesics.
  3. Antibiotics for bacterial sinusitis; nasal steroid spray for allergy.
  4. Functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) for chronic sinusitis.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Respiratory Disorders
question: What is atelectasis? How is it prevented after surgery?
answer_html:
Atelectasis is the incomplete expansion or collapse of part or all of a lung, so that alveoli contain little or no air.

Causes – shallow breathing after surgery and anaesthesia (pain, sedation), mucus plug or obstruction (tumour, foreign body), compression by effusion or pneumothorax. Features – breathlessness, tachypnoea, reduced breath sounds, low-grade fever (often on the first post-operative day), low SpO₂.

Prevention after surgery

  1. Deep breathing, coughing and incentive spirometry every hour while awake.
  2. Adequate pain relief and splinting of the incision.
  3. Early ambulation and frequent change of position.
  4. Adequate hydration, chest physiotherapy and suction of secretions.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Respiratory Disorders
question: What is pursed-lip breathing? State its benefits.
answer_html:
Pursed-lip breathing is a breathing exercise in which the patient breathes in slowly through the nose (for about 2 counts) and breathes out slowly through pursed lips (as if whistling or blowing a candle) for about 4 counts – making expiration twice as long as inspiration.

Benefits

  1. Creates back-pressure that keeps small airways open, reducing air trapping.
  2. Slows the respiratory rate and improves ventilation and oxygenation.
  3. Relieves breathlessness and anxiety during exertion.
  4. Gives the patient a sense of control; useful in COPD, emphysema and asthma.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Respiratory Disorders
question: What is peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR)? How is it measured?
answer_html:
Peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) is the maximum speed of air flow during a forceful expiration after a full inspiration, measured in litres per minute with a peak flow meter. Normal values depend on age, sex and height (roughly 450–650 L/min in adult men and 350–500 L/min in adult women).

Measurement

  1. Stand or sit upright; set the pointer to zero.
  2. Take a deep breath, seal the lips around the mouthpiece and blow out as hard and fast as possible.
  3. Repeat three times and record the best reading.

Uses – monitoring asthma control and response to treatment; zones: green (above 80% of personal best), yellow (50–80%), red (below 50% – emergency).

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Respiratory Disorders
question: What is silicosis? How can it be prevented?
answer_html:
Silicosis is an occupational lung disease (pneumoconiosis) caused by inhalation of crystalline silica dust, producing fibrotic nodules in the lungs. It is irreversible and progressive.

Occupations at risk (India) – stone quarrying and crushing, mining, sandblasting, glass and ceramic industries, slate-pencil and agate-grinding industries. Features – progressive breathlessness, dry cough, fatigue; high risk of tuberculosis (silico-tuberculosis) and lung cancer.

Prevention

  1. Dust control – wet drilling and cutting, ventilation, enclosure of processes.
  2. Respirators/masks and protective equipment for workers.
  3. Pre-placement and periodic medical examinations with chest X-rays.
  4. Health education; silicosis is a notified occupational disease with compensation for affected workers.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Digestive System Disorders
question: (a) Define acute pancreatitis and list its causes. (3 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features and diagnostic findings. (4 marks) (c) Describe the medical and nursing management of a patient with acute pancreatitis. (8 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Definition and causes (3 marks) Acute pancreatitis is an acute inflammatory condition of the pancreas caused by premature activation of pancreatic enzymes (especially trypsin) within the gland, leading to autodigestion, oedema, haemorrhage and sometimes necrosis of the pancreas and surrounding tissues. It ranges from a mild self-limiting illness to a severe disease with multi-organ failure.

Causes – memory aid "I GET SMASHED"

  • Idiopathic (no cause found in some patients).
  • Gallstones – the commonest cause (a stone blocks the common channel at the ampulla).
  • Ethanol (alcohol) – very common in Indian men.
  • Trauma – blunt abdominal injury, surgery.
  • Steroids and other drugs.
  • Mumps and other infections (viral, parasitic – Ascaris).
  • Autoimmune pancreatitis.
  • Scorpion sting (rare), Snake bite.
  • Hypertriglyceridaemia (above 1000 mg/dl), Hypercalcaemia.
  • ERCP (post-ERCP pancreatitis).
  • Drugs – azathioprine, valproate, thiazides, estrogens.

Pathophysiology (brief) – activated trypsin activates other enzymes (lipase, elastase, phospholipase) → digestion of pancreatic tissue, fat necrosis (calcium is used up – hypocalcaemia), blood-vessel damage (haemorrhage) → release of inflammatory mediators → systemic inflammatory response, capillary leak, shock, ARDS and kidney failure in severe cases.

(b) Clinical features and diagnostic findings (4 marks) Clinical features

  • Severe, constant epigastric pain of sudden onset, often after a heavy fatty meal or alcohol binge, radiating to the back; it is worse on lying flat and relieved by sitting up and leaning forward.
  • Nausea and repeated vomiting; vomiting does not relieve the pain.
  • Fever, tachycardia, sweating; hypotension and shock in severe cases.
  • Abdominal tenderness and guarding in the upper abdomen, distension, reduced bowel sounds (paralytic ileus).
  • Cullen's sign (bluish discoloration around the umbilicus) and Grey Turner's sign (bruising in the flanks) – signs of haemorrhagic pancreatitis.
  • Jaundice (gallstone obstruction), breathlessness (pleural effusion, ARDS), tetany (hypocalcaemia), confusion.

Diagnosis – two of the following three (Revised Atlanta criteria)

  1. Typical abdominal pain.
  2. Serum lipase or amylase at least three times the upper limit of normal (lipase is more specific and stays raised longer).
  3. Characteristic findings on imaging (contrast-enhanced CT, MRI or ultrasound).

Other investigations

  • Ultrasound abdomen – gallstones, dilated bile duct, oedematous pancreas.
  • CBC – leucocytosis; raised haematocrit (haemoconcentration); CRP above 150 mg/L at 48 hours suggests severe disease.
  • Blood sugar (raised), serum calcium (low), LFT (raised bilirubin, ALP in gallstone pancreatitis), triglycerides, urea and creatinine, ABG, chest X-ray (effusion, ARDS).
  • Contrast CT after 72 hours to detect necrosis and complications.

Severity (Revised Atlanta) – mild (no organ failure), moderately severe (organ failure for less than 48 hours or local complications), severe (organ failure lasting more than 48 hours). Scoring systems such as BISAP and Ranson's criteria help predict severity.

(c) Medical and nursing management (8 marks) 1. Medical management

  • Fluid resuscitation – early goal-directed IV fluids, preferably Ringer's lactate, guided by pulse, BP, urine output and haematocrit; avoid over-hydration, which can cause pulmonary oedema.
  • Pain relief – IV analgesics including opioids (morphine, fentanyl, tramadol) and paracetamol as ordered; pain control is a priority.
  • Oxygen to keep SpO₂ above 94%; ventilatory support for ARDS.
  • Nutrition
    • Mild pancreatitis – early oral feeding (within 24–72 hours) with a low-fat, soft diet as soon as pain and vomiting settle; prolonged "nil by mouth" is no longer recommended.
    • Severe pancreatitis – enteral feeding through a nasogastric or nasojejunal tube; parenteral nutrition only if enteral feeding is not possible.
    • Nasogastric suction only for persistent vomiting or ileus.
  • Antibiotics – not given routinely; used only for infected necrosis, cholangitis or other proven infections.
  • Treat the cause
    • ERCP with stone removal within 24 hours if there is cholangitis or persistent bile duct obstruction.
    • Cholecystectomy during the same admission after mild gallstone pancreatitis, to prevent recurrence.
    • Stop alcohol; insulin infusion or plasmapheresis for very high triglycerides.
  • Management of complications – pseudocyst (endoscopic or percutaneous drainage if symptomatic after 4–6 weeks), infected or walled-off necrosis (step-up approach – drainage, then necrosectomy), shock, ARDS, acute kidney injury, hypocalcaemia, hyperglycaemia (insulin), GI bleeding.

2. Nursing management (i) Acute pain related to inflammation and autodigestion of the pancreas

  • Assess pain regularly (0–10 scale); give analgesics on time and evaluate relief.
  • Position the patient sitting up, leaning forward, or in a side-lying position with knees flexed (fetal position) to reduce pain; semi-Fowler's to ease breathing.
  • Provide a calm environment; reduce stimulation of the pancreas (no oral intake while vomiting).

(ii) Deficient fluid volume related to vomiting, fluid shifts and haemorrhage

  • Monitor pulse, BP, CVP, urine output hourly (target at least 0.5 ml/kg/hour), skin turgor and mucous membranes.
  • Maintain IV fluids at the prescribed rate; keep an accurate intake–output chart, including NG aspirate.
  • Watch for signs of shock and report early.

(iii) Imbalanced nutrition: less than body requirements

  • Start feeds as ordered; progress from clear fluids to a low-fat, high-carbohydrate, high-protein soft diet.
  • Care of nasojejunal tube feeds – check position, flush, head elevated 30–45°.
  • Monitor blood glucose (hyperglycaemia is common) and weight.

(iv) Ineffective breathing pattern related to pain, pleural effusion and ARDS

  • Monitor respiratory rate, SpO₂ and ABG; encourage deep breathing and coughing; give oxygen; report increasing breathlessness.

(v) Risk for complications

  • Check serum calcium; watch for tetany, Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs; keep calcium gluconate ready.
  • Observe for bleeding, rising abdominal distension, fever (infected necrosis), oliguria (kidney injury) and confusion.
  • In alcoholic patients, watch for alcohol withdrawal (tremors, sweating, agitation, hallucinations, seizures) 6–72 hours after the last drink; give thiamine and sedation as ordered.

(vi) Comfort and hygiene

  • Oral care frequently while NPO or with NG tube; lubricate the lips and nostrils.
  • Skin care and position changes; prevent pressure ulcers in prolonged illness.

(vii) Anxiety and psychosocial care

  • Explain procedures; support the patient and family; counsel about alcohol de-addiction and refer to de-addiction services.

3. Discharge teaching

  • Avoid alcohol completely – even small amounts can cause recurrence.
  • Low-fat diet, small frequent meals; avoid heavy fried and spicy meals.
  • Complete planned cholecystectomy for gallstones.
  • Report recurrence of abdominal pain, fever, vomiting, jaundice or greasy, foul-smelling stools (steatorrhoea – may need pancreatic enzyme capsules).
  • Watch for symptoms of diabetes (thirst, frequent urination) after severe pancreatitis.
  • Keep follow-up appointments and control triglycerides.

4. Monitoring schedule (as ordered)

  • Hourly – pulse, BP, urine output (and CVP if available) in the first 24–48 hours.
  • Every 4 hours – temperature, respiratory rate, SpO₂, pain score, abdominal girth and bowel sounds.
  • Every 4–6 hours – blood glucose.
  • Daily – weight, electrolytes, calcium, urea, creatinine, CBC; CRP at 48 hours and further tests as ordered.

Nursing importance Acute pancreatitis can change rapidly from mild to life-threatening; close nursing monitoring of fluid balance, breathing, calcium, blood sugar and pain, together with early feeding and alcohol counselling, improves survival and prevents recurrence.

Conclusion Acute pancreatitis is autodigestion of the pancreas, mainly due to gallstones and alcohol; early fluids, pain relief, early nutrition, treatment of the cause and careful nursing care form the basis of management.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Digestive System Disorders
question: (a) Define appendicitis and list its causes. (2 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features and diagnosis of acute appendicitis. (5 marks) (c) Describe the pre-operative and post-operative nursing management of a patient undergoing appendicectomy. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Clinical signs in acute appendicitis
labels: McBurney's point one-third of the way from anterior superior iliac spine to umbilicus; shifting of pain from periumbilical region to right iliac fossa; Rovsing's sign; psoas and obturator manoeuvres

answer_html:
(a) Definition and causes (2 marks) Appendicitis is inflammation of the vermiform appendix. Acute appendicitis is the commonest surgical emergency of the abdomen, most often between 10 and 30 years of age.

Causes – obstruction of the lumen of the appendix by

  1. Faecolith (hardened faecal matter) – the commonest cause in adults.
  2. Lymphoid hyperplasia – in children and young adults, after viral infections.
  3. Foreign bodies (seeds), worms (Ascaris, Enterobius).
  4. Tumours (carcinoid), strictures. Pathophysiology – obstruction → mucus collects → pressure rises → venous congestion and ischaemia → bacterial invasion → gangrene → perforation (often within 24–36 hours) → localised abscess, appendicular mass or generalised peritonitis.

(b) Clinical features and diagnosis (5 marks) Clinical features

  • Abdominal pain – starts as vague, periumbilical (central) pain, then shifts to the right iliac fossa within 12–24 hours and becomes sharp and localised; worse on movement and coughing.
  • Anorexia (almost always present), nausea and vomiting – usually after the onset of pain.
  • Low-grade fever (37.5–38.5 °C), tachycardia, coated tongue, bad breath.
  • Signs
    • Tenderness at McBurney's point (junction of the lateral one-third and medial two-thirds of a line from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus).
    • Rebound tenderness (Blumberg's sign) and guarding.
    • Rovsing's sign – pressure in the left iliac fossa causes pain in the right iliac fossa.
    • Psoas sign (retrocaecal appendix) – pain on extending the right hip.
    • Obturator sign (pelvic appendix) – pain on internal rotation of the flexed right hip.
    • Pelvic appendix may cause frequency of urine or diarrhoea.
  • Perforation – sudden temporary relief of pain followed by generalised pain, high fever, rigidity and signs of shock.
  • Atypical presentation in children, elderly and pregnant women (pain higher up as the uterus displaces the appendix).

Diagnosis

  • Mainly clinical, supported by the Alvarado score (MANTRELS) – Migration of pain (1), Anorexia (1), Nausea/vomiting (1), Tenderness in right iliac fossa (2), Rebound tenderness (1), Elevated temperature (1), Leucocytosis (2), Shift to the left – neutrophilia (1); a score of 7 or more makes appendicitis likely.
  • CBC – leucocytosis with neutrophilia; CRP raised.
  • Urine routine – to exclude urinary tract infection or stone.
  • Ultrasound – non-compressible, enlarged appendix (more than 6 mm), fluid; CT scan in doubtful cases.
  • Pregnancy test in women of child-bearing age to exclude ectopic pregnancy.
  • Differential diagnosis – mesenteric lymphadenitis, ureteric colic, ectopic pregnancy, ovarian cyst torsion, pelvic inflammatory disease, gastroenteritis, typhoid ileitis, Meckel's diverticulitis.

(c) Nursing management of a patient undergoing appendicectomy (8 marks) Treatment in brief – appendicectomy (laparoscopic – preferred; or open through a grid-iron or Lanz incision) with antibiotics. An appendicular mass is treated conservatively (Ochsner–Sherren regimen – rest, NPO, IV fluids, antibiotics, monitoring) followed by interval appendicectomy after 6–8 weeks; an abscess is drained.

1. Pre-operative nursing care

  • Nil by mouth; start IV fluids to correct dehydration; maintain an intake–output chart.
  • Analgesics as ordered – modern practice does not withhold pain relief, as it does not mask the diagnosis.
  • IV antibiotics as ordered.
  • Do not give laxatives or enemas and do not apply heat to the abdomen – they may cause perforation.
  • Position – semi-Fowler's (or as comfortable) to localise any infection to the pelvis and ease breathing.
  • Monitor temperature, pulse, BP, pain character and abdomen every 1–2 hours; report signs of perforation (sudden relief then generalised pain, rigidity, high fever, rising pulse).
  • Pre-operative preparation – consent, investigations, skin preparation (clipping if needed), removal of jewellery, voiding, pre-medication and checklist; explain the operation and post-operative exercises; reassure the patient and parents.

2. Post-operative nursing care (i) Immediate care – PACU care: airway, breathing, circulation, level of consciousness, vital signs every 15 minutes until stable, pain and nausea control. (ii) Position – semi-Fowler's position once conscious – helps drainage of exudate to the pelvis (if peritonitis was present), reduces tension on the wound and eases breathing. (iii) Pain relief – regular analgesics (paracetamol, NSAIDs, opioids as ordered); teach splinting of the incision with a pillow while coughing. (iv) Respiratory care – deep breathing, coughing and incentive spirometry hourly while awake. (v) Early ambulation – within 12–24 hours (same day after laparoscopic surgery); prevents DVT, ileus and chest complications. (vi) Diet – sips of water when nausea settles and bowel sounds are present, then liquids → soft diet → normal diet; after uncomplicated laparoscopic appendicectomy, oral intake usually starts the same day; after perforation, feeding may be delayed and NG suction may be needed. (vii) Wound and drain care

  • Inspect the dressing for bleeding and discharge; aseptic dressing; record drain output (in perforated cases) and keep the drain patent.

  • Wound infection is the commonest complication – watch for redness, swelling, pain, pus and fever around days 3–5. (viii) Antibiotics – continue as ordered (longer course in perforated appendicitis). (ix) Elimination – watch for urinary retention; encourage voiding; prevent constipation with fluids and fibre. (x) Monitoring for complications

  • Intra-abdominal or pelvic abscess – persistent fever, abdominal pain, diarrhoea or tenesmus (pelvic abscess) after 5–7 days.

  • Paralytic ileus – distension, absent bowel sounds, vomiting.
  • Faecal fistula (rare), adhesive intestinal obstruction (later), haemorrhage, DVT. (xi) Psychological care – reassure the patient and family; explain progress.

3. Discharge teaching

  • Keep the wound clean and dry; suture or staple removal on about the 7th–10th day (or absorbable sutures).
  • Avoid heavy lifting and strenuous activity for about 2 weeks after laparoscopic and 4–6 weeks after open surgery; walking is encouraged.
  • Normal balanced diet with plenty of fluids and fibre.
  • Complete the antibiotic course.
  • Report fever, increasing abdominal pain, vomiting, wound redness or discharge, or inability to pass stool or flatus.
  • Return to school or work in about 1–2 weeks (light work), as advised.

4. Appendicitis in special groups

  • Children – cannot describe the pain well; present with vomiting, fever, irritability and refusal to walk; the omentum is small, so perforation occurs early.
  • Elderly – symptoms and signs are mild and fever may be absent, so diagnosis is delayed and perforation is more common.
  • Pregnant women – appendicitis is the commonest non-obstetric surgical emergency in pregnancy; the pain moves higher (towards the right upper quadrant) as the uterus enlarges; perforation increases the risk of preterm labour and fetal loss; laparoscopic surgery is safe; keep the patient in a left lateral tilt and monitor the fetus.

5. Common nursing diagnoses

  • Acute pain related to inflammation of the appendix or the surgical incision.
  • Risk for infection related to perforation and the surgical wound.
  • Risk for deficient fluid volume related to vomiting, fever and NPO status.
  • Anxiety related to emergency surgery; deficient knowledge regarding post-operative care.

Nursing importance Early recognition of appendicitis, avoidance of enemas and heat, careful monitoring for perforation and good post-operative care prevent peritonitis and shorten hospital stay.

Conclusion Acute appendicitis is caused by obstruction of the appendix lumen and presents with periumbilical pain shifting to the right iliac fossa; prompt appendicectomy with skilled pre- and post-operative nursing care gives excellent results.

question: (a) Define peptic ulcer and list its risk factors. (3 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features and diagnostic tests. (4 marks) (c) Describe the medical, surgical and nursing management, including the management of complications. (8 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Definition and risk factors (3 marks) Peptic ulcer disease (PUD) is a break in the mucosal lining of the stomach or duodenum (extending through the muscularis mucosae) in areas exposed to acid and pepsin. Duodenal ulcers are about four times more common than gastric ulcers.

Risk factors

  1. Helicobacter pylori infection – the most important cause; very common in India because of crowding and unsafe water.
  2. NSAIDs and aspirin – including over-the-counter painkillers for body ache and arthritis.
  3. Smoking and alcohol.
  4. Excess acid secretion – Zollinger–Ellison syndrome (gastrin-secreting tumour).
  5. Stress – severe burns (Curling's ulcer), head injury (Cushing's ulcer), ICU patients (stress ulcers).
  6. Corticosteroids with NSAIDs, anticoagulants, irregular meals, family history, blood group O, chronic diseases (cirrhosis, COPD, kidney failure).

(b) Clinical features and diagnostic tests (4 marks) Clinical features | Feature | Duodenal ulcer | Gastric ulcer | |---|---|---| | Age | 30–50 years | Above 50 years | | Pain | Epigastric burning 2–3 hours after meals and at night, relieved by food and antacids | Epigastric pain soon after meals, worsened by food | | Appetite and weight | Good appetite; weight may increase | Fear of eating; weight loss | | Vomiting | Less common | More common | | Malignancy | Almost never | Possible – biopsy needed | - Other features – heartburn, bloating, nausea, haematemesis or malaena (bleeding), anaemia; some patients (especially NSAID users and the elderly) have no pain until a complication occurs.

Diagnostic tests

  • Upper GI endoscopy (OGD) – investigation of choice; shows the ulcer; biopsy of gastric ulcers to exclude cancer; rapid urease test for H. pylori.
  • Non-invasive H. pylori tests – urea breath test, stool antigen test, serology.
  • CBC (anaemia), stool for occult blood.
  • Erect chest X-ray – free gas under the diaphragm in perforation.
  • Serum gastrin (if Zollinger–Ellison syndrome is suspected).

(c) Management (8 marks) 1. Medical management

  • Eradication of H. pylori – e.g., triple therapy (a proton-pump inhibitor + clarithromycin + amoxicillin for 14 days) or bismuth-based quadruple therapy as per local resistance; confirm eradication with a breath or stool test 4 weeks after therapy.
  • Acid suppression – proton-pump inhibitors (pantoprazole, omeprazole, esomeprazole) for 4–8 weeks; H₂-receptor blockers (famotidine); antacids for symptom relief; sucralfate as a mucosal protector.
  • Stop NSAIDs; if they are essential, give with a PPI or use safer alternatives (paracetamol).
  • Stop smoking and reduce alcohol.

2. Surgical management (now needed mainly for complications)

  • Perforation – laparoscopic or open closure with an omental (Graham's) patch and peritoneal lavage.
  • Bleeding not controlled by endoscopy – under-running of the bleeding vessel or angiographic embolisation.
  • Gastric outlet obstruction – endoscopic balloon dilatation or gastrojejunostomy.
  • Older elective operations – vagotomy with pyloroplasty, partial gastrectomy (Billroth I and II).

3. Management of complications

  • Upper GI bleeding (haematemesis, malaena) – resuscitation with IV fluids and blood, IV PPI in high doses, urgent endoscopic therapy (adrenaline injection, clips, thermal coagulation) within 24 hours, monitoring for rebleeding.
  • Perforation – sudden severe "knife-like" epigastric pain, board-like rigidity, shock: NPO, NG aspiration, IV fluids, IV antibiotics, analgesia and emergency surgery.
  • Gastric outlet obstruction – projectile vomiting of stale food, visible gastric peristalsis, succussion splash; NG decompression, correction of fluid and electrolyte loss (hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis), nutrition and definitive treatment.

4. Nursing management (i) Acute pain – assess pain pattern; give PPIs (30–60 minutes before breakfast) and antacids as ordered; encourage rest and relaxation. (ii) Diet and lifestyle

  • Regular, small, frequent meals; do not skip meals or eat late at night.
  • Avoid foods and drinks that cause discomfort (very spicy, fried food, excess tea and coffee, carbonated drinks); a strict bland or milk diet is not necessary (milk temporarily relieves but later increases acid).

  • Stop smoking; avoid alcohol. (iii) Medication teaching

  • Complete the full H. pylori regimen (side effects – metallic taste, diarrhoea).

  • Avoid NSAIDs and aspirin unless prescribed with protection; inform any doctor about the ulcer history. (iv) Monitoring for complications

  • Bleeding – black tarry stools, vomiting of blood or "coffee-ground" material, dizziness, pallor, tachycardia, falling BP.

  • Perforation – sudden severe pain, rigidity, shock – emergency.

  • Obstruction – repeated vomiting, distension, weight loss. (v) Care of a patient after gastric surgery

  • NG tube care – keep patent, do not reposition the tube (risk of damaging the suture line); record the aspirate.

  • Semi-Fowler's position, deep breathing (upper abdominal incision), early ambulation, pain control.
  • Gradual reintroduction of feeds; watch for dumping syndrome (small, frequent, dry meals high in protein, fluids between meals, lie down after meals).
  • Long-term – vitamin B₁₂ injections, iron and calcium supplements after gastrectomy. (vi) Stress management and emotional support – counselling, relaxation, adequate sleep.

5. Stress ulcer prophylaxis in critically ill patients

  • Patients on a ventilator for more than 48 hours, with coagulopathy, severe burns, head injury or shock are at risk of stress ulcers and bleeding.
  • Prevention – PPIs or H₂ blockers as ordered, early enteral feeding, correction of shock and hypoxia; monitor NG aspirate and stools for blood.

6. Long-term problems after gastrectomy

  • Dumping syndrome, iron-deficiency and vitamin B₁₂ deficiency anaemia (loss of intrinsic factor and acid), weight loss and malnutrition, bile reflux gastritis, osteoporosis (poor calcium absorption) and a small risk of cancer in the gastric stump; lifelong follow-up and supplements are needed.

7. Common nursing diagnoses

  • Acute pain related to acid irritation of the ulcer.
  • Risk for deficient fluid volume related to bleeding or vomiting.
  • Imbalanced nutrition related to pain, fear of eating or vomiting.
  • Anxiety related to symptoms and possible surgery.
  • Deficient knowledge regarding drugs, diet and lifestyle.

8. Health education for prevention of recurrence (Indian context)

  • Avoid self-medication with painkillers bought over the counter; many cold and pain combinations contain NSAIDs – read labels and ask the pharmacist.
  • Elderly patients with joint pain should use paracetamol first, topical NSAIDs, physiotherapy and weight reduction; when NSAIDs are essential they should be taken after food with a prescribed PPI.
  • Safe drinking water, hand washing and food hygiene reduce H. pylori spread in families.
  • Stop smoking, chewing tobacco and alcohol; eat at regular times; manage stress.
  • Complete the full course of eradication therapy and attend the test to confirm cure.

9. Follow-up

  • Repeat endoscopy after 6–8 weeks for gastric ulcers to confirm healing and to take further biopsies, because a non-healing gastric ulcer may be malignant.
  • Confirm H. pylori eradication with a breath or stool test (PPIs are stopped for 2 weeks before the test).
  • Long-term PPI is continued only when aspirin, NSAIDs or anticoagulants must be continued.

Nursing importance Most deaths from peptic ulcer are due to bleeding and perforation; nurses reduce these by teaching H. pylori treatment adherence and NSAID avoidance and by recognising complications early.

Conclusion Peptic ulcer disease is mainly caused by H. pylori and NSAIDs; eradication therapy, acid suppression, lifestyle changes and timely treatment of bleeding, perforation and obstruction, supported by good nursing care, lead to cure.

question: (a) Define cirrhosis of the liver and list its causes. (2 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features and complications. (5 marks) (c) Describe the medical and nursing management of a patient with cirrhosis. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Effects of portal hypertension in cirrhosis

answer_html:
(a) Definition and causes (2 marks) Cirrhosis is a chronic, diffuse, irreversible liver disease in which normal liver tissue is replaced by fibrosis and regenerative nodules, leading to loss of liver function and portal hypertension. Causes – alcohol, chronic hepatitis B and C, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (obesity, diabetes), autoimmune hepatitis, biliary cirrhosis, Wilson's disease, haemochromatosis, drugs and toxins, long-standing heart failure (cardiac cirrhosis) and unknown (cryptogenic).

(b) Clinical features and complications (5 marks) 1. Early (compensated) cirrhosis

  • May be silent; vague symptoms – fatigue, weakness, loss of appetite, nausea, weight loss, dull right upper abdominal discomfort, firm liver.

2. Features of liver cell failure

  • Jaundice, dark urine, itching.
  • Bleeding tendency – easy bruising, gum and nose bleeds (reduced clotting factors).
  • Hypoalbuminaemia – oedema of feet, muscle wasting.
  • Hormonal changes – spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia, testicular atrophy, loss of body hair, menstrual irregularities.
  • Clubbing, white nails, fetor hepaticus, low-grade fever, anaemia.

3. Features of portal hypertension

  • Splenomegaly (with low platelets), ascites, oesophageal and gastric varices, caput medusae, haemorrhoids.

4. Complications

  • Variceal bleeding – massive haematemesis and malaena; a leading cause of death.
  • Ascites and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) – fever, abdominal pain, worsening ascites or confusion.
  • Hepatic encephalopathy – confusion, sleep reversal, flapping tremor (asterixis), drowsiness, coma.
  • Hepatorenal syndrome – kidney failure due to poor kidney perfusion.
  • Hepatocellular carcinoma, coagulopathy, malnutrition, infections, hyponatraemia, hepatopulmonary syndrome.

(c) Medical and nursing management (8 marks) 1. Medical management

  • Treat the cause – total abstinence from alcohol; antivirals for hepatitis B (tenofovir, entecavir) and direct-acting antivirals for hepatitis C (available free under the National Viral Hepatitis Control Programme); weight reduction and diabetes control in fatty liver.
  • Ascites – sodium restriction (about 2 g sodium or 5 g salt a day); diuretics – spironolactone with furosemide (about 100:40 mg ratio) as ordered; therapeutic paracentesis for tense ascites with IV albumin (about 8 g per litre removed when large volumes are drained); TIPS for refractory cases.
  • Varices – non-selective β-blockers (propranolol, carvedilol) and endoscopic band ligation to prevent bleeding.
  • Acute variceal bleeding – resuscitation, blood transfusion, vasoactive drugs (terlipressin or octreotide), prophylactic antibiotics (ceftriaxone), urgent endoscopic band ligation within 12 hours; balloon tamponade (Sengstaken–Blakemore tube) as a temporary measure; TIPS if bleeding continues.
  • Hepatic encephalopathy – lactulose (titrated to give 2–3 soft stools a day), rifaximin, and correction of precipitating factors (bleeding, infection, constipation, dehydration, low potassium, sedatives); protein is not restricted.
  • SBP – IV antibiotics (cefotaxime/ceftriaxone) with albumin.
  • Nutrition – high-calorie (about 35 kcal/kg/day), adequate protein (1.2–1.5 g/kg/day), small frequent meals with a late-evening snack; vitamin supplements, thiamine in alcoholics.
  • Liver transplantation for end-stage disease.
  • Regular screening for liver cancer – ultrasound (± AFP) every 6 months.

2. Nursing management (i) Excess fluid volume (ascites, oedema)

  • Daily weight at the same time with the same scale and clothes; measure abdominal girth daily at the umbilicus (mark the site).
  • Strict intake–output; salt restriction (no pickles, papad, chips, salted snacks, processed food); fluid restriction if sodium is low, as ordered.
  • Semi-Fowler's position to ease breathing; elevate oedematous legs.
  • Assist with paracentesis – empty the bladder before, record the amount and colour of fluid, monitor BP and observe the site for leakage.
  • Monitor electrolytes and kidney function while on diuretics.

(ii) Risk for bleeding

  • Observe for haematemesis, malaena, bruising, bleeding gums; check stools for blood.
  • Use a soft toothbrush, electric razor; avoid IM injections when possible; apply pressure on puncture sites for longer; give vitamin K as ordered.
  • Teach the patient to avoid straining, forceful nose blowing and heavy lifting (raise variceal pressure).
  • In variceal bleeding – keep the patient lying on the side with the head raised, suction ready, two IV lines, blood ready; care of the balloon tamponade tube if used (traction, pressure checks, scissors at the bedside for emergency deflation).

(iii) Risk for injury – hepatic encephalopathy

  • Assess level of consciousness, orientation, handwriting and asterixis daily; report early changes.
  • Give lactulose as ordered and record the number of stools; avoid constipation.
  • Avoid sedatives, opioids and other drugs metabolised by the liver unless prescribed.
  • Safety – side rails, low bed, supervision; reorient the patient.

(iv) Imbalanced nutrition

  • Small, frequent, palatable meals; late-evening snack; oral care before meals; record food intake and weight; supplements as ordered.

(v) Impaired skin integrity

  • Oedematous, itchy and jaundiced skin breaks easily – frequent position changes, pressure-relieving mattress, gentle skin care, cool baths and calamine for itching, short nails, cotton clothes.

(vi) Risk for infection – hand hygiene, aseptic paracentesis, early reporting of fever or abdominal pain (SBP); vaccination against hepatitis A and B.

(vii) Ineffective breathing pattern – due to tense ascites; semi-Fowler's position, oxygen as needed, paracentesis.

(viii) Psychosocial care – counselling for alcohol de-addiction, support for depression and body-image changes; involve the family.

3. Health education

  • No alcohol at all; avoid NSAIDs, sedatives and unprescribed herbal remedies (some contain liver toxins); paracetamol only in small doses as advised (usually not more than 2 g a day).
  • Low-salt diet, adequate protein, daily weight checks at home.
  • Take lactulose, diuretics and β-blockers regularly; do not stop suddenly.
  • Report vomiting of blood, black stools, confusion, drowsiness, fever, abdominal pain, sudden weight gain or reduced urine immediately.
  • Regular follow-up, endoscopy and ultrasound screening.

4. Assessing severity – Child–Pugh classification

  • Five parameters are scored 1–3 each: serum bilirubin, serum albumin, prothrombin time/INR, ascites and hepatic encephalopathy.
  • Class A (5–6 points) – well-compensated; Class B (7–9) – significant functional compromise; Class C (10–15) – decompensated, with poor survival.
  • The MELD score (bilirubin, INR, creatinine, sodium) is used to prioritise patients for liver transplantation.

5. Prevention of cirrhosis (community role of the nurse)

  • Hepatitis B vaccination, including the birth dose under the Universal Immunisation Programme, and vaccination of health workers.
  • Safe injection practices, screening of donated blood, no sharing of razors or needles, safe sex.
  • Awareness about the harmful effects of alcohol; referral for de-addiction.
  • Prevention of fatty liver – weight control, regular exercise, control of diabetes and lipids.
  • Early testing and free treatment of hepatitis B and C under the National Viral Hepatitis Control Programme.

6. Nursing care during abdominal paracentesis (summary)

  • Before – explain, obtain consent, ask the patient to empty the bladder, record weight, abdominal girth and baseline vital signs; position upright or semi-Fowler's.
  • During – maintain asepsis, monitor pulse and BP, watch for pallor, sweating or dizziness, and control the rate of drainage as ordered.
  • After – record the amount and colour of fluid, send samples, apply a dressing, give albumin as ordered, and watch for hypotension, leakage from the site, infection and confusion (encephalopathy).

Nursing importance Cirrhosis patients deteriorate quickly with bleeding, infection or encephalopathy; daily weight and girth, careful observation of mental state and bleeding, salt restriction and teaching by nurses prevent many admissions and deaths.

Conclusion Cirrhosis is irreversible scarring of the liver causing liver failure and portal hypertension; treatment of the cause, control of ascites, varices and encephalopathy, good nutrition and vigilant nursing care improve survival and quality of life.

question: Explain the clinical features, management and post-operative nursing care of a patient with cholelithiasis.
answer_html:
Definition Cholelithiasis is the presence of stones (calculi) in the gallbladder. Gallstones are very common in northern and eastern India. Inflammation of the gallbladder is cholecystitis, and stones in the common bile duct are choledocholithiasis.

1. Types and risk factors

  • Cholesterol stones (most common), pigment stones (black – haemolysis, cirrhosis; brown – infection), mixed stones.
  • Risk factors – the "5 Fs": female, fat (obese), fertile (multiparous), forty, fair; pregnancy, oral contraceptives, rapid weight loss, diabetes, haemolytic anaemias (sickle cell disease, thalassaemia), cirrhosis, family history.

2. Clinical features

  • Many stones are silent (found on ultrasound).
  • Biliary colic – severe pain in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium, often after a fatty meal or at night, radiating to the right shoulder or scapula, lasting 30 minutes to a few hours, with nausea and vomiting.
  • Dyspepsia, flatulence, bloating and fat intolerance.
  • Complications – acute cholecystitis (fever, persistent pain, Murphy's sign), obstructive jaundice (dark urine, clay-coloured stools, itching), cholangitis (Charcot's triad – fever with rigors, jaundice, right upper quadrant pain), gallstone pancreatitis, empyema or gangrene of the gallbladder, and carcinoma of the gallbladder.

3. Diagnosis Ultrasound abdomen (investigation of choice), LFT (raised bilirubin and ALP in duct obstruction), CBC, serum lipase, MRCP for duct stones, ERCP (diagnostic and therapeutic).

4. Management

  • Biliary colic/cholecystitis – NPO, IV fluids, analgesics (NSAIDs such as diclofenac, opioids), antiemetics, IV antibiotics for cholecystitis.
  • Laparoscopic cholecystectomy – the gold standard for symptomatic gallstones (early cholecystectomy in acute cholecystitis).
  • ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction for common bile duct stones; open surgery with CBD exploration and T-tube when needed.
  • Ursodeoxycholic acid for small cholesterol stones in patients unfit for surgery (rarely used).

5. Post-operative nursing care (laparoscopic cholecystectomy)

  • PACU care, then semi-Fowler's position; vital signs as per protocol.
  • Shoulder-tip pain – due to CO₂ gas irritating the diaphragm; relieve with early ambulation, analgesics and reassurance (it settles in 1–2 days).
  • Pain relief and breathing exercises – deep breathing and coughing (especially after open surgery with a subcostal incision, which makes breathing painful).
  • Diet – sips of water and fluids within a few hours when nausea settles; progress to a light diet the same day or next day.
  • Wound care of port sites; drain care – record the amount and colour; report bile-stained drainage.
  • Watch for complications – bleeding, bile leak (increasing abdominal pain, fever, distension), jaundice, infection, retained duct stones.
  • Most patients go home within 24–48 hours.

6. Discharge teaching

  • Resume normal activities in 1–2 weeks; avoid heavy lifting for 2–4 weeks.
  • Diet – a low-fat diet for a few weeks if fatty food causes discomfort, then a normal balanced diet; avoid large heavy meals.
  • Some people have loose stools for a few weeks – usually settles.
  • Report fever, jaundice, dark urine, clay-coloured stools, severe abdominal pain or wound discharge.

Nursing importance Early recognition of complications such as cholangitis and bile leak, effective pain relief and teaching help patients recover quickly after cholecystectomy.

Conclusion Gallstones cause biliary colic and serious complications; laparoscopic cholecystectomy with good post-operative nursing care is the definitive treatment.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Digestive System Disorders
question: Explain stoma care with special reference to stoma complications and patient education.
answer_html:
Introduction A stoma is a surgically created opening of the bowel or urinary tract on the abdominal wall – colostomy (colon), ileostomy (ileum) or urostomy (ileal conduit). Good stoma care prevents skin damage and complications and helps the patient return to a normal life.

1. Post-operative assessment of the stoma

  • Colour – a healthy stoma is pink to beefy red and moist; a dusky, dark purple or black stoma indicates ischaemia or necrosis – report immediately.
  • Size and swelling – oedema is normal and settles over 6–8 weeks; measure the stoma regularly and adjust the appliance size.
  • Height – an ileostomy should protrude about 2–3 cm (so that the corrosive effluent drops into the pouch); a colostomy is flatter.
  • Output – an ileostomy starts working within 24–48 hours with liquid output; a colostomy usually within 2–5 days, with gradually formed stools.
  • Peristomal skin – should be intact and free of redness.

2. Pouching and skin care (brief)

  • Clean the skin with warm water and dry thoroughly; avoid soaps, oils and spirit.
  • Cut the base plate 2–3 mm larger than the stoma so the skin is protected without pressing on the stoma.
  • Use skin-barrier paste, powder or rings when needed.
  • Empty the drainable pouch when one-third to half full; change the appliance every 3–5 days or immediately if it leaks.

3. Stoma complications | Complication | Features | Nursing action | |---|---|---| | Necrosis | Dark, black stoma (early) | Report immediately | | Peristomal skin irritation | Redness, soreness, itching due to leakage of effluent or allergy | Correct fitting, barrier products, treat fungal infection | | High output (ileostomy) | Output above 1.5–2 litres/day, thirst, dizziness | Oral rehydration solution, fluids, salt; antidiarrhoeals as ordered | | Retraction | Stoma sinks below skin level | Convex appliance; surgeon review | | Prolapse | Bowel protrudes excessively | Larger pouch, report | | Stenosis | Narrowing, difficult passage of stool | Report; dilatation or surgery | | Parastomal hernia | Bulge around the stoma | Support belt; avoid heavy lifting | | Food bolus obstruction (ileostomy) | Cramps, no output, swelling | Avoid high-fibre foods; seek help |

4. Patient education

  • Self-care – teach and supervise emptying and changing the pouch; involve a family member.
  • Diet
    • Ileostomy – drink 2–3 litres of fluid daily and add a little extra salt; chew food well; introduce high-fibre foods (corn, nuts, coconut, mushrooms, raw vegetables, fruit skins) slowly to avoid blockage.
    • Foods that thicken output – banana, curd rice, boiled potatoes, white bread, khichdi.
    • Foods causing gas or odour – beans, cabbage, onion, eggs, fish, carbonated drinks – take in moderation.
  • Medicines – enteric-coated and slow-release tablets may pass out unabsorbed through an ileostomy; avoid laxatives unless advised.
  • Daily life – the patient can bathe with or without the pouch, wear normal clothes, travel (carry extra supplies), return to work, and resume sexual activity; avoid heavy lifting and contact sports.
  • Psychological support – address body-image concerns, fear of smell and leakage; link with ostomy support groups (for example, the Ostomy Association of India) and stoma nurses.
  • When to seek help – change in stoma colour, bleeding, no output for 6 hours or more (ileostomy) with cramps, very high output with dehydration, persistent skin breakdown.

Nursing importance Skilled stoma care and teaching restore the patient's independence and dignity and prevent complications such as dehydration and skin breakdown.

Conclusion Stoma care includes regular assessment of the stoma, correct pouching and skin care, early detection of complications and thorough education for self-care and normal living.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Digestive System Disorders
question: Explain the emergency management of a patient with upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
answer_html:
Definition Upper gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding is bleeding from the GI tract above the ligament of Treitz (oesophagus, stomach, duodenum). It presents as haematemesis (vomiting of fresh red blood or "coffee-ground" material) and/or malaena (black, tarry, foul-smelling stools); massive bleeding may cause fresh blood per rectum.

1. Common causes

  • Peptic ulcer (commonest), oesophageal and gastric varices (cirrhosis – common in India), erosive gastritis (NSAIDs, alcohol, stress), Mallory–Weiss tear (after forceful vomiting), oesophagitis, gastric cancer, vascular malformations.

2. Assessment

  • Amount and colour of blood vomited, stools, onset; history of NSAIDs, alcohol, liver disease, anticoagulants.
  • Signs of shock – tachycardia, hypotension, postural drop, cold clammy skin, oliguria, confusion; shock index above 0.9.
  • Risk scores – Glasgow-Blatchford score (helps decide who needs urgent intervention).

3. Emergency management

  1. Airway – position on the side with the head turned to prevent aspiration; suction ready; oxygen.
  2. Two large-bore IV cannulas; blood for grouping and cross-matching, CBC, coagulation profile, LFT, urea and creatinine.
  3. Fluid resuscitation with crystalloids; blood transfusion – usually when Hb is below 7 g/dl (8 g/dl in heart disease) or in active massive bleeding; FFP and platelets for coagulopathy.
  4. Nil by mouth until endoscopy.
  5. Drugs as ordered
    • IV proton-pump inhibitor (pantoprazole) for ulcer bleeding.
    • Suspected variceal bleeding – terlipressin or octreotide and prophylactic antibiotics (ceftriaxone).
  6. Urgent upper GI endoscopy – within 24 hours (within 12 hours for varices) for diagnosis and therapy: injection of adrenaline, clips, thermal coagulation, band ligation of varices.
  7. If endoscopy fails – balloon tamponade (varices), angiographic embolisation, TIPS or surgery.

4. Nursing responsibilities

  • Monitor vital signs every 15 minutes, SpO₂, level of consciousness and hourly urine output (urinary catheter).
  • Record the amount and character of vomitus and stools; check stools for malaena.
  • Safe transfusion – two-person check, monitoring for reactions and overload.
  • Oral hygiene after each episode of vomiting (blood leaves a bad taste and smell).
  • Calm, reassuring care; stay with the patient; explain procedures; support the family.
  • Prepare the patient for endoscopy (consent, NPO, removal of dentures, IV access) and care after it (watch for perforation – chest or abdominal pain, fever).
  • Watch for rebleeding – fresh haematemesis, malaena, rising pulse, falling BP or Hb.
  • In cirrhotic patients watch for hepatic encephalopathy after bleeding (give lactulose as ordered).

5. Health education Avoid NSAIDs, aspirin and alcohol; complete H. pylori treatment; take β-blockers and attend band-ligation sessions for varices; report black stools early.

Nursing importance Upper GI bleeding can quickly lead to shock and death; rapid resuscitation, close monitoring and early endoscopy, coordinated by the nurse, save lives.

Conclusion Upper GI bleeding needs immediate airway protection, IV access, fluid and blood replacement, specific drugs and urgent endoscopy, with careful nursing observation for shock and rebleeding.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Digestive System Disorders
question: Explain the causes, clinical features and management of intestinal obstruction.
answer_html:
Definition Intestinal obstruction is a partial or complete blockage of the forward passage of intestinal contents through the small or large bowel. It is a common surgical emergency.

1. Causes (a) Mechanical (dynamic) obstruction

  • Adhesions after previous abdominal surgery – commonest cause of small-bowel obstruction in adults.
  • Obstructed or strangulated hernia (inguinal, femoral, umbilical, incisional).
  • Volvulus (twisting of the bowel – sigmoid volvulus is common in parts of India), intussusception (infants and children).
  • Tumours – carcinoma of the colon (common in the elderly).
  • Strictures – ileocaecal tuberculosis, Crohn's disease.

  • Faecal impaction, worm bolus (Ascaris) in children, gallstone ileus, foreign bodies. (b) Adynamic (functional) obstruction – paralytic ileus

  • After abdominal surgery, peritonitis, hypokalaemia, spinal injury, drugs (opioids, anticholinergics). (c) Simple vs strangulated – in strangulation the blood supply is cut off, leading to gangrene and perforation – an emergency.

2. Clinical features (cardinal features)

  1. Colicky abdominal pain – central (small bowel) or lower abdominal (large bowel); constant severe pain suggests strangulation.
  2. Vomiting – early and bilious in high small-bowel obstruction; late and faeculent in low obstruction.
  3. Abdominal distension – more marked in large-bowel obstruction; visible peristalsis.
  4. Absolute constipation – no passage of stool or flatus. - Bowel sounds – high-pitched, tinkling in mechanical obstruction; absent in paralytic ileus. - Dehydration, tachycardia, oliguria; signs of strangulation – fever, tenderness, guarding, shock, raised WBC.

3. Investigations Erect and supine abdominal X-ray – dilated bowel loops with multiple air-fluid levels; CT abdomen (site and cause); serum electrolytes, urea, creatinine, CBC, ABG, serum lactate (strangulation).

4. Management

  • "Drip and suck" – nil by mouth, nasogastric tube decompression, IV fluids and electrolytes (especially potassium).
  • Urinary catheter and strict intake–output; analgesics; antibiotics as ordered.
  • Conservative treatment for adhesive obstruction and paralytic ileus (often resolves in 48–72 hours); water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin) may help.
  • Surgery – urgent laparotomy for strangulation, complete obstruction or failure of conservative treatment: release of adhesions, reduction and repair of hernia, resection and anastomosis, or stoma; endoscopic decompression for sigmoid volvulus.

5. Nursing management

  • Keep the NG tube patent; record the amount and nature of aspirate; give oral and nasal care.
  • Monitor vital signs, abdominal girth, bowel sounds, passage of flatus and stool, urine output and electrolytes.
  • Report signs of strangulation or perforation – continuous pain, fever, rising pulse, rigidity.
  • Semi-Fowler's position; pain relief; emotional support.
  • Pre- and post-operative care, including stoma care if a stoma is formed; early ambulation after surgery to prevent further adhesions and ileus.

Nursing importance Accurate fluid balance, NG decompression and early detection of strangulation by the nurse prevent bowel gangrene, perforation and death.

Conclusion Intestinal obstruction may be mechanical or paralytic; "drip and suck", correction of fluids and electrolytes and timely surgery, supported by close nursing observation, are the keys to management.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Digestive System Disorders
question: Define peritonitis. Explain its causes, clinical features and nursing management.
answer_html:
Definition Peritonitis is inflammation of the peritoneum, the serous membrane lining the abdominal cavity, usually due to bacterial infection or chemical irritation. It may be localised (abscess) or generalised, and is a life-threatening surgical emergency.

1. Types and causes

  • Primary (spontaneous) – infection of ascitic fluid without a perforation – spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in cirrhosis, peritonitis in nephrotic syndrome.
  • Secondary (commonest) – due to perforation or leakage of an abdominal organ:
    • Perforated peptic ulcer, perforated appendix, typhoid ileal perforation (important in India), perforated diverticulum or tumour.
