    • Strangulated bowel, abdominal trauma, anastomotic leak after surgery, ruptured ectopic pregnancy, pelvic inflammatory disease.
  • Chemical peritonitis – bile, pancreatic juice, gastric acid; later becomes infected.
  • Tuberculous peritonitis – chronic, with ascites and doughy abdomen.
  • Tertiary peritonitis – persistent infection in critically ill patients.

2. Clinical features

  • Severe abdominal pain, worse on movement and coughing; the patient lies still with knees drawn up.
  • Fever, tachycardia, nausea and vomiting, anorexia.
  • Tenderness, guarding, rebound tenderness and board-like rigidity (generalised peritonitis).
  • Abdominal distension, absent bowel sounds (paralytic ileus).
  • Dehydration, oliguria, hypotension and septic shock in late cases; sunken eyes and pinched face (Hippocratic facies).

3. Investigations CBC (leucocytosis), erect chest X-ray – free gas under the diaphragm in perforation, ultrasound and CT, serum electrolytes, urea, creatinine, lactate, blood culture; diagnostic paracentesis in ascites (neutrophils above 250/mm³ in SBP).

4. Management

  • Resuscitation – IV fluids, oxygen, correction of electrolytes; urinary catheter.
  • Nil by mouth and nasogastric aspiration to rest the bowel.
  • Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (covering Gram-negative and anaerobic organisms).
  • Analgesia.
  • Surgery for secondary peritonitis – laparotomy (or laparoscopy), closure of the perforation or removal of the source, thorough peritoneal lavage and drainage; sometimes a stoma.
  • SBP – IV antibiotics (cefotaxime/ceftriaxone) with albumin; no surgery.

5. Nursing management

  • Semi-Fowler's (Fowler's) position – helps localise pus in the pelvis (where absorption is slower) and eases breathing.
  • Monitor vital signs, SpO₂, urine output hourly, abdominal girth and level of consciousness; report signs of septic shock.
  • Maintain IV fluids and an accurate intake–output chart; keep the NG tube patent; oral and nasal care.
  • Give antibiotics and analgesics on time.
  • After surgery – drain care (record amount and nature), aseptic wound care, deep breathing, early ambulation, nutrition (enteral or parenteral when needed).
  • Watch for residual abscesses (subphrenic, pelvic) – persistent fever, pain, diarrhoea; wound infection and dehiscence.
  • Emotional support for the patient and family.

Nursing importance Peritonitis can progress rapidly to septic shock; early recognition, resuscitation, timely surgery and good post-operative nursing care greatly reduce deaths.

Conclusion Peritonitis is inflammation of the peritoneum, usually from perforation of an abdominal organ; resuscitation, antibiotics, surgical source control and vigilant nursing care are life-saving.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Digestive System Disorders
question: Explain the types, clinical features and nursing management of a patient with inguinal hernia undergoing hernioplasty.
answer_html:
Definition A hernia is the protrusion of a viscus or part of a viscus through a weakness or opening in the wall of the cavity that contains it. Inguinal hernia is the commonest type, especially in men.

1. Types (a) By site – inguinal, femoral (more common in women), umbilical and paraumbilical, incisional (through an old surgical scar), epigastric, hiatus hernia (diaphragm). (b) Inguinal hernia

  • Indirect – passes through the deep inguinal ring along the spermatic cord, may descend into the scrotum; congenital (patent processus vaginalis); commonest type at all ages.

  • Direct – bulges through a weak posterior wall (Hesselbach's triangle); acquired, in older men; rarely enters the scrotum. (c) By condition

  • Reducible – goes back on lying down or with gentle pressure.

  • Irreducible (incarcerated) – cannot be pushed back.
  • Obstructed – bowel in the hernia is obstructed.
  • Strangulated – blood supply is cut off – surgical emergency.

2. Risk factors (raised abdominal pressure) Chronic cough (smoking, COPD, TB), chronic constipation, straining at micturition (enlarged prostate), heavy lifting, obesity, pregnancy, ascites, previous surgery.

3. Clinical features

  • Swelling in the groin that appears on standing, coughing or straining and disappears on lying down; expansile cough impulse.
  • Dragging pain or discomfort; scrotal swelling in indirect hernia.
  • Strangulation – painful, tense, tender, irreducible swelling without cough impulse, vomiting, abdominal distension, fever, tachycardia.

4. Treatment

  • Surgery is the definitive treatment – hernioplasty (tension-free mesh repair – Lichtenstein repair – the standard), herniorrhaphy (suture repair), or laparoscopic repair (TEP/TAPP).
  • Treat the precipitating factor first – cough, constipation, prostate enlargement.
  • Strangulated hernia – emergency surgery with resection of gangrenous bowel.
  • A truss is used only if the patient is unfit for surgery.

5. Nursing management Pre-operative – treat cough and constipation; teach deep breathing and splinting; usual pre-operative preparation; check that the patient voids before surgery. Post-operative

  • Pain relief; apply an ice pack and scrotal support (suspensory bandage) to reduce scrotal swelling.
  • Avoid straining – stool softeners, high-fibre diet and fluids; splint the incision with the hand or a pillow while coughing or sneezing.
  • Early ambulation (same day); watch for urinary retention (common after spinal anaesthesia and in older men) – help the patient stand to void.

  • Wound care; watch for haematoma, infection and scrotal swelling. Discharge teaching

  • Avoid heavy lifting and strenuous work for about 4–6 weeks after open repair (about 2 weeks after laparoscopic repair); walking is encouraged.

  • Prevent recurrence – stop smoking, treat chronic cough, prevent constipation, reduce weight, use correct lifting technique (bend knees, keep back straight).
  • Report swelling, redness, fever or recurrence of the bulge.

Nursing importance Preventing straining and teaching safe activity after surgery reduce the risk of recurrence; early recognition of strangulation prevents bowel gangrene.

Conclusion Inguinal hernia is a protrusion through a weak groin wall; mesh hernioplasty with good post-operative care and correction of predisposing factors gives a lasting cure.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Digestive System Disorders
question: Explain haemorrhoids, fissure-in-ano and fistula-in-ano, with the post-operative nursing care.
answer_html:
Introduction Anorectal disorders – haemorrhoids, fissures and fistulas – are very common and are often hidden by patients out of embarrassment. Chronic constipation and a low-fibre diet are major causes.

1. Haemorrhoids (piles)

  • Definition – dilated, congested vascular cushions of the anal canal.
  • Types – internal (above the dentate line, painless) and external (below it, painful when thrombosed).
  • Grades of internal haemorrhoids – I: bleed, no prolapse; II: prolapse and reduce spontaneously; III: prolapse and need manual reduction; IV: permanently prolapsed.
  • Causes – chronic constipation and straining, low-fibre diet, pregnancy, prolonged sitting, heavy lifting, portal hypertension.
  • Features – painless bright red bleeding after defecation (splash in the pan or streaks on stool), prolapse, mucus discharge, itching, anaemia; pain if thrombosed.
  • Treatment – high-fibre diet, fluids, stool softeners (isabgol), sitz baths, topical agents; rubber band ligation, sclerotherapy, infrared coagulation (grades I–III); haemorrhoidectomy, stapled haemorrhoidopexy or laser for grades III–IV.

2. Fissure-in-ano

  • Definition – a longitudinal tear in the lining of the anal canal, usually in the posterior midline.
  • Cause – passage of hard stools; also childbirth, diarrhoea.
  • Features – severe sharp pain during and after defecation ("like passing broken glass"), lasting hours; streak of bright blood; a sentinel pile in chronic fissure; fear of passing stool worsens constipation.
  • Treatment – fibre, fluids, stool softeners, warm sitz baths, local anaesthetic gel, topical glyceryl trinitrate or diltiazem; lateral internal sphincterotomy for chronic fissures.

3. Fistula-in-ano

  • Definition – an abnormal tract connecting the anal canal or rectum to the perianal skin, usually after an anorectal abscess.
  • Features – recurrent discharge of pus or blood near the anus, perianal itching, pain and swelling when blocked.
  • Consider tuberculosis and Crohn's disease in recurrent cases.
  • Treatment – fistulotomy, fistulectomy, seton, advanced flap procedures; Kshar Sutra (a medicated Ayurvedic thread) is also used in India.

4. Post-operative nursing care (anorectal surgery)

  • Pain relief – analgesics on time; warm sitz baths 2–3 times a day and after each bowel movement (relieve pain and spasm, keep the area clean).
  • First bowel movement – may be painful; give stool softeners and laxatives as ordered; high-fibre diet and 2–3 litres of fluid; give analgesic before defecation.
  • Observe for bleeding – check dressings and stools; report heavy bleeding.
  • Urinary retention is common – encourage voiding; warm compress; catheterise if ordered.
  • Perianal hygiene – wash with water after defecation and pat dry; change pads; wound packing for fistula as ordered.
  • Position – side-lying or prone for comfort; sit on a soft cushion; avoid prolonged sitting.
  • Discharge teaching – avoid straining and constipation, respond promptly to the urge to defecate, regular exercise, avoid long periods on the toilet (no reading or mobile phones on the toilet), report bleeding, fever or discharge.

Nursing importance Sensitive, private care, good pain relief and teaching about diet and bowel habits help healing and prevent recurrence.

Conclusion Haemorrhoids, fissures and fistulas are common anorectal conditions; prevention of constipation, appropriate surgical or non-surgical treatment and good post-operative care give relief.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Digestive System Disorders
question: Explain gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and hiatus hernia with nursing management.
answer_html:
Definitions

  • Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is a condition in which reflux of stomach contents into the oesophagus causes troublesome symptoms or complications, usually due to a weak or inappropriately relaxing lower oesophageal sphincter (LES).
  • Hiatus hernia is the protrusion of part of the stomach through the oesophageal hiatus of the diaphragm into the chest. It weakens the anti-reflux barrier and often causes GERD.

1. Types of hiatus hernia

  • Sliding (type I, about 90%) – the gastro-oesophageal junction and upper stomach slide up into the chest; causes reflux.
  • Rolling (para-oesophageal, type II) – the fundus rolls up beside the oesophagus while the junction stays in place; may become strangulated.
  • Mixed types.

2. Risk factors Obesity, pregnancy, smoking, alcohol, large and late meals, lying down after eating, fatty and spicy foods, tea, coffee, chocolate, carbonated drinks, tight clothing, bending and lifting, and drugs (calcium-channel blockers, nitrates, theophylline, anticholinergics).

3. Clinical features

  • Heartburn – retrosternal burning after meals, worse on lying down or bending.
  • Regurgitation of sour or bitter fluid, water brash, belching.
  • Dysphagia or painful swallowing (oesophagitis, stricture).
  • Extra-oesophageal symptoms – chronic cough, hoarseness, asthma, dental erosion, chest pain (must be differentiated from angina).
  • Complications – oesophagitis, bleeding, stricture, Barrett's oesophagus (pre-cancerous), adenocarcinoma.

4. Diagnosis Clinical response to PPIs; upper GI endoscopy; barium swallow (hiatus hernia); 24-hour oesophageal pH monitoring and manometry.

5. Management

  • Lifestyle measures (the basis of treatment).
  • Drugs – antacids and alginates for quick relief; proton-pump inhibitors (most effective) taken 30–60 minutes before breakfast; H₂ blockers; prokinetics in selected patients.
  • Surgery – laparoscopic Nissen fundoplication for refractory GERD or large hiatus hernia; repair of para-oesophageal hernia to prevent strangulation.

6. Nursing management and patient education

  • Small, frequent meals; eat slowly; do not lie down for 2–3 hours after meals; avoid late-night dinners.
  • Raise the head end of the bed by 15–20 cm with blocks (extra pillows alone bend the abdomen and may worsen reflux).
  • Weight reduction; avoid tight belts and clothes.
  • Avoid trigger foods – fried and spicy food, chocolate, mint, citrus, excess tea and coffee, carbonated drinks; stop smoking and alcohol.
  • Avoid bending and heavy lifting after meals.
  • Take medicines correctly; review drugs that worsen reflux with the doctor.
  • Report difficulty in swallowing, weight loss, vomiting of blood or black stools (alarm features needing endoscopy).
  • After fundoplication – soft diet, small meals, avoid gas-forming foods; temporary difficulty in swallowing and inability to belch or vomit may occur.

Nursing importance Most patients with GERD improve with lifestyle changes and correct use of PPIs; the nurse's teaching is therefore central to management.

Conclusion GERD is reflux of gastric contents due to a weak LES, often with a hiatus hernia; lifestyle measures, PPIs and, when needed, fundoplication relieve symptoms and prevent complications.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Digestive System Disorders
question: Differentiate between amoebic and pyogenic liver abscess and explain the nursing management.
answer_html:
Definition A liver abscess is a localised collection of pus within the liver. In India, amoebic liver abscess is common because of poor sanitation and unsafe water, while pyogenic liver abscess is increasing among diabetics and elderly patients.

1. Differences | Feature | Amoebic liver abscess | Pyogenic liver abscess | |---|---|---| | Cause | Entamoeba histolytica (from intestinal amoebiasis via portal vein) | Bacteria – E. coli, Klebsiella (diabetics), streptococci, anaerobes | | Source | Contaminated food and water | Biliary infection (cholangitis), appendicitis, diverticulitis, bloodstream, trauma | | Patient | Young adult men, alcohol use | Elderly, diabetics, biliary disease, cancer | | Number and site | Usually single, right lobe | Often multiple | | Pus | Thick, chocolate-brown "anchovy sauce", odourless | Yellow, foul-smelling pus | | Onset | Subacute | Acute, toxic | | Diagnosis | Ultrasound, amoebic serology (ELISA) | Ultrasound/CT, blood and pus culture | | Treatment | Metronidazole + luminal agent; aspiration if needed | IV antibiotics + drainage |

2. Clinical features

  • Fever (with chills and rigors in pyogenic abscess), sweating, malaise, anorexia, weight loss.
  • Right upper quadrant pain, often referred to the right shoulder; pain on breathing or coughing.
  • Tender enlarged liver, intercostal tenderness; jaundice in some (more in pyogenic).
  • Chest X-ray – raised right hemidiaphragm, right pleural effusion.
  • Complications – rupture into the pleura, lung (coughing up "anchovy sauce" sputum), peritoneum or pericardium (left-lobe abscess – very dangerous), septicaemia.

3. Management

  • Amoebic – metronidazole 750 mg three times daily for 7–10 days, followed by a luminal amoebicide (diloxanide furoate or paromomycin) to clear intestinal cysts; ultrasound-guided aspiration if the abscess is large, in the left lobe, about to rupture, or not improving within 3–5 days.
  • Pyogenic – broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (for example, ceftriaxone with metronidazole) for several weeks, together with percutaneous needle aspiration or catheter (pigtail) drainage; surgery for rupture or multiloculated abscesses; treat the biliary source and control diabetes.

4. Nursing management

  • Fever care – tepid sponging, antipyretics, fluids; monitor temperature.
  • Pain relief; comfortable semi-Fowler's position; deep breathing (to prevent basal atelectasis).
  • Nutrition – high-calorie, high-protein diet with plenty of fluids.
  • Drug teaching – complete the full course; avoid alcohol with metronidazole (vomiting, flushing – disulfiram-like reaction); metallic taste is common.
  • Drain care – maintain patency, record output, aseptic care of the site.
  • Watch for rupture – sudden severe pain, breathlessness, chest pain, shock; monitor blood sugar in diabetics.
  • Prevention – safe drinking water (boiled or filtered), hand washing before eating and after using the toilet, food hygiene, sanitation (Swachh Bharat), treatment of intestinal amoebiasis and screening of family members.

Nursing importance Timely drug therapy, drain care and monitoring for rupture, together with health education on safe water and hygiene, ensure recovery and prevent recurrence.

Conclusion Amoebic liver abscess is single and responds to metronidazole, while pyogenic abscess is often multiple and needs antibiotics with drainage; good nursing care and hygiene education are essential.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Digestive System Disorders
question: Explain malabsorption syndrome with its nursing management.
answer_html:
Definition Malabsorption syndrome is a group of disorders in which there is defective digestion or absorption of nutrients (fats, proteins, carbohydrates, vitamins and minerals) from the small intestine, leading to diarrhoea, weight loss and nutritional deficiencies.

1. Causes

  • Maldigestion – chronic pancreatitis (lack of enzymes), bile salt deficiency (obstructive jaundice, liver disease), after gastrectomy.
  • Mucosal disease – coeliac disease (gluten sensitivity – increasingly diagnosed in north India), tropical sprue (common in India), Crohn's disease, intestinal tuberculosis, Giardia and other infections, HIV enteropathy.
  • Enzyme deficiency – lactose intolerance.
  • Short bowel syndrome after extensive resection; bacterial overgrowth.

2. Clinical features

  • Chronic diarrhoea; steatorrhoea – pale, bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stools that float and are hard to flush.
  • Abdominal bloating, flatulence, cramps; weight loss, fatigue and weakness.
  • Deficiency features
    • Iron, folate or vitamin B₁₂ – anaemia, glossitis, angular stomatitis.
    • Vitamin D and calcium – bone pain, osteomalacia, tetany.
    • Vitamin K – easy bruising and bleeding.
    • Vitamin A – night blindness.
    • Protein – oedema, muscle wasting; growth failure in children.

3. Investigations Stool for fat (Sudan stain, 72-hour faecal fat), stool for parasites; CBC, serum iron, B₁₂, folate, calcium, albumin; anti-tissue transglutaminase (tTG) antibodies for coeliac disease; upper GI endoscopy with duodenal biopsy; D-xylose test; lactose tolerance test; imaging for pancreatic disease.

4. Management

  • Coeliac disease – lifelong strict gluten-free diet – avoid wheat, barley and rye (chapati, bread, suji, maida, biscuits); allowed – rice, jowar, bajra, ragi, maize, pulses, millets, fruits, vegetables, milk, eggs, meat.
  • Tropical sprue – folic acid and tetracycline for 3–6 months; vitamin B₁₂.
  • Lactose intolerance – avoid or reduce milk; curd and buttermilk are usually tolerated.
  • Pancreatic insufficiency – pancreatic enzyme capsules with every meal; stop alcohol.
  • Treat infections (Giardia, TB); replace vitamins, iron, calcium, folate and B₁₂; medium-chain triglyceride oils in fat malabsorption.

5. Nursing management

  • Record stools – frequency, consistency, colour, presence of fat; maintain an intake–output chart; daily weight.
  • Fluid and electrolyte replacement – ORS, IV fluids if dehydrated; monitor potassium.
  • Dietary counselling with the dietitian – high-calorie, high-protein, easily digestible diet; gluten-free diet teaching with reading of food labels and avoiding hidden gluten (sauces, processed foods).
  • Give supplements and enzyme capsules correctly (with meals).
  • Perianal skin care – gentle washing, barrier cream.
  • Prevent infection and fatigue; plan rest periods.
  • Psychological support – lifelong diet changes are difficult; involve the family; regular follow-up of weight, Hb and growth.

Nursing importance The nurse's role in identifying deficiency signs, monitoring stools and weight and teaching diet is central, because most malabsorption disorders are controlled by diet and supplements.

Conclusion Malabsorption syndrome causes diarrhoea, weight loss and deficiencies; identifying the cause and providing the correct diet, supplements and nursing care restore nutrition.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Digestive System Disorders
question: List the clinical signs of acute appendicitis.
answer_html:
Clinical manifestations of acute appendicitis

  1. Periumbilical pain shifting to the right iliac fossa, with anorexia, nausea and vomiting, and low-grade fever.
  2. Tenderness at McBurney's point – one-third of the way from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus.
  3. Rebound tenderness (Blumberg's sign) and guarding in the right iliac fossa.
  4. Rovsing's sign – pressure on the left iliac fossa produces pain in the right iliac fossa.
  5. Psoas sign – pain on extension of the right hip (retrocaecal appendix).
  6. Obturator sign – pain on internal rotation of the flexed right hip (pelvic appendix).
  7. Pain on coughing (Dunphy's sign); tachycardia; leucocytosis.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Digestive System Disorders
question: What is dumping syndrome? How is it prevented?
answer_html:
Dumping syndrome is a group of symptoms caused by rapid emptying of hypertonic stomach contents into the jejunum, usually after gastrectomy or gastric bypass surgery.

  • Early dumping (10–30 minutes after a meal) – fluid shifts into the bowel → abdominal cramps, fullness, diarrhoea, palpitations, sweating, dizziness, flushing.
  • Late dumping (1–3 hours after a meal) – rapid sugar absorption causes excess insulin → hypoglycaemia (sweating, tremors, confusion).

Prevention

  1. Small, frequent meals – 6 a day.
  2. High protein and fat, low simple sugars (avoid sweets and sugary drinks).
  3. Avoid fluids with meals – drink 30–60 minutes before or after.
  4. Lie down for 20–30 minutes after meals; octreotide in severe cases.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Digestive System Disorders
question: Define hepatic encephalopathy. List its grades.
answer_html:
Hepatic encephalopathy is a reversible neuropsychiatric syndrome in patients with severe liver disease, caused mainly by ammonia and other toxins reaching the brain because the liver cannot detoxify them.

Precipitating factors – GI bleeding, infection, constipation, high protein load, dehydration, low potassium, sedatives, alcohol.

Grades (West Haven)

  1. Grade I – mild confusion, short attention span, sleep reversal.
  2. Grade II – drowsiness, disorientation, inappropriate behaviour, flapping tremor (asterixis).
  3. Grade III – somnolent but rousable, marked confusion, incoherent speech.
  4. Grade IV – coma.

Treatment – lactulose, rifaximin, correction of precipitating causes.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Digestive System Disorders
question: What are Cullen's sign and Grey Turner's sign?
answer_html:
Both are signs of retroperitoneal or intra-abdominal haemorrhage, in which blood tracks through tissue planes to the skin.

  1. Cullen's sign – bluish-purple discoloration (bruising) around the umbilicus.
  2. Grey Turner's sign – bruising of the flanks (loins).

Seen in – severe (haemorrhagic) acute pancreatitis (usually 24–48 hours after onset), ruptured ectopic pregnancy, ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm and blunt abdominal trauma. Significance – they indicate severe disease and a poorer prognosis; the patient needs close monitoring of pulse, BP, haemoglobin and urine output for shock, and the doctor should be informed at once.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Digestive System Disorders
question: What is Murphy's sign?
answer_html:
Murphy's sign is a clinical sign of acute cholecystitis.

Method – the examiner places the fingers or hand below the right costal margin in the mid-clavicular line (over the gallbladder) and asks the patient to take a deep breath. Positive sign – as the inflamed gallbladder descends and touches the examining hand, the patient feels sharp pain and suddenly stops breathing in (inspiratory arrest). The same manoeuvre on the left side does not cause pain.

A sonographic Murphy's sign is maximum tenderness when the ultrasound probe presses over the gallbladder.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Digestive System Disorders
question: What is a T-tube? Write the nursing care of a patient with a T-tube.
answer_html:
A T-tube is a T-shaped latex or silicone tube placed in the common bile duct after CBD exploration (choledocholithotomy). It drains bile while oedema of the duct subsides and allows a later T-tube cholangiogram.

Nursing care

  1. Connect to a closed sterile drainage bag kept below the level of the abdomen; prevent kinks and pulling.
  2. Measure and record bile output every shift – usually about 300–500 ml/day at first, decreasing as bile flows into the duodenum; report excessive drainage or sudden stoppage.
  3. Observe colour (golden-green), and watch for bile leakage, jaundice, clay stools, fever.
  4. Protect the skin around the tube (bile is irritant); aseptic dressing.
  5. Do not clamp unless ordered; clamping trials and removal (often after 10–14 days) are done by the surgeon.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Digestive System Disorders
question: What is achalasia cardia?
answer_html:
Achalasia cardia is a motility disorder of the oesophagus in which the lower oesophageal sphincter fails to relax during swallowing and peristalsis in the oesophageal body is absent, due to degeneration of the myenteric (Auerbach's) nerve plexus.

Features – progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids, regurgitation of undigested food (especially at night), chest pain, weight loss, aspiration pneumonia. Diagnosis – barium swallow ("bird's beak" narrowing with dilated oesophagus), manometry (confirmatory), endoscopy. Treatment – pneumatic balloon dilatation, laparoscopic Heller's myotomy, POEM (per-oral endoscopic myotomy), botulinum toxin injection. Nursing – small meals eaten slowly in an upright position, plenty of water with meals, head elevated during sleep.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Cardiovascular Disorders (including BCLS)
question: (a) Define hypertension and classify it. (3 marks) (b) Explain the risk factors, clinical features and complications of hypertension. (5 marks) (c) Describe the management and nursing care of a patient with hypertension, including health education. (7 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Definition and classification (3 marks) Hypertension is a condition in which the arterial blood pressure is persistently raised – in adults, a systolic BP of 140 mmHg or more and/or a diastolic BP of 90 mmHg or more, confirmed on repeated measurements on different occasions. It is called the "silent killer" because it usually causes no symptoms until organs are damaged. About one in four Indian adults has hypertension, and many do not know it.

Classification according to BP level (JNC-7, commonly used) | Category | Systolic (mmHg) | | Diastolic (mmHg) | |---|---|---|---| | Normal | below 120 | and | below 80 | | Pre-hypertension | 120–139 | or | 80–89 | | Stage 1 hypertension | 140–159 | or | 90–99 | | Stage 2 hypertension | 160 or more | or | 100 or more | (The American ACC/AHA 2017 guideline labels 130–139/80–89 as stage 1; Indian programmes use 140/90 as the cut-off for diagnosis and treatment.)

Classification according to cause

  1. Primary (essential) hypertension – no single identifiable cause; 90–95% of cases; results from genetic and lifestyle factors.
  2. Secondary hypertension – due to a known cause:
    • Kidney disease – chronic kidney disease, glomerulonephritis, renal artery stenosis.
    • Endocrine – Cushing's syndrome, primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's), phaeochromocytoma, thyroid disease.
    • Coarctation of the aorta; obstructive sleep apnoea.
    • Pregnancy-induced hypertension, pre-eclampsia.
    • Drugs – oral contraceptives, steroids, NSAIDs, decongestants.

Special forms

  • Isolated systolic hypertension – common in the elderly.
  • White-coat hypertension – high only in the clinic; masked hypertension – normal in the clinic but high at home.
  • Hypertensive crisis – BP 180/120 mmHg or more: urgency (no new organ damage) or emergency (with acute organ damage – stroke, encephalopathy, MI, pulmonary oedema, aortic dissection, eclampsia).

(b) Risk factors, clinical features and complications (5 marks) Risk factors

  • Non-modifiable – increasing age, family history, male sex (until menopause).
  • Modifiable
    • High salt intake – Indians consume about 8–11 g of salt a day against the WHO advice of less than 5 g (pickles, papad, namkeen, processed foods).
    • Overweight and obesity, especially abdominal (waist above 90 cm in men and 80 cm in women in Asians).
    • Physical inactivity, low fruit and vegetable intake (low potassium).
    • Tobacco (smoking and chewing) and alcohol.
    • Stress, poor sleep.
    • Associated diseases – diabetes, dyslipidaemia, chronic kidney disease.

Clinical features

  • Most patients have no symptoms; hypertension is often detected during screening or when complications appear.
  • Possible symptoms – headache (often occipital, in the morning), dizziness, palpitations, fatigue, nosebleeds (epistaxis), blurred vision, breathlessness on exertion, irritability.
  • Signs of target-organ damage – left ventricular hypertrophy, retinal changes, proteinuria.

Complications (target-organ damage)

  1. Heart – left ventricular hypertrophy, coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction, heart failure, arrhythmias.
  2. Brain – stroke (ischaemic and haemorrhagic), transient ischaemic attacks, hypertensive encephalopathy, vascular dementia.
  3. Kidneys – nephrosclerosis, chronic kidney disease, kidney failure.
  4. Eyes – hypertensive retinopathy (narrowed arteries, AV nicking, haemorrhages, papilloedema), loss of vision.
  5. Blood vessels – aortic dissection, aneurysm, peripheral arterial disease.

(c) Management and nursing care (7 marks) 1. Correct diagnosis and assessment

  • Correct BP measurement – patient seated and rested for 5 minutes, back supported, feet flat, arm supported at heart level, correct cuff size (bladder covering about 80% of arm circumference), no smoking, tea or coffee for 30 minutes before, bladder empty; take two readings 1–2 minutes apart and record the average; measure both arms at the first visit.
  • Confirm with repeat clinic readings, home BP monitoring or 24-hour ambulatory BP monitoring.
  • Investigations – urine for protein, serum creatinine and eGFR, electrolytes, blood sugar, lipid profile, ECG, echocardiography and fundoscopy as needed; tests for secondary causes in young or resistant patients.

2. Lifestyle modification (for every patient)

  • Salt restriction – less than 5 g a day (about one teaspoon of salt in total), avoiding pickles, papad, chips, sauces, bakery and processed foods; cook with less salt and do not add salt at the table.
  • DASH-type diet – plenty of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, pulses, low-fat milk; limit fried foods, sweets and red meat.
  • Weight reduction to a healthy BMI (18.5–22.9 kg/m² for Asians) and waist circumference.
  • Regular physical activity – brisk walking or cycling for at least 30 minutes on most days (150 minutes a week); yoga.
  • Stop tobacco in all forms; limit or avoid alcohol.
  • Stress management – relaxation, meditation, adequate sleep.

3. Drug therapy (as prescribed)

  • First-line groups – calcium-channel blockers (amlodipine), ACE inhibitors (enalapril, ramipril) or ARBs (telmisartan, losartan), and thiazide-like diuretics (chlorthalidone, indapamide); β-blockers in special situations (angina, after MI, heart failure).
  • Most patients need two or more drugs; once-daily long-acting drugs and fixed-dose combinations improve adherence.
  • Under the India Hypertension Control Initiative (IHCI), a simple protocol starts with amlodipine and adds telmisartan and chlorthalidone step by step; free drugs are given at government facilities.
  • Target BP – generally below 140/90 mmHg, and below 130/80 mmHg where tolerated (diabetes, kidney disease, high cardiovascular risk).

4. Management of hypertensive emergency

  • Admit to ICU; IV drugs such as labetalol, nicardipine, nitroglycerin or sodium nitroprusside as ordered.
  • Lower the BP gradually – usually by not more than 25% in the first hour, then towards 160/100 mmHg over the next 2–6 hours (rapid lowering can cause stroke or MI), except in aortic dissection where faster control is needed.
  • Continuous monitoring (arterial line), neurological checks, urine output.

5. Nursing care

  • Accurate BP monitoring and recording; report readings above the target or symptoms of target-organ damage (chest pain, severe headache, weakness, visual change, breathlessness, reduced urine).
  • Give drugs on time and observe for side effects:
    • Orthostatic hypotension – advise to rise slowly from lying to sitting to standing.
    • ACE inhibitors – dry cough, high potassium; CCBs – ankle swelling, flushing; diuretics – frequent urination (give in the morning), low potassium.
    • Never stop β-blockers or clonidine suddenly (rebound hypertension).
  • Assess adherence – common reasons for poor control are forgetting doses, stopping drugs when BP is normal, cost and side effects.
  • Plan care with the dietitian for low-salt, heart-healthy meals.

6. Health education

  • Hypertension is lifelong; drugs control but do not cure it – continue medicines even when BP is normal and feeling well.
  • Use pill boxes, phone reminders, link medicines to a daily routine.
  • Home BP monitoring with a validated digital machine; keep a BP diary.
  • Follow the lifestyle measures above; read food labels for sodium.
  • Avoid self-medication with NSAIDs and decongestants.
  • Regular follow-up at the PHC or Ayushman Arogya Mandir; annual tests for kidney, eyes, sugar and lipids.
  • Know warning signs – severe headache, chest pain, breathlessness, weakness or numbness of face or limbs, slurred speech, blurred vision – and seek care immediately.
  • Community role – population-based screening for NCDs of everyone above 30 years under the National Programme for Prevention and Control of NCDs (NP-NCD).

Common nursing diagnoses

  • Risk for decreased cardiac output related to increased afterload.
  • Ineffective health management related to lack of symptoms and complex regimen.
  • Deficient knowledge regarding diet, drugs and complications.
  • Risk for injury related to orthostatic hypotension.

Nursing importance Control of hypertension is one of the most effective ways to prevent strokes, heart attacks and kidney failure; nurses play the central role in screening, accurate measurement, adherence support and lifestyle counselling.

Conclusion Hypertension is persistently raised BP, mostly essential and symptomless, that damages the heart, brain, kidneys and eyes; correct measurement, lifelong lifestyle change, regular drugs and patient education keep it under control.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Cardiovascular Disorders (including BCLS)
question: (a) Define myocardial infarction and list its risk factors. (3 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features and diagnosis. (4 marks) (c) Describe the immediate and subsequent medical and nursing management, including cardiac rehabilitation. (8 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Definition and risk factors (3 marks) Myocardial infarction (MI), commonly called a heart attack, is the death (necrosis) of a part of the heart muscle due to prolonged lack of blood supply, usually caused by sudden blockage of a coronary artery by a thrombus formed over a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque. MI is part of the acute coronary syndrome (ACS), which includes unstable angina, NSTEMI (non-ST-elevation MI) and STEMI (ST-elevation MI). Indians develop coronary disease about a decade earlier than people in Western countries.

Risk factors

  • Non-modifiable – age (men above 45, women above 55 years), male sex, family history of premature heart disease, South Asian ethnicity.
  • Modifiable – smoking and tobacco chewing, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia (high LDL, low HDL, high triglycerides), obesity (especially abdominal), physical inactivity, unhealthy diet (trans fats, fried food, excess salt and sugar), stress, alcohol, air pollution.

(b) Clinical features and diagnosis (4 marks) Clinical features

  • Chest pain – severe, crushing, squeezing or heavy pressure behind the sternum, lasting more than 20–30 minutes, radiating to the left arm, shoulder, jaw, neck or back; not relieved by rest or sublingual nitroglycerin.
  • Sweating, nausea, vomiting, breathlessness, weakness, dizziness, anxiety and a feeling of impending death.
  • Atypical (silent) MI – common in diabetics, elderly and women: only breathlessness, epigastric pain (mistaken for "gas"), fatigue, confusion or fainting.
  • Signs – pallor, cold clammy skin, tachycardia or bradycardia, BP high or low, low-grade fever after 24 hours, crackles and a third heart sound in heart failure, arrhythmias.

Diagnosis

  • 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of arrival:
    • STEMI – ST elevation in two or more contiguous leads (or new left bundle branch block), followed by T-wave inversion and pathological Q waves.
    • NSTEMI/unstable angina – ST depression or T-wave inversion, or a normal ECG.
  • Cardiac biomarkers – a rise and fall of cardiac troponin (most sensitive and specific); CK-MB.
  • Echocardiography – regional wall-motion abnormality, ejection fraction, complications.
  • Other tests – CBC, electrolytes, blood sugar, lipid profile, kidney function, chest X-ray; coronary angiography to define the blocked artery.

(c) Management (8 marks) 1. Immediate management ("time is muscle")

  • Call for help; place the patient at rest in a semi-Fowler's position; reassure.
  • Continuous ECG monitoring, defibrillator at the bedside; IV access; draw blood for troponin and other tests.
  • Oxygen only if SpO₂ is below 90% (or with breathlessness, shock).
  • Aspirin 300–325 mg chewed immediately (unless allergic), plus a P2Y12 inhibitor (clopidogrel or ticagrelor) loading dose, as ordered.
  • Sublingual nitroglycerin 0.4 mg every 5 minutes up to three doses if systolic BP is above 90 mmHg (avoid in right ventricular infarction and after sildenafil use).
  • Morphine IV in small doses for pain not relieved by nitrates; antiemetic.
  • Anticoagulant (unfractionated heparin or enoxaparin), high-dose statin (atorvastatin 80 mg), β-blocker if there is no heart failure, bradycardia or shock.

2. Reperfusion therapy for STEMI (the most important step)

  • Primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) – angioplasty and stenting; ideally within 90 minutes of arrival (door-to-balloon time) at a PCI-capable hospital.
  • Thrombolysis (fibrinolysis) when PCI is not available within 120 minutes – within 30 minutes of arrival (door-to-needle time) and preferably within 12 hours of symptom onset – with streptokinase, tenecteplase (single bolus) or alteplase, followed by transfer for angiography (pharmaco-invasive strategy). Many Indian states run STEMI programmes with a hub-and-spoke model for this purpose.
  • Contraindications to thrombolysis – active bleeding, previous haemorrhagic stroke, ischaemic stroke within 3 months, recent major surgery or head injury, suspected aortic dissection, uncontrolled BP above 180/110 mmHg.
  • CABG (bypass surgery) for multivessel or left main disease.

3. Subsequent management in the CCU/ward

  • Monitoring for complications – arrhythmias (ventricular fibrillation is the commonest cause of early death), heart block, heart failure, cardiogenic shock, mechanical complications (papillary muscle rupture, ventricular septal rupture, free-wall rupture around days 3–7), pericarditis, thromboembolism, ventricular aneurysm.
  • Activity – bed rest for the first 12–24 hours, then progressive mobilisation (sitting, chair, walking in the corridor) as the patient remains pain-free and stable.
  • Diet – soft, light, low-fat, low-salt small meals; avoid heavy meals.
  • Stool softeners to avoid straining (Valsalva manoeuvre can cause arrhythmias).
  • Secondary prevention drugs – aspirin (lifelong), P2Y12 inhibitor (usually 12 months), statin, β-blocker, ACE inhibitor/ARB.

4. Nursing management (i) Acute pain related to myocardial ischaemia

  • Assess pain (location, character, score), give nitrates and morphine as ordered; record the response; obtain an ECG during pain. (ii) Decreased cardiac output / risk for arrhythmias

  • Continuous ECG monitoring; vital signs every 15–30 minutes initially; report arrhythmias, hypotension, crackles, falling urine output.

  • Keep the defibrillator and emergency drugs ready. (iii) Care during thrombolysis

  • Two IV lines; avoid IM injections and unnecessary punctures; observe for bleeding (gums, puncture sites, urine, stool, neurological change suggesting intracranial bleed), allergy and hypotension with streptokinase, and reperfusion arrhythmias; record time of drug and relief of pain and ST changes. (iv) Care after PCI

  • Check the radial or femoral puncture site for bleeding and haematoma; check distal pulses, colour and warmth; keep the leg straight for a few hours after femoral access; encourage fluids to protect kidneys from contrast dye. (v) Activity intolerance – plan rest periods; increase activity gradually; observe pulse, BP and symptoms during activity. (vi) Anxiety and fear – calm environment, explanations, allow family visits, reassurance; teach relaxation. (vii) Risk for bleeding due to antiplatelets and anticoagulants – soft toothbrush, observe stools and urine.

5. Cardiac rehabilitation

  • Phase I (in hospital) – early mobilisation, breathing exercises, education about the disease, risk factors and drugs.
  • Phase II (early outpatient, supervised, about 2–12 weeks after discharge) – supervised exercise training, risk-factor control, counselling.
  • Phase III (long-term maintenance) – lifelong regular exercise and healthy lifestyle in the community.

6. Discharge teaching

  • Stop smoking and all tobacco; control BP, sugar and cholesterol; heart-healthy diet with less salt, oil and sugar; maintain a healthy weight.
  • Regular walking, gradually increasing to 30 minutes on most days; avoid heavy lifting and exertion in cold weather or after meals.
  • Take medicines regularly, especially antiplatelets after stenting – never stop them without the cardiologist's advice (risk of stent thrombosis).
  • Sublingual nitroglycerin – sit down, take one tablet; if pain is not better or is worse after 5 minutes, call emergency services (108); a maximum of three tablets 5 minutes apart.
  • Return to work usually in 2–6 weeks; sexual activity when able to climb two flights of stairs without symptoms (usually after 1–2 weeks); driving as advised.
  • Recognise warning signs – chest pain, breathlessness, swelling of feet, palpitations, fainting.
  • Attend follow-up and cardiac rehabilitation; family members should learn CPR.

Nursing importance Survival after MI depends on rapid recognition, ECG within 10 minutes and early reperfusion; nurses also detect life-threatening arrhythmias early and guide the patient's long-term lifestyle change.

Conclusion MI is necrosis of heart muscle due to coronary thrombosis; immediate aspirin, pain relief, monitoring and early reperfusion (PCI or thrombolysis), followed by secondary prevention, cardiac rehabilitation and careful nursing care, save life and heart muscle.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Cardiovascular Disorders (including BCLS)
question: (a) Define heart failure and classify it. (3 marks) (b) Explain the causes, pathophysiology and clinical features of left- and right-sided heart failure. (5 marks) (c) Describe the management and nursing care of a patient with congestive heart failure. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: Features of left-sided and right-sided heart failure
labels: frothy sputum; right failure – raised JVP

answer_html:
(a) Definition and classification (3 marks) Heart failure (HF) is a clinical syndrome in which the heart is unable to pump enough blood to meet the metabolic needs of the body, or can do so only at high filling pressures. When fluid accumulates in the lungs and tissues it is called congestive heart failure (CHF).

Classification

  1. According to the side affected – left-sided, right-sided and biventricular (congestive) heart failure.
  2. According to ejection fraction (EF)
    • HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) – EF 40% or less (systolic failure).
    • HF with mildly reduced EF – EF 41–49%.
    • HF with preserved EF (HFpEF) – EF 50% or more (diastolic failure – stiff ventricle, common in elderly, hypertensive and diabetic women).
  3. According to onset – acute (sudden, e.g., after MI – acute pulmonary oedema) and chronic; acute decompensation of chronic HF.
  4. NYHA functional classification
    • Class I – no limitation of physical activity.
    • Class II – slight limitation; ordinary activity causes breathlessness or fatigue.
    • Class III – marked limitation; less than ordinary activity causes symptoms.
    • Class IV – symptoms at rest; unable to do any activity without discomfort.
  5. ACC/AHA stages – A (at risk), B (structural disease without symptoms), C (structural disease with symptoms), D (refractory HF).

(b) Causes, pathophysiology and clinical features (5 marks) Causes

  • Coronary artery disease and MI – the commonest cause.
  • Hypertension.
  • Valvular heart disease – especially rheumatic heart disease (mitral and aortic valve disease) in India.
  • Cardiomyopathies – dilated (alcohol, idiopathic), peripartum cardiomyopathy, hypertrophic.
  • Arrhythmias (atrial fibrillation), congenital heart disease, myocarditis.
  • High-output states – severe anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, beriberi, arteriovenous fistula.
  • Lung disease (COPD, pulmonary hypertension) causing right heart failure (cor pulmonale). Precipitating factors – infection (pneumonia), non-adherence to drugs or salt and fluid restriction, uncontrolled BP, new arrhythmia, MI, anaemia, NSAIDs, pregnancy, excessive IV fluids, kidney failure.

Pathophysiology

  • Weak or stiff ventricle → fall in cardiac output → body activates compensatory mechanisms:
    • Sympathetic stimulation – tachycardia, vasoconstriction.
    • Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system – sodium and water retention.
    • Ventricular dilatation and hypertrophy (remodelling).
  • These help at first but later increase the workload on the failing heart and cause fluid overload – a vicious cycle.
  • Back-pressure from the left ventricle causes pulmonary congestion; failure of the right ventricle causes systemic venous congestion.

Clinical features Left-sided heart failure (pulmonary congestion and low output)

  • Breathlessness on exertion, later at rest.
  • Orthopnoea (breathless on lying flat – uses extra pillows) and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea (wakes up breathless at night).
  • Cough, wheeze (cardiac asthma), pink frothy sputum in acute pulmonary oedema.
  • Basal crackles, third heart sound (gallop), tachycardia, pulsus alternans.

  • Fatigue, weakness, cold peripheries, cyanosis, reduced urine, confusion in the elderly. Right-sided heart failure (systemic venous congestion)

  • Dependent pitting oedema – ankles and feet, sacral oedema in bedridden patients.

  • Raised jugular venous pressure (JVP).
  • Tender hepatomegaly, ascites, weight gain.
  • Anorexia, nausea, abdominal fullness (congested gut), nocturia.

Investigations BNP or NT-proBNP (raised), echocardiography (EF, valves, wall motion), ECG, chest X-ray (cardiomegaly, upper-lobe diversion, Kerley B lines, pleural effusion), CBC, electrolytes, kidney, liver and thyroid function.

(c) Management and nursing care (7 marks) 1. Medical management

  • Treat the cause and precipitating factors – control BP, revascularise ischaemia, valve surgery, treat anaemia, infections and arrhythmias.
  • Drugs for HFrEF (guideline-directed medical therapy – "four pillars")
    • ARNI (sacubitril–valsartan) or ACE inhibitor/ARB.
    • β-blockers (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol) – started at a low dose and increased slowly.
    • Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (spironolactone).
    • SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin).
  • Diuretics (furosemide, torsemide) to relieve congestion and oedema.
  • Digoxin for atrial fibrillation with fast rate or persistent symptoms; ivabradine, hydralazine–nitrate in selected patients.
  • Devices and surgery – implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD), cardiac resynchronisation therapy, valve replacement, CABG, left ventricular assist device, heart transplantation.
  • Acute decompensated HF/pulmonary oedema – sit upright, oxygen, IV furosemide, nitrates, non-invasive ventilation, inotropes for low output.

2. Nursing management (i) Impaired gas exchange and breathlessness

  • High Fowler's position with arms supported on pillows, or sitting with legs hanging down (reduces venous return); oxygen as ordered.

  • Monitor respiratory rate, SpO₂, lung sounds (crackles) and the number of pillows needed. (ii) Excess fluid volume

  • Daily weight at the same time, on the same scale, with similar clothing, after voiding and before breakfast; report a gain of more than 1 kg in a day or 2 kg in 3 days.

  • Strict intake–output chart; fluid restriction (often 1.5–2 litres a day in severe HF) as ordered; salt restriction (less than 5 g salt a day; avoid pickles, papad, processed foods).

  • Assess oedema, JVP, abdominal girth; elevate oedematous legs (except when breathless lying flat). (iii) Decreased cardiac output

  • Monitor pulse (rate and rhythm), BP, urine output, mental state, skin colour and temperature.

  • Digoxin – check the apical pulse for one full minute; withhold and report if below 60/min (adults) or if there are signs of toxicity (anorexia, nausea, vomiting, visual disturbances such as yellow-green halos, new arrhythmias); monitor potassium (low potassium increases toxicity).
  • Diuretics – give in the morning; monitor potassium, BP and kidney function; watch for dehydration and dizziness.

  • ACE inhibitors and ARNI – watch for hypotension, cough, high potassium. (iv) Activity intolerance

  • Rest in the acute phase; gradually increase activity; plan care with rest periods; assist with daily activities.

  • Prevent complications of bed rest – leg exercises, DVT prophylaxis, position changes. (v) Risk for impaired skin integrity – oedematous skin breaks easily; frequent position changes, pressure-relieving mattress, gentle skin care. (vi) Nutrition – small, frequent, easily digestible meals low in salt; avoid heavy meals; stool softeners to prevent straining. (vii) Anxiety – calm reassurance, explanations, involvement of the family; adequate sleep (propped up).

3. Health education for self-care

  • Weigh daily and keep a record; follow salt and fluid limits.
  • Take medicines regularly; do not stop diuretics or β-blockers on your own; avoid NSAIDs and herbal products without advice.
  • Recognise warning signs – sudden weight gain, increased breathlessness, needing more pillows, waking up breathless, swelling of feet or abdomen, reduced urine – and seek care early.
  • Regular, light exercise (walking) as advised; cardiac rehabilitation.
  • Stop smoking and alcohol; take influenza and pneumococcal vaccines.
  • Plan for pregnancy only after cardiology advice (in women with heart disease).
  • Regular follow-up.

Common nursing diagnoses

  • Decreased cardiac output related to impaired contractility.
  • Excess fluid volume related to sodium and water retention.
  • Impaired gas exchange related to pulmonary congestion.
  • Activity intolerance related to reduced oxygen supply.

Nursing importance Most hospital readmissions in heart failure are due to poor adherence to drugs, salt and fluid limits and late reporting of weight gain; nurse-led education and monitoring greatly reduce readmissions and deaths.

Conclusion Heart failure is the inability of the heart to meet the body's needs, causing pulmonary and systemic congestion; treatment of the cause, modern drugs, salt and fluid control, daily weight monitoring and supportive nursing care improve symptoms and survival.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Cardiovascular Disorders (including BCLS)
question: (a) Define cardiogenic shock and list its causes. (3 marks) (b) Explain the pathophysiology and clinical features. (4 marks) (c) Describe the medical and nursing management of a patient with cardiogenic shock. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Vicious cycle of cardiogenic shock
labels: fall in stroke volume and cardiac output
more ischaemia; compensatory vasoconstriction increases afterload; raised filling pressure causes pulmonary congestion and hypoxia

answer_html:
(a) Definition and causes (3 marks) Cardiogenic shock is a state of critical tissue hypoperfusion caused by primary failure of the heart as a pump, in spite of an adequate circulating blood volume. It is a medical emergency with a very high death rate (around 40–50% even with modern treatment).

Haemodynamic criteria (for understanding)

  • Systolic BP below 90 mmHg for more than 30 minutes, or the need for vasopressors to maintain it.
  • Cardiac index below 2.2 L/min/m² with raised filling pressure (pulmonary capillary wedge pressure above 15–18 mmHg).
  • Signs of hypoperfusion – cold extremities, urine output below 30 ml/hour, altered mental state, raised lactate.

Causes

  1. Acute myocardial infarction – the commonest cause (usually a large anterior MI with loss of 40% or more of the left ventricular muscle).
  2. Mechanical complications of MI – papillary muscle rupture (acute mitral regurgitation), ventricular septal rupture, free-wall rupture.
  3. Right ventricular infarction.
  4. Severe arrhythmias – ventricular tachycardia, very slow heart rates (complete heart block).
  5. Acute myocarditis, end-stage cardiomyopathy, peripartum cardiomyopathy.
  6. Acute valve failure – severe aortic or mitral regurgitation, prosthetic valve thrombosis, critical aortic stenosis.
  7. After cardiac surgery, cardiac contusion, overdose of β-blockers or calcium-channel blockers. (Cardiac tamponade and massive pulmonary embolism cause obstructive shock with a similar picture.)

(b) Pathophysiology and clinical features (4 marks) Pathophysiology

  • Loss of contractility → fall in stroke volume and cardiac output → hypotension → reduced coronary blood flow → more myocardial ischaemia → further fall in contractility – a vicious cycle.
  • Compensatory vasoconstriction and tachycardia raise afterload and oxygen demand, worsening the failing heart.
  • Raised left ventricular filling pressure causes pulmonary congestion and oedema, leading to hypoxaemia.
  • Poor perfusion of organs causes lactic acidosis, acute kidney injury, liver injury, confusion and eventually multiple organ failure.

Clinical features

  • Hypotension (systolic below 90 mmHg, MAP below 65 mmHg), narrow pulse pressure.
  • Rapid, weak, thready pulse; arrhythmias.
  • Cold, clammy, pale or mottled skin, cyanosis, delayed capillary refill.
  • Oliguria (below 30 ml/hour).
  • Restlessness, confusion, drowsiness.
  • Breathlessness, tachypnoea, crackles, pink frothy sputum (pulmonary oedema); raised JVP; third heart sound.
  • Chest pain (if due to MI).
  • Investigations – ECG, troponin, echocardiography (essential – shows pump function and mechanical complications), chest X-ray, ABG and lactate, electrolytes, kidney and liver function, CBC; haemodynamic monitoring (arterial line, CVP, sometimes pulmonary artery catheter).

(c) Medical and nursing management (8 marks) 1. Medical management

  • Immediate resuscitation (ABC) – airway, oxygen, non-invasive or mechanical ventilation for respiratory failure and pulmonary oedema.
  • Early revascularisation – emergency PCI (or CABG) for MI-related shock is the single most effective treatment for improving survival; transfer to a PCI-capable centre.
  • Fluids – a cautious small bolus (e.g., 250 ml) only if there is no pulmonary congestion (for example, in right ventricular infarction); fluids are given carefully because the heart cannot handle excess volume.
  • Vasopressors and inotropes (through a central line, with infusion pumps), as ordered:
    • Noradrenaline – first-choice vasopressor to raise BP and maintain MAP of 65 mmHg or more.
    • Dobutamine – inotrope to improve contractility.
    • Adrenaline, milrinone or levosimendan in selected patients.
  • Diuretics and nitrates for pulmonary congestion only when BP allows.
  • Correction of arrhythmias – cardioversion, antiarrhythmic drugs, temporary pacing for bradycardia.
  • Correction of acidosis, electrolytes (potassium, magnesium) and blood sugar.
  • Antiplatelets and anticoagulants for MI.
  • Mechanical circulatory support – intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP), which inflates during diastole (improving coronary perfusion) and deflates just before systole (reducing afterload); Impella and VA-ECMO in advanced centres; left ventricular assist device or heart transplantation for end-stage disease.
  • Surgical repair of mechanical complications (septal rupture, papillary muscle rupture).

2. Nursing management (i) Continuous haemodynamic monitoring

  • ECG, invasive arterial BP (MAP target 65 mmHg or above), CVP, SpO₂, respiratory rate, temperature.
  • Hourly urine output (target at least 0.5 ml/kg/hour) via indwelling catheter.
  • Level of consciousness, skin colour, temperature, capillary refill, peripheral pulses, lung sounds.

  • ABG, lactate, electrolytes and kidney function as ordered; report trends early. (ii) Safe administration of vasoactive drugs

  • Use a dedicated central line and infusion pumps; calculate doses carefully (mcg/kg/min) and double-check with another nurse.

  • Never interrupt or flush a vasopressor line (sudden bolus or stop can cause dangerous BP changes); change syringes without a gap ("piggy-back" method).

  • Label all lines; watch for extravasation (tissue necrosis) and arrhythmias. (iii) Positioning and rest

  • Supine with the head slightly raised, or semi-Fowler's if pulmonary congestion is present; avoid the head-down position.

  • Reduce myocardial oxygen demand – complete bed rest, pain relief, treatment of fever, calm environment, minimal disturbance; cluster nursing activities. (iv) Respiratory care – oxygen, NIV or ventilator care, suctioning, VAP prevention, ABG monitoring. (v) IABP care (if used)

  • Keep the cannulated leg straight; head of bed not above 30°; check distal pulses, colour, warmth and sensation of the leg every hour (limb ischaemia); observe the insertion site for bleeding; monitor platelet count (heparin, mechanical damage); check timing and alarms; watch for blood in the tubing (balloon rupture). (vi) Fluid and nutrition – strict intake–output; careful fluids; early enteral nutrition as tolerated; blood glucose control. (vii) Prevention of complications – pressure ulcers (immobility, poor perfusion), DVT, infections of lines and catheters (bundles), stress ulcers. (viii) Psychosocial and family care – explain the condition and procedures, support the family, allow presence where possible, help with difficult decisions and end-of-life care when appropriate. (ix) Documentation of all parameters, drug doses and responses.

Common nursing diagnoses

  • Decreased cardiac output related to impaired contractility.
  • Ineffective tissue perfusion (cerebral, renal, peripheral) related to low output.
  • Impaired gas exchange related to pulmonary congestion.
  • Fear and anxiety of the patient and family.

3. How cardiogenic shock differs from hypovolaemic shock (bedside clues)

  • Neck veins – distended (raised JVP) in cardiogenic shock; flat in hypovolaemic shock.
  • Lungs – crackles and pulmonary oedema in cardiogenic shock; usually clear in hypovolaemic shock.
  • CVP and wedge pressure – high in cardiogenic shock; low in hypovolaemic shock.
  • Response to fluids – breathlessness worsens in cardiogenic shock; BP and pulse improve in hypovolaemic shock.
  • Heart – third heart sound, new murmur or arrhythmia point to a cardiac cause.
  • Treatment focus – inotropes, vasopressors and revascularisation versus fluids and blood.

4. Prevention

  • Early reperfusion of every STEMI reduces the size of the infarct and the risk of shock.
  • Close monitoring of high-risk MI patients – elderly, diabetic, large anterior MI, previous MI, low BP or tachycardia on arrival – with early transfer to a PCI centre.
  • Prompt treatment of arrhythmias, careful use of β-blockers and nitrates in borderline BP, and early detection of mechanical complications by echocardiography.

Nursing importance Cardiogenic shock changes minute by minute; continuous observation, accurate titration of vasoactive drugs and rapid reporting by the ICU nurse directly affect survival.

Conclusion Cardiogenic shock is pump failure, usually after a large MI, causing hypotension and organ hypoperfusion; early revascularisation, careful use of fluids, vasopressors, inotropes and mechanical support, with expert ICU nursing, offer the best chance of survival.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Cardiovascular Disorders (including BCLS)
question: (a) Define cardiopulmonary arrest and list its causes. (3 marks) (b) Explain the chain of survival and the steps of adult basic cardiac life support (BCLS), including the use of an AED. (8 marks) (c) Describe the post-resuscitation care and the nurse's responsibilities during a hospital "code blue". (4 marks)

diagram.caption: Adult basic life support algorithm for health-care providers

answer_html:
(a) Definition and causes (3 marks) Cardiopulmonary (cardiac) arrest is the sudden cessation of effective heart action and breathing, with loss of consciousness, absent pulse and absent or abnormal (gasping) breathing. Brain damage begins within 4–6 minutes without circulation, so immediate action is life-saving.

Causes

  • Cardiac – myocardial infarction and coronary artery disease (commonest), ventricular fibrillation, cardiomyopathy, heart block, valve disease.
  • Respiratory – airway obstruction (choking, vomitus), severe asthma, drowning, respiratory failure.
  • Reversible causes – the "Hs and Ts"
    • Hs – Hypovolaemia, Hypoxia, Hydrogen ion (acidosis), Hypo-/Hyperkalaemia, Hypothermia.
    • Ts – Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade (cardiac), Toxins (drug overdose, poisoning), Thrombosis – pulmonary (embolism), Thrombosis – coronary (MI).
  • Others – electric shock, trauma, severe bleeding, anaphylaxis, stroke.

Rhythms in cardiac arrest

  • Shockable – ventricular fibrillation (VF) and pulseless ventricular tachycardia (pVT).
  • Non-shockable – asystole and pulseless electrical activity (PEA).

(b) Chain of survival and adult BCLS (8 marks) 1. Chain of survival The AHA 2025 Guidelines use one unified chain of survival for all cardiac arrests – adult or child, in or out of hospital (the 2020 guidelines had separate in-hospital and out-of-hospital chains):

  1. Recognition and emergency activation – recognising the arrest quickly and calling for help (in hospital, the code team or "code blue"; outside, emergency services on 108/112).
  2. High-quality CPR.
  3. Defibrillation – early use of an AED or defibrillator.
  4. Advanced resuscitation – advanced airway, drugs and treatment of reversible causes by the code team or paramedics.
  5. Post-cardiac arrest care.
  6. Recovery and survivorship – rehabilitation and support for survivors and families. Prevention and preparedness come before the chain – in hospital, monitoring of ward patients, early warning scores and rapid response teams prevent many arrests.

2. Steps of adult BCLS (health-care provider)

  1. Ensure scene safety for yourself and the patient.
  2. Check responsiveness – tap the shoulders and shout, "Are you all right?"
  3. Shout for help, activate the emergency response (code blue) and ask someone to bring the AED/defibrillator and crash cart.
  4. Check breathing and pulse together – look for absent or only gasping breathing and feel the carotid pulse for no more than 10 seconds.
    • Normal breathing and pulse present – monitor and place in the recovery position.
    • No normal breathing but pulse present – give rescue breaths, 1 breath every 6 seconds (10 per minute); check pulse every 2 minutes; consider naloxone in suspected opioid overdose.
    • No breathing (or gasping) and no pulse – start CPR immediately.
  5. Chest compressions (C)
    • Patient on a firm surface (CPR board in hospital beds); kneel or stand at the side.
    • Place the heel of one hand on the lower half of the sternum (centre of the chest), the other hand on top, arms straight, shoulders over the hands.
    • Rate 100–120 compressions per minute; depth 5–6 cm in adults.
    • Allow full chest recoil after each compression; minimise interruptions (less than 10 seconds).
  6. Airway (A) – head-tilt chin-lift, or jaw thrust if neck injury is suspected; remove visible foreign material.
  7. Breathing (B) – give 2 breaths, each over 1 second, with a bag-valve mask (with oxygen) or pocket mask, enough to make the chest rise; avoid excessive ventilation.
  8. Compression–ventilation ratio 30:2 until an advanced airway is placed; after an advanced airway (endotracheal tube), give continuous compressions with 1 breath every 6 seconds.
  9. Use the AED/defibrillator as soon as it arrives.
  10. Change the compressor every 2 minutes (or earlier if tired) to maintain quality; check rhythm every 2 minutes.

3. Use of an automated external defibrillator (AED)

  1. Switch on the AED and follow the voice prompts.
  2. Attach the pads to the bare, dry chest – one below the right clavicle, the other on the left side of the chest below the armpit (anterolateral position); remove medication patches and wipe the chest if wet.
  3. Ensure no one touches the patient while the AED analyses the rhythm.
  4. If a shock is advised – shout "Stand clear", check that no one is touching the patient and press the shock button.
  5. Immediately resume CPR for 2 minutes, starting with compressions; do not check the pulse right after the shock.
  6. If no shock is advised, resume CPR immediately; continue until advanced help arrives or the patient shows signs of life.

4. High-quality CPR – key points

  • Push hard (5–6 cm) and fast (100–120/min); full recoil; minimal interruptions; avoid excessive ventilation; rotate compressors every 2 minutes; aim for compressions during at least 80% of the resuscitation time.

5. Advanced support (nurse assists)

  • IV/IO access; adrenaline 1 mg IV every 3–5 minutes; amiodarone (300 mg, then 150 mg) for persistent VF/pVT; advanced airway; capnography; treatment of reversible causes (Hs and Ts).

(c) Post-resuscitation care and code-blue responsibilities (4 marks) 1. Post-cardiac arrest care (after return of spontaneous circulation – ROSC)

  • Airway and breathing – secure airway, ventilation, SpO₂ 92–98% (avoid both hypoxia and excess oxygen), normal PaCO₂.
  • Circulation – keep systolic BP 90 mmHg or more and MAP 65 mmHg or more with fluids and vasopressors; continuous ECG.
  • 12-lead ECG – urgent coronary angiography/PCI if STEMI is present.
  • Temperature control – for patients who remain comatose, targeted temperature management (32–37.5 °C for at least 24 hours) and prevention of fever.
  • Control blood glucose, treat seizures, correct electrolytes; treat the cause of arrest.
  • Shift to ICU; neurological assessment; prognosis is usually judged after 72 hours.
  • Support the family and keep them informed.

2. Nurse's responsibilities during a code blue

  • Recognise arrest early, call the code using the hospital number, start CPR immediately and note the time of arrest.
  • Bring the crash cart and defibrillator; attach monitor/defibrillator pads; prepare suction, oxygen, bag-valve mask and intubation tray.
  • Take a role as assigned by the team leader – compressor, airway assistant, IV access and drugs, recorder (time-keeper), or runner.
  • Prepare and give drugs as ordered with closed-loop communication (repeat the order back).
  • Document – times of arrest, CPR start, rhythms, shocks, drugs, airway, ROSC or death, and team members.
  • Ensure the family is informed and supported; follow DNAR (do-not-attempt-resuscitation) orders where legally documented.
  • After the event – restock and check the crash cart, clean equipment, take part in debriefing.
  • Maintain own competency through regular BLS training.

3. Common errors to avoid during CPR

  • Compressions too slow or too shallow, or leaning on the chest so that it cannot recoil fully.
  • Long pauses for pulse checks, intubation or line insertion (keep interruptions below 10 seconds).
  • Over-ventilation – too many or too forceful breaths cause gastric inflation, vomiting and reduced venous return.
  • Wrong hand position (too low) causing rib and liver injuries.
  • Delay in defibrillation while waiting for a doctor – a trained nurse should use the AED as soon as it arrives.

Nursing importance In hospital, nurses are usually the first to find a patient in cardiac arrest; immediate high-quality CPR and defibrillation within minutes can double or triple the chances of survival.

Conclusion Cardiopulmonary arrest needs immediate recognition, calling for help, high-quality CPR at 30:2, early defibrillation with an AED and organised post-resuscitation care; trained nurses are the key link in the chain of survival.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Cardiovascular Disorders (including BCLS)
question: Explain the types, clinical features and management of heart block.

diagram.caption: ECG strips of heart block
labels: first-degree – long PR interval; Mobitz I – progressive PR lengthening then dropped beat; Mobitz II – constant PR with sudden dropped QRS; complete heart block – P waves and QRS complexes independent

answer_html:
Definition Heart block (atrioventricular or AV block) is a delay or interruption in the conduction of the electrical impulse from the atria to the ventricles through the AV node and bundle of His.

1. Causes

  • Inferior myocardial infarction (right coronary artery supplies the AV node), ischaemic heart disease.
  • Age-related fibrosis of the conducting system.
  • Drugs – digoxin, β-blockers, verapamil, diltiazem, amiodarone.
  • Hyperkalaemia, myocarditis, rheumatic fever, infective endocarditis, cardiac surgery, congenital (babies of mothers with SLE), increased vagal tone (athletes, sleep).

2. Types (degrees)

  • First-degree block – every impulse is conducted but delayed; PR interval longer than 0.20 second; usually no symptoms.
  • Second-degree block – some impulses are not conducted (dropped beats):
    • Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) – the PR interval lengthens progressively until a P wave is not followed by a QRS; usually at the AV node; often benign.
    • Mobitz type II – PR interval is constant, but some P waves are suddenly not conducted; lies lower in the conducting system; may progress to complete block – dangerous.
  • Third-degree (complete) heart block – no impulses pass; atria and ventricles beat independently (AV dissociation); a slow escape rhythm takes over (ventricular rate 20–40/min if ventricular, 40–60/min if junctional).

3. Clinical features

  • First-degree – none.
  • Higher degrees – bradycardia, fatigue, dizziness, breathlessness, chest pain, confusion, fainting attacks (Stokes–Adams attacks), hypotension, heart failure; irregular pulse in second-degree block; cannon "a" waves in the neck in complete block.

4. Management

  • Treat the cause – stop offending drugs, correct potassium, treat MI or myocarditis.
  • First-degree and Mobitz I – observation; avoid AV-blocking drugs.
  • Symptomatic bradycardia – atropine 1 mg IV (repeated every 3–5 minutes, maximum 3 mg), transcutaneous pacing, dopamine or adrenaline infusion, as ordered.
  • Temporary transvenous pacemaker for unstable patients.
  • Permanent pacemaker for Mobitz II and complete heart block.

5. Nursing management

  • Continuous ECG monitoring; monitor pulse (apical for one full minute), BP, level of consciousness; report pauses and slow rates.
  • Keep atropine, pacing equipment and defibrillator ready.
  • Fall precautions – the patient should not get up alone if dizzy.
  • Care after pacemaker insertion
    • Check the wound for bleeding, haematoma and infection; check ECG for pacing spikes and capture.
    • Limit movement of the arm on the side of the pacemaker (no lifting the arm above shoulder level for about 4–6 weeks) to prevent lead displacement.
    • Teach the patient to check the pulse daily, carry the pacemaker identity card, keep mobile phones at least 15 cm away from the device, inform staff before MRI, airport security or surgery (diathermy), and report dizziness, fainting, hiccups or a very slow pulse.

Nursing importance Mobitz II and complete heart block can suddenly cause cardiac arrest; close monitoring, ready pacing equipment and pacemaker teaching by nurses prevent deaths.

Conclusion Heart block ranges from harmless first-degree delay to life-threatening complete block; treatment depends on the degree and symptoms, with pacemakers for advanced blocks.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Cardiovascular Disorders (including BCLS)
question: Explain the types, clinical features and nursing management of angina pectoris.
answer_html:
Definition Angina pectoris is chest pain or discomfort caused by temporary myocardial ischaemia, when the oxygen demand of the heart muscle exceeds the supply through narrowed coronary arteries, without permanent damage (necrosis) of the muscle.

1. Types

  • Stable angina – predictable pain brought on by exertion or emotion, lasting a few minutes and relieved by rest or nitroglycerin.
  • Unstable angina – new, increasing, or occurring at rest; lasts longer; part of the acute coronary syndrome – an emergency (high risk of MI).
  • Variant (Prinzmetal) angina – due to coronary artery spasm; occurs at rest, often early morning, with transient ST elevation.
  • Microvascular angina – due to disease of small coronary vessels (often in women).

2. Precipitating factors Physical exertion, emotional stress, heavy meals, exposure to cold, smoking, sexual activity, anaemia, tachycardia.

3. Clinical features

  • Retrosternal heaviness, tightness, squeezing or burning, sometimes described as "gas" or indigestion.
  • Radiates to the left arm, shoulder, neck, jaw or back.
  • Duration usually 2–10 minutes; relieved by rest or sublingual nitroglycerin.
  • Breathlessness, sweating, nausea; the patient may press a clenched fist over the chest (Levine's sign).

4. Diagnosis ECG during pain (ST depression, T inversion), treadmill test (TMT), echocardiography, stress imaging, CT coronary angiography, coronary angiography; blood sugar, lipid profile; troponin to exclude MI.

5. Management (brief)

  • During an attack – stop activity, sit or lie down, sublingual nitroglycerin 0.4 mg (repeat every 5 minutes up to three doses), oxygen if SpO₂ is low, ECG.
  • Drugs – nitrates, β-blockers, calcium-channel blockers, antiplatelets (aspirin), statins, ACE inhibitors.
  • Revascularisation – PCI with stenting or CABG for severe disease or uncontrolled symptoms.

6. Nursing management

  • Assess pain (onset, site, character, radiation, duration, relieving factors); record ECG during pain; report pain lasting more than 15–20 minutes or not relieved by nitrates (possible MI).
  • Balance activity and rest – plan activities with rest periods; avoid exertion after meals.
  • Nitroglycerin teaching
    • Sit down before taking it (may cause dizziness, flushing, headache); place under the tongue and let it dissolve.
    • Keep tablets in the original dark glass bottle, away from heat, light and moisture; replace as per expiry instructions.
    • May be taken before exertion known to cause pain.
    • Never take it with sildenafil-type drugs (severe hypotension).
    • If pain is not relieved 5 minutes after the first tablet, call emergency services (108).
  • Risk-factor modification – stop smoking, control BP, diabetes and cholesterol, healthy diet, weight reduction, regular graded exercise, stress management, yoga.
  • Teach the patient to recognise unstable angina (pain at rest, more frequent, longer) and seek care immediately.
  • Emotional support; involve the family.

Nursing importance Patient education about nitrate use, risk factors and warning signs of unstable angina prevents many heart attacks and deaths.

Conclusion Angina is transient myocardial ischaemia relieved by rest and nitrates; drugs, revascularisation and lifestyle change, supported by nursing education, control symptoms and prevent MI.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Cardiovascular Disorders (including BCLS)
question: Write a note on thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger's disease) and the nursing care of a patient with peripheral arterial disease.
answer_html:
Introduction Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) is narrowing or blockage of arteries supplying the limbs, usually the legs. In older people, diabetics and smokers it is due to atherosclerosis. Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger's disease) is a special form seen mainly in young male smokers – common in India because of bidi and cigarette smoking.

1. Buerger's disease
