  • Definition – a non-atherosclerotic, inflammatory, occlusive disease of the small and medium-sized arteries and veins of the arms and legs, strongly linked to tobacco.
  • Features
    • Young men (usually below 45 years), heavy smokers.
    • Claudication in the foot (instep) or calf, later rest pain, especially at night.
    • Cold, pale or bluish fingers and toes; Raynaud's phenomenon; migratory superficial thrombophlebitis.
    • Absent distal pulses (dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial, radial).
    • Ulcers and gangrene of toes and fingers.
  • Diagnosis – clinical features, Doppler studies, angiography ("corkscrew" collaterals); exclusion of diabetes and atherosclerosis.
  • Treatment
    • Complete and permanent stopping of all tobacco – the only measure that halts the disease.
    • Pain relief, vasodilators (cilostazol), prostacyclin analogue (iloprost), lumbar sympathectomy, omentoplasty; amputation for gangrene.

2. Atherosclerotic PAD (brief)

  • Elderly, diabetics, smokers, hypertensives; intermittent claudication (calf pain on walking, relieved by rest); ankle–brachial index (ABI) below 0.9.
  • Statins, antiplatelets, supervised exercise, control of risk factors; angioplasty or bypass surgery.

3. Nursing care of a patient with peripheral arterial disease

  • Tobacco cessation counselling – repeated, firm and supportive; involve the family; refer to tobacco cessation centres.
  • Positioning – keep the legs level or slightly dependent (gravity improves arterial flow); avoid elevating the legs (unlike venous disease); avoid crossing legs and tight socks or garters.
  • Warmth – keep limbs warm with socks and blankets; never apply hot water bottles or heating pads (numb, ischaemic skin burns easily).
  • Foot care – wash and dry daily, inspect for cuts and colour changes (use a mirror), moisturise (not between toes), cut nails straight, wear well-fitting footwear, never walk barefoot, treat injuries early.
  • Exercise – walk until pain begins, rest, then walk again (graded walking for 30–45 minutes a day) to develop collateral circulation.
  • Pain management – analgesics, comfortable position (patients often hang the legs over the bed edge at night).
  • Wound care of ulcers; watch for infection and spreading gangrene.
  • Monitor pulses, colour, temperature, capillary refill and sensation.
  • Prepare and support the patient if amputation is needed; rehabilitation and prosthesis.

Nursing importance Because Buerger's disease progresses as long as tobacco is used, the nurse's counselling for complete cessation can save the patient's limbs.

Conclusion Buerger's disease is an inflammatory occlusive disease of young smokers; total tobacco cessation, foot care, exercise and careful nursing are the main measures to prevent gangrene and amputation.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Cardiovascular Disorders (including BCLS)
question: Explain the causes, clinical features and management of varicose veins with nursing care.
answer_html:
Definition Varicose veins are dilated, elongated and tortuous superficial veins, usually in the lower limbs, caused by incompetent valves and increased venous pressure. The great saphenous vein is most commonly affected.

1. Causes and risk factors

  • Prolonged standing – traffic police, teachers, nurses, shopkeepers, factory workers.
  • Pregnancy (pressure of the uterus and hormones), obesity, female sex, family history, increasing age.
  • Previous deep vein thrombosis (secondary varicose veins), chronic constipation, pelvic tumours.

2. Clinical features

  • Visible, dilated, twisted veins on the legs.
  • Aching, heaviness and tiredness of the legs, worse at the end of the day and on standing, relieved by elevation.
  • Night cramps, ankle swelling, itching.
  • Skin changes – brown pigmentation, eczema, hardening (lipodermatosclerosis).
  • Complications – venous ulcer (usually above the medial malleolus), bleeding from a ruptured vein, superficial thrombophlebitis.

3. Diagnosis Clinical examination, Trendelenburg test and Doppler/duplex ultrasound (to locate incompetent valves and exclude DVT).

4. Management

  • Conservative – leg elevation, graduated compression stockings, regular walking (calf-muscle pump), weight reduction, avoiding prolonged standing.
  • Sclerotherapy – injection of a sclerosing agent (polidocanol) for small veins.
  • Endovenous laser ablation (EVLA) or radiofrequency ablation – minimally invasive, day-care procedures.
  • Surgery – Trendelenburg operation (saphenofemoral ligation) with stripping of the vein, and removal of tributaries.
  • Venous ulcer care – compression bandaging, dressings, elevation, treatment of infection.

5. Nursing care Conservative and preventive

  • Teach to elevate the legs above heart level for 15–30 minutes several times a day and raise the foot end of the bed.
  • Correct use of compression stockings – put on in the morning before getting out of bed, remove at night, correct size, no wrinkles.
  • Avoid standing or sitting for long; move the legs, do ankle exercises, walk during breaks; avoid crossing legs and tight garters.
  • Weight control, high-fibre diet to avoid constipation.

  • Protect the legs from injury; moisturise dry skin. After surgery or ablation

  • Elevate the legs; apply elastic bandage or stockings as ordered.

  • Early ambulation – walk for short periods frequently; avoid standing still or sitting with legs down.
  • Check distal pulses, colour, temperature and sensation; observe for bleeding and bruising.
  • Pain relief; watch for DVT (calf pain, swelling).
  • Discharge teaching – continue stockings for several weeks, gradual return to activities.

Nursing importance Nurses themselves are at risk of varicose veins; teaching simple preventive measures and post-operative care prevents ulcers and recurrence.

Conclusion Varicose veins result from valve incompetence and venous hypertension; elevation, compression, exercise and minimally invasive or surgical treatment, with good nursing care, relieve symptoms and prevent complications.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Cardiovascular Disorders (including BCLS)
question: Explain the clinical features and nursing management of a patient with mitral stenosis due to rheumatic heart disease.
answer_html:
Introduction Mitral stenosis (MS) is narrowing of the mitral valve orifice that obstructs blood flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle. In India it is almost always due to rheumatic heart disease, and commonly affects young adults, especially women.

1. Pathophysiology (brief)

  • The normal mitral valve area is 4–6 cm²; symptoms appear when it becomes less than about 2.5 cm², and stenosis is severe below 1.5 cm².
  • Blood dams back in the left atrium → left atrial enlargement → atrial fibrillation and clot formation → raised pulmonary venous pressure → pulmonary congestion → pulmonary hypertension → right heart failure.

2. Clinical features

  • Breathlessness on exertion, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea; acute pulmonary oedema with fast heart rate, fever or pregnancy.
  • Haemoptysis, cough, recurrent chest infections.
  • Palpitations (atrial fibrillation), fatigue.
  • Embolic events – stroke, limb ischaemia.
  • Mitral facies (pinkish-purple flush on cheeks), hoarseness (pressure on the recurrent laryngeal nerve), features of right heart failure (oedema, raised JVP, hepatomegaly).
  • Auscultation – loud first heart sound, opening snap, low-pitched mid-diastolic rumbling murmur at the apex (heard best with the bell in the left lateral position).
  • Echocardiography confirms the diagnosis and valve area.

3. Management

  • Secondary prophylaxis of rheumatic fever – benzathine penicillin 1.2 million units IM every 3 weeks (as per Indian guidelines) for many years.
  • Diuretics and salt restriction for congestion; β-blockers or rate-control drugs to slow the heart and lengthen diastolic filling.
  • Anticoagulation (warfarin) for atrial fibrillation, left atrial clot or previous embolism (target INR usually 2–3).
  • Interventions
    • Balloon mitral valvotomy (percutaneous transvenous mitral commissurotomy – PTMC) – widely done in India for suitable valves.
    • Closed or open mitral commissurotomy.
    • Mitral valve replacement – mechanical valve (lifelong warfarin) or bioprosthetic valve.

4. Nursing management

  • Rest and activity balance; propped-up position; oxygen for breathlessness.
  • Monitor pulse rate and rhythm (apical–radial pulse deficit in AF), BP, respiratory rate, lung sounds, oedema, daily weight and intake–output.
  • Diuretics and salt restriction; watch potassium.
  • Watch for embolism – sudden weakness, speech problems, limb pain or coldness – and report.
  • Warfarin teaching – take at the same time daily; regular INR checks; watch for bleeding (gums, urine, black stools); keep green leafy vegetable intake steady (vitamin K); avoid NSAIDs and unprescribed medicines; inform dentists and doctors; avoid IM injections.
  • Penicillin prophylaxis adherence – explain why it is needed even when well; give the injection with proper technique and observe for allergy.
  • Dental hygiene and early treatment of infections to prevent infective endocarditis.
  • Pregnancy counselling – plan pregnancy after valve treatment; close antenatal care in a tertiary centre; suitable contraception.
  • Pre- and post-procedure care for PTMC or valve surgery.

Nursing importance Nurses ensure adherence to penicillin prophylaxis and anticoagulation, the two measures that prevent further valve damage and strokes in young patients.

Conclusion Mitral stenosis is mostly rheumatic; it causes pulmonary congestion, atrial fibrillation and embolism, and is managed with prophylaxis, drugs, anticoagulation, balloon valvotomy or valve replacement, with thorough nursing care and education.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Cardiovascular Disorders (including BCLS)
question: Explain pericarditis and cardiac tamponade with their nursing management.
answer_html:
Definitions

  • Pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardium (the double-layered sac around the heart).
  • Pericardial effusion is an abnormal collection of fluid in the pericardial sac.
  • Cardiac tamponade is compression of the heart by fluid (or blood) in the pericardial sac, which prevents the heart from filling – a life-threatening emergency causing obstructive shock.

1. Causes of pericarditis

  • Viral infection – the commonest cause overall.
  • Tuberculosis – an important cause in India; may lead to constrictive pericarditis.
  • Bacterial (purulent) infection, after MI (early pericarditis, or Dressler's syndrome weeks later), uraemia (kidney failure), autoimmune diseases (SLE, rheumatoid arthritis), rheumatic fever, cancer, radiation, trauma, cardiac surgery.

2. Clinical features of pericarditis

  • Sharp, stabbing chest pain, worse on lying flat, deep breathing and coughing, relieved by sitting up and leaning forward; may radiate to the shoulder.
  • Pericardial friction rub – a scratchy sound on auscultation.
  • Fever, malaise, breathlessness.
  • ECG – widespread concave (saddle-shaped) ST elevation and PR depression; echocardiography – effusion.

3. Features of cardiac tamponade

  • Beck's triad – hypotension, raised JVP (distended neck veins) and muffled (distant) heart sounds.
  • Pulsus paradoxus – fall of systolic BP by more than 10 mmHg during inspiration.
  • Tachycardia, breathlessness, restlessness, cold clammy skin, falling urine output; low-voltage ECG with electrical alternans; echocardiography shows compression of the heart chambers.

4. Management

  • Pericarditis – NSAIDs (ibuprofen or aspirin) with colchicine, rest, treatment of the cause (anti-TB treatment with steroids for tuberculous pericarditis, dialysis for uraemic pericarditis, antibiotics and drainage for purulent pericarditis).
  • Tamponade – emergency pericardiocentesis (needle aspiration of fluid, usually from below the xiphoid under echo guidance), surgical pericardial window or surgery for trauma; IV fluids to support filling while preparing; avoid diuretics and vasodilators.
  • Constrictive pericarditis – pericardiectomy.

5. Nursing management

  • Position – sitting up and leaning forward on an over-bed table with a pillow for pain relief.
  • Pain relief – NSAIDs/colchicine as ordered (with food); rest.
  • Monitor vital signs, pulsus paradoxus, JVP, heart sounds, respiration, SpO₂ and urine output; report signs of tamponade immediately.
  • Pericardiocentesis care
    • Before – consent, explanation, IV line, ECG monitoring, head raised 30–45°, emergency drugs and defibrillator ready.
    • During – monitor ECG (arrhythmias), BP, SpO₂; support the patient.
    • After – record the amount and character of fluid, send samples (cell count, culture, ADA, cytology), observe for re-accumulation, arrhythmias, pneumothorax and bleeding; drain care if a catheter is left.
  • Health education – complete anti-TB treatment; report recurrence of chest pain, breathlessness or fever.

Nursing importance Tamponade can kill within minutes; nurses who recognise Beck's triad and pulsus paradoxus and prepare quickly for pericardiocentesis save lives.

Conclusion Pericarditis causes positional chest pain and friction rub and is treated with NSAIDs, colchicine and treatment of the cause; cardiac tamponade is an emergency needing immediate pericardiocentesis and vigilant nursing care.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Cardiovascular Disorders (including BCLS)
question: Explain the emergency management of acute pulmonary oedema.
answer_html:
Definition Acute pulmonary oedema is the sudden accumulation of fluid in the interstitium and alveoli of the lungs, which interferes with gas exchange. It is usually cardiogenic – due to acute left ventricular failure – and is a medical emergency.

1. Causes

  • Acute myocardial infarction and ischaemia.
  • Hypertensive crisis.
  • Mitral stenosis (especially with fast atrial fibrillation or in pregnancy), aortic valve disease.
  • Arrhythmias, cardiomyopathy, decompensation of chronic heart failure.
  • Fluid overload – rapid IV fluids or blood transfusion, kidney failure. (Non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema occurs in ARDS, high altitude and some poisonings.)

2. Clinical features

  • Sudden, severe breathlessness, orthopnoea – the patient sits upright, gasping for air.
  • Cough with pink, frothy sputum.
  • Anxiety, restlessness, a feeling of suffocation.
  • Cyanosis, sweating, cold clammy skin.
  • Tachycardia, tachypnoea; BP often high (or low in shock).
  • Crackles throughout both lungs, wheeze ("cardiac asthma"), third heart sound.
  • SpO₂ falls; chest X-ray shows bilateral haziness ("bat-wing" shadows), Kerley B lines.

3. Emergency management (as ordered)

  1. Position – sit the patient upright with the legs hanging down to reduce venous return and ease breathing.
  2. High-flow oxygen to keep SpO₂ at 94% or more; start non-invasive ventilation (CPAP/BiPAP) early if breathing does not improve.
  3. IV loop diuretic – furosemide (for example, 40–80 mg IV) to remove excess fluid.
  4. Nitrates – sublingual or IV nitroglycerin infusion (if systolic BP is above about 100 mmHg) to reduce preload and afterload.
  5. Morphine in small IV doses only for severe distress (it is no longer used routinely).
  6. Treat the cause – control severe hypertension, urgent PCI for MI, control fast AF, stop IV fluids.
  7. Inotropes (dobutamine) or vasopressors if the BP is low (cardiogenic shock).
  8. Intubation and mechanical ventilation if the patient tires, becomes drowsy or SpO₂ remains low.
  9. Urinary catheter to monitor response to diuretics.

4. Nursing responsibilities

  • Stay with the patient, reassure calmly – fear increases breathlessness and heart rate.
  • Monitor respiratory rate, SpO₂, pulse, BP, ECG, level of consciousness and hourly urine output; listen to the lungs for change in crackles.
  • Prepare and manage NIV – correct mask fit, check leaks, watch for intolerance.
  • Secure IV access; give drugs on time; record the response.
  • Restrict fluids and salt; maintain a strict intake–output chart; daily weight.
  • Monitor potassium after diuretics; watch for hypotension.
  • Keep the defibrillator and emergency drugs ready.
  • After recovery – teach salt and fluid limits, daily weighing, regular medicines and early warning signs of heart failure.

Nursing importance Prompt positioning, oxygen, NIV and diuretics within the first minutes, together with calm nursing presence, often reverse acute pulmonary oedema and avoid intubation.

Conclusion Acute pulmonary oedema is a cardiac emergency; sitting the patient up, oxygen and NIV, diuretics, nitrates and treatment of the cause, with close nursing monitoring, are life-saving.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Cardiovascular Disorders (including BCLS)
question: Explain the nursing care of a patient undergoing cardiac catheterisation and coronary angiography.
answer_html:
Definition Cardiac catheterisation is an invasive procedure in which a thin catheter is passed through a peripheral artery (radial or femoral) or vein into the heart chambers and coronary arteries under X-ray (fluoroscopy) guidance. Coronary angiography is the injection of contrast dye into the coronary arteries to show blockages. The same route is used for PCI (angioplasty and stenting).

1. Purposes

  • Diagnose coronary artery disease and its severity; plan PCI or CABG.
  • Assess valve disease, congenital heart disease, cardiomyopathy; measure pressures and oxygen saturations in heart chambers.
  • Interventions – PCI, balloon valvotomy, device closure.

2. Pre-procedure care

  • Explain the procedure (done under local anaesthesia, patient awake, may feel warmth or flushing during dye injection); obtain informed consent.
  • Allergy history – contrast dye, iodine; previous reactions (pre-medication as ordered).
  • Check kidney function (creatinine/eGFR) – risk of contrast-induced kidney injury; ensure good hydration; withhold metformin as per protocol.
  • Check coagulation profile and anticoagulant use (warfarin stopped as advised); CBC, blood group.
  • Fasting for a few hours as per hospital policy; IV cannula (usually on the opposite arm from the access site).
  • Mark and record distal pulses (dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial for femoral access; radial and ulnar for radial access); baseline vital signs and ECG.
  • Skin preparation of the groin or wrist; removal of jewellery and dentures; void before the procedure; pre-medication if ordered.

3. Post-procedure care

  • Vital signs frequently (for example, every 15 minutes for the first hour, then every 30 minutes, then hourly) and ECG monitoring.
  • Puncture site – check for bleeding and haematoma each time; check distal pulses, colour, warmth and sensation of the limb.
  • Femoral access – keep the leg straight and the head of the bed at not more than 30° for the ordered period (usually 2–6 hours depending on the closure method); apply pressure if bleeding occurs and inform the doctor.
  • Radial access – the patient can sit up and walk early; the compression band is released gradually as per protocol; avoid BP measurement and cannulas on that arm; check hand circulation.
  • Hydration – encourage oral fluids (or IV fluids) to flush out the contrast, unless fluid-restricted; monitor urine output.
  • Watch for complications
    • Bleeding, haematoma, retroperitoneal bleeding (back or flank pain, hypotension, falling Hb).
    • Pseudoaneurysm, arterial thrombosis (cold, pale, pulseless limb).
    • Arrhythmias, chest pain (MI), stroke.
    • Contrast allergy (rash, breathlessness, hypotension) and contrast nephropathy (reduced urine, rising creatinine).
    • Vasovagal reaction (bradycardia, hypotension, sweating) during sheath removal.

4. Discharge teaching

  • Avoid heavy lifting and strenuous activity for a few days (radial access – about 2–3 days; femoral – about a week).
  • Keep the site clean and dry; small bruising is normal; if bleeding occurs, press firmly and seek help.
  • Report swelling, pain, numbness, coldness of the limb, fever or discharge.
  • Continue antiplatelet drugs after stenting without interruption; resume metformin only after kidney function is checked, as advised.

Nursing importance Most complications of cardiac catheterisation occur at the puncture site in the first few hours; careful nursing observation prevents serious bleeding and limb ischaemia.

Conclusion Cardiac catheterisation is a common invasive cardiac test; good preparation, monitoring of the puncture site and limb, hydration and patient teaching make it safe.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Cardiovascular Disorders (including BCLS)
question: Explain the procedure of recording a 12-lead ECG and the nurse's responsibilities.

diagram.caption: Placement of ECG chest leads V1 to V6
labels: V1 4th intercostal space right sternal border
V3 midway between V2 and V4
V6 mid-axillary line at level of V4

answer_html:
Definition An electrocardiogram (ECG) is a graphic recording of the electrical activity of the heart from the body surface. A standard 12-lead ECG uses 10 electrodes (4 limb and 6 chest) to view the heart from 12 different angles.

1. Purposes

  • Diagnosis of arrhythmias, myocardial ischaemia and infarction (ST changes, Q waves), conduction blocks.
  • Detection of electrolyte disturbances (potassium, calcium), drug effects (digoxin), chamber enlargement, pericarditis.
  • Pre-operative assessment and routine screening.

2. Electrode placement Limb leads (on the inner aspect of wrists and ankles, or upper arms and thighs, over soft tissue, not bone)

  • RA – right arm, LA – left arm, LL – left leg, RL – right leg (ground); colour codes as per the machine (for example, IEC system: red RA, yellow LA, green LL, black RL). Chest leads

  • V1 – 4th intercostal space at the right sternal border.

  • V2 – 4th intercostal space at the left sternal border.
  • V3 – midway between V2 and V4.
  • V4 – 5th intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line.
  • V5 – left anterior axillary line at the level of V4.
  • V6 – left mid-axillary line at the level of V4. (In women, place V4–V6 under the breast, not on it.)

3. Procedure

  1. Check the order; explain that the test is painless and takes a few minutes; provide privacy.
  2. Ask the patient to remove metal objects; expose the chest, wrists and ankles; position supine (or semi-recumbent if breathless), relaxed, arms by the side.
  3. Prepare the skin – clean with spirit or a gauze to remove oil and sweat; clip hair if needed for good contact.
  4. Attach the electrodes correctly; connect the cables without tension.
  5. Check machine settings – paper speed 25 mm/second and calibration 10 mm/mV.
  6. Ask the patient to lie still, breathe normally and not talk; record the ECG.
  7. Check the tracing for quality – artefacts due to movement, shivering, loose electrodes or electrical interference (wandering baseline, fuzzy lines); repeat if needed.
  8. Label with name, age, hospital number, date, time, and whether the patient had chest pain at the time.
  9. Remove electrodes, clean the skin, help the patient to dress; dispose of electrodes properly.
  10. Show the ECG to the doctor immediately if it is abnormal (for example, ST elevation) and file it in the record.

4. Nurse's responsibilities

  • Record an ECG within 10 minutes in any patient with chest pain.
  • For serial ECGs, mark the chest lead positions on the skin so that tracings are comparable.
  • Know basic interpretation – heart rate (300 ÷ number of large squares between R waves), rhythm, and dangerous patterns (VT, VF, complete heart block, ST elevation).
  • Maintain the machine – charged battery, paper, clean cables and electrodes.
  • Maintain patient dignity and infection control.

Nursing importance A correctly recorded ECG, taken at the right time and promptly shown to the doctor, can lead to life-saving treatment such as thrombolysis or primary PCI.

Conclusion Recording a 12-lead ECG requires correct electrode placement, good skin contact, a still patient and proper labelling; the nurse must recognise urgent abnormalities and report them immediately.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Cardiovascular Disorders (including BCLS)
question: What is a crash cart (emergency trolley)? Explain its contents and maintenance.
answer_html:
Definition A crash cart (emergency or resuscitation trolley) is a mobile trolley containing the equipment and drugs needed for cardiopulmonary resuscitation and other emergencies, kept ready in every ward, OT, emergency department and ICU so that life-saving care can begin within seconds.

1. Principles

  • Standard layout across the hospital so any nurse can find items quickly; a contents list fixed on the cart.
  • Placed in an easily accessible, unobstructed location known to all staff, near an electrical point and oxygen.

2. Contents (a) Top of the cart

  • Defibrillator/monitor (or AED) with pads, ECG electrodes and gel; portable suction with tubing; CPR board; sharps container; gloves. (b) Airway and breathing drawer

  • Oropharyngeal and nasopharyngeal airways of different sizes.

  • Bag-valve mask (Ambu bag) with masks and reservoir, oxygen tubing, face masks, nebuliser kit.

  • Laryngoscope handle with blades (Macintosh 3 and 4) and spare batteries/bulbs; endotracheal tubes (sizes 6.0–8.5), stylet, bougie, laryngeal mask airway, syringe for cuff, tube holder or tape, Magill forceps, suction catheters, Yankauer sucker. (c) Circulation drawer

  • IV cannulas (14–24 G), IV sets, syringes, needles, three-way stopcocks, tourniquet, adhesive dressings, blood sample tubes, ABG syringes; IV fluids – normal saline, Ringer's lactate. (d) Drug drawer (as per hospital list)

  • Adrenaline, atropine, amiodarone, adenosine, lignocaine.

  • Sodium bicarbonate, calcium gluconate, magnesium sulphate, 25%/50% dextrose.
  • Naloxone, hydrocortisone, chlorpheniramine, furosemide, nitroglycerin, salbutamol, midazolam/diazepam.

  • Vasopressors (noradrenaline, dopamine) for infusion. (e) Others

  • Torch, BP apparatus, glucometer, scissors, NG tube, urinary catheter, PPE, code-blue documentation forms.

3. Maintenance (nurse's responsibility)

  • Check daily (and after every use) using a checklist; sign and date.
  • Test the defibrillator daily (charge/self-test) and keep it plugged in for charging; check pads and paper.
  • Check expiry dates of drugs and sterile items (monthly) and replace early.
  • Lock or seal the cart with a numbered breakable seal after checking; record the seal number; open only in emergencies.
  • Restock immediately after each use; report shortages.
  • Keep the cart clean; do not use it as a storage place for routine items.
  • Conduct mock drills and orient new staff to its contents and location.

Nursing importance In cardiac arrest every second counts; a complete, checked crash cart prevents delays caused by missing drugs, flat batteries or empty oxygen cylinders.

Conclusion The crash cart holds all essentials for resuscitation – defibrillator, airway, circulation items and emergency drugs – and must be checked, sealed and restocked regularly by nurses.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Cardiovascular Disorders (including BCLS)
question: Define hypertension and classify it according to blood pressure levels.
answer_html:
Hypertension is a persistent elevation of arterial blood pressure – systolic 140 mmHg or more and/or diastolic 90 mmHg or more – on repeated measurements.

Classification (JNC-7)

  1. Normal – below 120/80 mmHg.
  2. Pre-hypertension – 120–139/80–89 mmHg.
  3. Stage 1 hypertension – 140–159/90–99 mmHg.
  4. Stage 2 hypertension – 160/100 mmHg or more.

By cause – primary (essential, 90–95%) and secondary (kidney disease, endocrine disorders, pregnancy, drugs). Hypertensive crisis – 180/120 mmHg or more (urgency without, emergency with, organ damage).

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Cardiovascular Disorders (including BCLS)
question: List four groups of antihypertensive drugs with one example each.
answer_html:
Groups of antihypertensive drugs

  1. Diuretics – thiazide (hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone), loop (furosemide), potassium-sparing (spironolactone).
  2. ACE inhibitors – enalapril, ramipril.
  3. Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) – telmisartan, losartan.
  4. Calcium-channel blockers – amlodipine, nifedipine.
  5. β-blockers – atenolol, metoprolol.
  6. α-blockers – prazosin; centrally acting – clonidine, methyldopa (in pregnancy); vasodilators – hydralazine, sodium nitroprusside.

Nursing points – check BP (and pulse for β-blockers) before giving; teach the patient to rise slowly (postural hypotension), to take diuretics in the morning, to report cough (ACE inhibitors) or ankle swelling (amlodipine), and never to stop drugs suddenly (rebound hypertension with clonidine and β-blockers).

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Cardiovascular Disorders (including BCLS)
question: Name the coronary arteries and the areas of the heart they supply.
answer_html:
The heart is supplied by two coronary arteries arising from the aortic sinuses just above the aortic valve; most filling occurs during diastole.

  1. Left coronary artery (left main) divides into:
    • Left anterior descending (LAD) – anterior wall of the left ventricle, apex and anterior two-thirds of the septum (blockage causes large anterior MI).
    • Left circumflex (LCx) – lateral and posterior walls of the left ventricle, left atrium.
  2. Right coronary artery (RCA) – right atrium, right ventricle, inferior wall of the left ventricle, posterior one-third of the septum, SA node (in about 60%) and AV node (in most people) – so inferior MI often causes bradycardia and heart block. Venous drainage – mainly through the coronary sinus into the right atrium.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Cardiovascular Disorders (including BCLS)
question: Differentiate between cardioversion and defibrillation.
answer_html:
Point Cardioversion Defibrillation
Shock Synchronised with the R wave (avoids the vulnerable T wave) Unsynchronised – delivered at any point
Used for Unstable tachyarrhythmias with a pulse – atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, SVT, VT with pulse Pulseless VF and pulseless VT (cardiac arrest)
Energy Lower (e.g., 50–200 J biphasic) Higher (120–200 J biphasic; 360 J monophasic)
Patient state Conscious – needs sedation and consent; may be elective (anticoagulation before AF cardioversion) Unconscious – immediate emergency, no sedation

Nursing points (both) – ensure no one touches the patient or bed at the time of shock ("all clear"), remove oxygen sources away from the chest, place pads correctly on dry skin, check the synchronisation marker before cardioversion, and monitor rhythm, BP and airway afterwards; inspect the skin for burns.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Cardiovascular Disorders (including BCLS)
question: List the links in the chain of survival for in-hospital cardiac arrest.
answer_html:
Chain of survival (AHA 2025 – one chain for in-hospital and out-of-hospital arrest)

  1. Recognition and emergency activation – early recognition of the arrest (in hospital helped by monitoring, early warning scores and rapid response teams) and calling "code blue".
  2. High-quality CPR – immediate chest compressions.
  3. Defibrillation with an AED/defibrillator as early as possible.
  4. Advanced resuscitation – advanced airway, IV drugs and treatment of reversible causes by the code team.
  5. Post-cardiac arrest care – ICU care, treatment of the cause, temperature control.
  6. Recovery and survivorship – rehabilitation and psychological support for the patient and family.

Each link must be strong; weakness in any link reduces survival. Prevention and preparedness (monitoring, trained staff, checked crash carts) come before the chain. Older (2020) texts show a separate in-hospital chain beginning with "early recognition and prevention". Outside hospital, the same chain begins with calling 108/112, bystander CPR and use of a public AED.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Cardiovascular Disorders (including BCLS)
question: What is atrial fibrillation? Write its nursing significance.
answer_html:
Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the commonest sustained arrhythmia, in which the atria discharge chaotically (350–600 impulses/min) and quiver instead of contracting, producing an "irregularly irregular" ventricular rhythm. ECG – no P waves, fibrillatory baseline, irregular R–R intervals.

Causes – rheumatic mitral valve disease, hypertension, coronary disease, heart failure, thyrotoxicosis, alcohol, old age. Features – palpitations, irregular pulse, pulse deficit (apical rate higher than radial), breathlessness, fatigue.

Nursing significance

  1. Count apical and radial pulse together for one full minute.
  2. Risk of stroke (clots in the left atrium) – give anticoagulants and teach bleeding precautions.
  3. Give rate-control drugs (β-blockers, digoxin) and monitor for heart failure.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Cardiovascular Disorders (including BCLS)
question: Define aneurysm and list its types.
answer_html:
An aneurysm is a localised, permanent dilatation of an artery to at least 1.5 times its normal diameter, due to weakness of the arterial wall.

Types

  1. By shape – fusiform (whole circumference dilated) and saccular (pouch from one side).
  2. True aneurysm (all three layers) and false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm) – a haematoma contained by surrounding tissue, e.g., after arterial puncture.
  3. Dissecting aneurysm – blood splits the layers of the aortic wall.
  4. By site – abdominal aortic (commonest), thoracic aortic, cerebral (berry) aneurysm (causes subarachnoid haemorrhage), popliteal.

Causes – atherosclerosis, hypertension, smoking, Marfan syndrome, syphilis, trauma, infection. Rupture causes severe pain and shock; treatment is BP control, monitoring, open repair or endovascular stenting (EVAR).

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Cardiovascular Disorders (including BCLS)
question: What is Raynaud's phenomenon?
answer_html:
Raynaud's phenomenon is episodic spasm of the small arteries of the fingers and toes, triggered by cold or emotional stress, producing a typical triphasic colour change:

  1. White (pallor – vasospasm and ischaemia), with numbness.
  2. Blue (cyanosis – deoxygenated blood).
  3. Red (reactive hyperaemia on rewarming), with tingling and throbbing pain.

Types – primary (Raynaud's disease) in young women without underlying disease; secondary to scleroderma, SLE, Buerger's disease, vibrating tools or β-blockers.

Management – keep hands and feet warm (gloves, socks), avoid cold and smoking, stop triggering drugs, calcium-channel blockers (nifedipine), protect fingers from injury, treat the underlying disease.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Haematological Disorders
question: (a) Define leukaemia and classify it. (3 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features and diagnosis of acute leukaemia. (4 marks) (c) Describe the management and nursing care of a patient with acute leukaemia. (8 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Definition and classification (3 marks) Leukaemia is a malignant disease of the blood-forming tissues in which there is uncontrolled proliferation of abnormal (immature) white blood cell precursors in the bone marrow. These cells crowd out normal marrow, spill into the blood and infiltrate organs such as the liver, spleen, lymph nodes and brain.

Classification

  1. According to course and maturity of cells
    • Acute leukaemia – sudden onset, rapid progress; marrow filled with immature blast cells (20% or more); fatal within weeks to months if untreated.
    • Chronic leukaemia – slow onset; more mature but abnormal cells; course of years.
  2. According to cell line
    • Lymphoid (lymphoblastic/lymphocytic) and myeloid (myeloblastic/myelogenous).
  3. Four main types
    • Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) – commonest cancer of children (peak 2–5 years); good cure rates with modern treatment.
    • Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) – mainly adults; acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL) is a special type with bleeding (DIC).
    • Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) – adults (30–60 years); Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) with the BCR-ABL gene; massive splenomegaly.
    • Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) – elderly; often found on a routine blood test.

Risk factors – ionising radiation, benzene and other chemicals, previous chemotherapy, smoking (AML), genetic conditions (Down syndrome, Fanconi anaemia), some viruses (HTLV-1).

(b) Clinical features and diagnosis of acute leukaemia (4 marks) Clinical features – mainly due to bone marrow failure and organ infiltration

  1. Anaemia (reduced RBCs) – pallor, fatigue, weakness, breathlessness, palpitations.
  2. Neutropenia (lack of functioning WBCs) – fever and repeated infections (sore throat, mouth ulcers, pneumonia, skin infections, septicaemia).
  3. Thrombocytopenia – bleeding: petechiae, bruises, gum bleeding, nosebleeds, heavy menstruation, blood in urine or stools; intracranial bleeding.
  4. Infiltration
    • Bone pain and sternal tenderness (children may refuse to walk).
    • Lymph node enlargement, hepatosplenomegaly.
    • Gum hypertrophy, skin nodules (AML).
    • CNS involvement (ALL) – headache, vomiting, cranial nerve palsies; testicular swelling.
  5. General – weight loss, night sweats, loss of appetite.
  6. Leucostasis with very high WBC counts – breathlessness, confusion, visual disturbance.

Diagnosis

  • CBC – anaemia, thrombocytopenia; WBC count may be high, normal or low.
  • Peripheral smear – blast cells; Auer rods in AML.
  • Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy – 20% or more blasts confirms acute leukaemia.
  • Flow cytometry (immunophenotyping), cytogenetics and molecular tests (e.g., Philadelphia chromosome, BCR-ABL) to classify the type and plan therapy.
  • Lumbar puncture (CSF for blasts in ALL); chest X-ray (mediastinal mass); coagulation profile (DIC in APL); uric acid, potassium, phosphate, calcium, LFT and RFT (baseline and tumour lysis); echocardiography before cardiotoxic drugs; HLA typing for transplant.

(c) Management and nursing care (8 marks) 1. Medical management

  • Combination chemotherapy in phases:
    • Induction – to achieve remission (no detectable blasts, normal blood counts).
    • Consolidation (intensification) – to destroy remaining leukaemic cells.
    • Maintenance (especially in ALL, for about 2–3 years) – oral drugs and periodic injections.
    • CNS prophylaxis in ALL – intrathecal methotrexate.
  • Targeted therapy – imatinib and other tyrosine kinase inhibitors for CML and Philadelphia-positive ALL; ATRA with arsenic trioxide for APL (very high cure rates).
  • Haematopoietic stem cell (bone marrow) transplantation for high-risk or relapsed disease.
  • Supportive care
    • Blood components – irradiated, leucodepleted packed cells and platelets.
    • Antibiotics, antifungals and antivirals; G-CSF in selected patients.
    • Prevention of tumour lysis syndrome – IV hydration, allopurinol or rasburicase, monitoring of potassium, phosphate, calcium and uric acid.
    • Nutrition, pain relief, psychosocial and palliative support.
  • In India, treatment is supported under PM-JAY, state schemes and charitable cancer centres; childhood ALL cure rates now exceed 70–80% in good centres.

2. Nursing care – nursing diagnoses and interventions (i) Risk for infection related to neutropenia and chemotherapy (absolute neutrophil count below 500/mm³ is high risk)

  • Hand hygiene by everyone – the single most important measure.
  • Protective (reverse barrier) isolation – single room, restricted visitors, no one with cold, fever or chickenpox; masks as per policy.
  • No fresh flowers, potted plants or stagnant water in the room.
  • Safe food – freshly cooked, hot food; boiled or filtered water; avoid raw salads, unpasteurised milk, street food and fruits that cannot be peeled.
  • Oral care after meals and at bedtime with a soft toothbrush and mild mouthwash; inspect the mouth daily.
  • Perineal hygiene; avoid rectal temperatures, suppositories and enemas.
  • Aseptic care of central lines (PICC, chemoport) and minimal invasive procedures.
  • Monitor temperature 4-hourly; febrile neutropenia (temperature 38.3 °C once or 38 °C for one hour) is an emergency – take blood cultures and start IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 60 minutes.

(ii) Risk for bleeding related to thrombocytopenia

  • Avoid IM injections, unnecessary punctures and rectal procedures; apply firm pressure for 5–10 minutes after needle removal.
  • Use a soft toothbrush, electric razor; avoid forceful nose blowing and straining (give stool softeners).
  • No aspirin or NSAIDs.
  • Observe for petechiae, bruises, gum bleeding, haematuria, malaena, heavy menstruation, headache or confusion (intracranial bleeding).
  • Pad side rails, prevent falls; give platelet transfusions as ordered.

(iii) Fatigue and activity intolerance related to anaemia

  • Plan rest periods; assist with daily activities; give packed red cells and oxygen as ordered; gradual increase in activity.

(iv) Care during chemotherapy

  • Safe handling of cytotoxic drugs – preparation in a biological safety cabinet, chemotherapy gloves and gown, spill kit, closed systems; dispose of cytotoxic waste in the designated yellow container as per BMW rules; pregnant staff should not handle these drugs.
  • Verify the drug, dose (calculated on body surface area) and patient with a second nurse.
  • Prevent extravasation of vesicant drugs – ensure a free-flowing line, check blood return, watch for pain, swelling or redness; if it occurs – stop the infusion, aspirate, inform the doctor, apply antidote and hot or cold packs as per drug.
  • Nausea and vomiting – give antiemetics before chemotherapy, small bland meals.
  • Mucositis – frequent saline mouthwashes, soft cool foods, topical anaesthetic gels, adequate analgesia.
  • Alopecia – counsel before it happens; scarf, cap or wig; reassure that hair regrows.
  • Tumour lysis syndrome – 2–3 litres or more of fluid daily, allopurinol, strict intake–output, monitor potassium, phosphate, calcium, uric acid and creatinine.

(v) Imbalanced nutrition – high-calorie, high-protein, small frequent meals; nutritional supplements; weigh regularly; treat mouth ulcers and nausea.

(vi) Acute pain (bone pain, mucositis, procedures) – regular analgesics (paracetamol, opioids; avoid NSAIDs), comfortable positioning, sedation or analgesia before bone marrow and lumbar punctures.

(vii) Anxiety, fear and grief – honest information, involvement of the family; for children, play therapy, continued schooling in hospital, parents' support; financial counselling and linking to support schemes and NGOs; spiritual care; palliative care in advanced disease.

3. Discharge teaching

  • Continue maintenance drugs exactly as prescribed; keep follow-up and blood-count appointments.
  • Report fever (38 °C or above), chills, bleeding, persistent headache, sore throat or mouth ulcers immediately.
  • Hand hygiene, safe food and water, avoid crowds and sick contacts; no live vaccines during treatment.
  • Care of the central line; adequate rest and nutrition; gradual return to school or work as advised.

Nursing importance Most deaths during leukaemia treatment are due to infection and bleeding, not the leukaemia itself; meticulous nursing – hand hygiene, early detection of fever, bleeding precautions and safe chemotherapy – greatly improves survival.

Conclusion Leukaemia is a malignant proliferation of immature white cells causing anaemia, infection and bleeding; combination chemotherapy, targeted drugs and stem cell transplantation can cure many patients when supported by expert, compassionate nursing care.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Haematological Disorders
question: (a) Define sickle cell disease and explain its inheritance. (3 marks) (b) Explain the pathophysiology and clinical features, including the types of crises. (5 marks) (c) Describe the management and nursing care of a patient in sickle cell crisis, with health education. (7 marks)
tags: National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission

diagram.caption: Sickling of red cells and vaso-occlusion
labels: sickled cells blocking a small vessel causing ischaemia and pain; inheritance chart of two carrier parents (AA 25%

answer_html:
(a) Definition and inheritance (3 marks) Sickle cell disease (SCD) is an inherited (autosomal recessive) disorder of haemoglobin in which an abnormal haemoglobin, HbS, is formed because of a point mutation in the β-globin gene (glutamic acid is replaced by valine at position 6). When deoxygenated, HbS polymerises and the red cells become rigid and sickle (crescent)-shaped, causing chronic haemolytic anaemia and episodes of vaso-occlusion (crises).

Forms

  • Sickle cell anaemia (HbSS) – inherited from both parents; causes the disease.
  • Sickle cell trait (HbAS) – a carrier state with one abnormal gene; usually no symptoms.
  • Compound forms – HbS with β-thalassaemia (HbS-β-thal).

Inheritance

  • If both parents are carriers (AS × AS), in each pregnancy there is a 25% chance of a child with sickle cell disease (SS), 50% chance of a carrier (AS) and 25% chance of a normal child (AA).
  • If one parent has the disease and the other is a carrier, there is a 50% chance of each child having the disease.

Indian context

  • SCD is common among tribal and some non-tribal communities of central and western India – Maharashtra (Vidarbha – Nagpur, Gadchiroli, Chandrapur, Bhandara, Gondia), Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Gujarat, Jharkhand and parts of south India.
  • The National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (launched in July 2023) aims at universal screening of people aged 0–40 years in affected areas, issue of genetic status (sickle cell) cards, counselling and care, to eliminate SCD as a public health problem by 2047. Maharashtra has also run a state sickle cell programme for many years.

(b) Pathophysiology and clinical features (5 marks) Pathophysiology

  • Triggers – hypoxia, dehydration, infection and fever, cold, acidosis, emotional stress, strenuous exercise, high altitude, pregnancy.
  • Under low oxygen, HbS molecules stick together and distort the red cell into a sickle shape.
  • Two main consequences
    1. Haemolysis – sickle cells survive only 10–20 days (normal 120) → chronic haemolytic anaemia, jaundice, gallstones.
    2. Vaso-occlusion – rigid sickle cells block small vessels → ischaemia and infarction of bones, lungs, spleen, brain, kidneys → severe pain and organ damage.
  • Repeated splenic infarction causes "autosplenectomy" (shrunken, non-functioning spleen) → high risk of serious infections (pneumococcus, Salmonella).

Clinical features

  • Chronic anaemia (Hb often 6–9 g/dl), fatigue, jaundice, pallor.
  • Infants – dactylitis (hand–foot syndrome): painful swelling of hands and feet; splenomegaly in early childhood.
  • Growth retardation, delayed puberty.
  • Recurrent infections, pneumonia, osteomyelitis (Salmonella), malaria (severe).
  • Chronic organ damage – leg ulcers, avascular necrosis of the femoral head, stroke (especially in children), retinopathy, kidney damage (inability to concentrate urine, haematuria), priapism, pulmonary hypertension, gallstones.

Types of sickle cell crises

  1. Vaso-occlusive (painful) crisis – the commonest; sudden severe pain in bones (back, limbs, chest), joints and abdomen, lasting hours to days; may have fever and swelling.
  2. Acute chest syndrome – chest pain, fever, cough, breathlessness, hypoxia and a new infiltrate on X-ray; a leading cause of death – an emergency.
  3. Splenic sequestration crisis (young children) – sudden pooling of blood in the spleen → rapid enlargement of the spleen, sharp fall in Hb, shock.
  4. Aplastic crisis – temporary stop in red-cell production, usually after parvovirus B19 infection; severe anaemia with very low reticulocytes.
  5. Haemolytic crisis – increased haemolysis with worsening anaemia and jaundice.
  6. Other acute events – stroke, priapism, severe infection.

Diagnosis Solubility test and sickling (sodium metabisulphite) slide test for screening; point-of-care rapid tests; HPLC or haemoglobin electrophoresis (confirmatory); newborn screening by dried blood spot; CBC, peripheral smear (sickle cells, target cells), reticulocyte count, LFT (bilirubin), chest X-ray in chest symptoms.

(c) Management and nursing care of a patient in crisis (7 marks) 1. Medical management of crisis

  • Rapid and adequate analgesia – within 30–60 minutes of arrival: paracetamol, NSAIDs (if kidneys are normal) and opioids (morphine) titrated to pain, sometimes by PCA.
  • Hydration – oral and IV fluids (about 1.5 times maintenance) to reduce sickling; avoid overload.
  • Oxygen if SpO₂ is below 95%.
  • Treat infection – blood cultures and broad-spectrum antibiotics for fever.
  • Blood transfusion – simple or exchange transfusion for acute chest syndrome, stroke, severe anaemia, splenic sequestration and aplastic crisis.
  • Incentive spirometry to prevent acute chest syndrome in chest or back pain.

2. Long-term (disease-modifying) management

  • Hydroxyurea – increases fetal haemoglobin (HbF), reducing crises, acute chest syndrome, transfusions and deaths; available free under the national mission; needs regular CBC monitoring.
  • Folic acid daily (increased red-cell turnover).
  • Penicillin prophylaxis in children (up to 5 years) and vaccines – pneumococcal, Hib, meningococcal, influenza, typhoid, hepatitis B.
  • Transcranial Doppler screening in children to predict stroke; chronic transfusion with iron chelation where needed.
  • Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation – the only established cure; gene therapies are emerging.
  • Regular follow-up at sickle cell clinics (district hospitals).

3. Nursing care (i) Acute pain – assess pain regularly with a pain scale; believe the patient's report; give analgesics on time (not "as needed" only); use warm compresses, gentle massage, positioning and distraction; avoid cold packs (cold causes vasoconstriction and more sickling). (ii) Risk for deficient fluid volume – encourage oral fluids, maintain IV fluids, strict intake–output, monitor urine colour and output. (iii) Impaired gas exchange – monitor SpO₂ and respiratory rate; oxygen as ordered; incentive spirometry every 2 hours while awake; report chest pain, cough, breathlessness (acute chest syndrome). (iv) Risk for infection – monitor temperature; fever of 38.5 °C or more is an emergency in SCD; hand hygiene; ensure prophylactic penicillin and vaccines. (v) Monitor for complications – neurological changes (stroke), sudden pallor and enlarging spleen (sequestration – teach parents to feel the spleen), priapism lasting more than 2–4 hours, jaundice, leg ulcers. (vi) Rest and warmth – rest during crisis, keep warm, avoid tight clothing and positions that restrict circulation. (vii) Psychosocial care – chronic pain, school absence and stigma cause stress; counselling, support groups, involvement of family and school.

4. Health education

  • Drink plenty of water daily (2–3 litres or more in adults), especially in summer, during fever and when travelling.
  • Avoid triggers – dehydration, extreme heat or cold, swimming in cold water, high altitudes, strenuous exercise without rest, alcohol and smoking.
  • Seek care immediately for fever, severe pain, breathlessness, chest pain, weakness or speech problems, sudden pallor or abdominal swelling, painful erection.
  • Take folic acid and hydroxyurea regularly; keep blood-test appointments; use contraception while on hydroxyurea and plan pregnancy with the doctor.
  • Complete vaccinations; use mosquito nets (malaria worsens SCD).
  • Genetic counselling – encourage premarital and antenatal screening; carry the sickle cell card; carriers (AS) should know the 25% risk if both partners are carriers; prenatal diagnosis (chorionic villus sampling at 10–12 weeks) is available for carrier couples.

Nursing importance In Vidarbha and other endemic areas, nurses are at the centre of screening, counselling and crisis care; adequate pain relief, hydration and early detection of acute chest syndrome save lives, while genetic counselling prevents new cases.

Conclusion Sickle cell disease is an inherited haemoglobin disorder causing haemolysis and painful vaso-occlusive crises; prompt analgesia, fluids, oxygen and treatment of infection in crises, hydroxyurea and folic acid in the long term, and screening with genetic counselling are the pillars of care.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Haematological Disorders
question: Explain the clinical features and nursing management of a patient with haemophilia.
answer_html:
Definition Haemophilia is an inherited, X-linked recessive bleeding disorder due to deficiency of a clotting factor – factor VIII (haemophilia A – about 80–85%) or factor IX (haemophilia B – Christmas disease). It affects males; females are usually carriers.

1. Severity

  • Severe – factor level below 1% – spontaneous bleeding into joints and muscles.
  • Moderate – 1–5% – bleeding after minor injuries.
  • Mild – 5–40% – bleeding only after surgery, tooth extraction or major injury.

2. Clinical features

  • Haemarthrosis – bleeding into knees, elbows and ankles – pain, swelling, warmth, restricted movement; repeated bleeds cause chronic haemophilic arthropathy (deformity and disability).
  • Muscle haematomas (thigh, calf, iliopsoas) – may compress nerves and vessels.
  • Prolonged bleeding after circumcision, tooth extraction, injections, cuts or surgery; easy bruising.
  • Bleeding in the mouth, nose, urine (haematuria), GI tract.
  • Intracranial haemorrhage after minor head injury – the commonest cause of death.

3. Laboratory findings Prolonged aPTT, normal PT, normal platelet count and bleeding time; low factor VIII or IX level on factor assay; inhibitor screening.

4. Management

  • Factor replacement – IV factor VIII or IX concentrate, either on demand (at the start of a bleed) or as prophylaxis (regular infusions to prevent bleeds, especially in children).
  • Emicizumab – a subcutaneous drug for prophylaxis in haemophilia A.
  • Cryoprecipitate or fresh frozen plasma only if concentrates are not available.
  • Desmopressin (DDAVP) for mild haemophilia A; tranexamic acid for mouth and nose bleeds.
  • Physiotherapy after bleeds; orthopaedic surgery for damaged joints.
  • In India, many states provide factor concentrates free through government hospitals and haemophilia treatment centres.

5. Nursing management

  • During a bleed – give factor concentrate as early as possible; follow RICE – Rest (splint the joint), Ice (wrapped, 15–20 minutes), Compression, Elevation; pain relief with paracetamol (no aspirin or NSAIDs).
  • Never give IM injections – use oral, IV or subcutaneous routes; apply pressure for at least 5 minutes after venepuncture.
  • Watch for signs of serious bleeding – headache, vomiting, drowsiness (intracranial), abdominal or groin pain (iliopsoas), airway swelling (neck bleeds).
  • Safe environment – soft toys and padded cot sides for toddlers, helmets and knee pads; avoid contact sports; encourage swimming and cycling to strengthen muscles.
  • Dental care – soft toothbrush, regular check-ups; factor cover before dental extraction.
  • Home therapy – teach parents and older children to give factor infusions at home; keep a bleeding diary.
  • Medical alert card or bracelet.
  • Genetic counselling – a carrier mother has a 50% chance of an affected son and 50% chance of a carrier daughter; carrier testing of sisters and daughters.
  • Psychological support, school education, and linking to the Haemophilia Federation (India) and support groups.

Nursing importance Early factor replacement and good nursing care at each bleed prevent joint destruction and disability, while teaching home therapy gives the child a near-normal life.

Conclusion Haemophilia is an X-linked deficiency of factor VIII or IX causing joint and muscle bleeds; factor replacement, RICE, avoidance of IM injections and NSAIDs, and education of the family are the key elements of care.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Haematological Disorders
question: Explain the causes, clinical features and nursing management of immune thrombocytopenia (ITP).
answer_html:
Definition Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), formerly called idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, is an autoimmune disorder in which antibodies coat the platelets, which are then destroyed in the spleen, leading to a low platelet count (below 1 lakh/µl) and bleeding. Platelet production may also be reduced.

1. Types

  • Acute ITP – mainly children, often 1–3 weeks after a viral infection or vaccination; sudden onset; usually resolves on its own within weeks to months.
  • Chronic ITP – mainly adults (women 20–40 years); lasts more than 12 months; may be associated with SLE, HIV, hepatitis C or H. pylori.

2. Clinical features

  • Petechiae and purpura (pinpoint red spots and bruises), especially on the legs.
  • Mucosal bleeding – nosebleeds, gum bleeding, blood blisters in the mouth, heavy menstrual bleeding, haematuria, GI bleeding.
  • Prolonged bleeding after injury; rarely intracranial haemorrhage.
  • The patient is otherwise well; spleen is not enlarged.

3. Diagnosis

  • CBC – low platelets with normal Hb and WBC (unless bleeding); peripheral smear – large platelets, rules out pseudothrombocytopenia (clumping).
  • Exclude other causes – dengue, malaria, drugs (heparin, quinine), HIV, hepatitis C, SLE, leukaemia, aplastic anaemia; bone marrow examination in doubtful or older patients.

4. Management

  • Observation – children and adults with platelets above about 30,000/µl and no significant bleeding.
  • Corticosteroids – prednisolone or high-dose dexamethasone (first-line).
  • IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) – rapid rise in platelets for serious bleeding or before surgery.
  • Second-line – thrombopoietin-receptor agonists (eltrombopag, romiplostim), rituximab, splenectomy (after pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib vaccination).
  • Platelet transfusion only for life-threatening bleeding (with IVIG and steroids), as transfused platelets are also destroyed.
  • H. pylori eradication if positive.

5. Nursing management

  • Bleeding precautions – avoid IM injections and unnecessary venepunctures; pressure for 5–10 minutes after punctures; soft toothbrush; electric razor; no aspirin or NSAIDs; stool softeners; avoid forceful nose blowing; safe environment to prevent falls; avoid contact sports.
  • Monitor – platelet counts, skin and mucosa for new bleeding, urine and stools, menstrual loss (pad count), vital signs, and neurological status (headache, vomiting, drowsiness – possible intracranial bleed).
  • Steroid therapy – give with food; monitor blood sugar, BP, weight, mood and signs of infection; do not stop suddenly.
  • After splenectomy – watch for bleeding and infection; teach lifelong risk of serious infections, need for vaccines and early treatment of fever.
  • Education – recognise warning signs of bleeding, avoid unprescribed medicines and herbal products that affect platelets, wear a medical alert card, regular follow-up; reassure parents of children with acute ITP that most recover fully.

Nursing importance Careful observation for bleeding and simple protective measures by nurses prevent serious haemorrhage while the platelet count recovers.

Conclusion ITP is autoimmune destruction of platelets causing mucocutaneous bleeding; observation, steroids, IVIG and second-line therapies, together with bleeding precautions and education, form the basis of care.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Haematological Disorders
question: Explain the causes, clinical features and nursing management of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).
answer_html:
Definition Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is an acquired, life-threatening syndrome in which there is widespread activation of coagulation within blood vessels, forming microthrombi in small vessels and consuming platelets and clotting factors, which then leads to bleeding. Thus the patient has both clotting and bleeding at the same time. DIC is always secondary to another serious condition.

1. Causes (triggers)

  • Sepsis – the commonest cause (Gram-negative septicaemia, meningococcaemia, falciparum malaria).
  • Obstetric – abruptio placentae, amniotic fluid embolism, retained dead fetus, severe postpartum haemorrhage, eclampsia and HELLP syndrome, septic abortion.
  • Trauma – major injuries, head injury, burns, crush injuries, fat embolism.
  • Malignancy – acute promyelocytic leukaemia, mucin-secreting adenocarcinomas.
  • Snake bite – especially Russell's viper envenomation in India.
  • Others – incompatible blood transfusion, acute pancreatitis, liver failure, heat stroke, shock.

2. Clinical features

  • Bleeding from multiple sites – oozing from venepuncture and IV sites, wounds and drains; gum bleeding, nosebleeds; haematuria, GI bleeding; petechiae, purpura, large bruises; heavy vaginal bleeding.
  • Thrombosis and ischaemia – cold, cyanosed, mottled fingers and toes, gangrene; organ dysfunction – acute kidney injury (oliguria), ARDS (breathlessness), confusion or stroke, liver dysfunction.
  • Shock – hypotension, tachycardia.

3. Laboratory findings Low platelet count, prolonged PT and aPTT, low fibrinogen, raised D-dimer and fibrin degradation products, fragmented red cells (schistocytes) on the smear; a scoring system (ISTH DIC score) helps in diagnosis. Whole-blood clotting time (20-minute WBCT) is used in snake bite.

4. Management

  • Treat the underlying cause – the most important step: antibiotics and source control in sepsis, delivery of the fetus and evacuation of the uterus in obstetric causes, anti-snake venom in viper bite, treatment of leukaemia.
  • Supportive care – oxygen, IV fluids, vasopressors for shock.
  • Blood component replacement in bleeding patients – platelets (if below about 50,000/µl), fresh frozen plasma (clotting factors), cryoprecipitate (if fibrinogen is low), packed red cells.
  • Heparin in selected patients in whom thrombosis predominates (as decided by the physician).

5. Nursing management

  • Monitor bleeding sites – IV and puncture sites, wounds, drains, mouth, urine, stools, vaginal bleeding; measure and record losses; check for new petechiae and bruising.
  • Minimise trauma – avoid IM injections and unnecessary punctures; apply pressure on sites for longer; gentle mouth care with soft swabs; avoid rectal temperatures; use soft restraints only if absolutely necessary.
  • Monitor perfusion – colour, temperature and pulses of extremities, urine output (hourly), level of consciousness, respiratory status and SpO₂.
  • Vital signs frequently; watch for shock.
  • Safe transfusion of blood components – correct identification, rates and monitoring for reactions and overload.
  • Accurate intake–output; monitor lab results (platelets, PT, fibrinogen, D-dimer) and report trends.
  • Support the patient and family – explain the condition; DIC is frightening because of visible bleeding.

Nursing importance The nurse is often the first to notice oozing from IV sites or new bruises, which may be the earliest sign of DIC; quick reporting allows early treatment of the cause.

Conclusion DIC is a secondary consumptive coagulopathy with simultaneous clotting and bleeding; treating the underlying cause, replacing blood components and careful nursing observation and protection are essential for survival.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Haematological Disorders
question: Explain the causes, clinical features and management of aplastic anaemia.
answer_html:
Definition Aplastic anaemia is a bone marrow failure syndrome in which the marrow becomes hypocellular (empty, replaced by fat) and fails to produce enough blood cells, leading to pancytopenia – low red cells, white cells and platelets.

1. Causes

  • Idiopathic / autoimmune – most cases; T cells attack the marrow stem cells.
  • Drugs – chloramphenicol, sulfonamides, anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, phenytoin), gold, NSAIDs (phenylbutazone), antithyroid drugs, cytotoxic chemotherapy.
  • Chemicals – benzene, insecticides and pesticides (important in agricultural areas), solvents.
  • Ionising radiation.
  • Viral infections – hepatitis (non-A to E), parvovirus B19, EBV, HIV.
  • Pregnancy; paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria.
  • Inherited – Fanconi anaemia (with short stature and thumb abnormalities).

2. Clinical features

  • Anaemia – pallor, fatigue, breathlessness, palpitations.
  • Neutropenia – recurrent infections, fever, mouth ulcers, sore throat.
  • Thrombocytopenia – bleeding: petechiae, bruising, gum and nose bleeds, menorrhagia.
  • No enlargement of liver, spleen or lymph nodes (unlike leukaemia).

3. Diagnosis

  • CBC – pancytopenia with very low reticulocytes; normal or large red cells.
  • Bone marrow aspiration and trephine biopsy – hypocellular, fatty marrow without abnormal cells.
  • Tests for causes – viral serology, B₁₂ and folate, PNH testing, chromosome breakage test (Fanconi).

4. Management

  • Remove the cause – stop suspected drugs, avoid chemical exposure.
  • Supportive – packed red cell and platelet transfusions (irradiated, leucodepleted; avoid using family donors if transplant is planned); antibiotics and antifungals for infections; G-CSF in some cases; iron chelation if transfused often.
  • Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation – treatment of choice for young patients with an HLA-matched sibling donor.
  • Immunosuppressive therapy – antithymocyte globulin (ATG) with ciclosporin, often with eltrombopag, for those not suitable for transplant.

5. Nursing management

  • Prevent infection – strict hand hygiene, protective isolation when neutropenic, safe food and water, oral and perineal hygiene, temperature monitoring and urgent action for fever.
  • Prevent bleeding – no IM injections, soft toothbrush, electric razor, no aspirin or NSAIDs, pressure on puncture sites, fall prevention.
  • Manage fatigue – rest periods, help with activities, transfusions as ordered.
  • Transfusion care – correct identification, monitoring for reactions, iron overload awareness.
  • Drug therapy – monitor for ATG reactions (fever, rigors, serum sickness) and ciclosporin side effects (high BP, kidney toxicity, gum hypertrophy, tremor).
  • Psychological support – long illness, frequent transfusions, cost of transplant; link to support schemes.
  • Education – avoid exposure to pesticides, benzene and unnecessary medicines; report fever or bleeding early.

Nursing importance Patients with aplastic anaemia die mostly from infection and bleeding; strict nursing precautions keep them alive until marrow recovery or transplantation.

Conclusion Aplastic anaemia is marrow failure causing pancytopenia; removal of the cause, supportive transfusions and anti-infective care, stem cell transplantation or immunosuppression, with meticulous nursing care, improve survival.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Haematological Disorders
question: Explain the causes, clinical features and management of megaloblastic anaemia.
answer_html:
Definition Megaloblastic anaemia is a macrocytic anaemia caused by impaired DNA synthesis in developing red cells, usually due to deficiency of vitamin B₁₂ or folic acid. The bone marrow shows large abnormal precursors called megaloblasts, and the red cells are large (MCV above 100 fl).

1. Causes Vitamin B₁₂ deficiency

  • Strict vegetarian diet – B₁₂ is found only in animal foods; very common in India.
  • Pernicious anaemia – autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor.
  • Gastrectomy, ileal resection or disease (Crohn's, tropical sprue), fish tapeworm.

  • Long-term metformin and proton-pump inhibitors. Folic acid deficiency

  • Poor diet (overcooking destroys folate), alcoholism.

  • Increased need – pregnancy and lactation, infancy, haemolytic anaemia.
  • Malabsorption; drugs – methotrexate, phenytoin, trimethoprim.

2. Clinical features

  • Anaemia – fatigue, breathlessness, palpitations, pallor with a mild lemon-yellow tint (mild jaundice due to ineffective erythropoiesis).
  • Glossitis (smooth, red, sore "beefy" tongue), angular stomatitis, loss of appetite, diarrhoea, weight loss.
  • Hyperpigmentation of knuckles (B₁₂ deficiency in Indians).
  • Neurological features (B₁₂ deficiency only) – tingling and numbness of hands and feet, loss of vibration and position sense, unsteady gait (ataxia), subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord, memory loss, depression, dementia.

3. Investigations

  • CBC – low Hb, high MCV, low reticulocytes; may have low WBC and platelets.
  • Peripheral smear – macro-ovalocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils (more than 5 lobes).
  • Serum B₁₂ and folate levels (low); raised LDH and indirect bilirubin.
  • Anti-intrinsic factor antibodies (pernicious anaemia); bone marrow (megaloblasts) in doubtful cases.

4. Management

  • Vitamin B₁₂ – IM injections (hydroxocobalamin or cyanocobalamin 1000 µg) frequently at first, then monthly; lifelong in pernicious anaemia and after gastrectomy; high-dose oral B₁₂ in dietary deficiency.
  • Folic acid 5 mg daily for about 4 months (longer if the cause continues).
  • Never treat B₁₂ deficiency with folic acid alone – the blood picture improves but nerve damage worsens.
  • Diet – B₁₂ sources: milk, curd, paneer, eggs, fish, meat, fortified foods; folate sources: green leafy vegetables, pulses, citrus fruits, liver.
  • Treat the cause; IFA supplementation under Anaemia Mukt Bharat; blood transfusion only for severe symptomatic anaemia (slowly, to avoid heart failure).

5. Nursing management

  • Assess neurological status and prevent falls (numbness, unsteady gait); protect numb feet from burns and injury.
  • Oral care for glossitis – soft, bland, non-spicy food; saline mouthwashes.
  • Give injections correctly and teach the importance of lifelong therapy where needed.
  • Monitor potassium early in treatment (it may fall as new red cells are formed) and watch for fluid overload in the elderly.
  • Rest and gradual activity; nutritious diet; diet counselling for vegetarians (milk and curd daily).
  • Follow-up – reticulocyte rise within a week, Hb recovery over weeks; neurological recovery may be slow or incomplete.

Nursing importance Early recognition and treatment of B₁₂ deficiency by nurses prevents permanent nerve damage, while diet counselling prevents recurrence.

Conclusion Megaloblastic anaemia is due to B₁₂ or folate deficiency causing macrocytic anaemia and, in B₁₂ deficiency, neurological damage; correct replacement, diet and treatment of the cause restore health.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Haematological Disorders
question: Differentiate between Hodgkin's lymphoma and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma and explain the nursing care.
answer_html:
Definition Lymphomas are malignant tumours of the lymphoid tissue (lymph nodes, spleen and other lymphoid organs) arising from lymphocytes. They are divided into Hodgkin's lymphoma (HL) and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (NHL).

1. Differences | Feature | Hodgkin's lymphoma | Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma | |---|---|---| | Frequency | Less common | More common (about 85%) | | Age | Two peaks – young adults (15–35) and above 55 | Mainly older adults; any age | | Characteristic cell | Reed–Sternberg cell | No Reed–Sternberg cells; mostly B-cell (diffuse large B-cell commonest) | | Spread | Orderly, to adjacent (contiguous) node groups | Non-contiguous; early spread | | Extranodal involvement | Uncommon | Common – GI tract, skin, CNS, bone marrow | | Associations | EBV | HIV, EBV, H. pylori (gastric MALT lymphoma), immunosuppression | | Typical treatment | ABVD chemotherapy ± radiotherapy | R-CHOP (rituximab-based) chemotherapy ± radiotherapy | | Prognosis | Very good (cure above 80%) | Variable – depends on type and stage |

2. Clinical features (both)

  • Painless, rubbery enlargement of lymph nodes, commonly in the neck, axilla or groin.
  • "B" symptoms – fever (may be cyclical – Pel–Ebstein fever in HL), drenching night sweats, weight loss of more than 10% in 6 months.
  • Itching (HL), fatigue, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly.
  • Pressure effects – breathlessness and cough (mediastinal nodes), superior vena cava obstruction, abdominal pain.

3. Diagnosis and staging Excision biopsy of a lymph node (essential), CBC, ESR, LDH, LFT, RFT, chest X-ray, PET-CT scan, bone marrow biopsy; Ann Arbor staging (I–IV) with "A" (no B symptoms) or "B".

4. Nursing care

  • Chemotherapy and immunotherapy care – antiemetics, oral care for mucositis, monitoring blood counts, infection prevention (neutropenia), bleeding precautions, management of infusion reactions (rituximab).
  • Radiotherapy care – skin in the field kept clean and dry, no creams or powders unless prescribed, loose cotton clothes, avoid sun; watch for dry mouth and difficulty swallowing in neck radiation.
  • B symptoms – tepid sponging, antipyretics, change damp linen after night sweats, extra fluids and calories.
  • Nutrition – high-calorie, high-protein small meals; weight monitoring.
  • Fertility counselling – sperm or egg preservation before treatment for young patients.
  • Psychosocial support – reassure about good cure rates (especially HL), body image (alopecia), financial and family support.
  • Long-term follow-up for relapse and late effects (thyroid problems after neck radiation, heart disease, second cancers).

Nursing importance Lymphomas are among the most curable cancers; nurses help patients complete intensive treatment safely by preventing infections and managing side effects.

Conclusion Hodgkin's lymphoma has Reed–Sternberg cells, contiguous spread and excellent prognosis, while non-Hodgkin's lymphoma is more varied and often extranodal; chemotherapy, radiotherapy and supportive nursing care can cure many patients.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Haematological Disorders
question: Explain the nurse's responsibilities in bone marrow aspiration and biopsy.
answer_html:
Definition Bone marrow aspiration is the removal of a small amount of liquid marrow with a needle for microscopic examination; bone marrow (trephine) biopsy is the removal of a core of bone with marrow to study marrow structure and cellularity. Both are usually done together.

1. Sites

  • Posterior superior iliac spine – the commonest and safest site in adults and children.
  • Anterior iliac crest.
  • Sternum – aspiration only, in adults (not for biopsy; risk of puncturing deeper structures).
  • Upper tibia – in infants below one year.

2. Indications Unexplained anaemia, leucopenia or thrombocytopenia; diagnosis and follow-up of leukaemia, aplastic anaemia, multiple myeloma; staging of lymphoma and other cancers; pyrexia of unknown origin (culture for TB, typhoid, kala-azar); assessment of iron stores; storage disorders.

3. Before the procedure

  • Explain the procedure and its purpose; obtain written consent.
  • Check platelet count and coagulation profile (correct severe abnormalities as ordered); note anticoagulant use and allergies.
  • Record baseline vital signs; give analgesic or sedative premedication as ordered (children often need sedation).
  • Prepare the tray – sterile bone marrow aspiration needle (Salah or Klima) and trephine needle (Jamshidi), local anaesthetic, syringes, glass slides, EDTA and heparin tubes, formalin container, sterile drapes, gloves, antiseptic, dressing.
  • Position – lateral (knees flexed) or prone for the posterior iliac crest; supine for the sternum.

4. During the procedure

  • Maintain strict asepsis; help with skin cleaning and draping.
  • Support and reassure the patient; warn that a brief sharp, pulling pain is felt when marrow is aspirated; encourage slow breathing.
  • Help prepare smears quickly (aspirate clots fast); put samples in the correct containers – EDTA for morphology and flow cytometry, heparin for cytogenetics, culture bottles if ordered; place the trephine core in 10% formalin.
  • Label all specimens correctly and send with requisition forms promptly.
  • Observe the patient's colour, pulse and response.

5. After the procedure

  • Apply firm pressure for 5–10 minutes (longer if platelets are low) and a sterile pressure dressing.
  • Ask the patient to lie on the back (for posterior iliac site) for 30–60 minutes to maintain pressure, or rest as advised.
  • Monitor vital signs and the site for bleeding or haematoma; give analgesics (paracetamol; avoid aspirin and NSAIDs).
  • Keep the dressing dry for 24 hours; watch for infection (redness, swelling, fever) over the next few days.
  • Document the procedure, site, samples sent and the patient's condition.

Nursing importance Good preparation, support during the painful step, correct specimen handling and post-procedure care make the test safe and ensure accurate diagnosis.

Conclusion Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy are key diagnostic procedures in blood disorders; the nurse ensures consent, positioning, asepsis, specimen handling, haemostasis and comfort.
