subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Haematological Disorders
question: What is thalassaemia? Write its management.
answer_html:
Thalassaemia is an inherited (autosomal recessive) disorder in which there is reduced or absent synthesis of α- or β-globin chains of haemoglobin, causing ineffective erythropoiesis, haemolysis and microcytic hypochromic anaemia.

β-thalassaemia major presents at 6–12 months with severe anaemia, failure to thrive, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice and thalassaemic facies (frontal bossing, prominent cheek bones). The minor (trait) form is a mild carrier state often mistaken for iron-deficiency anaemia.

Management

  1. Regular blood transfusions every 2–4 weeks to keep pre-transfusion Hb at about 9–10.5 g/dl.
  2. Iron chelation – deferasirox (oral), deferoxamine (subcutaneous), deferiprone; folic acid.
  3. Stem cell transplantation (cure); splenectomy in selected cases.
  4. Prevention – carrier screening (HbA2 above 3.5% on HPLC), premarital and antenatal screening, prenatal diagnosis.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Haematological Disorders
question: Define leukaemia and list its types.
answer_html:
Leukaemia is a malignant proliferation of abnormal white blood cell precursors in the bone marrow, which replace normal marrow and appear in the blood, causing anaemia, infection and bleeding.

Types

  1. Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) – commonest childhood cancer.
  2. Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) – mainly adults.
  3. Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) – adults; Philadelphia chromosome; massive splenomegaly.
  4. Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) – elderly.

Basis of classification – course (acute or chronic) and cell line (lymphoid or myeloid). Diagnosis is by blood smear and bone marrow examination.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Haematological Disorders
question: What is sickle cell trait? Name the tests used to screen for sickle cell disease.
answer_html:
Sickle cell trait (HbAS) is the carrier state in which a person inherits one sickle gene and one normal gene. The person usually has no symptoms and a normal life, but can pass the gene to children; if both partners are carriers, each child has a 25% chance of sickle cell disease. Severe dehydration or very high altitude may rarely cause problems.

Screening and diagnostic tests

  1. Sickling (slide) test with sodium metabisulphite.
  2. Solubility test (dithionite tube test).
  3. Point-of-care rapid tests (lateral-flow cards) used in field screening.
  4. HPLC or haemoglobin electrophoresis – confirmatory; distinguishes AS, SS and other variants.
  5. Newborn screening by dried blood spot; status recorded on the sickle cell (genetic status) card under the national mission.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Haematological Disorders
question: What is polycythaemia vera?
answer_html:
Polycythaemia vera is a myeloproliferative neoplasm in which the bone marrow produces too many red cells (often with increased WBCs and platelets), usually due to a JAK2 gene mutation.

Features – ruddy (plethoric) face, headache, dizziness, blurred vision, itching after a hot bath, burning pain in hands and feet, splenomegaly, gout, and risk of thrombosis (stroke, MI, DVT) and bleeding. Hb and haematocrit are high (Hb above 16.5 g/dl in men, 16 g/dl in women).

Management

  1. Venesection (phlebotomy) to keep haematocrit below 45%.
  2. Low-dose aspirin; hydroxyurea or ruxolitinib in high-risk patients.
  3. Nursing – adequate hydration, leg exercises, avoid iron supplements, report thrombosis signs.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Haematological Disorders
question: What is multiple myeloma?
answer_html:
Multiple myeloma is a malignant proliferation of plasma cells in the bone marrow that produce a monoclonal immunoglobulin (M-protein), mainly in the elderly.

Clinical features – "CRAB"

  1. Calcium raised – hypercalcaemia (thirst, confusion, constipation).
  2. Renal failure.
  3. Anaemia – fatigue, pallor.
  4. Bone lesions – back pain, punched-out lytic lesions in the skull, pathological fractures. Also recurrent infections and hyperviscosity.

Diagnosis – serum protein electrophoresis (M band), urine Bence-Jones protein, bone marrow plasma cells, skeletal imaging. Treatment – bortezomib, lenalidomide, dexamethasone, stem cell transplant, bisphosphonates; nursing focuses on pain relief, fracture prevention, 2–3 litres of fluid daily and infection prevention.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Haematological Disorders
question: What is agranulocytosis? Mention its causes and nursing care.
answer_html:
Agranulocytosis is a severe reduction or absence of granulocytes (neutrophils) in the blood – absolute neutrophil count usually below 500/µl – leaving the patient highly prone to serious infections.

Causes – drugs (antithyroid drugs such as carbimazole, clozapine, sulfonamides, chloramphenicol, metamizole, cytotoxic chemotherapy), radiation, autoimmune disease, severe infections. Features – sudden high fever, chills, severe sore throat, mouth ulcers, pneumonia and septicaemia.

Nursing care

  1. Stop the offending drug immediately; take blood cultures; give IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and G-CSF as ordered.
  2. Protective isolation, strict hand hygiene, safe food and oral care.
  3. Teach patients on antithyroid drugs and clozapine to report fever or sore throat at once and to attend regular blood counts.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Endocrine Disorders
question: (a) Define diabetes mellitus and list its types. (2 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features and diagnostic criteria. (4 marks) (c) Describe the medical and nursing management of a patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus, including insulin administration and patient education. (9 marks)

diagram.caption: Insulin injection sites and rotation
labels: upper outer buttocks; rotation within a site 2.5 cm apart; pen held at 90 degrees

answer_html:
(a) Definition and types (2 marks) Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a chronic metabolic disorder characterised by persistent hyperglycaemia resulting from defects in insulin secretion, insulin action or both, with disturbances of carbohydrate, fat and protein metabolism. India has more than 10 crore people with diabetes, and many are undiagnosed.

Types

  1. Type 1 DM – autoimmune destruction of β-cells → absolute insulin deficiency; usually children and young adults; needs insulin for life.
  2. Type 2 DM – insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency; about 90–95% of cases; adults (increasingly young Indians), linked to obesity, inactivity and family history.
  3. Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) – diabetes first detected in pregnancy.
  4. Other specific types – due to pancreatic disease (chronic pancreatitis, fibrocalculous pancreatic diabetes), drugs (steroids), endocrine disorders (Cushing's), genetic defects (MODY).

(b) Clinical features and diagnostic criteria (4 marks) Clinical features

  • Classic symptoms – polyuria (frequent urination, nocturia), polydipsia (excessive thirst), polyphagia (excessive hunger), weight loss (more in type 1).
  • Fatigue, weakness, blurred vision, tingling and numbness of feet.
  • Recurrent infections – boils, carbuncles, vulvovaginal candidiasis, urinary infections, slow-healing wounds.
  • Many type 2 patients are asymptomatic and are detected on screening or with complications (heart attack, foot ulcer, vision loss).

Diagnostic criteria (ADA/WHO) – any one, confirmed by repeat testing unless symptoms are clear:

  • Fasting plasma glucose 126 mg/dl or more (after at least 8 hours' fast).
  • 2-hour plasma glucose 200 mg/dl or more during a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test.
  • HbA1c 6.5% or more (standardised laboratory method).
  • Random plasma glucose 200 mg/dl or more with classic symptoms. Prediabetes – fasting glucose 100–125 mg/dl, 2-hour glucose 140–199 mg/dl or HbA1c 5.7–6.4%.

(c) Medical and nursing management (9 marks) 1. Goals of treatment (individualised)

  • HbA1c below 7% for most adults; fasting glucose 80–130 mg/dl; post-meal glucose below 180 mg/dl.
  • BP below 130/80 mmHg, LDL cholesterol below 100 mg/dl (lower with heart disease), healthy weight, no smoking.
  • Avoid hypoglycaemia; prevent complications.

2. Medical nutrition therapy (diet)

  • Regular meal timings; do not skip meals or overeat; avoid long fasts and feasts (counsel for religious fasts and festivals).
  • "Diabetes plate" – half the plate non-starchy vegetables, one quarter whole grains or millets, one quarter protein (dal, pulses, curd, paneer, egg, fish, chicken).
  • Prefer low glycaemic index foods – millets (jowar, bajra, ragi), whole wheat, brown or parboiled rice in small amounts, whole pulses, sprouts, vegetables.
  • Avoid sugar, jaggery, honey, sweets, bakery items, maida, fried snacks, sweetened drinks and fruit juices; whole fruits in moderation (guava, apple, orange, papaya) rather than mango, chikoo and grapes in large amounts.
  • Limit oil, salt and alcohol; plenty of fibre and water.
  • Weight reduction of 5–10% in overweight patients improves control markedly.

3. Physical activity

  • At least 150 minutes a week of moderate activity (brisk walking 30 minutes, 5 days a week) plus resistance exercises 2–3 days a week; yoga.
  • Check blood sugar before exercise if on insulin or sulfonylureas; carry sugar; wear proper footwear; avoid exercise when glucose is very high with ketones or very low.

4. Drug therapy (as prescribed)

  • Oral drugs – metformin (first-line; take with meals), sulfonylureas (glimepiride, gliclazide – risk of hypoglycaemia), DPP-4 inhibitors (sitagliptin, teneligliptin), SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin – also protect heart and kidneys), pioglitazone; injectable GLP-1 agonists.
  • Insulin – when oral drugs fail, in pregnancy, illness, surgery and type 1 diabetes:
    • Rapid-acting (lispro, aspart), short-acting (regular/soluble), intermediate (NPH), long-acting (glargine, degludec) and premixed (30/70).

5. Insulin administration – nursing responsibilities

  • Check the order, type, strength (match U-40 or U-100 syringe to the vial), dose, expiry, appearance (clear or uniformly cloudy) and the blood glucose before giving.
  • Storage – unopened insulin in the refrigerator (2–8 °C), never frozen; the vial or pen in use can be kept at room temperature (below about 30 °C) for about 28 days, away from sunlight; in hot Indian summers keep it in a cool place (for example, an earthen-pot cooler) when there is no fridge.
  • Mixing – roll cloudy insulin gently 10–20 times (do not shake); when mixing regular and NPH in one syringe, draw clear (regular) before cloudy (NPH).
  • Sites – abdomen (fastest absorption; avoid 5 cm around the umbilicus), front and outer thighs, back of upper arms, upper outer buttocks.
  • Rotate sites systematically (each injection about 2.5 cm away from the previous one) to prevent lipohypertrophy (fatty lumps that cause erratic absorption).
  • Technique – clean, dry skin; pinch up a skin fold if needed; insert the needle at 90° (45° in very thin people); inject slowly; with a pen, keep the needle in for 10 seconds; do not massage the site.
  • Timing – regular insulin about 30 minutes before meals; rapid-acting insulin just before (0–15 minutes) the meal; ensure the patient eats after the injection.
  • Sharps disposal – in a puncture-proof container (a hard plastic bottle at home); do not reuse needles many times.
  • Watch for hypoglycaemia, lipohypertrophy and allergy; teach self-injection with return demonstration.

6. Self-monitoring and follow-up

  • Self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG) with a glucometer – frequency according to treatment; keep a record.
  • HbA1c every 3 months until controlled, then every 6 months.
  • Annual screening for complications – dilated eye examination, urine albumin–creatinine ratio and eGFR, lipid profile, ECG; foot examination at every visit; dental check.
  • Vaccinations – influenza, pneumococcal, hepatitis B.

7. Common nursing diagnoses and interventions

  • Risk for unstable blood glucose – monitor glucose, give drugs on time, coordinate meals with insulin, teach recognition and treatment of high and low sugar.
  • Imbalanced nutrition: more than body requirements – diet counselling with the dietitian, weight monitoring.
  • Risk for infection and impaired skin integrity – hygiene, foot and skin care, early treatment of wounds.
  • Risk for injury – peripheral neuropathy and hypoglycaemia; safe footwear, fall prevention.
  • Deficient knowledge / ineffective health management – structured education.

8. Patient education (diabetes self-management)

  • Diabetes is lifelong but controllable; complications are preventable.
  • Diet, exercise, medicines, glucose monitoring and regular follow-up.
  • Hypoglycaemia – symptoms (sweating, shaking, hunger, confusion) and "Rule of 15" treatment; always carry glucose or sugar and a diabetes identity card.
  • Sick-day rules – never stop insulin during illness; check sugar every 4 hours; drink plenty of fluids; take small frequent carbohydrate-containing fluids; check ketones if possible; seek help if vomiting, unable to eat or sugar persistently above 300 mg/dl.
  • Foot care – daily inspection, washing and drying between toes, moisturising, proper footwear, never walking barefoot, careful nail cutting, immediate care of injuries.
  • Stop tobacco and alcohol; control BP and cholesterol; dental hygiene.
  • Women – plan pregnancy with good sugar control.
  • Free screening and drugs are available at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs under the NP-NCD programme; generic medicines at Jan Aushadhi Kendras.

Nursing importance Diabetes is a self-managed disease; the nurse's teaching of diet, insulin technique, glucose monitoring, foot care and sick-day rules decides whether the patient stays healthy or develops blindness, kidney failure and amputation.

Conclusion Diabetes mellitus is chronic hyperglycaemia due to insulin deficiency or resistance; diet, exercise, oral drugs or insulin, regular monitoring and thorough self-management education, coordinated by the nurse, control the disease and prevent complications.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Endocrine Disorders
question: (a) Define hyperthyroidism and list its causes. (3 marks) (b) Describe the clinical features of hyperthyroidism. (4 marks) (c) Explain the pre-operative preparation and post-operative nursing care of a patient undergoing thyroidectomy, including its complications. (8 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Definition and causes (3 marks) Hyperthyroidism is a condition in which the thyroid gland produces excessive thyroid hormones (T₃ and T₄), producing a hypermetabolic state. Thyrotoxicosis is the clinical syndrome caused by excess circulating thyroid hormones from any source.

Causes

  1. Graves' disease – the commonest cause; autoimmune; TSH-receptor-stimulating antibodies cause diffuse goitre, hyperthyroidism and eye signs; mostly women aged 20–40 years.
  2. Toxic multinodular goitre – older people, often in iodine-deficient areas.
  3. Toxic adenoma – a single hyperfunctioning nodule.
  4. Thyroiditis – subacute (painful, de Quervain's), postpartum and silent thyroiditis (temporary release of stored hormone).
  5. Excess iodine (iodine-induced, Jod–Basedow), amiodarone.
  6. Excess intake of thyroxine (overtreatment or misuse for weight loss).
  7. Rare – TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma, hCG-producing molar pregnancy, struma ovarii.

(b) Clinical features (4 marks) 1. General (hypermetabolic)

  • Weight loss despite increased appetite, heat intolerance, excessive sweating, warm moist skin, fatigue, muscle weakness (proximal myopathy). 2. Cardiovascular

  • Palpitations, tachycardia (raised sleeping pulse), atrial fibrillation (especially in the elderly), wide pulse pressure, breathlessness, heart failure. 3. Nervous system and mind

  • Nervousness, anxiety, irritability, emotional instability, restlessness, insomnia, fine tremor of the outstretched hands, brisk reflexes. 4. Gastrointestinal – frequent bowel movements or diarrhoea. 5. Reproductive – scanty or absent periods, infertility; gynaecomastia in men. 6. Eye signs (Graves' ophthalmopathy)

  • Lid retraction and lid lag, staring look, exophthalmos (proptosis), grittiness, watering, swelling of the conjunctiva, double vision; severe cases – corneal ulceration and optic nerve compression. 7. Thyroid gland – diffuse goitre with a bruit (Graves'), nodular goitre (toxic multinodular). 8. Others – pretibial myxoedema, thinning of hair, brittle nails, osteoporosis; apathetic hyperthyroidism in the elderly (weight loss, AF, depression without classic signs). Investigations – low TSH with high free T₄/T₃, TSH-receptor antibodies, radioactive iodine uptake scan, thyroid ultrasound.

Treatment options (brief) – antithyroid drugs (carbimazole/methimazole; propylthiouracil in early pregnancy) with β-blockers (propranolol) for symptoms; radioactive iodine (I-131); surgery (total or near-total thyroidectomy) for large goitres, pressure symptoms, suspicion of cancer, drug failure, or patient choice.

(c) Thyroidectomy – pre-operative preparation and post-operative nursing care (8 marks) 1. Pre-operative preparation

  • Make the patient euthyroid with antithyroid drugs before surgery (to prevent thyroid storm); propranolol to control pulse.
  • Lugol's iodine or potassium iodide for about 7–10 days before surgery, as ordered, to reduce the vascularity of the gland (give diluted in milk or juice through a straw to avoid staining teeth).
  • Investigations – thyroid function tests, serum calcium (baseline), CBC, coagulation, ECG; indirect laryngoscopy to check vocal cord movement before surgery (medico-legal baseline).
  • Nutrition – high-calorie, high-protein diet; rest; reduce anxiety in a quiet room.
  • Teach – deep breathing, coughing, and how to support the head and neck with the hands when moving after surgery; explain that speaking will be checked frequently.
  • Routine pre-operative preparation and consent.

2. Post-operative nursing care (i) Position and airway

  • After recovery from anaesthesia, semi-Fowler's position with the head and neck supported by pillows in a neutral position – avoid flexion or hyperextension of the neck (strain on the suture line).
  • Keep at the bedside – tracheostomy set, suction, oxygen, and suture or clip remover (to open the wound in case of a compressing haematoma), and calcium gluconate.

  • Observe for respiratory distress, stridor, restlessness and cyanosis – caused by haematoma, laryngeal oedema or bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury. (ii) Haemorrhage and neck haematoma

  • Check the dressing including the back of the neck (blood collects posteriorly), drain output, and any increasing neck swelling, tightness of the dressing, difficulty in swallowing or breathing.

  • A haematoma compressing the trachea is an emergency – call the surgeon immediately; the wound may need to be opened at the bedside to release the clot. (iii) Voice and recurrent laryngeal nerve injury

  • Ask the patient to speak (for example, to say their name or "ee") every 1–2 hours; mild hoarseness is common due to oedema and intubation, but persistent hoarseness suggests unilateral nerve injury; stridor and airway obstruction suggest bilateral injury – emergency.

  • Discourage unnecessary talking in the first day; provide a writing pad. (iv) Hypocalcaemia (parathyroid damage or removal)

  • Usually appears 24–72 hours after surgery.

  • Watch for tingling around the mouth and in fingers and toes, muscle cramps, positive Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs, carpopedal spasm, laryngospasm and seizures.

  • Monitor serum calcium as ordered; give IV calcium gluconate slowly for symptoms and oral calcium with vitamin D as prescribed. (v) Thyroid storm (thyrotoxic crisis)

  • A rare but life-threatening flare, usually in poorly prepared patients, within the first 12–48 hours: high fever (above 38.5 °C), marked tachycardia, AF, agitation, delirium, vomiting, diarrhoea, heart failure.

  • Emergency care as ordered – cooling (tepid sponging, cooling blankets; avoid aspirin), antithyroid drugs (PTU/methimazole), iodine given one hour after the antithyroid drug, propranolol, hydrocortisone, IV fluids, oxygen and ICU care. (vi) Pain, diet and comfort

  • Analgesics as ordered; cold sips and soft, cool foods at first (swallowing is painful), progressing to a normal diet.

  • Support the head when the patient sits up or turns; humidified air if needed. (vii) Wound care

  • Aseptic dressing; drain usually removed within 24–48 hours; clips or sutures removed early (as ordered) for a better scar; observe for infection.

  • Gentle neck movements (range-of-motion exercises) after the first days, as advised, to prevent stiffness. (viii) Monitoring – vital signs, temperature, SpO₂, intake–output; record voice, calcium symptoms and wound condition.

3. Discharge teaching

  • After total thyroidectomy, lifelong levothyroxine is needed – take on an empty stomach in the morning, 30–60 minutes before breakfast, separate from calcium and iron tablets; regular TSH checks.
  • Watch for symptoms of hypothyroidism (tiredness, weight gain, cold intolerance) or hypocalcaemia (tingling, cramps) and report them.
  • Wound care; scar massage after healing; protect the scar from sun.
  • Follow-up for histopathology report, voice and calcium levels.

Common nursing diagnoses

  • Risk for ineffective airway clearance related to haematoma, laryngeal oedema or nerve injury.
  • Risk for injury (tetany) related to hypocalcaemia.
  • Acute pain related to the surgical incision.
  • Impaired verbal communication related to hoarseness.

4. Nursing care of the medically treated patient and eye care

  • Antithyroid drugs – teach to take them regularly for the full course (often 12–18 months); report sore throat, fever or mouth ulcers at once (agranulocytosis) and yellowing of eyes or skin (liver injury); regular blood counts and thyroid tests.
  • High-calorie, high-protein diet with plenty of fluids; avoid tea, coffee and colas (stimulants) and iodine supplements.
  • Cool, quiet environment, light clothing, adequate rest and sleep; reduce emotional stress.
  • Eye care in exophthalmos – dark glasses, lubricating eye drops, elevate the head end of the bed to reduce periorbital swelling, tape the eyelids closed at night if they do not close fully, and report pain or reduced vision; stop smoking (worsens eye disease).

Nursing importance The first 48–72 hours after thyroidectomy carry the risks of airway obstruction, haemorrhage, hypocalcaemia and thyroid storm; vigilant nursing observation and ready emergency equipment save lives.

Conclusion Hyperthyroidism, usually due to Graves' disease, causes a hypermetabolic state with typical eye, cardiac and nervous system features; when thyroidectomy is chosen, careful preparation and expert post-operative nursing care prevent its serious complications.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Endocrine Disorders
question: Explain the acute complications of diabetes mellitus and their management.
answer_html:
Introduction Diabetes mellitus causes acute (short-term) complications, which are emergencies, and chronic complications due to damage to blood vessels and nerves. The three acute complications are diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS) and hypoglycaemia.

1. Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)

  • Cause – severe insulin deficiency; mainly type 1 DM; triggered by missed insulin, infection, new-onset diabetes, MI, stress.
  • Mechanism – high glucose → osmotic diuresis and dehydration; fat breakdown → ketone bodies → metabolic acidosis.
  • Features – polyuria, polydipsia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, deep rapid (Kussmaul) breathing, fruity (acetone) breath, dehydration, tachycardia, hypotension, drowsiness, coma.
  • Lab – glucose usually above 250 mg/dl, pH below 7.3, bicarbonate below 18 mEq/L, ketones in blood/urine.
  • Management – IV fluids (normal saline about 1 litre in the first hour, then as ordered); IV insulin infusion (about 0.1 unit/kg/hour) once potassium is above 3.3 mEq/L; potassium replacement (potassium falls with insulin); add dextrose when glucose falls to about 200–250 mg/dl; treat the cause; monitor glucose hourly, potassium and ABG 2–4 hourly, urine output, and level of consciousness (cerebral oedema in children).

2. Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS)

  • Who – elderly type 2 diabetics; triggered by infection, stroke, MI, poor fluid intake, steroids or diuretics.
  • Features – very high glucose (often above 600 mg/dl), severe dehydration, high serum osmolality (above 320 mOsm/kg), little or no ketosis, confusion, seizures, coma; develops over days.
  • Management – large volumes of IV fluids (main treatment), gradual lowering of glucose with lower-dose insulin, potassium replacement, treatment of the cause, DVT prophylaxis; high mortality.

3. Hypoglycaemia

  • Definition – blood glucose below 70 mg/dl (serious below 54 mg/dl).
  • Causes – excess insulin or sulfonylurea, missed or delayed meal, extra exercise, alcohol, kidney failure.
  • Features – sweating, trembling, palpitations, hunger, anxiety; then headache, confusion, blurred vision, slurred speech, abnormal behaviour, seizures and coma.
  • Management
    • Conscious – Rule of 15: give 15 g of fast-acting sugar (3 teaspoons of sugar or glucose in water, 150 ml fruit juice), recheck after 15 minutes, repeat if still low, then a snack.
    • Unconscious – nothing by mouth; IV 25% dextrose (about 50–100 ml) or glucagon 1 mg IM/SC; recovery position.
    • Find and correct the cause; sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia needs prolonged observation.

4. Chronic complications (brief list) Microvascular – retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy; macrovascular – coronary disease, stroke, peripheral arterial disease; diabetic foot, infections, cataract, periodontal disease.

5. Nursing responsibilities

  • Recognise early signs; check bedside glucose in any diabetic who is unwell or confused.
  • Maintain IV lines, fluid and insulin infusions with pumps; monitor glucose, electrolytes, ABG, urine output, vital signs and neurological status.
  • Teach sick-day rules, hypoglycaemia recognition and treatment, regular meals and medicine adherence.

Nursing importance DKA, HHS and hypoglycaemia are preventable and treatable emergencies; prompt recognition and correct management by nurses prevent deaths.

Conclusion The acute complications of diabetes – DKA, HHS and hypoglycaemia – require rapid fluids, insulin or glucose and electrolyte correction, together with education to prevent recurrence.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Endocrine Disorders
question: Explain the clinical features, management and nursing care of hypothyroidism.
answer_html:
Definition Hypothyroidism is a condition in which the thyroid gland produces too little thyroid hormone, slowing down body metabolism. Severe hypothyroidism with skin and tissue changes is called myxoedema. It is much more common in women.

1. Causes

  • Hashimoto's (autoimmune) thyroiditis – the commonest cause.
  • Iodine deficiency (endemic goitre areas).
  • After thyroidectomy or radioactive iodine therapy.
  • Drugs – lithium, amiodarone, antithyroid drugs.
  • Congenital hypothyroidism (cretinism if untreated); pituitary or hypothalamic disease (secondary).

2. Clinical features

  • Tiredness, lethargy, slowness of thought and movement, cold intolerance.
  • Weight gain with poor appetite, constipation.
  • Dry, coarse, cold skin, hair loss (including the outer third of the eyebrows), puffy face and eyelids, hoarse voice, slow speech.
  • Bradycardia, high cholesterol, pericardial effusion.
  • Menorrhagia, infertility, reduced libido.
  • Depression, poor memory, muscle cramps, carpal tunnel syndrome, delayed relaxation of ankle reflexes, non-pitting oedema.
  • Children – growth and mental retardation (cretinism); newborn screening detects it early.
  • Lab – high TSH and low free T₄ in primary hypothyroidism; anti-TPO antibodies in Hashimoto's.

3. Management

  • Levothyroxine daily for life; start with a low dose in the elderly and heart patients and increase slowly (a sudden increase in metabolism can cause angina or MI); check TSH after 6–8 weeks and adjust the dose.
  • Myxoedema coma (in elderly, often triggered by cold, infection or sedatives – hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation, low sodium and sugar, coma): ICU care with IV levothyroxine, IV hydrocortisone, ventilatory support, cautious fluids, correction of glucose and sodium, and passive rewarming with blankets (active external heating can cause vasodilatation and shock).

4. Nursing care

  • Medication teaching – take levothyroxine on an empty stomach in the morning, 30–60 minutes before breakfast, separated from calcium, iron and antacids by about 4 hours; lifelong therapy; do not stop when feeling well.
  • Teach signs of over-dosage – palpitations, tremor, insomnia, weight loss – and under-dosage – persistent tiredness, cold intolerance.
  • Provide a warm environment and extra clothing; avoid heating pads on insensitive skin.
  • Prevent constipation – high-fibre diet, fluids, activity.
  • Low-calorie, high-fibre diet, gradual increase in activity.
  • Skin care – mild soap, moisturisers.
  • Monitor pulse, weight, bowel habits and mental status; avoid sedatives and opioids (patients are very sensitive).
  • Emotional support – slowness and depression improve with treatment.
  • Pregnant women need dose adjustment and close monitoring; ensure newborn screening.

Nursing importance With regular levothyroxine the patient can live a completely normal life; the nurse's teaching on correct intake and lifelong adherence is the key to success.

Conclusion Hypothyroidism slows all body systems; it is easily diagnosed by TSH and treated with lifelong levothyroxine, supported by nursing care and education.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Endocrine Disorders
question: Explain the causes, clinical features and nursing management of Cushing's syndrome.
answer_html:
Definition Cushing's syndrome is a condition caused by prolonged exposure to excess glucocorticoids (cortisol). When it is due to an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma, it is called Cushing's disease.

1. Causes

  • Exogenous (iatrogenic) – long-term corticosteroid therapy – the commonest cause; in India also hidden steroids in some unlabelled "herbal" or "desi" powders used for joint pain and asthma.
  • Pituitary adenoma secreting ACTH (Cushing's disease) – commonest endogenous cause.
  • Adrenal adenoma or carcinoma.
  • Ectopic ACTH – small-cell lung cancer, carcinoid tumours.

2. Clinical features

  • Central (truncal) obesity with thin arms and legs, moon face, buffalo hump (fat over upper back), supraclavicular fat pads.
  • Purple striae (wide stretch marks) on abdomen, thighs and breasts; thin, fragile skin, easy bruising, poor wound healing, acne.
  • Proximal muscle weakness (difficulty climbing stairs or rising from a chair).
  • Hypertension, hyperglycaemia/diabetes, osteoporosis and fractures, kidney stones.
  • Frequent infections.
  • Hirsutism, menstrual irregularity, reduced libido.
  • Mood changes – depression, irritability, psychosis, insomnia.
  • Hypokalaemia (especially ectopic ACTH).

3. Diagnosis 24-hour urinary free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol, overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test; then plasma ACTH, MRI of the pituitary or CT of the adrenals to locate the cause.

4. Management

  • Iatrogenic – gradual tapering of steroids under supervision (never stop suddenly – risk of adrenal crisis); use the lowest effective dose.
  • Transsphenoidal removal of pituitary adenoma; adrenalectomy for adrenal tumours (bilateral adrenalectomy needs lifelong replacement); treatment of ectopic tumours.
  • Drugs that block cortisol synthesis (ketoconazole, metyrapone) when surgery is not possible.

5. Nursing management

  • Monitor BP, blood glucose, weight, intake–output and potassium.
  • Prevent infection – hand hygiene, avoid exposure to infected people, careful skin care; signs of infection may be masked.
  • Protect fragile skin – gentle handling, avoid adhesive tapes, pressure-relieving mattress, prompt wound care.
  • Prevent falls and fractures – safe environment, assistance with mobility, calcium and vitamin D.
  • Diet – low-calorie, low-salt, low-carbohydrate, high-protein, potassium- and calcium-rich foods.
  • Body image and emotional support – reassure that appearance improves after treatment; watch for depression.
  • After adrenalectomy – give steroid replacement exactly as ordered; watch for adrenal insufficiency (hypotension, weakness, vomiting).
  • Education – patients on long-term steroids must carry a steroid card, never stop drugs abruptly, and seek advice before taking any unlabelled medicine.

Nursing importance Many cases are caused by unsupervised steroid use; nurses can prevent them through education and can reduce complications such as infection, fractures and skin breakdown.

Conclusion Cushing's syndrome results from excess cortisol, most often from steroid medicines; treatment of the cause, careful steroid withdrawal and supportive nursing care reverse most features.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Endocrine Disorders
question: Explain Addison's disease and the emergency management of adrenal crisis.
answer_html:
Definition Addison's disease (primary adrenocortical insufficiency) is a condition in which the adrenal cortex is destroyed or fails, causing deficiency of cortisol and aldosterone (and adrenal androgens). Adrenal (Addisonian) crisis is a sudden, life-threatening worsening of adrenal insufficiency.

1. Causes

  • Autoimmune adrenalitis – commonest worldwide.
  • Tuberculosis of the adrenals – an important cause in India.
  • Fungal infections, HIV-related infections, metastatic cancer, haemorrhage into the adrenals (severe meningococcal sepsis, anticoagulants), bilateral adrenalectomy.
  • Secondary adrenal insufficiency – pituitary disease or sudden stopping of long-term steroid therapy (the commonest cause of adrenal insufficiency in hospitals).

2. Clinical features

  • Fatigue, weakness, weight loss, loss of appetite.
  • Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhoea.
  • Postural hypotension, dizziness, fainting.
  • Hyperpigmentation of skin creases, knuckles, scars, gums and inner cheeks (due to high ACTH – only in primary disease).
  • Salt craving, low blood sugar, depression, loss of body hair in women.
  • Lab – low sodium, high potassium, low glucose, raised urea; low morning cortisol and high ACTH; poor response to the short Synacthen (ACTH stimulation) test.

3. Adrenal crisis

  • Triggers – infection, surgery, trauma, dehydration, vomiting, or abrupt withdrawal of steroids in a person with adrenal insufficiency.
  • Features – severe hypotension and shock, severe abdominal pain, vomiting, fever, confusion, hypoglycaemia, hyperkalaemia.
  • Emergency management (as ordered)
    1. IV hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately, then 50 mg every 6 hours (or 200 mg over 24 hours).
    2. Rapid IV fluids – normal saline (about 1 litre in the first hour), with dextrose to correct hypoglycaemia.
    3. Correct electrolytes; treat the trigger (antibiotics for infection).
    4. Monitor BP, pulse, urine output, glucose and electrolytes closely.

4. Long-term management

  • Hydrocortisone in divided doses (larger dose in the morning, smaller in the afternoon) – mimics normal cortisol rhythm.
  • Fludrocortisone (mineralocorticoid) in primary disease; adequate salt intake.
  • Treat the cause (anti-TB therapy).

5. Nursing care and education

  • Monitor postural BP, weight, intake–output, blood glucose and electrolytes; fall precautions.
  • Give steroids on time with food; never miss doses.
  • Sick-day rules – double the hydrocortisone dose during fever or illness; take injectable hydrocortisone if vomiting; seek medical help early.
  • Carry a steroid emergency card or bracelet; inform doctors and dentists before procedures (extra steroid cover for surgery).
  • Balanced diet with adequate salt and fluids; avoid strenuous activity in hot weather.

Nursing importance Adrenal crisis is fatal if missed but responds dramatically to hydrocortisone and fluids; nurses must recognise it and teach patients sick-day rules to prevent it.

Conclusion Addison's disease is deficiency of adrenal cortical hormones causing weakness, hypotension and pigmentation; lifelong replacement, sick-day rules and prompt treatment of adrenal crisis keep patients safe.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Endocrine Disorders
question: Explain acromegaly and the nursing care after transsphenoidal hypophysectomy.
answer_html:
Definition Acromegaly is a chronic disorder caused by excess growth hormone (GH) after closure of the epiphyses (in adults), usually due to a GH-secreting pituitary adenoma. Excess GH before epiphyseal closure causes gigantism.

1. Clinical features

  • Enlargement of hands and feet – increasing ring and shoe size; thick, spade-like hands.
  • Coarse facial features – frontal bossing, large nose and lips, protruding lower jaw (prognathism), widely spaced teeth, enlarged tongue, deep voice.
  • Thick, oily skin, excessive sweating, skin tags.
  • Joint pain (arthropathy), carpal tunnel syndrome, obstructive sleep apnoea.
  • Hypertension, diabetes, heart enlargement (cardiomyopathy), colon polyps.
  • Pressure effects of the tumour – headache, bitemporal hemianopia (loss of outer visual fields due to pressure on the optic chiasm), hypopituitarism.

2. Diagnosis Raised IGF-1, failure of GH suppression during an oral glucose tolerance test, MRI of the pituitary, visual field testing.

3. Treatment

  • Transsphenoidal surgery – removal of the adenoma through the nose or under the upper lip and sphenoid sinus – the treatment of choice.
  • Somatostatin analogues (octreotide, lanreotide), GH-receptor antagonist (pegvisomant), dopamine agonists; radiotherapy for residual tumour.

4. Nursing care after transsphenoidal hypophysectomy

  • Position – head of the bed elevated about 30° to reduce pressure on the sella and promote venous drainage.
  • Nasal packing for 24–72 hours – the patient breathes through the mouth; give frequent mouth care; moisten the lips; no toothbrushing over the incision under the upper lip for about 10 days (use mouthwash/swabs).
  • Prevent CSF leak – teach the patient not to blow the nose, sneeze forcefully (sneeze with the mouth open), cough, bend down or strain (stool softeners) for several weeks; avoid straws.
  • Watch for CSF rhinorrhoea – clear watery nasal drip or post-nasal drip with a salty taste; test drainage for glucose; a "halo" ring on gauze; report immediately (risk of meningitis).
  • Neurological and visual checks – level of consciousness, pupils, visual fields and acuity.
  • Diabetes insipidus – common after pituitary surgery; monitor hourly urine output and specific gravity; report urine output above about 200–250 ml/hour for 2 hours with specific gravity below 1.005; give desmopressin as ordered; maintain fluid balance and check sodium.
  • Hormone replacement – give hydrocortisone as ordered (risk of adrenal insufficiency); later thyroid and sex hormones if needed.
  • Watch for meningitis (fever, headache, neck stiffness).
  • Discharge teaching – avoid nose blowing and heavy lifting for about a month, take hormones regularly, carry an identity card, report excessive thirst and urination, clear nasal drip, headache or fever.

Nursing importance Early detection of CSF leak, diabetes insipidus and adrenal insufficiency by careful nursing observation prevents serious complications after pituitary surgery.

Conclusion Acromegaly is due to GH excess from a pituitary adenoma, producing characteristic body changes; transsphenoidal surgery is the main treatment, and post-operative nursing focuses on airway, CSF leak prevention, fluid balance and hormone replacement.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Endocrine Disorders
question: Explain the nursing responsibilities in radioactive iodine therapy for hyperthyroidism.
answer_html:
Introduction Radioactive iodine (RAI, I-131) therapy is a common, effective and safe treatment for hyperthyroidism (Graves' disease, toxic nodules) and for thyroid cancer after surgery. The thyroid takes up the radioactive iodine, which destroys overactive thyroid tissue over weeks to months. It is given as a capsule or drink in a nuclear medicine department.

1. Indications and contraindications

  • Indications – Graves' disease (especially after relapse on drugs), toxic multinodular goitre, toxic adenoma; ablation after thyroidectomy for cancer.
  • Contraindications – pregnancy and breastfeeding; caution in severe active thyroid eye disease (may worsen – steroid cover).

2. Preparation

  • Explain the treatment, expected effects and precautions; obtain consent.
  • Pregnancy test in women of reproductive age; stop breastfeeding (should not be resumed for that child).
  • Stop antithyroid drugs for a few days before (as ordered) and avoid iodine-containing drugs, contrast dyes and iodine-rich foods (sea fish, iodised salt in excess) for 1–2 weeks as advised (a low-iodine diet improves uptake).
  • β-blockers may be continued to control symptoms.
  • Fasting for a few hours before and after the capsule, as per protocol.

3. Radiation safety precautions after treatment (for a few days, as advised by the nuclear medicine team)

  • Keep a distance (about 1–2 metres) from others, especially pregnant women and children; avoid close contact such as hugging and sleeping in the same bed.
  • Sleep alone; use separate towels, utensils and bedding, and wash them separately.
  • Drink plenty of fluids and void frequently – most radioactive iodine leaves in the urine; flush the toilet twice and wash hands well; men should sit to urinate to avoid splashes.
  • Suck sour candy if advised (stimulates saliva and protects salivary glands).
  • Avoid public transport for long journeys and crowded places for the advised period; inform airport security if travelling (detectors may be triggered).
  • Avoid pregnancy for at least 6 months (women) and fathering a child for about 4 months (men).
  • Hospital staff follow time, distance and shielding rules; disposal of the patient's waste follows radiation-safety regulations.

4. Side effects and follow-up

  • Mild neck tenderness or swelling, temporary worsening of thyrotoxic symptoms, nausea, altered taste.
  • Hypothyroidism develops in most patients within months to a year – lifelong levothyroxine is then needed; this is an expected outcome, not a complication.
  • Thyroid function tests at about 6–8 weeks and then regularly.
  • Watch for worsening eye symptoms.

5. Nursing responsibilities

  • Educate the patient and family clearly in simple language, with written instructions.
  • Reassure the patient that the dose for hyperthyroidism is safe and does not cause cancer or infertility in later life when precautions are followed.
  • Ensure follow-up and teach symptoms of hypothyroidism (tiredness, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation).

Nursing importance Clear instructions from the nurse protect family members from unnecessary radiation and ensure that post-treatment hypothyroidism is detected and treated early.

Conclusion Radioactive iodine is a simple and effective treatment for hyperthyroidism; careful preparation, radiation-safety precautions at home and regular thyroid function follow-up are the nurse's main teaching points.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Endocrine Disorders
question: What is diabetes insipidus? Write its management.
answer_html:
Diabetes insipidus (DI) is a disorder in which the body passes large volumes of dilute urine because of deficiency of antidiuretic hormone (ADH/vasopressin) – central DI (head injury, pituitary surgery, tumours) – or kidney resistance to ADH – nephrogenic DI (lithium, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia, kidney disease).

Features – polyuria (3–20 litres/day), urine specific gravity below 1.005, intense thirst (craving for cold water), nocturia, dehydration and hypernatraemia if water intake is inadequate.

Management

  1. Desmopressin (DDAVP) – nasal spray, tablet or injection for central DI.
  2. Thiazide diuretics, low-salt diet and treatment of the cause for nephrogenic DI.
  3. Nursing – strict intake–output, daily weight, urine specific gravity, serum sodium; free access to water.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Endocrine Disorders
question: What is diabetic foot? Write Wagner's classification.
answer_html:
Diabetic foot is infection, ulceration or destruction of deep tissues of the foot in a person with diabetes, associated with peripheral neuropathy (loss of protective sensation) and/or peripheral arterial disease. It is the commonest cause of non-traumatic lower-limb amputation in India.

Wagner's classification

  • Grade 0 – no ulcer; high-risk foot (deformity, callus).
  • Grade 1 – superficial ulcer.
  • Grade 2 – deep ulcer reaching tendon, bone or joint capsule.
  • Grade 3 – deep ulcer with abscess or osteomyelitis.
  • Grade 4 – localised gangrene (toes or forefoot).
  • Grade 5 – gangrene of the whole foot.

Prevention – daily foot inspection, proper footwear, no barefoot walking, nail care, offloading of pressure areas.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Endocrine Disorders
question: What is the "Rule of 15" in the management of hypoglycaemia?
answer_html:
The "Rule of 15" is a simple method for treating hypoglycaemia (blood glucose below 70 mg/dl) in a conscious patient who can swallow:

  1. Give 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate – 3 teaspoons of sugar or glucose dissolved in water, about 150 ml fruit juice or regular soft drink, or 3–4 glucose tablets.
  2. Wait 15 minutes and recheck blood glucose.
  3. If still below 70 mg/dl, repeat the 15 g.
  4. Once glucose is normal, give a snack or meal with complex carbohydrate (for example, roti or biscuits with milk) to prevent recurrence.

Unconscious patients – nothing by mouth; give IV dextrose or glucagon and place in the recovery position.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Endocrine Disorders
question: Differentiate between the Somogyi effect and the dawn phenomenon.
answer_html:
Point Somogyi effect Dawn phenomenon
Meaning Rebound morning hyperglycaemia following night-time hypoglycaemia Early-morning hyperglycaemia without preceding hypoglycaemia
Cause Excess evening insulin → hypoglycaemia at night (2–3 a.m.) → counter-regulatory hormones (glucagon, adrenaline, cortisol, GH) raise sugar Normal early-morning surge of GH and cortisol with insufficient insulin
2–3 a.m. glucose Low Normal or high
Management Reduce evening/bedtime insulin or add a bedtime snack Increase or shift the evening intermediate/long-acting insulin dose to bedtime, as ordered

Nursing point – check blood glucose at 2–3 a.m. for a few nights to distinguish the two.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Endocrine Disorders
question: What is the syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH)?
answer_html:
SIADH is a condition in which ADH is secreted in excess even though the blood is dilute, causing the kidneys to retain water, which leads to dilutional hyponatraemia and concentrated urine.

Causes – brain disorders (head injury, meningitis, stroke), lung disease (small-cell lung cancer, pneumonia, TB), drugs (carbamazepine, antidepressants, cyclophosphamide), post-operative pain and nausea. Features – reduced urine output, weight gain without oedema, symptoms of low sodium – headache, nausea, confusion, seizures.

Management

  1. Fluid restriction (about 800–1000 ml/day) and treatment of the cause.
  2. Hypertonic saline for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia; tolvaptan; slow correction of sodium.
  3. Nursing – daily weight, intake–output, neurological checks and seizure precautions.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Endocrine Disorders
question: What is phaeochromocytoma?
answer_html:
Phaeochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumour of the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla (rarely outside the adrenal), producing excess adrenaline and noradrenaline.

Features – paroxysmal or sustained hypertension with the classic triad of headache, sweating and palpitations; pallor, anxiety, tremor, chest pain, hyperglycaemia, weight loss; attacks may be triggered by abdominal pressure, exertion, anaesthesia or certain drugs. Diagnosis – raised plasma or urinary metanephrines; CT/MRI of adrenals.

Management

  1. α-blocker first (phenoxybenzamine or prazosin) for 10–14 days with liberal salt and fluids, then β-blocker (never β-blocker first – it can cause a hypertensive crisis).
  2. Laparoscopic adrenalectomy; post-operatively watch for hypotension and hypoglycaemia.
  3. Nursing – frequent BP monitoring; avoid palpating the abdomen firmly.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Integumentary Disorders
question: (a) Define psoriasis. (2 marks) (b) Explain the types, causes and clinical features of psoriasis. (5 marks) (c) Describe the management and nursing care of a patient with psoriasis. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Psoriasis – typical plaque and common sites
labels: well-demarcated red plaque with silvery scales; sites – scalp

answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks) Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated, non-infectious inflammatory skin disease characterised by well-demarcated, red, raised plaques covered with silvery-white scales, due to rapid proliferation of epidermal cells (skin cells mature in about 3–4 days instead of the normal 28 days). It runs a chronic course with remissions and relapses, and is not contagious.

(b) Types, causes and clinical features (5 marks) Causes and triggers

  • Genetic predisposition – family history in about one-third of patients (HLA-Cw6).
  • Immune mechanism – activated T-lymphocytes and cytokines (TNF-α, IL-17, IL-23) drive inflammation and rapid cell turnover.
  • Triggers
    • Streptococcal throat infection (guttate psoriasis), HIV.
    • Skin injury – cuts, scratches, burns, tattoos (Koebner phenomenon – new lesions at sites of trauma).
    • Emotional stress.
    • Smoking, alcohol, obesity.
    • Drugs – β-blockers, lithium, antimalarials (chloroquine), NSAIDs; sudden withdrawal of oral steroids (can cause pustular flare).
    • Cold, dry weather (winter worsening).

Types

  1. Plaque psoriasis (psoriasis vulgaris) – commonest (80–90%); sharply defined red plaques with silvery scales on extensor surfaces – elbows, knees, scalp, lower back, umbilicus.
  2. Guttate psoriasis – many small drop-like papules on the trunk in children and young adults, 2–3 weeks after a streptococcal sore throat.
  3. Inverse (flexural) psoriasis – smooth, red, non-scaly patches in skin folds (axillae, groin, under breasts).
  4. Pustular psoriasis – sterile pustules; localised (palms and soles) or generalised (von Zumbusch) with fever – an emergency.
  5. Erythrodermic psoriasis – redness and scaling over more than 90% of the body – an emergency (loss of heat, fluid and protein; infection; heart failure).
  6. Nail psoriasis – pitting, onycholysis (separation of the nail), "oil-drop" discoloration, thickening.
  7. Scalp psoriasis – thick scales extending beyond the hairline.
  8. Psoriatic arthritis – in about 10–30%; affects finger and toe joints (distal joints), "sausage" digits, back.

Clinical features and signs

  • Red plaques with silvery scales; itching (variable), burning, cracking and bleeding of plaques on palms and soles.
  • Candle-grease sign – scraping produces silvery scales like candle wax.
  • Auspitz sign – pinpoint bleeding when scales are removed.
  • Koebner phenomenon.
  • Psychological effects – embarrassment, depression, social isolation (misbelief that it is contagious).
  • Associated conditions – metabolic syndrome, diabetes, heart disease, depression.
  • Severity – assessed by body surface area involved (mild less than 3%, moderate 3–10%, severe more than 10%), PASI score and effect on quality of life.
  • Diagnosis is mainly clinical; skin biopsy in doubtful cases.

(c) Management and nursing care (8 marks) 1. Topical therapy (mild psoriasis and as add-on)

  • Emollients (petroleum jelly, liquid paraffin, coconut oil) – reduce scaling and itching; used daily.
  • Keratolytics – salicylic acid (3–6%) to soften and remove thick scales so that other medicines penetrate.
  • Topical corticosteroids – potency chosen according to site (mild on face and folds); used in short courses.
  • Vitamin D analogues – calcipotriol (often combined with a steroid).
  • Coal tar preparations and tar shampoos – effective but messy, smelly, stain clothes and increase sun sensitivity.
  • Dithranol (short-contact therapy) – stains skin and clothes purple-brown; not used on face or folds.
  • Tacrolimus ointment for face and flexures; tazarotene gel.

2. Phototherapy

  • Narrowband UVB (311 nm) two to three times a week – safe and effective for widespread psoriasis.
  • PUVA (psoralen tablets followed by UVA light) – wear UV-protective glasses for 24 hours after psoralen, avoid sunlight; long-term risk of skin cancer.
  • Controlled sun exposure under advice.

3. Systemic therapy (moderate to severe disease, arthritis, erythrodermic or pustular psoriasis)

  • Methotrexate – given once a week (never daily – fatal toxicity), with folic acid; monitor CBC, liver and kidney function; avoid alcohol; teratogenic.
  • Ciclosporin – monitor BP and kidney function.
  • Acitretin (oral retinoid) – teratogenic; women must avoid pregnancy during and for 3 years after treatment.
  • Apremilast; biologics – anti-TNF (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab), anti-IL-17 (secukinumab), anti-IL-12/23 (ustekinumab); biosimilars have reduced costs in India; screen for TB before biologics.
  • Avoid systemic steroids – they cause severe rebound flares on withdrawal.

4. Nursing care – nursing diagnoses and interventions (i) Impaired skin integrity

  • Lukewarm baths (not hot) with mild, soap-free cleanser or oil; soak plaques to soften scales; gently remove loosened scales – do not pick or scrub.
  • Apply medicines correctly – thin layer, on the lesion only, in the direction of hair growth; wear gloves when applying steroids, tar or dithranol; protect normal skin around dithranol with petroleum jelly.
  • "Soak and seal" – apply emollient within a few minutes after bathing.
  • Occlusive dressings or plastic wraps as ordered for thick plaques.

  • Soft, loose cotton clothing; keep nails short to prevent scratch injuries (Koebner). (ii) Impaired comfort (itching)

  • Emollients, cool compresses, calamine; antihistamines at night as ordered; distraction. (iii) Disturbed body image and social isolation

  • Encourage the patient to express feelings; correct the myth that psoriasis is contagious or due to "impure blood"; involve the family; link to support groups; refer for counselling if depressed. (iv) Deficient knowledge

  • Explain the chronic, relapsing nature – it can be controlled but not cured; adherence to treatment; recognising and avoiding triggers.

  • Avoid self-medication with unlabelled creams containing strong steroids, and quacks promising permanent cure.
  • Safe use of methotrexate (weekly), contraception with retinoids and methotrexate, regular blood tests.

  • Lifestyle – stop smoking and alcohol, reduce weight, exercise, manage stress (yoga, relaxation); treat throat infections early. (v) Care in erythrodermic or generalised pustular psoriasis (emergency)

  • Admit; maintain a warm room (heat loss), monitor temperature, fluid balance and electrolytes, high-protein diet (protein loss in scales), prevent infection, wet dressings and emollients, monitor for heart failure. (vi) Scalp and nail care

  • Tar or salicylic acid shampoos; oil the scalp overnight to soften scales; keep nails short and protected; avoid trauma. (vii) Joint care – report joint pain and swelling early (psoriatic arthritis); physiotherapy.

5. Health education summary Daily moisturising, short lukewarm baths, adherence to treatment, regular follow-up, sun exposure in moderation as advised, avoidance of triggers and harmful creams, healthy lifestyle and emotional support.

6. Common nursing diagnoses

  • Impaired skin integrity related to rapid epidermal turnover and scaling.
  • Impaired comfort (itching, pain) related to dry, cracked plaques.
  • Disturbed body image and social isolation related to visible lesions and stigma.
  • Deficient knowledge regarding the chronic nature of the disease, triggers and safe use of medicines.
  • Risk for infection related to cracked skin and immunosuppressive therapy.

7. Psoriasis and pregnancy, children and the elderly (brief)

  • Pregnancy – methotrexate and acitretin are contraindicated; emollients, mild topical steroids and narrowband UVB are preferred; planning is needed before conception.
  • Children – guttate psoriasis after sore throat is common; gentle topical therapy; school support against teasing.
  • Elderly – dry, fragile skin, many medicines (β-blockers may worsen psoriasis); careful monitoring of systemic drugs.

Nursing importance Psoriasis affects quality of life as much as heart disease or diabetes; nurses help patients through correct application of treatment, education about triggers and drugs, and support against stigma.

Conclusion Psoriasis is a chronic immune-mediated disease with rapid skin turnover and silvery scaly plaques; topical agents, phototherapy and systemic or biologic drugs control it, while skin care, trigger avoidance, education and emotional support by the nurse improve the patient's life.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Integumentary Disorders
question: (a) Explain the nursing assessment of a patient with a skin disorder, including primary and secondary skin lesions. (6 marks) (b) Describe the general nursing management of patients with dermatological disorders – topical therapy, therapeutic baths, wet dressings and care of pruritus. (9 marks)
answer_html:
Introduction Skin diseases are among the commonest health problems in India, especially in hot, humid conditions and crowded living. Although they are rarely fatal, they cause itching, pain, sleeplessness, disfigurement and social stigma. Careful assessment and skilled topical and supportive nursing care are central to dermatology nursing.

(a) Nursing assessment (6 marks) 1. History

  • Onset, duration, site of first lesion, spread; course (acute, chronic, relapsing).
  • Symptoms – itching (worse at night in scabies), pain, burning, discharge, bleeding.
  • Triggers and exposures – new soaps, cosmetics, hair dye, jewellery (nickel), rubber gloves, plants (parthenium weed), detergents and cement (occupation), foods, insect bites, sun exposure.
  • Medicines – oral and topical, including over-the-counter steroid combination creams and home remedies.
  • Contacts – similar lesions in family or hostel (scabies, fungal infection, impetigo).
  • Past and family history – atopy (asthma, allergic rhinitis, eczema), psoriasis, diabetes, HIV.
  • Psychosocial effects – sleep, work, self-esteem, relationships.

2. Physical examination

  • Examine the entire skin, hair, nails and mucous membranes in good natural light, maintaining privacy.
  • Colour – erythema, pallor, cyanosis, jaundice, hyper- and hypopigmentation; temperature, moisture, texture, turgor, oedema.
  • Describe each lesion – type, size (measure in mm/cm), shape, colour, margin, surface (scaly, crusted, moist), arrangement (linear, annular, grouped, dermatomal), distribution (localised, generalised, symmetrical, flexural, extensor, sun-exposed areas), and whether it blanches on pressure (diascopy).
  • Hair – loss, lice, nits; nails – pitting, discoloration, thickening.
  • Lymph nodes; signs of systemic disease.

3. Primary skin lesions (first lesions of a disease)

  • Macule – flat, coloured spot less than 1 cm (freckle); patch – flat area more than 1 cm (vitiligo).
  • Papule – raised, solid, less than 1 cm (wart); plaque – raised, flat-topped, more than 1 cm (psoriasis).
  • Nodule – solid, deeper lesion more than 1 cm; tumour – larger solid mass.
  • Vesicle – fluid-filled blister less than 1 cm (chickenpox, herpes); bulla – blister more than 1 cm (pemphigus, burns).
  • Pustule – pus-filled lesion (acne, pustular psoriasis).
  • Wheal – transient, itchy, oedematous swelling (urticaria).
  • Cyst – sac containing fluid or semi-solid material; petechiae and purpura – small and larger bleeding spots that do not blanch.

4. Secondary skin lesions (changes due to progression, scratching or treatment)

  • Scale – flakes of dead skin (psoriasis); crust – dried exudate (impetigo – honey-coloured).
  • Erosion – loss of epidermis only (heals without scar); ulcer – loss of epidermis and dermis (heals with scar).
  • Excoriation – scratch marks; fissure – linear crack (athlete's foot, cracked heels).
  • Lichenification – thickened skin with exaggerated markings due to chronic scratching (chronic eczema).
  • Scar, keloid (overgrown scar), atrophy (thin skin – steroid misuse).

5. Diagnostic tests (nurse assists and collects samples)

  • KOH mount of scrapings (fungal hyphae); Wood's lamp (tinea capitis, vitiligo); Tzanck smear (herpes, pemphigus); skin scraping for scabies mites.
  • Patch test (allergic contact dermatitis); skin biopsy (punch biopsy) with immunofluorescence; slit-skin smear (leprosy); swab culture; blood tests (CBC, sugar, HIV, thyroid).

(b) General nursing management of dermatological disorders (9 marks) 1. Principles of topical therapy

  • Choose the right vehicle – the rule is "if it is wet, dry it; if it is dry, wet it":
    • Lotions and solutions – for acute, weeping lesions and hairy areas.
    • Creams – for moist or acute lesions; cosmetically acceptable.
    • Ointments – greasy, occlusive; best for dry, thick, chronic lesions; better absorption.
    • Gels – scalp and face; pastes – protect localised areas; powders – skin folds (antifungal dusting powder); shampoos – scalp.
  • Application – wash hands, wear gloves for potent drugs, clean the area, apply a thin layer gently in the direction of hair growth, preferably after a bath on slightly damp skin; wash hands afterwards.
  • Fingertip unit (FTU) – the amount squeezed from the tip of the index finger to the first crease (about 0.5 g) covers an area equal to two adult palms; helps to give the correct quantity of steroid.
  • Topical steroids – use the lowest effective potency for the shortest time; mild steroids for the face, folds and children; side effects – skin thinning, striae, telangiectasia, acne, steroid-dependent rosacea and steroid-modified tinea. In India, misuse of over-the-counter steroid–antifungal–antibiotic combination creams is a major cause of chronic fungal infection – teach patients to avoid them.
  • Ensure adherence; explain how long and how often to apply.

2. Therapeutic (medicated) baths

  • Purposes – cleanse the skin, remove crusts and scales, relieve itching, hydrate the skin and apply medication over large areas.
  • Types – emollient/oil baths (dry skin, eczema), colloidal oatmeal baths (itching), potassium permanganate baths (1:10,000 – light pink solution) for weeping, infected or blistering conditions (pemphigus, infected eczema), saline baths, tar baths (psoriasis).
  • Procedure points – water lukewarm (about 32–38 °C), 15–20 minutes; keep the room warm to prevent chilling; prevent slipping (oil makes the tub slippery); pat dry (do not rub); apply emollient or medicine within 3 minutes of the bath ("soak and seal"); KMnO₄ stains skin, nails and clothes and must be fully dissolved (crystals burn the skin).

3. Wet dressings (compresses)

  • Uses – acute, oozing, inflamed or crusted lesions; they cool, soothe, dry the lesion, remove crusts and reduce itching.
  • Types – open (evaporative) dressings, left uncovered so that water evaporates (cooling, drying); closed (occlusive) dressings covered with plastic to keep the area moist and improve drug penetration.
  • Solutions – normal saline, Burow's solution (aluminium acetate), dilute potassium permanganate.
  • Technique – soft cotton cloth or gauze soaked and wrung until it stops dripping; applied for 15–30 minutes, 3–4 times a day; re-moisten as it dries; treat not more than one-third of the body at a time to prevent chilling; use clean cloths each time.

4. Care of pruritus (itching)

  • Find and treat the cause – dry skin, scabies, allergy, fungal infection, diabetes, liver or kidney disease, drugs.
  • Keep the skin moisturised; avoid hot baths, strong soaps, woollen and synthetic clothing; use loose cotton clothes.
  • Cool environment; cool compresses, calamine or menthol lotions.
  • Keep nails short; cotton gloves at night for children; gently pat or press instead of scratching.
  • Oral antihistamines as ordered (sedating ones at night); break the itch–scratch cycle with distraction and relaxation.

5. Prevention of infection

  • Hand hygiene; aseptic dressing of eroded skin; contact precautions in contagious conditions (scabies, impetigo, chickenpox); clean linen; treat family contacts.

6. Nutrition and fluids

  • High-protein, high-calorie diet with vitamins A, C and zinc for healing; extra fluids in extensive skin loss (erythroderma, pemphigus); avoid known food triggers.

7. Psychosocial care

  • Visible skin diseases (vitiligo, psoriasis, leprosy, acne) cause stigma, anxiety and depression; listen, correct myths, involve family, refer to counselling and support groups; maintain dignity during examination and treatment.

8. Health education

  • Correct use of medicines and emollients; avoid self-medication; personal hygiene; not sharing towels, combs and clothes; sun protection (shade, clothing, sunscreen SPF 30 or more); follow-up.

Nursing importance Accurate description of lesions helps diagnosis, and correctly applied topical treatment, baths and wet dressings – mostly carried out by nurses – largely decide how quickly a skin disease improves.

Conclusion Assessment of skin disorders involves a careful history and systematic description of primary and secondary lesions; general nursing management includes correct topical therapy, medicated baths, wet dressings, relief of itching, infection prevention, nutrition, psychosocial support and education.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Integumentary Disorders
question: Define eczema. Explain its types, clinical features and nursing management.
answer_html:
Definition Eczema (dermatitis) is a non-infectious inflammatory reaction of the skin characterised by itching, redness, vesicles and oozing in the acute stage and scaling, thickening (lichenification) and pigmentation in the chronic stage. The terms eczema and dermatitis are often used interchangeably.

1. Types (a) Endogenous (constitutional)

  • Atopic dermatitis – common in children; associated with personal or family history of asthma and allergic rhinitis; affects face and cheeks in infants and flexures (elbow and knee creases) in older children; dry, itchy skin.
  • Seborrhoeic dermatitis – greasy scaling of scalp (dandruff), eyebrows, nasolabial folds, chest; cradle cap in infants.
  • Discoid (nummular) eczema – coin-shaped itchy plaques.
  • Pompholyx (dyshidrotic) – deep itchy vesicles on palms and soles.

  • Stasis (venous) eczema – lower legs in patients with varicose veins. (b) Exogenous

  • Irritant contact dermatitis – due to detergents, soaps, cement, solvents; common in housewives ("housewives' hand eczema") and construction workers.

  • Allergic contact dermatitis – type IV allergy to nickel (jewellery, belt buckles), hair dye (paraphenylenediamine), cosmetics, rubber gloves, medicines (neomycin) and plants – parthenium (congress grass) dermatitis is common in India.

2. Clinical features

  • Acute stage – intense itching, redness, swelling, vesicles, oozing, crusting.
  • Subacute stage – scaling, crusting, less oozing.
  • Chronic stage – dry, thickened, lichenified skin, fissures, hyperpigmentation.
  • Sleep disturbance; secondary bacterial infection (pustules, honey-coloured crusts); eczema herpeticum (widespread herpes infection – an emergency).

3. Management

  • Identify and avoid triggers – patch testing for allergic contact dermatitis.
  • Emollients – the cornerstone; applied liberally and often.
  • Topical corticosteroids for flares; tacrolimus for face and folds.
  • Wet compresses or wet wraps for oozing lesions; potassium permanganate soaks for infected eczema.
  • Antihistamines for itching; antibiotics for infection.
  • Severe disease – ciclosporin, methotrexate, dupilumab (biologic), phototherapy.

4. Nursing management

  • "Soak and seal" – short lukewarm bath with soap-free cleanser, pat dry, apply emollient immediately.
  • Apply topical medicines correctly and in the right amounts (fingertip units).
  • Reduce itching – cool environment, cotton clothes, nails short, gloves at night for children.
  • Protect hands – cotton gloves under rubber gloves for wet work; avoid harsh detergents; moisturise after washing.
  • Teach to avoid hair dyes or do a patch test before use in sensitive persons; avoid nickel contact.
  • Watch for infection; report sudden painful spreading blisters.
  • Support parents of children with atopic eczema – explain the chronic nature, need for daily care and myths about diet.

Nursing importance Eczema control depends mainly on daily skin care and trigger avoidance taught by the nurse rather than on strong medicines.

Conclusion Eczema is an itchy inflammatory skin reaction of endogenous or contact origin; emollients, avoidance of triggers, topical anti-inflammatory therapy and good nursing care control the condition.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Integumentary Disorders
question: Write a note on malignant melanoma.
answer_html:
Definition Malignant melanoma is a malignant tumour arising from melanocytes (pigment-producing cells) of the skin, and occasionally of the eye or mucous membranes. Though less common in Indians than in fair-skinned populations, it is the most aggressive skin cancer and is often detected late.

1. Risk factors

  • Ultraviolet exposure and sunburns, especially in childhood; tanning beds.
  • Fair skin, many moles or atypical (dysplastic) naevi, family history.
  • Immunosuppression; previous melanoma.

2. Types

  • Superficial spreading melanoma – commonest in fair-skinned people.
  • Nodular melanoma – raised, grows quickly in depth; aggressive.
  • Lentigo maligna melanoma – sun-damaged face of the elderly.
  • Acral lentiginous melanoma – on palms, soles and under the nails – the commonest type in Indians and darker-skinned people; dark streak under a nail spreading to the nail fold (Hutchinson's sign).
  • Amelanotic and mucosal melanomas (mouth, nose, genital tract).

3. Warning signs – the ABCDE rule

  • Asymmetry – one half unlike the other.
  • Border – irregular, notched or blurred.
  • Colour – varied shades of brown, black, red, white or blue.
  • Diameter – more than 6 mm.
  • Evolving – change in size, shape, colour or elevation; new symptoms such as itching or bleeding.
  • An "ugly duckling" mole that looks different from the others.

4. Diagnosis and staging Dermoscopy, excision biopsy (full thickness; shave biopsy is avoided), Breslow thickness (depth of invasion – the most important prognostic factor), sentinel lymph node biopsy, CT/PET scan for spread; TNM staging.

5. Management

  • Wide local excision with a margin of normal skin (1–2 cm depending on thickness), skin graft or flap if needed.
  • Sentinel lymph node biopsy and lymph node dissection when nodes are involved.
  • Immunotherapy (anti-PD-1 drugs – nivolumab, pembrolizumab; ipilimumab) and targeted therapy (BRAF and MEK inhibitors) for advanced disease; radiotherapy for symptomatic metastases.

6. Nursing management

  • Post-operative care – wound and graft care, pain relief, observation of flap colour, infection prevention.
  • After lymph node dissection – prevent lymphoedema (limb elevation, exercises, avoid injections and injury on that limb, skin care).
  • Monitor and report side effects of immunotherapy – rash, diarrhoea (colitis), jaundice, fatigue, thyroid and other hormonal problems.
  • Psychological support – fear of cancer, disfigurement; involve family.
  • Education for prevention and early detection
    • Sun protection – avoid strong sun (10 a.m.–4 p.m.), wear protective clothing and hats, use broad-spectrum sunscreen SPF 30 or more and reapply every 2 hours outdoors; avoid tanning beds.
    • Monthly skin self-examination, including palms, soles, nails and between toes; report any changing mole or non-healing dark lesion.
    • Regular follow-up after treatment.

Nursing importance Early detection by recognising the ABCDE signs, especially on the soles and nails in Indian patients, greatly improves survival.

Conclusion Malignant melanoma is an aggressive melanocytic cancer; early excision cures thin lesions, while advanced disease needs immunotherapy or targeted therapy; prevention and early detection through education are key nursing roles.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Integumentary Disorders
question: Explain the clinical features, treatment and nursing management of scabies.
answer_html:
Definition Scabies is a highly contagious skin infestation caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei var. *hominis, which burrows into the epidermis and lays eggs. It spreads by close, prolonged skin-to-skin contact* (family members, hostels, orphanages, prisons, sexual partners) and occasionally through shared clothing and bedding.

1. Clinical features

  • Intense itching, worse at night (nocturnal pruritus); several family members are often affected.
  • Burrows – fine, greyish, wavy lines; papules, vesicles and excoriations.
  • Typical sites – web spaces of fingers, sides of fingers, flexor aspect of wrists, elbows, axillae, around the nipples (women), umbilicus, waist, buttocks, genitals (itchy nodules on penis and scrotum in men).
  • Face and scalp are usually spared in adults but may be involved in infants (along with palms and soles).
  • Complications – secondary bacterial infection (impetigo, pustules) and, after streptococcal infection, acute glomerulonephritis.
  • Crusted (Norwegian) scabies – in elderly, immunocompromised and disabled persons – thick crusts containing thousands of mites; extremely contagious; mild itching.

2. Diagnosis Clinical history and distribution; skin scraping under the microscope (mites, eggs, faecal pellets); dermoscopy.

3. Treatment

  • Permethrin 5% cream (drug of choice) – apply to the whole body from the neck down to the toes (including web spaces, under nails, genitals; also scalp and face in infants and elderly), on cool, dry skin at night; leave for 8–12 hours and wash off; repeat after one week.
  • Alternatives – benzyl benzoate 25% lotion (adults; irritant), crotamiton; oral ivermectin (200 µg/kg, two doses one week apart) – not in pregnancy or children below 15 kg; useful in crusted scabies and institutional outbreaks.
  • Antihistamines for itching; antibiotics for secondary infection.
  • Treat all household and close contacts at the same time, even if they have no symptoms.

4. Nursing management

  • Contact precautions (gloves, gown) until 24 hours after effective treatment; single room for crusted scabies.
  • Teach correct application – trim nails, apply to every part from neck to toes, re-apply to hands after washing them during the treatment period.
  • Linen and clothing care – wash clothes, towels and bed linen used in the last 3 days in hot water and dry in strong sunlight or iron them; items that cannot be washed are sealed in a plastic bag for about a week.
  • Explain that itching may persist for 2–4 weeks after successful treatment (not treatment failure); emollients and antihistamines help.
  • Treat secondary infection; keep nails short.
  • Health education in schools, hostels and institutions – personal hygiene, not sharing clothes and bedding, early treatment and treatment of all contacts.

Nursing importance Scabies recurs mainly because contacts are not treated together or the cream is applied incorrectly; nurse-led teaching breaks the chain of transmission.

Conclusion Scabies is a contagious mite infestation causing nocturnal itching with burrows at typical sites; permethrin or ivermectin for the patient and all contacts, linen care and education cure it.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Integumentary Disorders
question: Explain pemphigus vulgaris and its nursing management.
answer_html:
Definition Pemphigus vulgaris is a chronic, autoimmune blistering disease in which IgG autoantibodies against desmoglein (proteins that hold epidermal cells together) cause loss of adhesion between skin cells (acantholysis), producing flaccid blisters and painful erosions of the skin and mucous membranes. It usually affects adults aged 40–60 years and was frequently fatal before steroids.

1. Clinical features
