  • Painful oral erosions – often the first sign, months before skin lesions; difficulty in eating and swallowing.
  • Flaccid bullae on apparently normal skin of the scalp, face, chest, back, groin, which rupture easily, leaving large, raw, painful, oozing erosions that crust and may smell foul.
  • Nikolsky's sign positive – gentle lateral pressure on normal-looking skin causes the upper layer to slide off.
  • Complications – secondary infection and septicaemia, fluid, electrolyte and protein loss, hypothermia, malnutrition; side effects of long-term steroids.

2. Diagnosis Tzanck smear (acantholytic cells), skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence (intercellular IgG in a "fish-net" pattern), ELISA for anti-desmoglein antibodies.

3. Treatment

  • Systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone) – main treatment initially.
  • Rituximab – now a first-line steroid-sparing therapy.
  • Dexamethasone–cyclophosphamide pulse (DCP) therapy – a regimen developed in India.
  • Immunosuppressants (azathioprine, mycophenolate), IVIG.
  • Supportive care – antibiotics for infection, fluids, nutrition, pain relief.

4. Nursing management (similar to care of burns)

  • Protective isolation, strict asepsis, sterile linen; handle the patient gently (lift with a sheet; avoid friction and adhesive tapes).
  • Skin care – potassium permanganate (1:10,000) or saline baths/soaks, non-adherent dressings (paraffin gauze), topical antibiotics on erosions as ordered; aspirate large intact bullae aseptically if ordered, leaving the roof as a natural dressing.
  • Oral care – soft toothbrush or swabs, mild mouthwashes, topical anaesthetic gel before meals; soft, cool, bland diet; avoid spicy and hot foods.
  • Fluid and electrolyte balance – intake–output, daily weight, serum electrolytes and albumin.
  • High-protein, high-calorie diet with supplements.
  • Pain relief before dressings.
  • Monitor for infection (fever, pus, odour) and steroid side effects – blood sugar, BP, GI bleeding, infections, mood, osteoporosis.
  • Maintain a warm environment (heat loss from raw skin).
  • Psychological support – disfigurement, prolonged treatment; involve family.
  • Education – take drugs exactly as prescribed, never stop steroids suddenly, report new blisters or fever, regular follow-up.

Nursing importance Infection and fluid loss are the main causes of death in pemphigus; meticulous aseptic skin care, oral care and nutrition by nurses save lives.

Conclusion Pemphigus vulgaris is an autoimmune blistering disease with fragile bullae and painful erosions; immunosuppressive therapy and burn-like nursing care with strict asepsis are essential.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Integumentary Disorders
question: Explain acne vulgaris and its management with nursing education.
answer_html:
Definition Acne vulgaris is a chronic inflammatory disease of the pilosebaceous units (hair follicles and sebaceous glands), characterised by comedones, papules, pustules, nodules and cysts on the face, chest and back. It mainly affects adolescents and often continues into adulthood, especially in women.

1. Causes (pathogenesis)

  1. Increased sebum production – stimulated by androgens at puberty.
  2. Blockage of follicles by excess keratin – forming comedones.
  3. Bacterial colonisation – Cutibacterium (Propionibacterium) acnes.
  4. Inflammation. Aggravating factors – hormonal changes (before menses, PCOS), oily cosmetics and hair oils, stress, squeezing and picking, drugs (steroids, anabolic steroids, lithium, isoniazid), high glycaemic diet and excess dairy in some people, humid climate.

2. Clinical features

  • Non-inflammatory lesions – open comedones (blackheads) and closed comedones (whiteheads).
  • Inflammatory lesions – red papules, pustules, painful nodules and cysts.
  • Sites – face, forehead, chest, upper back, shoulders.
  • Grades – mild (mainly comedones), moderate (papules and pustules), severe (nodules, cysts, scarring).
  • Sequelae – scars (ice-pick, boxcar), post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (very common in Indian skin), low self-esteem, anxiety, depression.

3. Management

  • Topical – benzoyl peroxide (2.5–5%), topical retinoids (adapalene, tretinoin), topical antibiotics (clindamycin – always with benzoyl peroxide to prevent resistance), azelaic acid.
  • Oral antibiotics – doxycycline or minocycline for moderate acne (about 3 months).
  • Hormonal therapy in women – combined oral contraceptives, spironolactone (PCOS).
  • Oral isotretinoin for severe or scarring acne – highly effective; teratogenic (strict contraception), dryness of lips and skin, raised lipids and liver enzymes, mood changes; regular monitoring.
  • Procedures – comedone extraction, chemical peels, and for scars – microneedling, laser resurfacing.

4. Nursing education

  • Wash the face gently twice daily with a mild cleanser; avoid harsh scrubbing.
  • Do not squeeze or pick lesions – causes scarring and pigmentation.
  • Use oil-free, non-comedogenic cosmetics and sunscreen; avoid heavy hair oils on the forehead; wash hair regularly (dandruff worsens acne).
  • Apply retinoids at night in a thin layer; use sunscreen during the day (photosensitivity).
  • Be patient – improvement takes 6–8 weeks; continue treatment as advised.
  • Avoid steroid creams and unprescribed "fairness" creams that may contain steroids (they worsen acne).
  • Balanced diet, adequate sleep, stress management.
  • Correct myths – acne is not caused by dirt and is not contagious; address emotional distress and refer for counselling if needed.

Nursing importance Acne seriously affects young people's self-image; correct information and support from the nurse improve adherence and prevent permanent scars.

Conclusion Acne vulgaris is a chronic pilosebaceous disorder of adolescents; topical and systemic treatments are effective when combined with correct skin care, patience and avoidance of harmful creams.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Integumentary Disorders
question: Explain dermatophytosis (tinea infections) and the nursing management, with reference to the Indian situation.
answer_html:
Definition Dermatophytosis (tinea or ringworm) is a superficial fungal infection of keratinised tissues – skin, hair and nails – caused by dermatophytes (Trichophyton, Microsporum and Epidermophyton).

1. The Indian situation India is facing an epidemic of chronic, widespread and recurrent dermatophytosis, often caused by Trichophyton indotineae. Contributing factors are the hot, humid climate, sweating, tight synthetic clothing, sharing of towels and clothes, crowding, poor adherence to treatment and, most importantly, misuse of over-the-counter steroid–antifungal–antibiotic combination creams, which suppress symptoms but make the infection spread (steroid-modified tinea or tinea incognito) and contribute to drug resistance.

2. Types and clinical features

  • Tinea corporis (body) – ring-shaped (annular) itchy plaques with a raised, scaly, active border and central clearing.
  • Tinea cruris (groin – "dhobi itch") – itchy red plaques on inner thighs and groin.
  • Tinea pedis (athlete's foot) – scaling, maceration and fissures between the toes.
  • Tinea capitis (scalp, mainly children) – scaly patches with hair loss; kerion (boggy, inflamed swelling).
  • Tinea unguium (onychomycosis) – thickened, discoloured, crumbling nails.
  • Tinea faciei, tinea manuum (hands), tinea barbae (beard).
  • Steroid-modified tinea – extensive lesions with ill-defined borders, less scaling, persistent itching.

3. Diagnosis KOH mount of skin scrapings, hair or nail clippings (fungal hyphae), fungal culture, Wood's lamp (some scalp infections).

4. Treatment

  • Topical antifungals – luliconazole, clotrimazole, miconazole, terbinafine, sertaconazole, amorolfine – applied twice daily to the lesion and 2 cm beyond its edge, continued for about 2 weeks after the skin looks normal (usually 4–6 weeks).
  • Oral antifungals – terbinafine or itraconazole for extensive, recurrent, scalp and nail infections, for the duration advised (often several weeks; nails need months).
  • Stop steroid combination creams.
  • Antihistamines for itching; treat all affected family members at the same time.

5. Nursing management and education

  • Keep the skin dry – dry thoroughly after bathing, especially folds and between toes; use antifungal dusting powder in folds.
  • Loose cotton clothing; change undergarments and socks daily; avoid tight jeans and synthetic fabrics.
  • Do not share towels, clothes, combs, caps or bedding.
  • Wash clothes and towels in hot water and dry them in strong sunlight; iron clothes, including undergarments.
  • Complete the full course of treatment even after itching stops.
  • Never use over-the-counter steroid creams for itching or rashes.
  • Treat pets with skin lesions; control diabetes and obesity; keep feet dry and wear open footwear where possible.

Nursing importance Health education by nurses about hygiene, dry skin, full-course treatment and avoidance of steroid creams is essential to control the ongoing epidemic of tinea in India.

Conclusion Dermatophytosis is a common superficial fungal infection that has become chronic and recurrent in India due to climate, hygiene factors and steroid misuse; correct antifungal therapy, completion of treatment and hygiene measures cure it.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Integumentary Disorders
question: Define psoriasis. Mention its characteristic signs.
answer_html:
Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated, non-infectious inflammatory skin disease with well-demarcated red plaques covered by silvery-white scales, due to rapid epidermal cell turnover (3–4 days instead of 28). It runs a course of remissions and relapses.

Characteristic signs

  1. Candle-grease sign – scraping produces silvery scales.
  2. Auspitz sign – pinpoint bleeding on removal of scales.
  3. Koebner phenomenon – new lesions at sites of skin injury.
  4. Nail pitting and onycholysis. Common sites – scalp, elbows, knees, lower back (extensor surfaces).

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Integumentary Disorders
question: What is alopecia? List its types.
answer_html:
Alopecia is loss of hair from areas where it normally grows, especially the scalp.

Types

  1. Non-scarring alopecia (follicles preserved – hair may regrow)
    • Androgenetic alopecia – male and female pattern baldness.
    • Alopecia areata – autoimmune; sudden round, smooth bald patches.
    • Telogen effluvium – diffuse shedding 2–3 months after fever (dengue, typhoid, COVID-19), childbirth, surgery, crash dieting or stress.
    • Anagen effluvium – chemotherapy.
    • Traction alopecia (tight hairstyles), tinea capitis, nutritional (iron, protein) and thyroid causes.
  2. Scarring alopecia – permanent loss due to destruction of follicles (lichen planopilaris, discoid lupus, burns).

Management – treat the cause; minoxidil, intralesional steroids (areata); counselling, wigs or scarves.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Integumentary Disorders
question: What is urticaria? Write its management.
answer_html:
Urticaria (hives) is a condition with transient, itchy, raised, pink or pale swellings (wheals) of the skin that appear and disappear within 24 hours, due to release of histamine from mast cells. Deeper swelling of lips, eyelids or tongue is angioedema.

Types – acute (less than 6 weeks – foods, drugs such as penicillin and NSAIDs, insect stings, infections) and chronic (more than 6 weeks – often spontaneous/autoimmune, or physical – pressure, cold, heat, exercise, dermographism).

Management

  1. Identify and avoid the trigger; keep a diary.
  2. Non-sedating antihistamines (cetirizine, levocetirizine, fexofenadine) – dose may be increased as advised.
  3. Cool compresses, calamine; short course of steroids for severe acute urticaria; omalizumab for chronic cases.
  4. IM adrenaline if there is throat swelling, breathing difficulty or hypotension (anaphylaxis).

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Integumentary Disorders
question: What is vitiligo? Mention the nurse's role.
answer_html:
Vitiligo is an acquired depigmenting disorder in which melanocytes are destroyed (usually by an autoimmune process), producing milky-white, well-defined patches on the skin, commonly on the face, around the mouth and eyes, hands, feet and genitals. It may be associated with thyroid disease, diabetes and other autoimmune disorders.

Treatment – topical steroids or tacrolimus, narrowband UVB phototherapy, oral mini-pulse steroids for spreading disease, surgical grafting for stable patches, cosmetic camouflage and sunscreen.

Nurse's role

  1. Correct myths – vitiligo is not contagious, not leprosy, and not caused by eating fish with milk.
  2. Counselling to reduce stigma and anxiety (marriage-related concerns are common in India).
  3. Teach sun protection and correct use of medicines; encourage follow-up.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Integumentary Disorders
question: What is impetigo? Write its nursing care.
answer_html:
Impetigo is a highly contagious superficial bacterial skin infection caused by Staphylococcus aureus and/or Streptococcus pyogenes, common in children aged 2–5 years, especially in hot, humid weather.

Features – red spots that form vesicles and pustules which rupture to leave honey-coloured crusts, usually around the nose and mouth; bullous impetigo shows flaccid blisters. Complications – cellulitis and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

Nursing care

  1. Soak and gently remove crusts with saline or soap and water; apply mupirocin or fusidic acid ointment as ordered; oral antibiotics for extensive lesions.
  2. Hand hygiene, short nails, separate towels and clothes; wash linen.
  3. Keep the child away from school until 24 hours after starting antibiotics or until lesions crust; treat underlying scabies.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Musculoskeletal Disorders
question: (a) Classify fractures and list the clinical features of a fracture of the tibia. (4 marks) (b) Explain the medical and surgical management of fracture of the shaft of the tibia. (4 marks) (c) Describe the nursing management of the patient, including prevention of complications. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: Types of fracture patterns in the tibia
labels: open fracture with bone through the skin; intramedullary interlocking nail and external fixator for fixation

answer_html:
Introduction The tibia is the commonest long bone to fracture, and because its front surface lies just beneath the skin, many tibial fractures are open (compound). In India, most are due to road traffic accidents (especially two-wheelers), falls and sports injuries. The fracture heals slowly – often 16–20 weeks or more – because the lower third of the tibia has a poor blood supply.

(a) Classification of fractures and clinical features (4 marks) Classification of fractures

  1. According to the relation with the skin
    • Closed (simple) – skin intact.
    • Open (compound) – the fracture communicates with the outside through a wound; graded by the Gustilo–Anderson classification (type I – wound below 1 cm, clean; type II – 1–10 cm; type III – extensive soft-tissue damage, contamination, vascular injury).
  2. According to the fracture line (pattern) – transverse, oblique, spiral, comminuted (more than two fragments), segmental, greenstick (children), impacted, avulsion, compression.
  3. According to displacement – undisplaced or displaced (angulated, shortened, rotated).
  4. According to cause – traumatic, pathological (weak bone – tumour, osteoporosis), stress (fatigue) fractures.
  5. According to site – tibial plateau (upper end), shaft (upper, middle, lower third), distal end (pilon) and ankle.

Clinical features of fracture of the tibia

  • History of injury, severe pain and inability to bear weight.
  • Swelling, bruising, tenderness over the fracture.
  • Deformity – angulation, shortening, rotation of the leg.
  • Abnormal mobility and crepitus (not to be elicited deliberately).
  • Loss of function.
  • Open wound with or without visible bone in compound fractures.
  • Signs of associated injuries – absent foot pulses (vascular injury), foot drop and numbness (common peroneal nerve injury, especially with upper fibular fractures), tense swollen calf (compartment syndrome).
  • Investigations – X-ray of the whole leg (AP and lateral, including knee and ankle); CT for plateau and pilon fractures; Doppler if pulses are weak; blood tests before surgery.

(b) Medical and surgical management (4 marks) 1. Emergency care

  • Primary survey (ABCDE); control bleeding; splint the limb in the position found (including the knee and ankle); analgesia; IV fluids.
  • Open fractures – IV antibiotics within one hour (e.g., cefazolin, plus gentamicin for heavily contaminated wounds), tetanus prophylaxis, remove gross contamination, cover the wound with a sterile saline-soaked dressing, photograph the wound, and take the patient for debridement and irrigation in the OT as early as possible.
  • Check and record neurovascular status before and after any manipulation.

2. Conservative treatment (stable, undisplaced closed fractures)

  • Closed reduction and above-knee plaster of Paris (POP) cast, followed after some weeks by a patellar-tendon-bearing (PTB) cast or functional brace that allows walking.

3. Operative treatment

  • Intramedullary interlocking nailing – the standard treatment for most displaced tibial shaft fractures; allows early mobilisation.
  • Plating (open or minimally invasive) for fractures near the ends of the bone.
  • External fixator – for open fractures with soft-tissue damage, severe swelling or multiple injuries (damage control); later converted to internal fixation.
  • Ilizarov ring fixator – for complex fractures, bone loss, infection and non-union.
  • Soft-tissue cover with flaps or skin grafts in open fractures; fasciotomy for compartment syndrome.

(c) Nursing management and prevention of complications (7 marks) 1. Neurovascular assessment – every hour for the first 24–48 hours, then 4-hourly

  • The "6 Ps" – Pain (especially pain out of proportion or on passive stretching of toes), Pallor, Pulselessness (dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses), Paraesthesia, Paralysis (ability to move toes), Poikilothermia (coldness); also capillary refill (less than 2 seconds).
  • Report immediately any increasing pain, numbness or inability to move toes – possible compartment syndrome.

2. Positioning and swelling control

  • Elevate the limb on pillows (slightly above heart level) and apply ice packs (wrapped) for the first 48 hours to reduce swelling – except when compartment syndrome is suspected, when the limb is kept at heart level.
  • Encourage toe movements frequently.

3. Pain management

  • Regular analgesics; immobilisation and support of the limb during movement; diversion.

4. Care of POP cast (if applied)

  • Allow the cast to dry fully (keep exposed, do not cover); handle with palms, not fingertips, while wet.
  • Check edges, skin around the cast, colour and temperature of toes; ask about tightness, burning or pressure spots; split the cast if circulation is compromised (as ordered).
  • Do not allow the patient to push objects inside the cast; keep it dry.

5. Care of external fixator (pin-site care)

  • Clean pin sites daily (or as per protocol) with normal saline or chlorhexidine using a separate swab for each pin; observe for redness, discharge, loosening and pain (pin-tract infection).
  • Check that clamps and bars are secure; never use the frame as a handle to lift the leg without instruction.

6. Post-operative care after nailing or plating

  • Vital signs, wound and drain care, antibiotics, pain relief.
  • Early mobilisation – sitting up on the first day; walking with a walker or crutches, initially non-weight bearing or touch-down weight bearing, progressing as advised by the surgeon.
  • Exercises – quadriceps setting, straight-leg raising, knee and ankle range-of-motion, and exercises for the other limbs.

7. Prevention of complications | Complication | Prevention / nursing action | |---|---| | Compartment syndrome | Neurovascular checks; avoid tight bandages/casts; report early for fasciotomy | | Infection / osteomyelitis (open fractures) | Early antibiotics, aseptic wound and pin-site care, nutrition | | Deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism | Leg and ankle exercises, early mobilisation, anticoagulants and stockings (other limb) as ordered | | Fat embolism (24–72 hours) | Early immobilisation; watch for breathlessness, confusion, petechiae on chest and axillae; oxygen | | Delayed union / non-union | Good immobilisation, nutrition, no smoking, follow-up X-rays | | Malunion, joint stiffness, muscle wasting | Correct reduction, regular exercises, physiotherapy | | Pressure ulcers, chest infection, constipation, UTI | Position changes, breathing exercises, fluids and fibre, mobility | | Common peroneal nerve palsy (foot drop) | Avoid pressure at the fibular head; padding; foot splint |

8. Nutrition and general care

  • Diet rich in protein, calcium, vitamin D, vitamin C and zinc; adequate fluids and fibre.
  • Hygiene, bladder and bowel care; diversional activities.

9. Psychological support and rehabilitation

  • Long recovery may cause anxiety about work and income; counselling, family involvement and physiotherapy referral.

10. Discharge teaching

  • Crutch walking correctly with prescribed weight bearing; safety at home (remove loose mats, good lighting).
  • Care of cast or pin sites; keep follow-up appointments for X-rays.
  • Stop smoking (delays bone healing).
  • Report increasing pain, swelling, numbness, coldness, fever, wound discharge or calf pain immediately.

Common nursing diagnoses

  • Acute pain related to fracture and soft-tissue injury.
  • Risk for peripheral neurovascular dysfunction related to swelling and immobilisation.
  • Impaired physical mobility and self-care deficit.
  • Risk for infection related to open wound, surgery and pins.

Nursing importance Many disabilities after tibial fractures – foot drop, contractures, non-union, infection and compartment syndrome – are preventable by careful nursing observation, early reporting and supervised mobilisation.

Conclusion Fracture of the tibia, often open and slow to heal, is managed by immobilisation or, more often, interlocking nailing or external fixation; skilled nursing care with neurovascular monitoring, wound and pin care, early exercises and rehabilitation prevents complications.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Musculoskeletal Disorders
question: (a) Define rheumatoid arthritis. (2 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features and diagnosis. (5 marks) (c) Describe the medical and nursing management of a patient with rheumatoid arthritis. (8 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks) Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic, systemic, autoimmune inflammatory disease that mainly affects the synovial joints in a symmetrical manner, causing synovitis, destruction of cartilage and bone, joint deformities and disability; it can also affect other organs. It is about three times more common in women, usually starting between 30 and 50 years.

Pathophysiology (brief) – an autoimmune reaction (in genetically susceptible people – HLA-DR4 – triggered by factors such as smoking and infections) causes inflammation of the synovial membrane; the thickened, inflamed synovium (pannus) erodes cartilage and bone, and ligaments and tendons are damaged, leading to deformities.

(b) Clinical features and diagnosis (5 marks) Joint features

  • Insidious onset with pain, swelling and stiffness of joints over weeks.
  • Symmetrical polyarthritis of small joints of hands and feet – MCP and PIP joints (DIP joints usually spared), wrists, MTP joints; later knees, ankles, elbows, shoulders and cervical spine (atlanto-axial instability – care during intubation and neck movements).
  • Morning stiffness lasting more than one hour, improving with activity.
  • Joints are warm, tender and boggy (soft) swollen; reduced grip strength and function.
  • Deformities – ulnar deviation of fingers, swan-neck and boutonnière deformities, Z-thumb, wrist subluxation; claw toes and painful forefoot.

Systemic and extra-articular features

  • Fatigue, low-grade fever, weight loss, anaemia of chronic disease.
  • Rheumatoid nodules over pressure areas (elbows).
  • Eyes and glands – dry eyes and mouth (Sjögren's syndrome), scleritis.
  • Lungs – pleural effusion, interstitial lung disease; heart – pericarditis, increased risk of coronary disease.
  • Vasculitis, carpal tunnel syndrome, osteoporosis; Felty's syndrome (RA with splenomegaly and neutropenia).

Diagnosis

  • ACR/EULAR 2010 classification criteria – based on number and size of joints involved, serology (RF, anti-CCP), acute-phase reactants (ESR, CRP) and duration of symptoms (6 weeks or more); a score of 6 or more out of 10 indicates RA.
  • Blood tests – rheumatoid factor (positive in about 70–80%), anti-CCP antibodies (more specific), raised ESR and CRP, anaemia on CBC; LFT and RFT before drugs.
  • Imaging – X-ray of hands and feet (periarticular osteopenia, joint-space narrowing, erosions); ultrasound or MRI for early synovitis.
  • Synovial fluid analysis if needed.

(c) Medical and nursing management (8 marks) 1. Medical management

  • Early treatment with disease-modifying drugs within the first 3–6 months ("window of opportunity") prevents joint damage; the aim is remission or low disease activity ("treat to target").
  • Conventional DMARDs
    • Methotrexate – the anchor drug; given once a week with folic acid; monitor CBC and liver function; avoid alcohol; contraception needed.
    • Hydroxychloroquine (yearly eye check), sulfasalazine, leflunomide.
  • Biologic and targeted DMARDs – anti-TNF agents (etanercept, adalimumab, infliximab), tocilizumab, rituximab, abatacept; JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib); screen for tuberculosis and hepatitis B before starting.
  • NSAIDs and low-dose corticosteroids for short periods to control pain and inflammation while DMARDs start working (with gastric protection).
  • Physiotherapy and occupational therapy, splints and orthoses.
  • Surgery – synovectomy, tendon repair, arthrodesis, joint replacement (knee, hip, small joints of the hand).

2. Nursing management (i) Chronic pain and stiffness

  • Give analgesics and NSAIDs with food; time them so that they act before morning activities.
  • Warm shower or bath in the morning, warm compresses or paraffin wax baths for hands to relieve stiffness; cold packs for acutely inflamed, hot joints.

  • Rest the inflamed joints during flares with splints in the functional position; avoid pillows under the knees (contractures). (ii) Impaired physical mobility

  • Range-of-motion exercises (active or assisted) daily, within pain limits; isometric exercises to maintain muscle strength; avoid vigorous exercise of acutely inflamed joints.

  • Physiotherapy referral; walking aids if needed; correct footwear. (iii) Self-care deficit – joint protection and assistive devices

  • Joint protection principles – use larger, stronger joints (carry bags on the forearm, not the fingers), avoid tight gripping and twisting (opening jars), use both hands, avoid staying in one position for long, alternate activity and rest.

  • Assistive devices – long-handled reachers, built-up handles for spoons and toothbrushes, raised toilet seats, chairs with arms, Velcro fastenings, slip-on shoes. (iv) Fatigue – 8–10 hours of sleep and rest periods during the day; energy conservation – plan and pace activities, sit while working. (v) Nutrition – balanced diet with adequate protein, calcium and vitamin D; maintain a healthy weight (reduces load on joints); omega-3-rich foods; iron and folate for anaemia. (vi) Safe drug therapy and monitoring

  • Teach that methotrexate is taken once a week only, with folic acid on another day; report mouth ulcers, fever, cough, bleeding or jaundice.

  • On biologics – watch for infections, avoid live vaccines, ensure TB screening; vaccines (influenza, pneumococcal) as advised.

  • Monitor blood counts, liver and kidney function, BP and blood sugar (steroids). (vii) Disturbed body image and anxiety/depression

  • Encourage expression of feelings; counselling; involve the family; support groups; discuss sexuality and work adjustments. (viii) Health education

  • RA is chronic but controllable; continue DMARDs even when feeling better; regular follow-up.

  • Stop smoking; dental hygiene; foot care.
  • Plan pregnancy with the rheumatologist (methotrexate and leflunomide must be stopped beforehand).
  • Recognise flares and seek early review; avoid unproven remedies and quacks.

Common nursing diagnoses

  • Chronic pain related to joint inflammation.
  • Impaired physical mobility related to stiffness and deformity.
  • Fatigue related to disease activity and anaemia.
  • Disturbed body image related to deformities.

3. Care during an acute flare

  • Rest the inflamed joints with splints; reduce daily activities for a few days but continue gentle range-of-motion movements once or twice a day to prevent stiffness.
  • Cold packs on hot, swollen joints; analgesics and NSAIDs as ordered; short "bridging" steroid course or intra-articular injection as prescribed.
  • Watch for a single joint that is much hotter and more painful than the others, with fever – it may be septic arthritis (especially on immunosuppressive drugs) and must be reported at once.
  • Review adherence to DMARDs and look for triggers such as infection or stopping medicines.

4. Special situations

  • Pregnancy – RA often improves during pregnancy and may flare after delivery; methotrexate and leflunomide must be stopped before conception (leflunomide needs a wash-out), while hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine and low-dose prednisolone are generally used if needed.
  • Elderly – greater risk of falls, osteoporosis and drug side effects; simplify medicines and make the home safe.
  • Surgery and anaesthesia – inform the anaesthetist about cervical spine involvement (neck X-ray before intubation) and long-term steroid use (steroid cover may be needed).

5. Rehabilitation and community support

  • Occupational therapy for work adjustments; home modifications (handrails, raised seats, lever taps).
  • Inform eligible patients about disability certification and benefits under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016.
  • Encourage regular, gentle physical activity such as walking, swimming and yoga, and participation in patient support groups.

Nursing importance Early diagnosis, adherence to DMARDs and daily joint-protection practices taught by nurses prevent deformity and keep patients working and independent.

Conclusion Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic autoimmune symmetrical polyarthritis that can destroy joints; early DMARD therapy, physiotherapy, joint protection and comprehensive nursing care preserve function and quality of life.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Musculoskeletal Disorders
question: Define rheumatoid arthritis. List its clinical features.
answer_html:
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic, systemic autoimmune disease causing symmetrical inflammation of synovial joints, leading to joint destruction and deformity; commoner in women aged 30–50 years.

Clinical features

  1. Symmetrical pain and swelling of small joints of hands (MCP, PIP), wrists and feet.
  2. Morning stiffness lasting more than one hour.
  3. Fatigue, low-grade fever, weight loss, anaemia.
  4. Deformities – ulnar deviation, swan-neck and boutonnière deformities.
  5. Rheumatoid nodules, dry eyes and mouth, lung and heart involvement. Tests – RF, anti-CCP, raised ESR and CRP; X-ray erosions.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Musculoskeletal Disorders
question: Define amputation and list its indications.
answer_html:
Amputation is the surgical removal of a limb or part of a limb (it may also occur traumatically). The level is chosen to remove all diseased tissue while keeping the longest useful stump (below-knee is preferred to above-knee to preserve the knee).

Indications – "the 3 Ds"

  1. Dead limb – gangrene due to diabetes, peripheral arterial disease, Buerger's disease, frostbite, severe burns, electrical injury.
  2. Dangerous limb – malignant bone or soft-tissue tumours, gas gangrene or spreading infection, crush injury with sepsis.
  3. "Damn nuisance" – useless, deformed or painful limb, non-healing ulcers, failed reconstruction.

Nursing points – stump bandaging (figure-of-eight), prevent contractures (prone lying), phantom pain care, early prosthesis (e.g., Jaipur Foot) and rehabilitation.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Musculoskeletal Disorders
question: What is phantom limb pain? How is it managed?
answer_html:
Phantom limb pain is pain felt in the part of the limb that has been amputated – burning, cramping, shooting or crushing pain – experienced by a majority of amputees, usually starting within days to weeks. It is real pain due to changes in the nerves, spinal cord and brain, and must be distinguished from phantom sensation (non-painful feeling that the limb is present) and stump pain.

Management

  1. Reassure the patient that the pain is real and common.
  2. Analgesics; gabapentin/pregabalin, amitriptyline.
  3. Mirror therapy, TENS, stump massage and desensitisation, early use of a prosthesis.
  4. Relaxation, distraction and psychological support.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Musculoskeletal Disorders
question: What is Volkmann's ischaemic contracture? How can it be prevented?
answer_html:
Volkmann's ischaemic contracture is a permanent flexion deformity of the wrist and fingers caused by ischaemic necrosis and fibrosis of the forearm flexor muscles, following untreated compartment syndrome of the forearm – classically after a supracondylar fracture of the humerus in children (brachial artery injury or kinking) or a tight plaster cast.

Features – claw-like hand; fingers can be straightened only when the wrist is flexed; weakness and numbness.

Prevention

  1. Monitor the radial pulse, capillary refill, colour and sensation after elbow injuries and plaster application.
  2. Pain on passive extension of fingers is an early warning – report immediately.
  3. Avoid tight casts and excessive elbow flexion when swollen; split the cast; urgent fasciotomy for compartment syndrome.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Musculoskeletal Disorders
question: Differentiate between scoliosis, kyphosis and lordosis.
answer_html:
1. Scoliosis – lateral (sideways) curvature of the spine with rotation of vertebrae; commonest is idiopathic adolescent scoliosis in girls; also congenital and neuromuscular (polio, cerebral palsy). Signs – uneven shoulders and hips, rib hump on forward bending (Adams test). Treatment – observation, bracing, spinal fusion for severe curves.
  2. Kyphosis – exaggerated forward (posterior convex) curvature of the thoracic spine ("hunchback"); causes – poor posture, osteoporotic vertebral fractures in elderly women, Scheuermann's disease, tuberculosis of the spine (gibbus).
  3. Lordosis – exaggerated inward (anterior convex) curvature of the lumbar spine ("swayback"); seen in pregnancy, obesity, spondylolisthesis and hip flexion contractures.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Musculoskeletal Disorders
question: What is osteomalacia?
answer_html:
Osteomalacia is softening of bones in adults due to defective mineralisation of bone matrix, most often from vitamin D deficiency (the same disease in children is rickets).

Causes – lack of sunlight exposure (indoor life, covered clothing, pollution, dark skin), poor diet, malabsorption, chronic kidney or liver disease, long-term anticonvulsants. Features – diffuse bone pain and tenderness (pelvis, spine, ribs), proximal muscle weakness with waddling gait, difficulty climbing stairs, fractures (pseudofractures); low calcium and phosphate, high ALP, low vitamin D. Treatment – vitamin D₃ (cholecalciferol) in therapeutic doses, calcium supplements, sunlight exposure (15–30 minutes on face and arms) and calcium-rich diet.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Musculoskeletal Disorders
question: What is Paget's disease of bone?
answer_html:
Paget's disease of bone (osteitis deformans) is a chronic disorder of bone remodelling in which excessive bone resorption by osteoclasts is followed by disorganised new bone formation, producing enlarged, deformed, weak and highly vascular bones. It usually affects people above 55 years and is rare in India.

Sites and features – pelvis, skull, spine, femur and tibia (bowing); often painless and found by a raised alkaline phosphatase; bone pain, deformity, enlarging skull, deafness, fractures, warmth over affected bone, rarely heart failure or osteosarcoma. Treatment – bisphosphonates (single IV zoledronic acid), analgesics, calcium and vitamin D; surgery for fractures and deformities; fall prevention.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Musculoskeletal Disorders
question: Explain the risk factors, clinical features, management and nursing care of osteoporosis.
answer_html:
Definition Osteoporosis is a metabolic bone disease characterised by low bone mass and deterioration of bone micro-architecture, leading to fragile bones and an increased risk of fractures with minimal trauma. It is called a "silent disease" because there are no symptoms until a fracture occurs.

1. Risk factors

  • Non-modifiable – female sex, especially after menopause (loss of oestrogen), increasing age, family history, small body frame, Asian ethnicity.
  • Modifiable
    • Low calcium intake and vitamin D deficiency (very common in India because of indoor life, covered clothing and pollution).
    • Physical inactivity, prolonged immobilisation.
    • Smoking, excess alcohol, excess tea, coffee and colas, low body weight.
  • Diseases and drugs – long-term corticosteroids, thyroid hormone excess, anticonvulsants, heparin; rheumatoid arthritis, hyperparathyroidism, chronic kidney and liver disease, early menopause, malabsorption.

2. Clinical features

  • Fragility fractures – vertebral compression fractures (back pain, loss of height, kyphosis – "dowager's hump"), fracture of the neck of femur (hip) and distal radius (Colles' fracture) after minor falls.
  • Chronic back pain, stooped posture, breathlessness or abdominal discomfort due to kyphosis.

3. Diagnosis

  • DEXA scan (bone mineral density) – T-score of −2.5 or lower = osteoporosis; between −1.0 and −2.5 = osteopenia.
  • X-rays (vertebral fractures); serum calcium, phosphate, vitamin D, ALP, thyroid and kidney function; FRAX tool for 10-year fracture risk.

4. Management

  • Calcium (about 1000–1200 mg/day from diet and supplements) and vitamin D₃ (to maintain normal levels).
  • Bisphosphonates – alendronate (weekly tablet), risedronate, zoledronic acid (yearly IV infusion).
  • Others – denosumab (6-monthly injection), teriparatide (bone-forming daily injection for severe disease), raloxifene, hormone therapy in selected women.
  • Treatment of fractures – fixation or joint replacement for hip fractures, vertebroplasty for painful vertebral fractures.

5. Nursing care and education

  • Diet – calcium-rich foods: milk, curd, paneer, ragi, sesame (til), green leafy vegetables, soybean, small fish with bones; adequate protein.
  • Sunlight – 15–30 minutes of sunlight on face and arms on most days.
  • Weight-bearing and muscle-strengthening exercises – brisk walking, stair climbing, yoga; balance exercises.
  • Alendronate teaching – take on an empty stomach in the morning with a full glass of plain water, remain upright for at least 30 minutes, and take no food or other medicines for 30 minutes (prevents oesophageal irritation and ensures absorption).
  • Fall prevention – remove loose rugs, provide good lighting and night lights, grab bars in the toilet, non-slip mats, well-fitting footwear, eye check-up, avoid sedatives; hip protectors for high-risk elderly.
  • Safe body mechanics – avoid lifting heavy objects and bending forward with the back.
  • Stop smoking, limit alcohol and caffeine.
  • Pain relief and support for patients with vertebral fractures; encourage early mobilisation.

Nursing importance Osteoporotic hip fractures in the elderly cause disability and death; nurses prevent them by teaching calcium, vitamin D, exercise and fall prevention, and by ensuring correct use of medicines.

Conclusion Osteoporosis is a silent loss of bone strength that leads to fragility fractures; diagnosis by DEXA, calcium, vitamin D, bone-protective drugs, exercise and fall prevention are the mainstays of care.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Musculoskeletal Disorders
question: Differentiate between rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis. Explain the management of osteoarthritis of the knee.
answer_html:
Introduction Arthritis means inflammation of a joint. The two commonest chronic types are rheumatoid arthritis (RA), an autoimmune inflammatory disease, and osteoarthritis (OA), a degenerative joint disease caused by wear and breakdown of articular cartilage. Knee OA is very common in India, especially in women and people who squat and sit cross-legged for long periods.

1. Differences between RA and OA | Feature | Rheumatoid arthritis | Osteoarthritis | |---|---|---| | Nature | Autoimmune, inflammatory, systemic | Degenerative ("wear and tear"), mainly local | | Age and sex | 30–50 years; women 3:1 | Above 50 years; women more for knees | | Joints | Small joints of hands and feet (MCP, PIP, wrists), symmetrical | Weight-bearing joints – knees, hips, spine; DIP and PIP of hands | | Morning stiffness | More than 1 hour | Less than 30 minutes | | Pain | At rest and with activity; improves with activity | Worse with activity, relieved by rest | | Swelling | Soft, boggy (synovitis), warm | Bony hard enlargement (Heberden's, Bouchard's nodes) | | Systemic features | Fatigue, fever, anaemia, nodules | Absent | | Laboratory | RF/anti-CCP positive, raised ESR/CRP | Normal | | X-ray | Periarticular osteopenia, erosions | Joint-space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis |

2. Clinical features of knee OA Knee pain on walking, climbing stairs and squatting, short morning stiffness, crepitus, swelling, reduced movement, bow-leg deformity (genu varum), limping and difficulty in sitting on the floor or using an Indian-style toilet.

3. Management of knee osteoarthritis (a) Non-pharmacological (the foundation)

  • Weight reduction – each kilogram lost reduces load on the knee several-fold.
  • Exercises – quadriceps strengthening (static quadriceps, straight-leg raising), hamstring stretching, low-impact aerobic exercise (walking on level ground, cycling, swimming); yoga.
  • Activity modification – avoid prolonged squatting, sitting cross-legged and climbing many stairs; use a Western toilet and chairs of suitable height.
  • Walking stick in the hand opposite the affected knee; knee brace; cushioned footwear, lateral-wedge insoles.

  • Hot fomentation or ice packs for pain; physiotherapy (ultrasound, TENS). (b) Drugs

  • Paracetamol, topical NSAIDs (diclofenac gel); oral NSAIDs for short periods with gastric protection; duloxetine for chronic pain.

  • Intra-articular corticosteroid injections for flares; hyaluronic acid injections in some patients. (c) Surgery

  • Arthroscopic procedures in selected cases, high tibial osteotomy (younger patients with varus deformity), and total knee replacement (TKR) for severe pain and disability.

4. Nursing responsibilities

  • Assess pain, function and gait; teach and supervise exercises.
  • Diet counselling for weight loss; calcium and vitamin D.
  • Teach joint protection and correct use of walking aids; home safety to prevent falls.
  • Explain the safe use of analgesics (avoid long-term NSAID self-medication).
  • Pre- and post-operative care and rehabilitation after knee replacement.

Nursing importance Most patients with knee OA improve with weight loss, exercise and activity modification taught by nurses, delaying or avoiding surgery.

Conclusion RA is a symmetrical inflammatory autoimmune arthritis of small joints, whereas OA is degenerative arthritis of weight-bearing joints; knee OA is managed mainly by weight loss, exercise, aids and analgesics, with joint replacement for severe disease.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Musculoskeletal Disorders
question: Explain the use of walking aids – cane, walker and crutches – with special reference to the four-point gait.
answer_html:
Introduction Walking (ambulatory) aids support patients with weakness, pain, injury or poor balance, allowing safe mobility and partial or no weight bearing on an affected limb. The common aids are canes (walking sticks), walkers and crutches. The four-point gait is the most stable crutch gait.

1. Cane (walking stick)

  • Uses – mild weakness or pain of one leg (hip or knee OA, after stroke), balance support.
  • Height – the handle at the level of the greater trochanter or wrist crease, with the elbow flexed about 15–30°.
  • Use – hold the cane in the hand opposite the affected leg; move the cane and the affected leg together, then the good leg.

2. Walker

  • Uses – elderly, generalised weakness, poor balance, after hip and knee surgery.
  • Types – standard (pick-up) walker, two-wheeled walker, rollator (four wheels with brakes and seat).
  • Height – handgrips at the wrist crease, elbows slightly flexed.
  • Use – stand inside the frame; lift and move the walker forward about 15–20 cm, step forward with the affected leg, then the good leg; do not step too close to the front bar; never use the walker to pull up from sitting – push up from the chair arms.

3. Crutches

  • Types – axillary crutches and forearm (elbow) crutches.
  • Measurement of axillary crutches
    • Patient standing with shoes on: crutch tip about 15 cm in front and 15 cm to the side of the foot.
    • Top of the crutch 2–3 finger-breadths (about 5 cm) below the axilla.
    • Handgrip at the wrist crease, with the elbow flexed 20–30°.
  • Weight is borne on the hands, not on the axillae – pressure on the axilla can injure the radial nerve (crutch palsy).

4. Four-point gait

  • Indication – patients who can bear partial weight on both legs but have weakness or poor coordination of both legs (for example, bilateral arthritis, cerebral palsy, muscle weakness).
  • Features – the most stable and safest gait because three points are always on the ground; but it is slow.
  • Sequence
    1. Right crutch forward.
    2. Left foot forward.
    3. Left crutch forward.
    4. Right foot forward. - Repeat; the patient may count aloud "1-2-3-4" to keep rhythm.
  • Two-point gait is a faster version: right crutch with left foot, then left crutch with right foot. Three-point gait is used when one leg cannot bear weight.

5. Stairs with crutches

  • Going up – "up with the good": step up with the good leg first, then bring up the crutches and the affected leg.
  • Going down – "down with the bad": crutches and affected leg go down first, then the good leg.
  • Use a handrail when available.

6. Nurse's responsibilities

  • Assess strength (especially arms and shoulders), balance, endurance and understanding before teaching.
  • Check the aid – correct height, rubber tips intact and non-slip, padding, brakes on rollators.
  • Teach and supervise with return demonstration; walk beside the patient on the weaker side; use a gait belt.
  • Environment – clear pathways, dry floors, good lighting, remove loose rugs; well-fitting, non-slip footwear.
  • Teach safe sitting and standing and how to rest; watch for fatigue, dizziness and axillary pressure.

Nursing importance Correctly measured aids and proper gait training prevent falls, nerve injuries and further damage to injured limbs.

Conclusion Canes, walkers and crutches promote safe mobility; the four-point gait gives maximum stability when both legs can bear some weight, and the nurse ensures correct measurement, technique and safety.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Musculoskeletal Disorders
question: Define traction. Explain its types and the nursing care of a patient in traction.
answer_html:
Definition Traction is the application of a pulling force to a part of the body, with an equal counter-traction in the opposite direction, to reduce and immobilise fractures, maintain alignment, relieve muscle spasm and pain, and prevent or correct deformities.

1. Purposes

  • Reduce and maintain alignment of fractures (femur, cervical spine) before or instead of surgery.
  • Relieve muscle spasm and pain (back pain, hip conditions).
  • Rest inflamed joints; prevent and correct contractures and deformities.

2. Types (a) Manual traction – applied by hand during reduction or plaster application. (b) Skin traction – force applied through the skin with adhesive or non-adhesive strips and bandages.

  • Buck's extension traction – lower limb (hip and knee conditions, temporary for fracture neck of femur); weight usually limited to about 3–5 kg (skin cannot tolerate more).
  • Russell's traction, pelvic belt traction (low back pain), cervical halter traction.
  • Bryant's (gallows) traction – both legs vertically suspended in children below 2 years for fracture of the femur. (c) Skeletal traction – force applied directly to the bone through a Steinmann pin or Kirschner wire (through the tibial tuberosity, calcaneum or lower femur) or skull tongs (Gardner–Wells, Crutchfield) for cervical spine injuries; heavier weights for longer periods; often used with a Thomas splint (balanced suspension).

3. Principles of effective traction

  • Counter-traction must be present (patient's body weight; foot end of bed raised).
  • Continuous traction – weights are not removed unless ordered.
  • Weights hang freely – not resting on the bed or floor; ropes run freely in pulleys, knots secure and away from pulleys.
  • The line of pull is maintained; the patient is centred in the bed and does not slide down.
  • No pressure on the line of traction (bed clothes, footboard).

4. Nursing care of a patient in traction

  • Neurovascular checks of the limb – colour, warmth, capillary refill, pulses, sensation and movement – frequently.
  • Skin traction – inspect the skin under and around bandages daily for blisters, allergy and pressure areas; protect the fibular head (common peroneal nerve – foot drop) and the heel; re-apply bandages as ordered.
  • Skeletal traction – pin-site care – clean pin sites daily or as per protocol with saline or chlorhexidine; watch for redness, discharge, pain and loosening (pin-tract infection, osteomyelitis); cover pin ends to prevent injury.
  • Pressure area care – sacrum, heels, elbows, back of the head; pressure-relieving mattress; trapeze bar over the bed to help the patient move.
  • Prevent complications of immobility – deep breathing and coughing, exercises of all free joints, ankle pumps of the unaffected leg, DVT prophylaxis, plenty of fluids and fibre (constipation, kidney stones), bladder care.
  • Positioning and alignment – check daily; keep the foot in a neutral position (prevent foot drop).
  • Elimination – fracture bedpan; maintain privacy.
  • Nutrition – high-protein, calcium-rich diet; adequate fluids.
  • Psychological care – long immobilisation causes boredom and depression; diversional activities, visits, explanations.
  • Documentation of weights, alignment and checks.

Nursing importance Effective, safe traction depends almost entirely on the nurse's daily checks of the apparatus, the limb and the skin, and on prevention of immobility complications.

Conclusion Traction may be manual, skin or skeletal; correct principles (counter-traction, free weights, line of pull) and meticulous nursing care of the skin, pins and immobilised patient ensure good results.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Musculoskeletal Disorders
question: Explain compartment syndrome and its emergency management.
answer_html:
Definition Compartment syndrome is a condition in which increased pressure within a closed osteofascial compartment (muscles enclosed by fascia) reduces blood flow to the muscles and nerves within it, causing ischaemia and, if untreated, permanent muscle and nerve death. Acute compartment syndrome is a surgical emergency.

1. Causes

  • Internal – fractures (especially tibia – anterior compartment of the leg – and forearm, including supracondylar fracture of the humerus in children), crush injuries, bleeding into muscles (haemophilia, anticoagulants), reperfusion after vascular repair, burns, snake bite with severe swelling, prolonged lying on a limb (drug overdose, unconsciousness).
  • External – tight plaster casts, bandages or splints.

2. Clinical features – the "6 Ps"

  1. Pain – the earliest and most important sign: severe, out of proportion to the injury, not relieved by analgesics, and increased by passive stretching of the muscles in the compartment (e.g., moving the toes or fingers).
  2. Paraesthesia – tingling, numbness.
  3. Pallor.
  4. Paralysis – weakness of the muscles (late).
  5. Pulselessness – late sign; pulses are often present even in established compartment syndrome.
  6. Poikilothermia – cold limb. - The compartment is tense, swollen and shiny. - Diagnosis – mainly clinical; compartment pressure measurement (pressure above about 30 mmHg, or diastolic BP minus compartment pressure less than 30 mmHg).

3. Emergency management

  1. Inform the surgeon immediately.
  2. Release external pressure – loosen bandages; split (bivalve) the plaster cast down to the skin, including the padding.
  3. Position the limb at heart level – do not elevate (elevation reduces arterial inflow) and do not apply ice.
  4. Give oxygen, maintain BP with IV fluids (low BP worsens ischaemia); analgesics.
  5. Urgent fasciotomy – surgical opening of the fascia of all involved compartments, ideally within about 6 hours; wounds are left open and closed later or skin-grafted.

4. Complications

  • Muscle necrosis and Volkmann's ischaemic contracture.
  • Rhabdomyolysis – myoglobin released from dead muscle causes dark (cola-coloured) urine and acute kidney injury, hyperkalaemia.
  • Nerve damage, infection, limb loss.

5. Nursing responsibilities

  • Prevention – avoid tight casts and bandages, elevate injured limbs in the early period (before signs develop), and teach patients to report increasing pain, numbness or tightness.
  • Neurovascular observation every hour for 24–48 hours after injury or surgery; record and report early warning signs (pain on passive stretch).
  • After fasciotomy – sterile dressing of open wounds, monitor urine output and colour, CK and potassium; IV fluids; pain relief; physiotherapy.

Nursing importance Because the window for saving muscle is only a few hours, the nurse's early recognition of pain on passive stretch and prompt action can save the limb.

Conclusion Compartment syndrome is raised pressure in a closed compartment causing ischaemia; early recognition, release of external pressure and urgent fasciotomy prevent permanent damage.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Musculoskeletal Disorders
question: Explain sprain, strain and dislocation with their management.
answer_html:
Introduction Injuries of soft tissues and joints are very common in sports, falls and road accidents. They include contusions, sprains, strains, dislocations and subluxations.

1. Definitions

  • Contusion – a bruise; injury to soft tissue with bleeding under intact skin.
  • Sprain – stretching or tearing of a ligament around a joint (commonest at the ankle, also knee and wrist); graded I (stretch), II (partial tear) and III (complete tear).
  • Strain – stretching or tearing of a muscle or tendon ("pulled muscle") – hamstrings, calf, back.
  • Dislocation – complete displacement of the bone ends forming a joint, with loss of contact between articular surfaces; subluxation is partial displacement.

2. Clinical features

  • Sprain/strain – pain, swelling, bruising, tenderness, difficulty using the limb; joint instability in severe sprains.
  • Dislocation – severe pain, visible deformity (abnormal contour), loss of movement, shortening or rotation of the limb; e.g., anterior shoulder dislocation (commonest – flattened shoulder, arm held away from the body), posterior hip dislocation after "dashboard" injuries (leg shortened, flexed, adducted and internally rotated).
  • Complications of dislocation – nerve injury (axillary nerve in shoulder, sciatic nerve in hip), vascular injury, associated fractures, avascular necrosis of the femoral head (if hip reduction is delayed), recurrent dislocation, stiffness.

3. Management (a) Sprains and strains – "PRICE"

  • Protection – avoid further injury (splint, brace).
  • Rest the part for 24–72 hours.
  • Ice – wrapped ice pack for 15–20 minutes every 2–3 hours for the first 48–72 hours (no heat in this period).
  • Compression – elastic (crepe) bandage, not too tight.
  • Elevation of the limb above heart level.
  • Analgesics; gradual exercises and physiotherapy; surgical repair for complete (grade III) ligament tears.

(b) Dislocations

  • Emergency – immobilise in the position found, check and record neurovascular status, analgesia; X-ray to confirm and exclude fracture.
  • Closed reduction as early as possible under sedation or anaesthesia (hip dislocation is reduced within about 6 hours to reduce the risk of avascular necrosis); check neurovascular status and X-ray again after reduction.
  • Immobilisation – sling for 2–3 weeks after shoulder dislocation; traction or bracing for hip as advised.
  • Open reduction if closed reduction fails; surgery for recurrent dislocations.
  • Rehabilitation – graduated exercises to restore movement and strength.

4. Nursing responsibilities

  • Apply PRICE correctly; monitor circulation distal to bandages.
  • Neurovascular checks before and after reduction; sling and splint care.
  • Pain relief; teach exercises and gradual return to activity.
  • Prevention – warm-up before sports, proper footwear, safe floors, helmets and seat belts.

Nursing importance Correct first-hour care (PRICE, immobilisation and early reduction) reduces swelling, pain and long-term complications such as instability and avascular necrosis.

Conclusion Sprains and strains are ligament and muscle injuries treated by PRICE and rehabilitation, while dislocations need early reduction, immobilisation and neurovascular monitoring.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Musculoskeletal Disorders
question: Explain the post-operative nursing care of a patient after total hip replacement.
answer_html:
Introduction Total hip replacement (THR, total hip arthroplasty) is the surgical replacement of the damaged femoral head and acetabulum with prosthetic components. It relieves pain and restores mobility.

1. Indications Osteoarthritis of the hip, rheumatoid arthritis, avascular necrosis of the femoral head, displaced fracture of the neck of femur in the elderly, ankylosing spondylitis, failed earlier surgery.

2. Post-operative nursing care (a) Positioning and prevention of dislocation (posterior approach – as advised by the surgeon)

  • Keep the operated leg in slight abduction with an abduction pillow or wedge between the legs.
  • Hip precautions for about 6–12 weeks:
    • Do not bend the hip more than 90° (no low chairs, low toilets or bending to pick things up).
    • Do not cross the legs or bring the operated leg past the midline.
    • Do not turn the operated leg inwards (internal rotation).
  • Turn the patient with a pillow between the legs, as ordered.
  • Signs of dislocation – sudden severe pain, shortening and rotation of the leg, inability to move – report immediately.

(b) Monitoring

  • Vital signs, neurovascular checks of the operated limb (pulses, colour, sensation, movement – sciatic nerve injury causes foot drop).
  • Wound and drain – amount and colour; dressing soakage; haemoglobin.
  • Urine output; urinary retention is common.

(c) Prevention of DVT and pulmonary embolism

  • Ankle pumps and quadriceps exercises hourly while awake; compression stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression; anticoagulants (LMWH, rivaroxaban) as ordered; early mobilisation.

(d) Pain management – multimodal analgesia; nerve blocks; pain relief before physiotherapy.

(e) Early mobilisation and exercises

  • Walking with a walker usually from the day of surgery or the next day, with weight bearing as allowed.
  • Exercises – quadriceps and gluteal setting, ankle pumps, hip abduction (as taught by the physiotherapist).
  • Use of a raised toilet seat, high firm chair with arms.

(f) Infection prevention – prophylactic antibiotics, aseptic wound care, glucose control in diabetics; report fever or wound discharge (prosthetic infection is serious).

(g) Other care – deep breathing, fluids and fibre, pressure area care, nutrition.

3. Discharge teaching

  • Continue hip precautions; use a long-handled reacher, sock aid and shoe horn; sit on high chairs; use a Western toilet.
  • Sleep on the back with a pillow between the legs; get in and out of bed on the side advised.
  • Continue anticoagulants and exercises; walk regularly; avoid heavy lifting, twisting and jumping.
  • Home safety – remove loose mats, install grab bars, good lighting.
  • Driving and return to work as advised (often after about 6 weeks).
  • Inform doctors and dentists about the prosthesis; report pain, swelling, fever, wound discharge, calf pain or leg shortening.

Nursing importance Most early complications after THR – dislocation, DVT and infection – are preventable by correct positioning, hip precautions, anticoagulation and asepsis supervised by the nurse.

Conclusion After total hip replacement, nursing care focuses on preventing dislocation, DVT and infection, controlling pain and promoting early, safe mobilisation and independence.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Musculoskeletal Disorders
question: Explain the clinical features and nursing management of a patient with prolapsed intervertebral disc.
answer_html:
Definition Prolapsed intervertebral disc (PIVD), or herniated disc, is the protrusion of the nucleus pulposus through a tear in the annulus fibrosus, which may compress spinal nerve roots or, rarely, the cauda equina or spinal cord. The commonest levels are L4–L5 and L5–S1 in the lumbar spine and C5–C6 and C6–C7 in the neck.

1. Causes and risk factors Disc degeneration with age (30–50 years), lifting heavy weights with a bent and twisted back, heavy manual work, prolonged sitting or driving, obesity, smoking, trauma.

2. Clinical features Lumbar disc

  • Low back pain radiating down the buttock and leg below the knee (sciatica), worse on coughing, sneezing, straining and sitting.
  • Numbness and tingling along the nerve distribution; weakness (e.g., foot drop with L5 root), reduced ankle reflex (S1).
  • Muscle spasm, restricted movement, list of the spine.
  • Positive straight-leg-raising (SLR) test – pain down the leg when the straight leg is raised between 30° and 70°. Cervical disc – neck pain radiating to the shoulder and arm, numbness of fingers, weakness of hand muscles. Cauda equina syndrome (emergency) – saddle anaesthesia, retention or incontinence of urine and stool, bilateral leg weakness – needs urgent MRI and decompression.

3. Diagnosis MRI of the spine (investigation of choice); X-rays; nerve conduction studies in selected cases.

4. Management

  • Conservative (most patients improve in 6–12 weeks) – short rest (1–2 days only) and early return to normal activities, analgesics, NSAIDs, muscle relaxants, neuropathic pain drugs (pregabalin), hot or cold packs, physiotherapy (back extension and core-strengthening exercises), short-term lumbar support, epidural steroid injection.
  • Surgery – microdiscectomy, endoscopic discectomy, laminectomy, spinal fusion; indicated for cauda equina syndrome, progressive weakness or intractable pain not relieved by conservative care.

5. Nursing management

  • Pain relief – medicines on time; heat or cold application; relaxation.
  • Positioning – firm mattress; lying on the back with a pillow under the knees, or on the side with knees bent and a pillow between the knees.
  • Neurological checks – leg sensation, power and bladder and bowel function; report cauda equina signs immediately.
  • After surgery – log-rolling (turning the body as one unit) for the first day or as advised; check the wound for bleeding or CSF leak (clear fluid); monitor voiding; early ambulation as ordered; avoid sitting for long periods initially.
  • Education – back care and body mechanics
    • Bend the knees, not the back, when lifting; keep the load close to the body; avoid twisting while lifting; do not lift heavy weights.
    • Maintain good posture; take breaks every 30–45 minutes from sitting; use a chair with back support.
    • Regular back and core-strengthening exercises, walking, weight reduction, stop smoking.
    • Avoid sudden jerks, bending forward to lift and sleeping on soft sagging mattresses.

Nursing importance Most patients recover without surgery when nurses ensure pain control, correct positioning and back-care education, and recognise emergencies such as cauda equina syndrome early.

Conclusion PIVD is herniation of disc material compressing nerve roots and causing sciatica; conservative care with physiotherapy and education suffices for most, while surgery is needed for neurological emergencies or persistent pain.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Musculoskeletal Disorders
question: Explain the causes, clinical features and management of gout.
answer_html:
Definition Gout is a metabolic disorder caused by hyperuricaemia (serum uric acid above about 6.8–7 mg/dl), in which monosodium urate crystals deposit in joints and tissues, causing recurrent attacks of acute inflammatory arthritis, tophi and kidney stones.

1. Causes and risk factors

  • Increased production or reduced excretion of uric acid.
  • Diet – purine-rich foods (red meat, organ meats such as liver and kidney, seafood), alcohol (especially beer), sugary drinks and fructose.
  • Obesity, hypertension, diabetes, metabolic syndrome, chronic kidney disease.
  • Drugs – thiazide and loop diuretics, low-dose aspirin, ciclosporin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol (anti-TB drugs).
  • Tumour lysis during cancer chemotherapy; men above 40 and post-menopausal women; family history.

2. Clinical features

  • Acute gouty arthritis – sudden, excruciating pain, swelling, redness and warmth of one joint, classically the first metatarsophalangeal joint (big toe – podagra), often at night after a heavy meal or alcohol; ankle, knee and wrist may be involved; low-grade fever. The attack settles in 1–2 weeks.
  • Recurrent attacks with symptom-free intervals.
  • Chronic tophaceous gout – tophi (chalky urate deposits) on the ear helix, elbows, fingers, Achilles tendon; joint damage and deformity.
  • Kidney – uric acid stones, urate nephropathy.

3. Diagnosis Joint aspiration – needle-shaped, negatively birefringent urate crystals (gold standard); serum uric acid (may be normal during an attack); X-ray (punched-out erosions in chronic gout); kidney function.

4. Management (a) Acute attack

  • Rest and elevation of the joint; ice packs; a bed cradle to keep sheets off the painful joint.
  • NSAIDs (naproxen, indomethacin), low-dose colchicine, or corticosteroids (oral or intra-articular).

  • Do not start or stop urate-lowering drugs during an attack (continue if already taking). (b) Long-term

  • Urate-lowering therapy for recurrent attacks, tophi or stones – allopurinol (start low, increase gradually to keep uric acid below 6 mg/dl), febuxostat, probenecid; colchicine cover for the first few months.

  • Lifestyle – weight reduction, limit red meat, organ meat, seafood, alcohol and sugary drinks; 2–3 litres of water a day; low-fat dairy products are beneficial.
  • Review diuretics and other contributing drugs.

5. Nursing responsibilities

  • Pain relief and protection of the inflamed joint; record the joints affected.
  • Diet teaching and encouragement of fluids; weight control.
  • Teach regular use of allopurinol and report skin rash at once (allopurinol hypersensitivity can be severe).
  • Monitor uric acid and kidney function; watch for stones (strain urine if ordered).

Nursing importance Patient education on diet, fluids, weight and adherence to urate-lowering therapy prevents recurrent attacks, joint damage and kidney stones.

Conclusion Gout results from urate crystal deposition due to hyperuricaemia; acute attacks respond to NSAIDs, colchicine or steroids, while long-term control needs urate-lowering drugs and lifestyle changes.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Musculoskeletal Disorders
question: Write a note on bone tumours with special reference to osteosarcoma.
answer_html:
Introduction Bone tumours may be benign or malignant, and malignant tumours may be primary (arising in bone) or secondary (metastatic). Metastatic bone disease is the commonest malignant bone condition in adults, while osteosarcoma is the commonest primary malignant bone tumour of adolescents.

1. Classification

  • Benign – osteochondroma (commonest benign tumour, bony outgrowth near joints), osteoid osteoma (night pain relieved by aspirin/NSAIDs), enchondroma, giant cell tumour (ends of long bones in young adults; locally aggressive).
  • Primary malignant – osteosarcoma, Ewing's sarcoma (children 5–15 years; shaft of long bones; fever mimics osteomyelitis; "onion-peel" X-ray), chondrosarcoma (older adults), multiple myeloma (commonest primary bone malignancy in older adults).
  • Secondary (metastatic) – from cancers of the breast, prostate, lung, kidney and thyroid – spine, pelvis, ribs and long bones.

2. Osteosarcoma

  • Age – mainly 10–25 years (growth spurt); also in the elderly with Paget's disease or previous radiation.
  • Site – metaphysis of long bones, especially around the knee (lower femur, upper tibia) and upper humerus.
  • Features – persistent bone pain, worse at night, swelling or a mass, limp, warmth, restricted movement, pathological fracture; spreads early to the lungs.
  • Investigations – X-ray (destructive lesion with "sunburst" appearance and Codman's triangle), MRI of the limb, CT chest (lung metastases), bone scan or PET-CT, raised ALP and LDH, biopsy (planned by the treating surgeon so that the biopsy track can be removed later).

3. Management of osteosarcoma

  • Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (methotrexate, doxorubicin, cisplatin, ifosfamide) to shrink the tumour.
  • Surgery – limb-salvage surgery (wide excision with endoprosthesis or bone graft) in most patients; amputation when salvage is not possible.
  • Adjuvant chemotherapy after surgery; removal of lung metastases where possible.
  • Survival has improved to about 60–70% for non-metastatic disease.

4. Nursing management

  • Pain management – regular analgesics including opioids; positioning and support of the limb.
  • Prevent pathological fracture – handle the limb gently, support it during movement, avoid weight bearing as advised, use aids.
  • Chemotherapy care – hydration and leucovorin rescue with high-dose methotrexate; monitoring kidney function and hearing with cisplatin and heart function with doxorubicin; infection and bleeding precautions; antiemetics; mucositis care.
  • Post-operative care – neurovascular checks, wound and drain care, DVT prevention; after amputation – stump care, phantom pain management, prosthesis and rehabilitation.
  • Psychosocial care – adolescents fear loss of limb, hair and school life; counselling, education continuity, peer support, fertility counselling, family support and financial help.
  • Long-term follow-up for recurrence and late effects.

Nursing importance Persistent bone pain in a teenager must not be dismissed as "growing pains"; early referral and comprehensive nursing support during long treatment improve survival and quality of life.

Conclusion Bone tumours range from benign osteochondromas to aggressive osteosarcoma and metastases; osteosarcoma of adolescents is treated with chemotherapy and limb-salvage surgery, supported by skilled nursing care and rehabilitation.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Communicable Diseases
question: (a) Define COVID-19 and explain its mode of transmission. (3 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features, classification of severity and diagnosis. (4 marks) (c) Describe the management, nursing care and infection control measures for a patient with COVID-19. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Sequence of donning and doffing personal protective equipment

answer_html:
(a) Definition and mode of transmission (3 marks) COVID-19 (coronavirus disease 2019) is an acute infectious respiratory disease caused by the novel coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 (severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus-2), an RNA virus of the family Coronaviridae. First identified in Wuhan, China, in December 2019, it was declared a pandemic by the WHO in March 2020; the global emergency phase ended in May 2023, and COVID-19 is now an ongoing endemic disease with periodic waves caused by new variants (such as Omicron sub-lineages).

Mode of transmission

  1. Respiratory droplets and aerosols – released when an infected person coughs, sneezes, talks, sings or breathes; aerosols can remain in the air and spread further in crowded, poorly ventilated indoor spaces.
  2. Close contact – within about 1–2 metres of an infected person, especially for more than 15 minutes.
  3. Contaminated surfaces (fomites) – touching contaminated hands, surfaces or objects and then the eyes, nose or mouth (less important).
  4. Aerosol-generating procedures (AGPs) in hospitals – intubation, suctioning, nebulisation, non-invasive ventilation, bronchoscopy, CPR. - Incubation period – 2–14 days (usually about 3–5 days with recent variants); people can transmit the infection 1–2 days before symptoms and even without symptoms.

(b) Clinical features, severity and diagnosis (4 marks) Clinical features

  • Fever, dry cough, sore throat, runny or blocked nose, fatigue, body ache, headache.
  • Loss of smell or taste, nausea, diarrhoea, conjunctivitis, skin rashes.
  • Breathlessness, chest pain or pressure, low oxygen saturation (sometimes without breathlessness – "silent hypoxia"), confusion, bluish lips.
  • Complications – viral pneumonia, ARDS, thrombo-embolism (DVT, pulmonary embolism, stroke), myocarditis and arrhythmias, acute kidney injury, secondary bacterial and fungal infections – including mucormycosis ("black fungus"), seen in India in 2021 with uncontrolled diabetes and steroid misuse – multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C) and post-COVID ("long COVID") symptoms.
  • High-risk groups – age above 60, diabetes, hypertension, heart, lung and kidney disease, obesity, cancer, immunosuppression, pregnancy.

Classification of severity (Indian clinical guidance)

  • Mild – upper respiratory symptoms and/or fever without breathlessness or hypoxia.
  • Moderate – breathlessness with respiratory rate 24/min or more and/or SpO₂ 90–93% on room air.
  • Severe – respiratory rate above 30/min and/or SpO₂ below 90% on room air, or ARDS, shock, organ failure.

Diagnosis

  • RT-PCR of a nasopharyngeal/oropharyngeal swab – the gold standard; CBNAAT/TrueNat.
  • Rapid antigen test (RAT) – quick bedside test; a negative result in a symptomatic person may need confirmation by RT-PCR.
  • Chest X-ray / CT chest – bilateral ground-glass opacities.
  • Laboratory markers – CBC (lymphopenia), CRP, D-dimer, ferritin, LDH, IL-6, procalcitonin, blood sugar, kidney and liver function, ABG; continuous pulse oximetry.

(c) Management, nursing care and infection control (8 marks) 1. Medical management (according to severity)

  • Mild – home isolation with symptomatic care: rest, oral fluids, paracetamol for fever, steam inhalation or warm gargles; monitor temperature and SpO₂ at home; seek care if SpO₂ falls to 93% or below, breathlessness develops or fever persists beyond 5 days. Unnecessary antibiotics, ivermectin and hydroxychloroquine are not recommended, and steroids are not used in mild disease. High-risk patients may receive oral antivirals where available.
  • Moderate – admission; oxygen to keep SpO₂ at 92–96% (88–92% in COPD); awake prone positioning; corticosteroids (e.g., dexamethasone 6 mg daily for up to 10 days); prophylactic anticoagulation (low-molecular-weight heparin); remdesivir in selected patients early in the illness; careful monitoring.
  • Severe – ICU care; high-flow nasal oxygen, non-invasive ventilation, or mechanical ventilation with a lung-protective strategy and prone ventilation; steroids; IL-6 inhibitor (tocilizumab) in selected patients; management of shock, organ failure and secondary infections.

2. Nursing care (i) Impaired gas exchange
