  • Monitor SpO₂, respiratory rate, work of breathing, heart rate, BP, temperature and level of consciousness regularly; record trends and report early deterioration (rising respiratory rate, falling SpO₂).
  • Give oxygen with the correct device (nasal cannula, face mask, non-rebreather mask, HFNC); humidify; check flow and cylinder levels.
  • Awake prone positioning in conscious patients (if tolerated) – rotate positions: prone (lying on the abdomen) 30 minutes to 2 hours → right lateral → sitting up (30–60°) → left lateral → prone again; avoid within an hour after meals; watch SpO₂ during position changes.
  • Encourage deep breathing exercises and incentive spirometry (avoid in infectious aerosol settings without precautions). (ii) Hyperthermia and fluid balance – antipyretics, tepid sponging, adequate oral fluids; intake–output; avoid fluid overload. (iii) Nutrition – high-protein, high-calorie, easily digestible diet; small frequent meals; vitamin and zinc supplements as ordered. (iv) Risk for unstable blood glucose – steroids raise blood sugar; monitor glucose closely in all patients on steroids, especially diabetics, and give insulin as ordered (good control prevents mucormycosis). (v) Risk for thrombosis – leg exercises, early mobilisation, anticoagulants as ordered; watch for calf pain, sudden breathlessness and chest pain. (vi) Anxiety, fear and social isolation – explain care, provide information, allow video calls with family, counselling; address stigma; spiritual support. (vii) Care of the critically ill – ventilator and VAP bundle care, sedation, pressure-area care, eye and mouth care, prone-position care. (viii) Discharge and home care – teach self-monitoring, warning signs, gradual return to activity, management of post-COVID fatigue and breathlessness, vaccination and follow-up.

3. Infection prevention and control measures

  • Screening and triage at hospital entry; separate fever/respiratory clinics and patient flow.
  • Isolation – single rooms or cohort wards for confirmed patients with good ventilation; airborne infection isolation rooms (negative pressure) for aerosol-generating procedures where available; limit the number of staff and visitors.
  • Standard precautions + droplet and contact precautions, with airborne precautions (N95 respirators) for aerosol-generating procedures and in high-risk areas.
  • Personal protective equipment (PPE) chosen according to risk – N95 respirator, gown or coverall, gloves, goggles or face shield; correct donning sequence (hand hygiene → gown → respirator → goggles/face shield → gloves) and doffing sequence (gloves → hand hygiene → goggles/face shield → gown → hand hygiene → respirator removed outside the room → hand hygiene); fit-check the N95 every time.
  • Hand hygiene with alcohol-based hand rub or soap and water at all five moments.
  • Respiratory hygiene – surgical masks for patients, cough etiquette, tissues disposed of in covered bins.
  • Environmental cleaning – frequently touched surfaces cleaned and disinfected with 1% sodium hypochlorite or 70% alcohol (for small surfaces) as per protocol; terminal cleaning after discharge.
  • Biomedical waste management – COVID-19 waste collected in double-layered, labelled bags in the appropriate colour-coded bins as per CPCB guidelines.
  • Linen and equipment – dedicated equipment (BP apparatus, stethoscope, thermometer) for each patient; soiled linen handled as infectious.
  • Staff safety – training, vaccination, symptom monitoring, adequate rest; reporting of exposures.
  • Contact tracing, testing and home isolation advice for contacts as per current guidelines; safe and dignified management of dead bodies as per guidelines.

4. Prevention in the community Vaccination (India's COVID-19 vaccination programme began in January 2021, with precaution doses for high-risk groups), staying home when unwell, masks in crowded indoor places during waves, hand hygiene, good ventilation and early testing of high-risk persons.

Common nursing diagnoses

  • Impaired gas exchange related to viral pneumonia.
  • Hyperthermia related to infection.
  • Anxiety and social isolation related to the disease and isolation measures.
  • Risk for infection transmission to others.

Nursing importance During the pandemic, nurses were at the front line; early detection of hypoxia, correct oxygen therapy, prone positioning, glucose control and strict infection control saved lives and protected health workers.

Conclusion COVID-19 is a SARS-CoV-2 infection spread mainly by droplets and aerosols; management depends on severity – home care for mild disease, oxygen, steroids and anticoagulation for moderate to severe disease – supported by vigilant nursing and strict infection control.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Communicable Diseases
question: (a) Define pulmonary tuberculosis and explain its mode of transmission and risk factors. (3 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features and diagnosis under the National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP). (4 marks) (c) Describe the treatment under NTEP and the nursing management of a patient with pulmonary tuberculosis. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Sputum collection and treatment under NTEP
labels: two sputum samples (spot and early morning)
treatment – 2 months HRZE then 4 months HRE

answer_html:
(a) Definition, transmission and risk factors (3 marks) Pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) is a chronic infectious disease of the lungs caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, characterised by the formation of granulomas with caseation and cavitation. India has the highest TB burden in the world (about a quarter of global cases), and the government aims to end TB under the National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP) and TB Mukt Bharat.

Mode of transmission

  • Airborne – when a patient with sputum-positive pulmonary TB coughs, sneezes, sings or talks, tiny droplet nuclei are released and inhaled by others; prolonged close contact in crowded, poorly ventilated homes increases risk.
  • One untreated infectious patient can infect 10–15 people a year; patients become much less infectious within a few weeks of effective treatment.
  • Extrapulmonary TB is usually not infectious.

Risk factors

  • HIV infection, diabetes, malnutrition (BMI below 18.5), smoking, alcohol use.
  • Close contact with a TB patient (household contacts, health workers).
  • Poverty, overcrowding, poor ventilation; migrants, prisoners, slum dwellers.
  • Silicosis, chronic kidney disease, cancer, immunosuppressive drugs (steroids, anti-TNF agents), elderly and young children.

(b) Clinical features and diagnosis under NTEP (4 marks) Clinical features

  • Cough for 2 weeks or more (dry, later productive), haemoptysis.
  • Fever, typically low-grade with evening rise, night sweats.
  • Weight loss, loss of appetite, fatigue.
  • Chest pain, breathlessness (in advanced disease or effusion).
  • Presumptive TB (NTEP) – a person with cough for 2 weeks or more, fever for 2 weeks or more, significant weight loss, haemoptysis or night sweats, or any abnormality on chest X-ray suggestive of TB; contacts and high-risk groups are screened actively.

Diagnosis under NTEP

  • Sputum examination – two samples (one spot sample and one early-morning sample) collected correctly.
  • Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT) – CBNAAT/TrueNat – the preferred first test; detects M. tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance within hours.
  • Sputum smear microscopy (Ziehl–Neelsen or fluorescent staining) where NAAT is not available.
  • Universal drug susceptibility testing (UDST) – every diagnosed patient is tested for drug resistance (NAAT, line probe assay, liquid culture).
  • Chest X-ray (including portable/hand-held X-rays in active case finding) – infiltrates, cavities, effusion.
  • Culture (liquid MGIT) and line probe assay for resistance patterns.
  • Tests for TB infection (Mantoux/TST, IGRA) in contacts before preventive treatment.
  • HIV testing and blood sugar for every TB patient (bi-directional screening).
  • Notification – TB is a notifiable disease; every case (government and private) is notified and registered on the Ni-kshay portal.

(c) Treatment under NTEP and nursing management (8 marks) 1. Treatment of drug-sensitive TB (as per NTEP)

  • Intensive phase – 2 months: isoniazid (H), rifampicin (R), pyrazinamide (Z) and ethambutol (E) given daily.
  • Continuation phase – 4 months: H, R and E given daily.
  • Drugs are given as weight-band-based fixed-dose combinations (FDCs); the total duration is 6 months (longer for some extrapulmonary forms).
  • Adherence support – treatment supporters, family DOT, digital adherence technologies (99DOTS, medication monitors), counselling.

  • Follow-up – clinical review and sputum examination at the end of the intensive phase and end of treatment; weight monitoring. 2. Drug-resistant TB

  • Treated with newer all-oral regimens containing bedaquiline; the 6-month BPaLM regimen (bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, with or without moxifloxacin) has been introduced under NTEP for MDR/rifampicin-resistant TB. 3. Patient support under NTEP

  • Free diagnosis and drugs in government and private sectors.

  • Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana – direct benefit transfer of ₹1,000 per month for nutritional support for the entire duration of treatment; energy-dense nutritional supplements for undernourished patients (BMI below 18.5).
  • Pradhan Mantri TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan – Ni-kshay Mitras (individuals, organisations) adopt patients and families and provide food baskets and other support.
  • TB preventive treatment (TPT) for household contacts and people living with HIV (e.g., 3HP – weekly isoniazid and rifapentine for 3 months, or 6 months of isoniazid).

4. Common side effects of first-line drugs | Drug | Important side effects | Nursing action | |---|---|---| | Isoniazid | Peripheral neuropathy, hepatitis | Pyridoxine; report tingling, jaundice | | Rifampicin | Orange-red urine, sweat and tears (harmless), hepatitis, flu-like illness, reduces effect of oral contraceptives | Reassure; use non-hormonal contraception; LFT if jaundice | | Pyrazinamide | Hepatitis, joint pains (raised uric acid) | Report joint pain, jaundice | | Ethambutol | Optic neuritis – blurred vision, red–green colour blindness | Check vision; stop and report visual change |

5. Nursing management (i) Airborne infection control

  • Teach cough etiquette – cover the mouth and nose with a cloth or tissue, turn away from others; patient wears a surgical mask around others in the early weeks.
  • Separate, well-ventilated room or bed near a window; sunlight; avoid crowded rooms.
  • Sputum disposal – into a covered container with disinfectant (or as per BMW rules), never spit in the open.

  • Health workers use N95 respirators in high-risk settings (DR-TB wards, sputum induction). (ii) Adherence and education

  • Explain that TB is completely curable if treatment is taken daily for the full duration; never stop when symptoms improve – incomplete treatment causes drug-resistant TB.

  • Teach how to take FDCs (preferably on an empty stomach or as advised, at the same time daily), recognise side effects and attend follow-up.
  • Link the patient with the treatment supporter, ASHA and Ni-kshay benefits (bank account details for DBT). (iii) Monitoring for side effects – jaundice, vomiting and abdominal pain (hepatitis), tingling, visual disturbance, rash; report promptly. (iv) Nutrition – high-calorie, high-protein diet (milk, eggs, pulses, groundnuts, soybean); small frequent meals; Ni-kshay Poshan support; weigh monthly. (v) Symptom care – fever care and sponging; haemoptysis – reassure, position on the affected side, keep a container for sputum, report large bleeds; adequate rest with gradual return to activity. (vi) Comorbidities – control diabetes, test and treat HIV, help to stop smoking and alcohol (de-addiction support). (vii) Contact screening and prevention – screen all household contacts for symptoms; arrange chest X-ray and TPT; ensure BCG for newborns. (viii) Psychosocial care – address stigma, fear of discrimination at work and in marriage; involve the family; maintain confidentiality. (ix) Records – treatment card, Ni-kshay entries, follow-up dates.

Common nursing diagnoses

  • Ineffective airway clearance related to secretions and cough.
  • Imbalanced nutrition: less than body requirements related to anorexia and increased metabolic needs.
  • Risk for infection transmission to contacts.
  • Risk for non-adherence related to long treatment duration and side effects.

Nursing importance Nurses are central to ending TB in India – through case finding, correct sputum collection, adherence support, side-effect monitoring, nutrition support, contact screening and reduction of stigma.

Conclusion Pulmonary TB is an airborne bacterial disease that is curable with 6 months of daily HRZE/HRE under NTEP; rapid NAAT diagnosis, universal drug-susceptibility testing, nutritional and social support, preventive treatment for contacts and dedicated nursing care are essential to achieve a TB-free India.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Communicable Diseases
question: (a) Define viral hepatitis and classify it. (3 marks) (b) Explain the modes of transmission and clinical features. (4 marks) (c) Describe the management, nursing care and prevention of viral hepatitis. (8 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Definition and classification (3 marks) Viral hepatitis is inflammation of the liver caused by hepatotropic viruses, producing liver cell damage, raised liver enzymes and often jaundice. It may be acute (lasting less than 6 months) or chronic (persisting beyond 6 months), leading to cirrhosis and liver cancer.

Classification – five main hepatitis viruses | Feature | Hepatitis A | Hepatitis B | Hepatitis C | Hepatitis D | Hepatitis E | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Virus | RNA | DNA | RNA | RNA (defective – needs HBV) | RNA | | Main route | Faeco-oral | Blood, sexual, mother to child | Blood (unsafe injections, transfusion) | Blood (with HBV) | Faeco-oral (water-borne) | | Incubation | 2–6 weeks | 6 weeks–6 months | 2 weeks–6 months | Same as HBV | 2–8 weeks | | Chronic infection | No | Yes (especially if infected at birth) | Yes (most infected) | Yes | Rarely (immunosuppressed) | | Vaccine | Yes | Yes (UIP) | No | Prevented by HBV vaccine | Not widely available | | Special risk | Severe in adults with liver disease | Cirrhosis, liver cancer | Cirrhosis, liver cancer | Severe, rapid cirrhosis | High mortality in pregnancy |

Other viruses (CMV, EBV, herpes simplex, yellow fever) can also cause hepatitis.

(b) Modes of transmission and clinical features (4 marks) Modes of transmission

  • Hepatitis A and E (enteric) – contaminated water and food, poor sanitation, unwashed hands, raw vegetables and street foods; outbreaks after floods and water-pipeline contamination; hepatitis E causes large water-borne epidemics in India.
  • Hepatitis B, C and D (parenteral) – unsafe injections and reuse of needles and syringes, transfusion of unscreened blood, needle-stick injuries in health workers, sharing razors, toothbrushes and needles (drug users), tattooing and piercing with unsterile instruments, dialysis, unprotected sex (especially HBV), and mother-to-child transmission at birth (HBV).

Clinical features (acute hepatitis)

  1. Pre-icteric (prodromal) phase – 3–10 days: loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, malaise, low-grade fever, headache, aversion to food and smoking, dull right upper abdominal pain; joint pain and rash (HBV).
  2. Icteric phase – jaundice (yellow eyes and skin), dark (tea-coloured) urine, pale or clay-coloured stools, itching, tender enlarged liver; appetite and well-being often improve when jaundice appears.
  3. Recovery (post-icteric) phase – gradual disappearance of jaundice; fatigue may continue for weeks. - Many infections (especially in children, and HCV) are asymptomatic.

Complications

  • Fulminant (acute) liver failure – deepening jaundice, confusion and drowsiness (encephalopathy), bleeding (prolonged INR), vomiting – especially hepatitis E in pregnant women (high maternal and fetal mortality in the third trimester) and hepatitis A in older adults.
  • Chronic hepatitis (B, C, D) → cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma; extrahepatic manifestations.

Investigations LFT (markedly raised ALT and AST, raised bilirubin, ALP), prothrombin time/INR (severity), serology – IgM anti-HAV, HBsAg, IgM anti-HBc, HBeAg, HBV DNA, anti-HCV and HCV RNA, IgM anti-HEV, anti-HDV; ultrasound abdomen.

(c) Management, nursing care and prevention (8 marks) 1. Medical management

  • Acute hepatitis – mainly supportive: rest, nutrition, fluids, antiemetics, treatment of itching; avoid alcohol and hepatotoxic drugs (sedatives, unnecessary medicines, herbal preparations; paracetamol only in small doses as advised).
  • Hospital admission for persistent vomiting, dehydration, pregnancy, elderly, or signs of liver failure (confusion, bleeding, rising INR).
  • Fulminant hepatic failure – ICU care, management of encephalopathy, cerebral oedema, bleeding and infection; liver transplantation.
  • Chronic hepatitis B – tenofovir or entecavir (long-term); chronic hepatitis C – direct-acting antivirals (e.g., sofosbuvir-based combinations for 12 weeks) with cure rates above 95%; both are available free of cost under the National Viral Hepatitis Control Programme (NVHCP) at designated centres.

2. Nursing care (i) Activity intolerance and fatigue – bed rest during the acute phase, with gradual increase in activity as jaundice and LFT improve; avoid strenuous work for some weeks. (ii) Imbalanced nutrition

  • High-calorie, adequate protein, easily digestible diet; small, frequent meals; most calories in the morning when nausea is less; fruit juices, glucose water, khichdi, curd rice, dal, fruits.
  • A strict fat-free diet is not necessary, but heavy, fried and spicy foods are avoided if they cause nausea; no alcohol.
  • Plenty of fluids (2–3 litres a day) unless restricted; antiemetics before meals as ordered.

  • (Traditional remedies such as sugarcane juice should be clean and hygienically prepared; unverified herbal medicines should be avoided.) (iii) Impaired comfort (itching) – cool baths, calamine lotion, loose cotton clothes, short nails, antihistamines or cholestyramine as ordered. (iv) Monitoring for complications – degree of jaundice, colour of urine and stools, mental state (confusion, drowsiness), bleeding (gums, bruises, black stools), vomiting, intake–output, LFT and INR; report early signs of liver failure. (v) Infection prevention in hospital

  • Hepatitis A and E – enteric precautions: strict hand washing, safe disposal of faeces, separate toilet or disinfection after use, gloves when handling excreta, separate or well-cleaned utensils.

  • Hepatitis B, C and D – standard (blood and body fluid) precautions, safe injection practices and sharps disposal, no sharing of razors, toothbrushes or nail cutters; post-exposure prophylaxis for needle-stick injuries (HBV vaccine and HBIG as per immune status). (vi) Psychosocial care – reassurance, explanation of the disease, confidentiality and counselling for chronic HBV/HCV carriers; screening and vaccination of family members. (vii) Health education at discharge – avoid alcohol for at least 6 months (lifelong in chronic hepatitis), avoid unprescribed drugs, attend follow-up LFT, recognise warning signs, safe sex, and do not donate blood (HBV/HCV).

3. Prevention (a) Hepatitis A and E

  • Safe drinking water – boiled, filtered or chlorinated; sanitation and safe disposal of human excreta (Swachh Bharat).
  • Hand washing with soap after using the toilet and before eating and cooking; food hygiene; avoid raw and street foods during outbreaks.

  • Hepatitis A vaccine (available in the private sector); protection of pregnant women from contaminated water (hepatitis E). (b) Hepatitis B, C and D

  • Hepatitis B vaccination under the Universal Immunisation Programme – birth dose within 24 hours, then pentavalent vaccine at 6, 10 and 14 weeks; vaccination of all health-care workers.

  • Hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) with vaccine for newborns of HBsAg-positive mothers; antenatal screening for HBsAg.
  • Screening of blood and organs, safe injection practices (auto-disable syringes, no reuse), safe dialysis, sterile tattoo and piercing practices.
  • Safe sex (condoms), harm reduction for people who inject drugs.
  • NVHCP (launched in 2018) aims to eliminate hepatitis C and reduce hepatitis B and its complications through awareness, free testing, treatment and vaccination; World Hepatitis Day – 28 July.

Common nursing diagnoses

  • Fatigue related to liver inflammation.
  • Imbalanced nutrition related to anorexia and nausea.
  • Risk for infection transmission related to the mode of spread.
  • Deficient knowledge regarding prevention and follow-up.

Nursing importance Nurses prevent viral hepatitis through hygiene education, safe injection practices and vaccination (including the hepatitis B birth dose), and they detect early liver failure in hospitalised patients.

Conclusion Viral hepatitis is caused mainly by viruses A–E; A and E spread through contaminated water and food, while B, C and D spread through blood and body fluids; supportive care, antiviral therapy for chronic B and C, and prevention through sanitation, safe injections and vaccination are the cornerstones of management.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Communicable Diseases
question: Define fever. List the common communicable diseases that present with fever in India.
answer_html:
Fever (pyrexia) is an elevation of body temperature above the normal daily range (oral temperature above about 37.5–38 °C) due to resetting of the hypothalamic set-point by pyrogens released during infection or inflammation.

Common communicable diseases presenting with fever

  1. Vector-borne – malaria, dengue, chikungunya, filarial fever, Japanese encephalitis.
  2. Enteric – typhoid, viral hepatitis (A, E), acute gastroenteritis.
  3. Respiratory – influenza (H1N1), COVID-19, pneumonia, tuberculosis (evening rise), diphtheria.
  4. Exanthematous (with rash) – measles, chickenpox.
  5. Others – scrub typhus, leptospirosis (monsoon), meningitis, HIV, brucellosis, urinary tract infection.

Nursing point – record a temperature chart, send early tests (malaria RDT/smear, dengue NS1) and give paracetamol; avoid aspirin and NSAIDs until dengue is ruled out.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Communicable Diseases
question: What is the nurse's role in collecting a blood smear for malaria? Differentiate thick and thin smears.
answer_html:
Nurse's role

  1. Collect blood before giving antimalarial drugs, preferably during or just before the fever peak.
  2. Clean the side of the ring finger, prick, wipe away the first drop, and use the next drops.
  3. Prepare one thick and one thin smear on a clean, labelled slide; dry it horizontally, protected from dust and flies; do not heat.
  4. Send it promptly with a completed form (name, age, address, date, fever history); perform a rapid diagnostic test (RDT) where available.
Point Thick smear Thin smear
Blood 2–3 drops spread in a circle of about 1 cm 1 small drop spread as a thin "tongue"
Fixation Not fixed (red cells lysed) Fixed with methanol
Purpose Detects parasites – more sensitive; parasite count Identifies the species (P. vivax, P. falciparum)

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Communicable Diseases
question: List the types of viral hepatitis with their modes of transmission.
answer_html:
Types of viral hepatitis and transmission

  1. Hepatitis A – faeco-oral (contaminated water and food); no chronic infection; vaccine available.
  2. Hepatitis B – blood, unsafe injections, sexual contact, mother to child at birth; may become chronic; vaccine in UIP (birth dose).
  3. Hepatitis C – mainly blood-borne (unsafe injections, transfusion, needle sharing); often chronic; curable with antivirals; no vaccine.
  4. Hepatitis D – blood-borne; occurs only with hepatitis B; prevented by HBV vaccination.
  5. Hepatitis E – faeco-oral (water-borne); causes epidemics; dangerous in pregnancy.

Prevention – safe water and sanitation for A and E; vaccination, safe injections and blood screening for B, C and D.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Communicable Diseases
question: What is chikungunya? Write its management.
answer_html:
Chikungunya is an acute viral fever caused by the chikungunya virus (an alphavirus), transmitted by the day-biting Aedes aegypti and *Aedes albopictus mosquitoes. The name means "that which bends up"*, describing the stooped posture due to joint pain.

Features – sudden high fever, severe pain and swelling of multiple joints (wrists, ankles, fingers, knees), headache, muscle pain, rash; joint pain may persist for weeks to months. Diagnosis – IgM ELISA, RT-PCR.

Management

  1. No specific antiviral – rest, plenty of fluids, paracetamol; NSAIDs only after dengue is excluded.
  2. Cold compresses and gentle joint exercises; physiotherapy for chronic arthritis.
  3. Prevention – eliminate Aedes breeding sites, use repellents, nets and full-sleeved clothes.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Communicable Diseases
question: What is swine flu (H1N1 influenza)? How are patients categorised for management in India?
answer_html:
Swine flu is influenza caused by the influenza A (H1N1)pdm09 virus, which caused the 2009 pandemic and now circulates as a seasonal influenza strain in India, spreading by droplets and contaminated hands.

Features – fever, cough, sore throat, runny nose, body ache, headache; severe cases – breathlessness, chest pain, low SpO₂.

MoHFW categorisation

  1. Category A – mild fever, cough, sore throat – home isolation, symptomatic treatment; no testing or oseltamivir needed.
  2. Category B – high fever and severe sore throat (B1), or mild illness in high-risk groups – children under 5, pregnant women, elderly, chronic diseases (B2) – oseltamivir and home isolation.
  3. Category C – breathlessness, chest pain, drowsiness, low BP, blood-stained sputum, cyanosis – hospital admission, testing and oseltamivir. Prevention – cough etiquette, hand hygiene, masks, annual influenza vaccine for high-risk persons and health workers.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Communicable Diseases
question: Write a short note on diphtheria.
answer_html:
Diphtheria is an acute infectious disease caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae, spread by droplets, mostly affecting unimmunised children.

Features – sore throat, low-grade fever, a greyish-white adherent pseudomembrane on the tonsils and pharynx that bleeds when removed, "bull neck" (swollen neck glands), hoarseness and airway obstruction; the toxin causes myocarditis and nerve palsies (palate, eyes, limbs).

Management

  1. Diphtheria antitoxin (DAT) as early as possible, plus penicillin or erythromycin.
  2. Droplet isolation until two negative throat cultures; airway care (tracheostomy if needed); bed rest and cardiac monitoring.
  3. Contacts – throat swab, erythromycin and booster vaccination. Prevention – DPT/pentavalent vaccine and boosters under UIP, Td for adolescents.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Communicable Diseases
question: Write a short note on pertussis (whooping cough).
answer_html:
Pertussis (whooping cough) is a highly contagious respiratory infection caused by Bordetella pertussis, spread by droplets, most dangerous in infants.

Stages

  1. Catarrhal stage (1–2 weeks) – cold-like symptoms; most infectious.
  2. Paroxysmal stage (2–6 weeks) – bouts of rapid coughing followed by a high-pitched inspiratory "whoop", vomiting after coughing, red or blue face; apnoea in young infants.
  3. Convalescent stage – gradual recovery over weeks. Complications – pneumonia, seizures, subconjunctival haemorrhage, hernia, malnutrition.

Management – azithromycin or erythromycin; suction, oxygen, small frequent feeds (re-feed after vomiting), quiet environment; droplet isolation. Prevention – DPT/pentavalent vaccination under UIP.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Communicable Diseases
question: Write a short note on poliomyelitis and AFP surveillance.
answer_html:
Poliomyelitis is an acute viral infection caused by poliovirus (an enterovirus), spread by the faeco-oral route. Most infections are silent; less than 1% cause acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) – sudden, asymmetrical paralysis, usually of the legs, without sensory loss. India was certified polio-free in 2014 (last case in January 2011).

AFP surveillance

  1. Every child below 15 years with sudden onset of flaccid paralysis (and any suspected polio at any age) is reported immediately.
  2. Two stool samples, 24 hours apart, within 14 days of onset are sent to the laboratory in a cold chain.
  3. Follow-up examination after 60 days for residual paralysis.

Prevention – bivalent OPV (birth, 6, 10, 14 weeks and booster) and fractional IPV under UIP; Pulse Polio campaigns.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Communicable Diseases
question: What is gas gangrene? Write its management.
answer_html:
Gas gangrene is a rapidly spreading, life-threatening necrotising infection of muscles (myonecrosis) caused by toxin-producing anaerobic bacteria, mainly Clostridium perfringens, in deep, contaminated wounds – road accidents, crush and war injuries, unclean surgery or abortion, diabetic foot.

Features – severe pain out of proportion to the wound, swelling, bronze-to-black skin, blisters, foul sweetish discharge, crepitus (gas in tissues), high fever, toxaemia and shock.

Management

  1. Emergency surgical debridement of all dead tissue, fasciotomy; amputation if needed.
  2. High-dose IV penicillin with clindamycin; hyperbaric oxygen where available.
  3. ICU care for shock; mark the spreading edge and monitor hourly. Prevention – early thorough wound cleaning and debridement; contaminated wounds are left open (delayed closure).

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Communicable Diseases
question: Differentiate between isolation and quarantine.
answer_html:
Point Isolation Quarantine
Who Infected persons (cases) or carriers Healthy persons (contacts) who have been exposed
Purpose Prevent spread from the sick person to others Prevent spread if the exposed person becomes infected
Duration Period of communicability of the disease Maximum incubation period of the disease
Examples TB, COVID-19, chickenpox, cholera patients Contacts of COVID-19, travellers from yellow fever areas, plague contacts
Types Standard, contact, droplet, airborne, protective (reverse) isolation Complete (absolute), modified, segregation; home or institutional

Nursing point – isolation and quarantine must be explained to patients and families with respect and without stigma; the person's basic needs, mental health and communication with family are maintained, and confidentiality is protected.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Communicable Diseases
question: Write a short note on mumps.
answer_html:
Mumps is an acute viral infection caused by the mumps virus (a paramyxovirus), spread by droplets and saliva, mainly in children aged 5–15 years; incubation about 16–18 days.

Features – fever, headache, painful swelling of one or both parotid glands (swelling in front of and below the ear), earache, pain on chewing and with sour foods. Complications – orchitis (in males after puberty), oophoritis, pancreatitis, aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, deafness.

Management – symptomatic: paracetamol, warm or cold compresses, soft diet, plenty of fluids, oral hygiene, scrotal support and ice for orchitis; isolation for 5 days after the onset of swelling. Prevention – MMR vaccine (available privately; the UIP gives MR vaccine).

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Communicable Diseases
question: Write a short note on plague.
answer_html:
Plague is an acute, severe bacterial zoonosis caused by Yersinia pestis, maintained in wild rodents and spread to humans mainly by the bite of infected rat fleas (Xenopsylla cheopis); pneumonic plague spreads person to person by droplets. India had outbreaks in Surat (1994), Himachal Pradesh (2002) and Uttarakhand (2004).

Types – bubonic (fever with very painful swollen lymph nodes – buboes – in groin or axilla), septicaemic, and pneumonic (cough, bloody sputum – most dangerous and highly infectious). Management – streptomycin or gentamicin, doxycycline or ciprofloxacin; droplet isolation for pneumonic plague; chemoprophylaxis of contacts (doxycycline); flea control (insecticide) before rodent control; plague is notifiable internationally.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Communicable Diseases
question: Explain the clinical features, management and nursing care of a patient with dengue fever.
answer_html:
Definition Dengue is an acute viral febrile illness caused by the dengue virus (a flavivirus with four serotypes, DENV-1 to 4) and transmitted by the bite of the day-biting Aedes aegypti mosquito, which breeds in clean stagnant water (coolers, tyres, flower pots, overhead tanks, discarded containers). Infection with a second, different serotype increases the risk of severe dengue.

1. Classification (WHO)

  • Dengue without warning signs.
  • Dengue with warning signs.
  • Severe dengue – severe plasma leakage (shock, fluid accumulation with breathlessness), severe bleeding or severe organ involvement (liver, brain, heart).

2. Clinical features – three phases (a) Febrile phase (days 1–3/7)

  • Sudden high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes (retro-orbital pain), muscle and joint pain ("break-bone fever"), flushed face, rash, nausea, vomiting.

  • Mild bleeding – petechiae, gum bleeding, positive tourniquet test. (b) Critical phase (around the time the fever falls, days 3–7)

  • Plasma leakage – rising haematocrit, rapidly falling platelets, pleural effusion, ascites; may lead to shock (cold extremities, narrow pulse pressure, low urine output).

  • Warning signs – abdominal pain or tenderness, persistent vomiting, clinical fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding, lethargy or restlessness, liver enlargement, rise in haematocrit with a rapid fall in platelets. (c) Recovery phase

  • Reabsorption of leaked fluid; improving appetite; itchy convalescent rash; risk of fluid overload if IV fluids continue unchecked; bradycardia.

3. Diagnosis NS1 antigen (days 1–5), IgM ELISA (after day 5), RT-PCR; CBC – platelet count, haematocrit, leucopenia; LFT; ultrasound for effusion.

4. Management

  • No specific antiviral – treatment is supportive.
  • Fever – paracetamol and tepid sponging; avoid aspirin, ibuprofen and other NSAIDs and IM injections (bleeding risk).
  • Oral fluids – ORS, coconut water, juices, rice water, soups (about 2.5–3 litres a day in adults).
  • IV crystalloids for patients with warning signs or shock, as per national protocol, guided by haematocrit, vital signs and urine output.
  • Blood transfusion for significant bleeding; platelet transfusion is not given routinely – only when platelets are very low (below about 10,000/µl) or there is significant bleeding, as per guidelines.
  • Watch for and manage fluid overload in the recovery phase.

5. Nursing care

  • Monitor vital signs, pulse pressure, capillary refill, urine output (at least 0.5 ml/kg/hour), haematocrit and platelets as ordered, and warning signs; record a fluid balance chart.
  • Bleeding precautions – soft toothbrush, avoid IM injections, pressure on puncture sites; observe for bleeding gums, nosebleeds, black stools, heavy periods.
  • Rest, nutritious soft diet, oral hygiene.
  • Mosquito net even in the daytime for the patient (prevents spread to others).
  • Health education – complete rest, fluids, warning signs needing hospital care, avoid self-medication with painkillers and unproven remedies.

6. Prevention

  • Source reduction – empty, clean and cover water containers once a week ("dry day"), remove discarded tyres and containers, change cooler water, larvicides (temephos), fogging during outbreaks.
  • Personal protection – full-sleeved clothes, repellents, window screens, nets during daytime sleep.
  • Community participation; National Dengue Day – 16 May.
  • Vaccine – India's first dengue vaccine (Qdenga) received regulatory approval in 2026 for people aged 4–60 years (two doses three months apart); it is available in the private sector and is not part of the UIP.

Nursing importance Close nursing observation during the critical phase – haematocrit, warning signs and urine output – and careful fluid management prevent most dengue deaths.

Conclusion Dengue is an Aedes-borne viral fever with febrile, critical and recovery phases; supportive care, careful fluid management, avoidance of NSAIDs and close monitoring, together with mosquito control, form the basis of care.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Communicable Diseases
question: Explain the clinical features, treatment and nursing management of malaria.
answer_html:
Definition Malaria is an acute and sometimes chronic parasitic disease caused by Plasmodium species – in India mainly P. vivax and *P. falciparum – transmitted by the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito (night-biting). India aims to eliminate malaria by 2030* under the National Framework for Malaria Elimination.

1. Clinical features (a) Typical malarial paroxysm

  • Cold stage (15–60 minutes) – intense chills and rigors, shivering, rapid pulse.
  • Hot stage (2–6 hours) – high fever (up to 40–41 °C), flushed face, headache, vomiting, body ache.
  • Sweating stage (2–4 hours) – profuse sweating, fall in temperature, the patient feels better and sleeps.

  • Fever may recur every 48 hours (vivax) or be irregular (falciparum); anaemia, splenomegaly, mild jaundice. (b) Severe (complicated) malaria – mostly P. falciparum

  • Cerebral malaria (impaired consciousness, seizures), severe anaemia, hypoglycaemia, acute kidney injury (dark urine – blackwater fever), jaundice, ARDS, shock, bleeding (DIC), acidosis; high risk in pregnancy (abortion, stillbirth, low birth weight).

2. Diagnosis Peripheral blood smear (thick and thin – gold standard) and bivalent rapid diagnostic test (RDT), used even by ASHAs in villages.

3. Treatment (as per national guidelines)

  • P. vivax – chloroquine for 3 days plus primaquine (0.25 mg/kg daily for 14 days) for radical cure (to kill liver stages and prevent relapse); primaquine is avoided in pregnancy, infants and G6PD deficiency.
  • P. falciparum (uncomplicated) – artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) – artesunate + sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine for 3 days (artemether–lumefantrine in north-eastern states), with single-dose primaquine to stop transmission.
  • Severe malaria – IV (or IM) artesunate, followed by a full course of ACT; supportive ICU care.
  • Treatment of pregnant women as per the specific national recommendations.

4. Nursing management

  • Fever care according to the stage – cold stage: warm blankets, hot drinks; hot stage: tepid sponging, antipyretics, cool fluids; sweating stage: change wet clothes and linen, dry the skin, fluids.
  • Collect the blood smear or RDT before the first dose of antimalarials.
  • Give drugs with food; give primaquine after food; ensure the full course is completed.
  • Monitor temperature, pulse, BP, level of consciousness, blood sugar, urine output and colour, jaundice and Hb; report confusion, seizures, dark urine or breathlessness (severe malaria).
  • Seizure precautions and airway care in cerebral malaria; hypoglycaemia monitoring with quinine and in pregnancy.
  • Nutrition and fluids; rest; iron and folic acid for anaemia.

5. Prevention

  • Vector control – indoor residual spraying, long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs), larval source management (filling ditches, larvivorous fish such as Gambusia and guppy).
  • Personal protection – nets, repellents, full-sleeved clothes, screens.
  • Early diagnosis and complete treatment of every case; surveillance and health education.

Nursing importance Early testing, complete treatment and close monitoring for complications – especially in falciparum malaria – prevent deaths and transmission.

Conclusion Malaria is a mosquito-borne parasitic disease with cyclical chills, fever and sweating; prompt diagnosis, correct species-specific treatment, good nursing care and vector control are essential to reach malaria elimination.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Communicable Diseases
question: Explain the clinical features, complications, management and nursing care of typhoid fever.
answer_html:
Definition Typhoid (enteric) fever is an acute systemic infection caused by Salmonella Typhi (and S. Paratyphi A, B in paratyphoid), transmitted by the faeco-oral route through contaminated water and food, often from carriers (bacteria persist in the gallbladder). Incubation is usually 10–14 days. India carries a large share of the world's typhoid burden.

1. Clinical features

  • Fever rising in a "step-ladder" pattern during the first week, becoming high and continuous.
  • Headache, malaise, loss of appetite, body ache, abdominal pain, constipation in adults or diarrhoea (especially children).
  • Coated tongue, relative bradycardia (pulse slower than expected for the fever), tender abdomen, hepatosplenomegaly, rose spots on the trunk (rarely seen).
  • Toxic, apathetic appearance in the second week ("typhoid state").

2. Complications (usually in the 2nd–3rd week)

  • Intestinal haemorrhage (malaena) and intestinal perforation of the terminal ileum (sudden abdominal pain, rigidity, shock) – surgical emergencies.
  • Encephalopathy, myocarditis, hepatitis, cholecystitis, pneumonia, relapse and a chronic carrier state.

3. Diagnosis Blood culture (first week – the best test), bone marrow culture (most sensitive), stool and urine culture (later); Widal test (limited value); CBC (leucopenia).

4. Management

  • Antibiotics as per sensitivity and guidelines – azithromycin (oral) for uncomplicated typhoid, ceftriaxone IV for severe cases, cefixime; fluoroquinolone resistance is widespread in India; usual duration 7–14 days.
  • Antipyretics (paracetamol), fluids and electrolytes.
  • Surgery for perforation; transfusion for haemorrhage.

5. Nursing care

  • Fever care – tepid sponging, antipyretics, cool environment, monitor temperature 4-hourly.
  • Nutrition – soft, high-calorie, high-protein, easily digestible, low-residue diet in small frequent feeds; plenty of fluids.
  • Rest and pressure-area care; oral hygiene (coated tongue).
  • Enteric precautions – strict hand washing; safe disposal and disinfection of stools and urine; separate utensils; gloves for handling excreta.
  • Observe for complications – sudden abdominal pain, distension, rigidity, malaena, falling BP, rising pulse; avoid laxatives and enemas (risk of perforation).
  • Complete the antibiotic course; follow-up stool cultures in food handlers.

6. Prevention

  • Safe drinking water (boiled or chlorinated), sanitation, hand washing with soap, food hygiene; avoid raw salads and street food.
  • Screening and treatment of food handlers and carriers.
  • Vaccination – typhoid conjugate vaccine (TCV), recommended by the national technical advisory group, is available in the private sector; Vi polysaccharide vaccine.

Nursing importance Good nursing – fever care, nutrition, enteric precautions and early recognition of perforation and bleeding – reduces deaths from typhoid, while health education prevents its spread.

Conclusion Typhoid is a faeco-orally spread systemic Salmonella infection with step-ladder fever; correct antibiotics, supportive care, vigilance for complications and sanitation-based prevention are the keys to control.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Communicable Diseases
question: Explain the assessment of dehydration and the management of a patient with acute diarrhoea and cholera.
answer_html:
Introduction Acute diarrhoea is the passage of three or more loose or watery stools in 24 hours, lasting less than 14 days. It may be caused by viruses (rotavirus, norovirus), bacteria (Vibrio cholerae, E. coli, Shigella, Salmonella), parasites (Giardia, Entamoeba) or food poisoning. Cholera causes the most rapid and severe dehydration – painless, profuse "rice-water" stools with vomiting, leading to shock within hours.

1. Assessment of dehydration (WHO) | Sign | No dehydration | Some dehydration | Severe dehydration | |---|---|---|---| | General condition | Well, alert | Restless, irritable | Lethargic or unconscious | | Eyes | Normal | Sunken | Very sunken | | Thirst | Drinks normally | Drinks eagerly, thirsty | Drinks poorly or unable to drink | | Skin pinch | Goes back quickly | Goes back slowly | Goes back very slowly (more than 2 seconds) | Also check pulse, BP, urine output, weight loss and mucous membranes.

2. Management

  • Plan A (no dehydration – home care) – extra fluids (ORS after every loose stool, rice water, buttermilk, soups), zinc for children (20 mg daily for 14 days; 10 mg below 6 months), continue feeding and breastfeeding, return if danger signs appear.
  • Plan B (some dehydration) – ORS about 75 ml/kg over 4 hours under observation, then reassess.
  • Plan C (severe dehydration) – IV Ringer's lactate (or normal saline) 100 ml/kg – in adults 30 ml/kg in the first 30 minutes and 70 ml/kg over the next 2½ hours (slower in infants); ORS as soon as the patient can drink.
  • Antibiotics – cholera (doxycycline single dose in adults; azithromycin in children and pregnant women) and dysentery (bloody diarrhoea – azithromycin or as per guidelines); not for most watery diarrhoea.
  • Avoid antimotility drugs in children and in bloody diarrhoea.

3. Nursing management

  • Intake–output chart, stool chart (frequency, volume, character), daily weight, vital signs and urine output.
  • Monitor for electrolyte imbalance (low potassium – weakness, ileus; acidosis – deep breathing).
  • Teach correct ORS preparation – one packet in one litre of clean drinking water, give small frequent sips (by spoon in children), use within 24 hours.
  • Nutrition – continue feeding with easily digestible foods (khichdi, curd, banana, dal water).
  • Perianal skin care – gentle washing, barrier cream.
  • Enteric precautions – hand hygiene, disinfection of stools and soiled linen (1% sodium hypochlorite), safe disposal; notify cholera and outbreaks (IDSP).

4. Prevention Safe drinking water, sanitation (open-defecation-free villages), hand washing with soap, food hygiene, exclusive breastfeeding, rotavirus vaccine (UIP), oral cholera vaccine in outbreak-prone areas.

Nursing importance Almost all deaths from diarrhoea and cholera are preventable by timely rehydration; nurses' assessment of dehydration and teaching of ORS and zinc save lives.

Conclusion Acute diarrhoea and cholera are managed by correct assessment of dehydration, ORS or IV fluids as per Plans A–C, zinc for children, antibiotics when indicated, continued feeding and strict hygiene.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Communicable Diseases
question: Explain the classification, clinical features, treatment and nursing management of leprosy.
answer_html:
Definition Leprosy (Hansen's disease) is a chronic infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae, which mainly affects the skin, peripheral nerves, eyes and nasal mucosa. It spreads through droplets from the nose and mouth of untreated patients during prolonged close contact; the incubation period is long (on average 3–5 years). It is curable, and India runs the National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP).

1. Cardinal signs (any one confirms leprosy)

  1. Hypopigmented or reddish skin patch with definite loss of sensation.
  2. Thickened or enlarged peripheral nerve with loss of sensation and/or weakness of muscles supplied (ulnar, median, radial cutaneous, common peroneal, posterior tibial, great auricular).
  3. Positive slit-skin smear for acid-fast bacilli.

2. Classification (for treatment)

  • Paucibacillary (PB) – 1–5 skin lesions, no nerve or only one nerve involved, smear negative.
  • Multibacillary (MB) – 6 or more lesions, more than one nerve involved, or smear positive. (Ridley–Jopling spectrum – TT, BT, BB, BL, LL.)

3. Complications

  • Nerve damage → loss of sensation, claw hand, foot drop, lagophthalmos (inability to close the eye) → injuries, plantar ulcers, deformities, blindness.
  • Lepra reactions – type 1 (reversal) – inflamed patches and painful nerves; type 2 (ENL) – painful red nodules, fever, neuritis, eye and joint involvement; both need prompt treatment (steroids) to prevent disability.

4. Treatment – multidrug therapy (MDT)

  • Three drugs – rifampicin (monthly, supervised), clofazimine (monthly supervised dose plus daily dose) and dapsone (daily).
  • PB leprosy – 6 months; MB leprosy – 12 months (India now uses the three-drug regimen for PB cases as well).
  • MDT is free; patients become non-infectious soon after starting MDT – no isolation is required.
  • Side effects – red urine (rifampicin), reversible darkening of the skin (clofazimine), anaemia and allergy (dapsone).

5. Nursing management

  • Early detection – examine contacts; support case-detection campaigns; refer suspected patches.
  • Counselling – leprosy is curable, not hereditary, not a curse or due to sin; continue normal family life.
  • Adherence to the full MDT course; explain side effects.
  • Watch for reactions – new pain or tenderness of nerves, weakness, redness of patches, painful nodules, eye redness – and refer immediately.
  • Self-care for prevention of disability – daily soaking of anaesthetic hands and feet in water, oiling, scraping of hard skin, inspection for injuries, protective footwear (MCR chappals), gloves or cloth when handling hot utensils, eye care (protective glasses, lubricant drops, blinking exercises), exercises for weak muscles.
  • Ulcer care – cleaning, dressing, rest and off-loading.
  • Rehabilitation – reconstructive surgery, vocational and social rehabilitation; disability benefits.
  • Stigma reduction – Anti-Leprosy Day (30 January) and the Sparsh Leprosy Awareness Campaign.

6. Prevention Early diagnosis and MDT, single-dose rifampicin post-exposure prophylaxis for eligible contacts, BCG vaccination (partial protection) and community awareness.

Nursing importance Disability in leprosy is preventable; nurses' role in early detection, MDT adherence, recognition of reactions and teaching self-care protects patients from deformity and stigma.

Conclusion Leprosy is a curable chronic infection of skin and nerves; classification into PB and MB guides 6- or 12-month MDT, while self-care, management of reactions and stigma reduction are central nursing responsibilities.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Communicable Diseases
question: Explain the clinical features, management and nursing care of a patient with tetanus.
answer_html:
Definition Tetanus is an acute, often fatal disease caused by the toxin (tetanospasmin) of Clostridium tetani, whose spores live in soil, dust and animal faeces and enter the body through wounds – puncture wounds, burns, crush injuries, unclean deliveries and cord care (neonatal tetanus), ear infections and IV drug use. The toxin blocks inhibitory nerve signals, causing muscle rigidity and painful spasms. India has eliminated maternal and neonatal tetanus (validated in 2015), but adult tetanus still occurs.

1. Clinical features

  • Incubation 3–21 days (shorter incubation means more severe disease).
  • Trismus (lockjaw) – the earliest sign; difficulty in opening the mouth and swallowing.
  • Risus sardonicus – fixed sardonic smile due to facial muscle spasm.
  • Neck stiffness, board-like abdominal rigidity, back muscle spasm causing opisthotonus (arched back).
  • Generalised reflex spasms triggered by noise, light, touch or movement; very painful; the patient remains fully conscious.
  • Laryngospasm and respiratory muscle spasm – asphyxia.
  • Autonomic instability – fever, sweating, tachycardia, fluctuating BP, arrhythmias.
  • Neonatal tetanus – a baby who sucks well at birth stops sucking after 3–4 days, becomes stiff and has spasms.

2. Management

  • ICU care in a dark, quiet room.
  • Wound care – thorough debridement.
  • Neutralise unbound toxin – human tetanus immunoglobulin (TIG) IM as ordered.
  • Antibiotics – metronidazole (preferred) or penicillin.
  • Control spasms – diazepam or midazolam, magnesium sulphate, and muscle relaxants with mechanical ventilation in severe cases.
  • Airway – early tracheostomy in severe cases; oxygen and suction.
  • Fluids and nutrition through a nasogastric tube or parenterally; treatment of autonomic instability.
  • Active immunisation (Td) after recovery, as the disease does not give immunity.

3. Nursing care

  • Minimise stimulation – dim light, quiet room, cluster nursing care, gentle handling, limited visitors.
  • Airway management – suction, oxygen, tracheostomy care; observe for laryngospasm.
  • Record spasms – frequency, duration and triggers; give sedatives on time.
  • Monitor vital signs, temperature and autonomic signs, SpO₂, urine output.
  • Safety – padded side rails; prevent tongue bites and injuries.
  • Nutrition and hydration – tube feeding, intake–output.
  • Oral, eye, skin and pressure-area care; bladder and bowel care; prevention of aspiration pneumonia and DVT.
  • Psychological support – the patient is conscious and frightened; explain procedures and reassure.

4. Prevention

  • Immunisation under UIP – DPT/pentavalent in infancy, DPT boosters at 16–24 months and 5–6 years, Td at 10 and 16 years, and Td for pregnant women.
  • Wound management – cleaning and debridement, with Td and/or TIG according to immunisation status.
  • Clean delivery and cord care practices (institutional deliveries).

Nursing importance Tetanus is entirely preventable by vaccination, yet once established it needs intensive nursing – minimal stimulation, airway care and spasm control – for survival.

Conclusion Tetanus is a toxin-mediated disease causing lockjaw and painful spasms; wound debridement, TIG, metronidazole, spasm control, airway support and skilled nursing are essential, while immunisation prevents it.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Communicable Diseases
question: Explain the clinical features, management and nursing care of a patient with bacterial meningitis.
answer_html:
Definition Meningitis is inflammation of the meninges (pia and arachnoid mater) and the CSF surrounding the brain and spinal cord. Bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency; viral meningitis is usually milder, and tuberculous meningitis is an important subacute form in India.

1. Causes

  • Bacterial – Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcus), Haemophilus influenzae type b (children), Listeria (newborns, elderly), group B streptococci and E. coli (newborns).
  • Viral (enteroviruses), tuberculous, fungal (cryptococcus in HIV).
  • Spread through the blood or directly from ear and sinus infections, skull fractures or neurosurgery.

2. Clinical features

  • Fever, severe headache and neck stiffness (classic triad); photophobia, nausea and vomiting.
  • Altered consciousness, irritability, confusion, seizures.
  • Kernig's sign – pain and resistance when the knee is extended with the hip flexed; Brudzinski's sign – bending the neck causes flexion of the hips and knees.
  • Meningococcal meningitis – non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash and rapid septic shock.
  • Infants – fever, poor feeding, vomiting, irritability, high-pitched cry, bulging fontanelle, seizures.
  • Complications – raised intracranial pressure, hydrocephalus, deafness, cranial nerve palsies, brain abscess, SIADH, septic shock, DIC.

3. Diagnosis Lumbar puncture – CSF cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain, culture, CBNAAT/ADA (TB), PCR; blood culture; CT scan before LP if there are signs of raised ICP or focal deficits.

4. Management

  • Start empirical IV antibiotics immediately – ceftriaxone (with vancomycin where resistance is common; ampicillin for Listeria risk); do not delay antibiotics for investigations.
  • Dexamethasone with or just before the first antibiotic dose (reduces hearing loss and deaths, especially in pneumococcal meningitis).
  • Anti-TB drugs with steroids for tuberculous meningitis; acyclovir for suspected herpes encephalitis.
  • Supportive – oxygen, careful IV fluids, antipyretics, anticonvulsants, management of raised ICP (head elevation, mannitol), treatment of shock.
  • Chemoprophylaxis for close contacts of meningococcal disease (rifampicin, ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone).

5. Nursing care

  • Droplet precautions for the first 24 hours of effective antibiotics (meningococcal and Hib meningitis).
  • Neurological observations – GCS, pupils, limb movements – hourly at first; watch for raised ICP (worsening headache, vomiting, drowsiness, rising BP with slowing pulse and irregular breathing) and report immediately.
  • Head end elevated 30°, neutral neck position; quiet, dimly lit room (photophobia).
  • Seizure precautions – padded side rails, suction ready, anticonvulsants on time.
  • Fever control, pain relief, oral and eye care, pressure-area care.
  • Fluid balance – intake–output, daily weight, serum sodium (SIADH).
  • Hearing assessment after recovery; follow-up for development in children.
  • Support and education for the family; contact tracing and prophylaxis.

6. Prevention Hib and pneumococcal (PCV) vaccines under UIP; BCG (protects against TB meningitis in children); meningococcal vaccine for travellers (Hajj) and outbreaks.

Nursing importance Bacterial meningitis can kill or disable within hours; prompt antibiotics and vigilant neurological nursing observations improve survival and reduce deafness and brain damage.

Conclusion Bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, neck stiffness and altered consciousness; immediate antibiotics and dexamethasone, careful supportive care and close nursing monitoring are life-saving, while vaccination prevents many cases.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Communicable Diseases
question: Explain chickenpox and herpes zoster with their nursing management.
answer_html:
Introduction Both diseases are caused by the varicella-zoster virus (VZV). Chickenpox (varicella) is the primary infection, common in children; the virus then remains dormant in sensory nerve ganglia and may later reactivate as herpes zoster (shingles), usually in older or immunocompromised adults.

1. Chickenpox (varicella)

  • Transmission – airborne/droplet and direct contact with vesicle fluid; highly contagious; incubation 14–16 days (10–21); infectious from 1–2 days before the rash until all lesions have crusted.
  • Features – mild fever and malaise, then an itchy rash that appears first on the trunk (centripetal) and spreads to the face and limbs; lesions progress rapidly from macule → papule → vesicle ("dewdrop on a rose petal") → pustule → crust; lesions of different stages are present together; mouth ulcers.
  • Complications – secondary bacterial infection and scarring, varicella pneumonia (adults, smokers, pregnant women), encephalitis and cerebellar ataxia, Reye's syndrome (with aspirin), fetal and neonatal varicella, severe disease in the immunocompromised.
  • Treatment – symptomatic care (paracetamol – no aspirin; NSAIDs are avoided), calamine lotion, antihistamines; acyclovir or valacyclovir for adolescents, adults, pregnant women and immunocompromised patients (IV acyclovir in severe cases); varicella-zoster immunoglobulin for exposed high-risk persons.
  • Prevention – varicella vaccine (live; available privately, not in UIP).

2. Herpes zoster (shingles)

  • Cause – reactivation of latent VZV, triggered by ageing, stress, HIV, cancer, steroids and immunosuppressive drugs.
  • Features – burning pain, tingling or itching in one dermatome for 2–3 days, followed by clusters of painful vesicles on a red base in a band-like distribution on one side of the body (commonly the chest), not crossing the midline; fever, malaise.
  • Special forms – ophthalmic zoster (forehead, eye; vesicles on the tip of the nose suggest eye involvement – urgent eye care), Ramsay Hunt syndrome (facial palsy with ear vesicles).
  • Complications – post-herpetic neuralgia (pain persisting more than 3 months, especially in the elderly), secondary infection, scarring, dissemination.
  • Treatment – antivirals (acyclovir, valacyclovir) ideally within 72 hours, analgesics; for neuralgia – gabapentin, pregabalin, amitriptyline; zoster vaccine for older adults (privately available).

3. Nursing management

  • Isolation – chickenpox: airborne and contact precautions until all lesions are crusted; exclusion from school or work; herpes zoster: cover lesions, contact precautions (airborne for disseminated zoster or immunocompromised patients).
  • Non-immune and pregnant staff should not care for these patients.
  • Skin care – keep the skin clean and dry, cool baths, calamine, loose cotton clothing; cut nails short, mittens for infants; avoid scratching and picking crusts.
  • Fever and pain management – paracetamol, analgesics, comfortable positioning; cool compresses for zoster.
  • Oral care for mouth ulcers – soft, bland, cool diet; plenty of fluids.
  • Eye care in ophthalmic zoster – lubricant drops, protect the eye, urgent ophthalmology referral.
  • Observe for complications – breathlessness (pneumonia), drowsiness or unsteadiness (encephalitis), spreading redness or pus (infection).
  • Health education – period of infectivity, avoidance of aspirin, vaccination, and early treatment of zoster.

Nursing importance Nurses prevent spread in wards and schools through isolation, and reduce scarring, infection and post-herpetic pain by good skin care and early antiviral therapy.

Conclusion Chickenpox is a highly contagious primary VZV infection with a pleomorphic vesicular rash, and herpes zoster is its painful dermatomal reactivation; isolation, skin care, symptom relief and timely antivirals are the main elements of care.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Communicable Diseases
question: Explain the clinical features, complications and nursing management of measles.
answer_html:
Definition Measles (rubeola) is an acute, highly contagious viral disease of childhood caused by the measles virus (a paramyxovirus), transmitted by the airborne route and droplets. It remains an important cause of child deaths, especially in malnourished children. Incubation is about 10–14 days, and a patient is infectious from 4 days before to 4 days after the onset of rash.

1. Clinical features (a) Prodromal stage (3–4 days)

  • High fever with the "3 Cs" – cough, coryza (running nose) and conjunctivitis (red, watery eyes, photophobia).

  • Koplik's spots – small bluish-white spots on a red base on the inner cheek opposite the lower molars, appearing 1–2 days before the rash – diagnostic. (b) Eruptive stage

  • A red maculopapular rash begins behind the ears and along the hairline/face around the 4th day, then spreads downwards to the trunk and limbs over 3 days; fever peaks with the rash. (c) Recovery stage

  • The rash fades in the same order, leaving brownish staining and fine peeling; fever settles.

2. Complications

  • Pneumonia (the commonest cause of death), diarrhoea and dehydration, otitis media, croup.
  • Malnutrition (measles can precipitate kwashiorkor), vitamin A deficiency with corneal damage and blindness.
  • Encephalitis, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) years later.
  • Temporary immune suppression – flare-up of TB, secondary infections.

3. Management

  • Supportive – antipyretics, fluids, nutrition (continue breastfeeding), rest.
  • Vitamin A – two doses on two consecutive days (50,000 IU below 6 months, 100,000 IU at 6–11 months, 200,000 IU at 12 months and above), and a third dose after 2–4 weeks if eye signs are present.
  • Treat complications – antibiotics for pneumonia and otitis, ORS for diarrhoea, oxygen for breathlessness.

4. Nursing management

  • Airborne isolation until 4 days after the onset of rash; non-immune staff should not care for the child.
  • Fever care – tepid sponging, paracetamol, light clothing.
  • Eye care – clean the eyes with sterile saline, keep the room dimly lit; watch for corneal changes.
  • Oral and nasal care; skin care – keep clean and dry.
  • Nutrition and fluids – small, frequent, nutritious feeds; ORS; prevent malnutrition after illness.
  • Monitor respiratory rate, chest indrawing, SpO₂, hydration and level of consciousness for complications.
  • Notify the case (measles is under surveillance for elimination).

5. Prevention

  • Measles–rubella (MR) vaccine under UIP – first dose at 9–12 months, second dose at 16–24 months; catch-up campaigns towards measles and rubella elimination.
  • Vaccination of contacts within 72 hours of exposure; good nutrition and vitamin A supplementation.

Nursing importance Measles deaths are largely due to pneumonia, diarrhoea and malnutrition; nursing care with vitamin A, nutrition and early detection of complications, along with full immunisation coverage, saves children's lives.

Conclusion Measles is a highly contagious viral illness with prodromal 3 Cs, Koplik's spots and a downward-spreading rash; supportive care, vitamin A, isolation and treatment of complications, together with MR vaccination, are essential.

subject: Adult Health Nursing I with integrated pathophysiology (including BCLS module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Communicable Diseases
question: Explain lymphatic filariasis and the role of the nurse in its control, with reference to Maharashtra.
answer_html:
Definition Lymphatic filariasis (LF), commonly called "hathipaon" (elephantiasis), is a chronic parasitic disease caused by filarial worms – mainly Wuchereria bancrofti in India – that live in the lymphatic system, transmitted by the bite of the Culex quinquefasciatus mosquito, which breeds in dirty, polluted water (drains, cesspools, septic tanks) and bites at night. India has the world's largest LF burden and aims to eliminate it by 2027. Several districts of Maharashtra, especially in Vidarbha (for example, Nagpur, Bhandara, Gondia, Chandrapur and Gadchiroli), are endemic.

1. Clinical features

  • Asymptomatic microfilaraemia – most infected people have no symptoms but have hidden lymphatic damage.
  • Acute attacks (acute dermato-lymphangio-adenitis) – fever with chills, painful red swelling of a limb or genitals, lymphangitis, lymphadenitis.
  • Chronic disease
    • Lymphoedema progressing to elephantiasis of legs, arms, breasts.
    • Hydrocele (commonest chronic sign in men), scrotal swelling.
    • Chyluria (milky urine).
  • Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia – night-time cough and wheeze with high eosinophils.
  • Disability, loss of work and social stigma, especially for women.

2. Diagnosis Night blood smear (microfilariae show nocturnal periodicity – collected between 10 p.m. and 2 a.m.), filarial antigen test (FTS) at any time of the day, ultrasound ("filarial dance sign").

3. Treatment and control strategy

  • Individual treatment – diethylcarbamazine (DEC), albendazole, doxycycline as prescribed.
  • Mass drug administration (MDA – "Sarva Dawa Sevan") – an annual single dose of anti-filarial drugs to the whole eligible population in endemic areas – DEC + albendazole (DA) or the triple-drug therapy IDA (ivermectin + DEC + albendazole) used in districts such as Nagpur; pregnant women, children below 2 years and seriously ill persons are excluded.
  • Morbidity management and disability prevention (MMDP) – limb care for lymphoedema and free hydrocele surgery.
  • Vector control – elimination of breeding sites, larvicides, and personal protection.

4. Role of the nurse

  • MDA participation – motivate families, ensure that tablets are swallowed in front of the health worker after food, explain that mild reactions (fever, headache, itching, nausea) show that the drugs are killing parasites and soon settle.
  • Night blood surveys and collection of samples; record keeping.
  • Teach limb hygiene to lymphoedema patients – wash the affected limb daily with soap and clean water, dry carefully (especially between toes and skin folds), apply antiseptic or antifungal cream to wounds, elevate the limb, exercise, wear comfortable footwear; treat acute attacks early (rest, cool compresses, analgesics, antibiotics).
  • Refer men with hydrocele for surgery; provide MMDP kits.
  • Vector control education – cover drains and septic-tank vent pipes, prevent water stagnation, use mosquito nets at night and repellents.
  • Reduce stigma and support affected persons; observe National Filaria Day (11 November) awareness activities.

Nursing importance High community coverage during MDA, achieved through nurses' motivation and supervision, is the key to stopping transmission, while simple limb care prevents progression of elephantiasis.

Conclusion Lymphatic filariasis is a Culex-borne parasitic disease causing lymphoedema and hydrocele; mass drug administration, vector control and morbidity management – driven by nurses and community health workers – are steadily moving India, including Vidarbha, towards elimination.
